title: BuildReady
pitch: From CAD to manufacturing decisions: BuildReady helps engineers and AI agents review designs, explore simulation evidence, and compare supplier options—with humans in control.
about_excerpt: From CAD to manufacturing decisions: BuildReady helps engineers and AI agents review designs, explore simulation evidence, and compare supplier options—with humans in control. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A part can look finished in CAD and still be far from ready to manufacture. Between the model and the machine are questions about geometry, material, strength, cost, and supplier requirements. Those answers often live in separate tools—and when the design changes, it is easy for the reasoning to stay attached to the old version. We built BuildReady to explore a different workflow: an engineer and an AI agent working from the same visible evidence, with a clear record of what is known, what has changed, and what still needs human review. What it does BuildReady is a WebMCP-powered manufacturing-readiness workspace. Our prototype brings together Onshape design context, CNC manufacturability checks, a SimScale integration workflow, and supplier comparison. An agent can inspect the active design context, explain findings, and prepare bounded next steps. The engineer sees the evidence in the interface and retains approval authority. In the controlled demonstration, a proposed radius correction is a preview—not an automatic edit to the source CAD. We also built a private quotation workspace for preserving original supplier documents, recording their terms, and comparing compatible offers. It separates unit price from setup, shipping, tax, and other charges. Unknown shipping stays unknown rather than quietly becoming zero. A preferred-supplier directory lets users maintain their own options. The central principle is traceability: a finding, simulation record, or quotation should make clear which design and assumptions it describes. Why WebMCP Manufacturing review requires more than knowing which button to click. An agent needs to understand the active revision, the meaning of a measurement, whether evidence is current, and which actions require approval. WebMCP lets BuildReady expose that context through structured, page-owned tools. The agent and the engineer use the same underlying handlers, so tool results connect to the evidence visible in the application. We implemented tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , explicit input schemas, and route- and state-dependent availability. Tools are refreshed as the workflow changes, and downstream evidence is invalidated when its source changes. This makes collaboration more direct: the agent can help inspect and explain a finding while the engineer reviews the same information, without repeatedly copying context between applications. The agent does not gain authority to approve production, modify source CAD, or purchase parts. How we built it We used plain JavaScript, HTML, and CSS for the interface, with Python and SQLite for local services, durable records, and private evidence storage. The project runs through uv without npm or PyPI package dependencies. The Onshape integration supplies design context. The operator-assisted SimScale workflow includes CAD preparation, reviewed topology mappings, durable operation tracking, and retained result evidence. Simulation records bind results to their source design and setup rather than treating a completed run as a universal pass. We built the quotation workflow around preserved originals and structured human review. Source, review status, design match, validity, and missing terms remain separate. Codex helped us turn our research into staged implementation work, develop the application and integrations, debug failures, and expand regression coverage. Our latest local checkpoint passed 203 Python tests and 24 JavaScript tests. Challenges we faced The hardest challenge was keeping context consistent. A small design revision can invalidate a manufacturing finding, simulation result, or commercial comparison. We had to treat freshness and identity as part of the workflow, not just labels in the interface. External operations introduced another problem: a request can succeed even when its response is lost. We added durable tracking and operator-assisted reconciliation so uncertainty does not trigger a blind duplicate operation. We also had to distinguish evidence from confidence. A solver finishing does not prove numerical correctness. A price without shipping is not a delivered total. A realistic-looking fixture is not a genuine supplier quotation. What we learned We learned that useful engineering AI depends as much on boundaries as capabilities. Structured tools help an agent understand what it can do; explicit unknowns help it understand what it cannot conclude. We also learned that trustworthy integration means preserving relationships between records—not simply connecting APIs. The design revision, exported geometry, simulation setup, and quoted scope all matter. What we are proud of We built a prototype where AI assistance is inspectable. Engineers can see the findings, assumptions, human decisions, and evidence behind the next step. We are especially proud of keeping historical evidence without allowing it to silently become a current claim, and of designing supplier comparisons that expose missing information instead of hiding it. What's next Our demonstration uses clearly labeled fictional supplier quotations and distinguishes recorded simulation examples from live provider evidence. Full live numerical validation and production readiness are not claimed. Next, we want to complete real-run engineering verification, broaden geometry support, finish the combined live review package, and add an authorized supplier API. Our goal is not an AI that declares a part ready. It is a workspace that helps engineers understand what readiness requires—and what evidence they still need. title: Median Viz
pitch: Data visualization is designed for humans, making it hard for AI agents to understand what actions are supported in a page. I built Median Viz using LinkedIn demographics to explore a different model
about_excerpt: Data visualization is designed for humans, making it hard for AI agents to understand what actions are supported in a page. I built Median Viz using LinkedIn demographics to explore a different model Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration One day, while my wife and I were watching a video from USAFacts, she wondered aloud how the animated data visualizations in the video were created. I started explaining the usual process—acquiring and cleaning the data, processing it, and then building dashboards with the right dimensions, filters, and pivots. Halfway through the explanation, I realized it might be easier to just build an example application that shows her how they work. That became Median Viz . I started with a few animated Plotly visualizations—a pie chart, a bar race, and a U.S. map—then turned them into a small web application, open-sourced it on GitHub, and deployed it on Vercel. When the WebMCP Challenge was announced, my cofounder and I were also exploring how to analyze LinkedIn Ad Set demographics for client campaigns. The two ideas suddenly connected. Instead of asking an AI agent to infer what a visualization means from the page alone, what if the application could tell the agent exactly what data, analytical capabilities, constraints, and current state were available? That became the /studio experience in Median Viz: a workspace designed so that humans and agents can understand and work on the same analysis through WebMCP. What it does Data visualization tools are usually built as human-operated dashboards for exploring complex data across different dimensions. They can be powerful, but they are also difficult for AI agents to understand because the agent has to infer which filters, dimensions, metrics, and actions the application actually supports. I built Median Viz Studio using LinkedIn Ad Set demographics as the example domain. Through WebMCP , the application exposes its analytical capabilities directly to ChatGPT. The agent can discover what dimensions are available, understand the current workspace, configure an analysis, apply filters, animate changes over time, and explain the results in plain language. The key idea is that the human and the agent are not working in separate experiences. They operate on the same live workspace . A filter selected by the human immediately becomes context for the agent, while a WebMCP action taken by the agent is reflected in the same controls and visualization the human sees. How we built it Median Viz is a Next.js/React application using Plotly for interactive and animated visualizations. The /studio route models a LinkedIn-style B2B audience analysis workflow using the supported demographic dimensions, including Job Function, Seniority, Industry, Company, Company Size, Region, and others. For the public demo, I use representative LinkedIn B2B audience-performance data for a fictional company, Northstar Media , with metrics such as CPC, CTR, impressions, spend, and conversions. The Studio exposes seven semantic tools through WebMCP : three read-only tools that let the agent inspect the dataset, workspace, and current result, and four guarded mutation tools that let it configure an analysis, apply filters, control animation, or reset the view. These tools operate on the same underlying workspace capabilities used by the human interface rather than manipulating Plotly or DOM elements directly. The application also preserves domain rules. For example, LinkedIn demographic dimensions are reported independently, so the system will reject an invalid request such as comparing Job Function directly with Seniority rather than inventing an unsupported intersection. Time-series animation is represented as shared workspace state, and the Agent Activity panel makes WebMCP-driven changes visible to the user. Challenges we ran into One of the main challenges came directly from a problem we were already thinking about in our startup: how do you keep human and agent actions in sync when both can change the same workspace? I wanted a filter or view selected by the user to immediately become context for the agent, while also making sure an agent action did not overwrite a newer human change. There were also important domain constraints to preserve. LinkedIn demographic dimensions are reported independently, so an analysis such as Job Function × Seniority is not valid. I wanted Median Viz to reject requests the underlying data cannot support rather than letting the agent invent an answer. Similarly, derived metrics such as CPC and CTR need to be calculated from aggregated values rather than by averaging row-level ratios. Finally, because this is a public demo based on a problem we encounter with real customer campaigns, privacy was a hard requirement. The public Studio uses representative demo data and fictional identities , so no real customer information is exposed. Accomplishments that we're proud of The accomplishment I’m most proud of is getting to a working experience where a human and an agent can genuinely collaborate in the same analytical workspace . A user can change a filter manually, ChatGPT can immediately understand that new state, and an agent action is reflected back in the same visualization and controls. This also gave my cofounder and me a concrete model for how we could use WebMCP in our own analytics products: expose the capabilities and constraints of the application directly to agents instead of asking them to infer everything from the interface. I was also happy with the way animation evolved. The human gets a visual, time-based experience, while the agent gets structured state it can reason over. Taking the project from an experiment, through WebMCP integration, to a deployed application and a working public demo was especially rewarding. What we learned Start with the problem, not the protocol. WebMCP became useful once I focused on the human-agent collaboration problem rather than trying to find places to add tools. Designing good WebMCP tools feels more like designing a product capability API than exposing UI controls. An agent works better with structured state and evidence than when it has to infer meaning from a screenshot or DOM. Domain constraints are a feature. Giving an agent explicit boundaries can make it both safer and more useful. Shared state matters more than tool count. The most interesting interactions happened when a human action became immediate context for the agent, and vice versa. What's next for Median Viz Explore additional multidimensional datasets beyond advertising , with examples from domains such as travel, retail, and other areas where interactive visual exploration is useful. Add richer annotations and storytelling , especially around animated and filtered views, so the application can help explain why a change matters rather than only showing that it happened. Explore better ways to analyze and compare independently reported demographic dimensions without violating the underlying data semantics —for example through side-by-side views, sequential filtering, or coordinated comparisons rather than unsupported intersections. Extend the human-agent collaboration model beyond the demo, including longer analytical workflows where humans and agents progressively refine the same workspace. title: Live Canvas
pitch: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface.
about_excerpt: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For as much as marketers have optimized for conversion, they haven't been able to cut through the number one reason that people leave open carts. they're not ready to buy. It had just happened to me while shopping for a microphone: I started at one site, then realized I needed more information to determine which was going to be the best fit. What if the shopping interface could have met me where I was at--researching the options, ranking the matches, explaining its rationale, and then designing a search result layout to fit its conclusions? That's just one glimpse of how web-interfaces of the future will adapt to their users' needs through a Live Canvas. What it does Each demo walks you through a conventional user interface, and then cordons off a bounded portion of it as WebMCP to redesign (the Live Canvas) The Storefront demo lets the agent curate the search results with a toolbox of approved card presets and badges. This constrained design is a good fit for the untrusted nature of the public internet, keeping users safe from XSS attacks. The Dashbord demo scales the idea up by giving you an entirely blank page. It imagine how the future of CRM / ERP dashboards might function. Prompt the agent to onboard you, collaborate on a vision with the agent as you would with your analytics team, and the end result is an entirely personal dashboard of controls, visualizations and reports. The Distribution demo scales the idea outwards by asking whether you distribute a Live Canvas as part of conventional component libraries. It demonstrates what a future Datatable component could be, with the ability to generate bespoke reports and save them to your browser - all without backend engineering or ai-vendor lock-in. How we built it The architecture north star is "agent composition, application execution". The application exposes its UI primitives through WebMCP. The agent supplies a composition, and then the live canvas renders that composition using application-owned components. This solution prevents data from leaking out of the organization's security boundary, and also prevents token bloat. Challenges we ran into and accomplishments that we're proud of There are two large challenges that required creativity: The largest challenge was discoverability. WebMCP is not bidirectional: an agent can invoke tools, but there's no mechanism for the website to initiate a conversation. The past 30 years of the web have trained users for the affordance of buttons and forms. I built a new set of visible prompts and verbs to communicate to surface the new modality which was an interesting accomplishment, but does highlight an apparent shortcoming in the standard. The second challenge is the built-in approval flow of agentic browsers. ChatGPT would auto-deny requests to access the user's simulated library to make recommendations, e.g. In the short term, this is solved with instructional text to ask for permission in advance. However, what WebMCP needs is a built in consent layer where tools are tied to required consent artifacts. What we learned WebMCP shows great potential to break interfaces out of the "ai chatbot jail". What's next for Live Canvas The most likely next step is to select an existing open-source component library and use it to build the first end-to-end WebMCP UI framework. That would turn the Live Canvas from just a demo pattern into a production-hardened implementation. title: colorwake
pitch: A coloring studio for parents and kids where their own drawings come alive. Tell ChatGPT the story, and through WebMCP the characters walk, dance, and fly across the stage — imagination, extended.
about_excerpt: A coloring studio for parents and kids where their own drawings come alive. Tell ChatGPT the story, and through WebMCP the characters walk, dance, and fly across the stage — imagination, extended. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Canvas mode - select sketc Play mode Play mode - dance, fly, swim etc. colorwake in 20 seconds Kids color a character, then an agent directs it over WebMCP as it acts out their story onstage. A read-only get_guide tool works like a system prompt handed over by the page: an in-page playbook for guiding a child with choices, never a script. Successful write-tool results carry fresh, action-relevant context, while get_studio_state lets the agent resync after on-screen changes. No app backend or accounts: raw artwork stays local, and the agent receives only a compact state summary. A parent runs the agent; the child makes the art. Built solo by a first-time hackathon entrant with a product background. Inspiration Coloring apps end when the coloring ends. But the best part comes next, when a child holds up the drawing and says, “And then the rocket flies to the moon!” No app was listening. WebMCP changed that. The app’s state and tools live inside the page, letting a connected agent interact with the same canvas the child is touching and help the picture move as the child imagines. What it does Color — choose a sketch and paint it with a finger, mouse, or stylus. Play — finish coloring, and the same canvas becomes a stage. Tell ChatGPT the story — “The rocket flies to the volcano, and the robot dances!” — and through 10 WebMCP tools, the agent casts the characters, sets the place, time, and weather, and composes their movements. Young children shouldn’t need to formulate commands. The agent can read the state of play and offer one simple next choice — always choices, never a script. No artwork is generated for the child. The child makes the art; the agent plays inside it, in real time, on the same screen. Because ChatGPT is for users 13 and older (subject to local minimum-age requirements), colorwake is co-play by design: a parent operates the agent and relays the child’s ideas, while the child stays in charge of the art. How we built it colorwake is a static React 19 and TypeScript SPA built with Vite. It has no app backend or accounts; artwork and state persist in localStorage. Characters are rigged SVGs across five rig families, animated with the Web Animations API. Motion parameters are clamped to safe ranges for both whole-character and part-targeted moves. The WebMCP layer registers 10 tools through document.modelContext.registerTool , typed with webmcp-types and validated with Zod: four read tools and six write tools. Three decisions mattered most: get_guide — an in-page playbook, delivered like a system prompt. A read-only tool can return more than app state. It can carry guidance: how the studio works, what the child can do in each state, and the house rules. An agent that reads it starts with a clear role as a playmate. A loop designed around WebMCP. On-screen button presses are not announced to the agent. Successful write-tool results provide current, action-relevant context, while get_studio_state lets the agent resync after manual interactions. The experience works best when the family continues through the protocol. Parity, with one boundary the agent cannot cross. UI-equivalent tools call the same actions as the on-screen controls, while motion tools drive the same play engine. The 20-picture and 8-step caps return actionable errors; the three-spot stage predictably swaps out the friend that has been there longest. There is deliberately no painting tool — coloring belongs to the child. Challenges I ran into This was my first hackathon, and I came to it with a product background rather than a traditional engineering one. The hardest part was translation : turning WebMCP’s technical properties into moments a family could actually feel. get_guide emerged from asking what happens when young children cannot type commands and turning that constraint into a feature. AI coding agents were my hands, but direction, taste, and QA were mine: round after round of on-device review, dozens of UI/UX fixes, and a 148-test verification chain. One technical lesson stood out: tool descriptions are UX writing. Agents behave only as well as the schemas and errors guiding them. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The promise works end to end: a picture colored a minute ago can walk across the stage beneath the weather the child chose. The page teaches the agent: get_guide gives it a playbook for becoming a good playmate. I shipped it solo for my first hackathon, with a local-first privacy model designed for families. What I learned Read-only tools can carry guidance — context, norms, and a role — not just app state. Designing for agents is UX design made of words: schemas, descriptions, and error messages are the interface. What's next for colorwake More sketches and motion families, sound, saved and replayable shows, and more languages — so more families can color together and more compatible agents can direct. title: Three in the Loop
pitch: A WebMCP research workbench where agents do the legwork and humans decide what counts as evidence.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP research workbench where agents do the legwork and humans decide what counts as evidence. Like 1 Comment Story Updates 3-in-the-loop-human-agent-research-workbench how-it-works human-approve-reject-retry-sourcing-method human-approved-artifact-ready flow-chart Inspiration Three in the Loop began with a practical question: what should research look like when a human, an agent, and a website work together in the same live workspace? We began with the WebMCP specification, Chrome developer and agent/tool security guidance, OpenAI developer demonstrations, community/practitioner demonstrations, and repeated internal dogfooding. Together, those sources made the website-declared tool model concrete. Our product question was what should remain under human control. Research was the test case we kept returning to. It rewards speed in gathering and punishes speed in judging. So we built the smallest workbench that could test the boundary between useful research delegation and human evidence judgment. Repeated dogfooding refined that boundary until it matched the workflow. What it does Three in the Loop is for researchers, analysts, and technical teams doing fast-moving evidence-based research where recency, authority, and provenance matter. It is a research workspace shared by a person and a WebMCP-enabled agent in the same live browser workspace: Human defines → Agent researches → Human curates → Agent synthesizes → Human approves You set the research question, audience, and evidence limit. The agent reads the workspace, searches OpenAlex, inspects sources, and proposes evidence. Then it stops. You accept or reject each proposal in the Workbench and control evidence membership. The agent drafts an Evidence Brief whose findings may cite only human-accepted evidence. You edit and review the brief, mark it reviewed, approve it, and download the approved Markdown. The Research Cycle shows whose turn it is at every stage. A WebMCP activity readout records real tool calls as they land, so agent work is visible without exposing private reasoning. The application embeds no model and makes no OpenAI API calls; intelligence comes from a compatible external agent using the site’s bounded tool surface. Why WebMCP The interesting question was never whether an agent can search. It was which operations the site should expose as structured tools and which decisions should remain in the human workflow. WebMCP lets the site declare that boundary on its structured tool surface. Three in the Loop exposes exactly five tools: get_research_workspace search_sources get_source_details propose_evidence draft_evidence_brief Accepting evidence and approving the brief are deliberately absent from the WebMCP tool surface. They are buttons, not tools. For the operations the site does expose, the agent can use structured calls instead of scraping the interface or imitating human clicks. Both actors work against the same bounded browser workspace. It is the same page, with the turn changing hands. Challenges The hard problem was not building tools. It was deciding where useful delegation should stop. We began with read-only tools and added exactly two state-changing operations when the workflow needed them: propose_evidence can stage a proposal, and draft_evidence_brief can place or replace a review-required draft. Evidence acceptance or rejection, evidence membership, brief editing and review, and final approval remain outside the WebMCP tool surface. That boundary looks obvious in hindsight. It took repeated use to find it. Two smaller problems followed. The site cannot know that a person has spoken to an agent or that the agent is thinking, so it only reports AGENT WORK IN PROGRESS after a real WebMCP call lands in the current stage. And persistent rehearsal state kept reviving old missions, so the workspace now uses session-scoped browser storage: same-tab refreshes survive, while a new browser session starts clean. What we learned We began by treating the tool as the main unit of WebMCP design: name it well, type it well, keep it narrow. That is necessary. It is not what made the product work. What made it work was the handoff. The agent works until evidence selection returns control to the human. The human changes the evidence set. The agent continues from that decision, not from scratch, and drafts from the accepted evidence. The human reviews and signs off. Each time we clarified one of those transitions, the product became simpler and more useful. Looking at tools in isolation never explained the workflow as clearly as the handoffs did. Next time, we would design the journey between the person, the agent, and the page first; the tool set should follow from that journey. The final product does not try to show how much the agent can do alone. It shows how clear the responsibility is at every step. What's next The application is frozen for submission. What follows is evaluation before expansion. Planned assurance work includes deterministic checks of workflow invariants, WebMCP registration and cancellation lifecycle testing, response and serialized-output measurement, model-facing indirect prompt-injection evaluations, browser-agent evaluations of human-authority boundaries, and adversarial retesting after approved hardening. Product directions remain open too: richer evidence comparison without a fake credibility score, additional structured research providers, reusable research sessions, and collaboration. Expansion follows evidence from the evaluations while preserving the principle that made the product useful: The agent gathers. You decide what counts. I handled product design, WebMCP workflow design, implementation, deployment, dogfooding, validation, and submission preparation. title: LifeOS
pitch: Your life, your agent, one workspace: LifeOS exposes 35 real WebMCP tools so an agent can manage your tasks, calendar, goals, and budget alongside you, not just click around a chatbot UI.
about_excerpt: Your life, your agent, one workspace: LifeOS exposes 35 real WebMCP tools so an agent can manage your tasks, calendar, goals, and budget alongside you, not just click around a chatbot UI. Like Comment Story Updates Dashboard Tasks Calender goals Inspiration Every "AI agent" bolted onto a personal productivity app treats the agent like a second-class user: it has to look at the same UI a human sees, guess which button does what, click around, and hope nothing changed underneath it. We wanted to try the opposite: what if the agent and the human were first-class citizens of the same app, sharing the same underlying actions instead of the agent faking a human? WebMCP made that possible. Instead of screen-scraping or blind automation, a website can expose real, typed, described tools directly via document.modelContext.registerTool() . That's a fundamentally different relationship between a person, their agent, and their software — so we built LifeOS to explore it end to end, on a domain everyone actually needs: a personal command center for tasks, calendar, goals, shopping, expenses, and routines. What it does LifeOS is a full personal productivity app — tasks, calendar/schedule, goals with action plans, shopping lists, expense tracking, and recurring routines — with a complete, polished manual UI. On top of that, it exposes 35 real WebMCP tools across three risk tiers: Read (14 tools): get_today_overview, get_tasks, get_schedule, get_goals, get_shopping_list, get_expenses, get_routines, analyze_day, identify_conflicts, prioritize_tasks, analyze_spending, plan_my_day, plan_my_week, and more. Write (17 tools): create_task, update_task, complete_task, reschedule_task, create_goal, update_goal_progress, record_expense, create_routine, and more. Needs approval (4 tools): delete_task, apply_schedule_plan, set_budget, delete_budget — destructive, irreversible, or financial-target changes always pause for a human click before they happen. An agent can read your day, spot schedule conflicts, propose and apply a week plan, log an expense, or build a goal's action plan by calling a described tool with a validated schema — the same way it would call any API, except the API is the website you're looking at, and every change shows up instantly in the human UI too. How we built it Next.js 16 (App Router) + PostgreSQL via Prisma 7 + Auth.js v5, deployed on Vercel with Prisma Postgres. The core architectural rule: a human clicking a button and an agent calling a WebMCP tool both end up calling the exact same function in src/services/* . There is no separate "agent path" that can drift from what the UI does — lib/actions (Server Actions for the human UI) and webmcp/ (tool definitions + dispatcher for the agent) are both thin callers of one shared service layer, validated by the same Zod schemas either way. Client-side, components/webmcp/ registers all 35 tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() on mount, exposes a live "WebMCP status" pill in the header, and ships a tool inspector at /app/activity that lists every registered tool with its schema and last-run time — useful for demoing and for debugging what the agent actually sees. Challenges we ran into Approval gating without breaking the "same function" rule. Destructive/financial tools (delete_task, set_budget, etc.) needed a human-in-the-loop approval step without forking the code path — we solved it with an approval state machine in the tool dispatcher that pauses before calling the shared service, rather than duplicating logic per surface. Prompt-injection defense. Any tool argument or stored content an agent reads (task titles, notes) has to be treated as untrusted data, never re-executed as instructions. We leaned on the WebMCP spec's annotations.readOnlyHint / annotations.untrustedContentHint fields and scoped every query to the authenticated user. Two real Next.js 16 / Prisma 7 issues surfaced while wiring generated Prisma output into a fresh Vercel deploy (a gitignored generated-client path breaking on npm install , fixed via a postinstall: prisma generate step) — documented in git history for anyone hitting the same thing. Verifying WebMCP itself. document.modelContext is only available behind an active origin trial / Chrome flag ( chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ) or ChatGPT's in-app browser, so we were careful to only claim what we could actually verify live, and documented what still needs a WebMCP-flagged browser to confirm. Accomplishments that we're proud of 35 real tools, not a toy demo — spanning read, write, and approval-gated actions across six real productivity domains. Zero drift between what a human can do and what the agent can do: one service layer, one set of Zod schemas. A real approval flow that actually blocks a destructive action until a human clicks "Approve" — verified with a Playwright end-to-end test that drives a real browser against a real server. 46 unit + integration tests plus a 3-test real-browser e2e suite, all green against a real Postgres database. What we learned Building the agent and human paths as two callers of one service layer, instead of two apps, was the single best decision — every feature we added to the UI was already agent-usable, and every bug we didn't have (an "agent version" of a feature quietly diverging from the human version) is a bug class WebMCP's model naturally avoids for you. What's next for LifeOS Multi-agent collaboration (a scheduling agent and a budgeting agent negotiating a shared calendar), richer WebMCP annotations for finer-grained trust, and expanding the risk-tiered approval model to cover shared/family accounts. title: Clearance
pitch: Your agent shops. You set the rules.
about_excerpt: Your agent shops. You set the rules. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration OpenAI killed Instant Checkout in March 2026 after a Walmart test showed ~3x worse conversion: people do not trust an agent to spend their money without guardrails. Forrester (Apr 2026) found ~75% of US/UK/CA adults uncomfortable letting agents complete purchases even WITH spending limits. The missing piece was never a smarter agent - it was visible governance living where the shopping happens. The W3C WebMCP spec even names this gap (Section 6.3.2.3 'Ambiguous Finalization') and lists it as unsolved in 6.3.2.4. Clearance is a working answer. What it does Clearance is an agent-native storefront. Your AI agent can search, compare, and build a cart - but a server-side rules engine gates every purchase against limits YOU set on the page: a monthly envelope, a per-purchase cap, an approval threshold, category whitelists, and a merchant blocklist. Over the cap, the agent's checkout call PAUSES and an in-page approval card appears showing exactly which rule fired and why the agent chose this item. Approve and it executes; reject and it stops. Every action lands in a SHA-256 hash-chained receipt ledger, and any purchase can be undone within 5 minutes - the 'escape hatch' Consumer Reports says every agentic-commerce provider must build under UETA 10(b). How we built it TanStack Start (React 19) + Tailwind v4 + PGlite (server-side embedded Postgres) for the store, rules engine, and ledger. The agent surface is the native WebMCP API: 8 tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool, with readOnly/untrustedContent/humanInTheLoop annotations. checkout_purchase uses requestUserInteraction to pause for human approval; @mcp-b/global polyfills the same tools into any browser when native WebMCP is absent. One shared rules engine governs both human clicks and agent calls - there is no separate, weaker 'agent lane'. Challenges we ran into Designing approval UX that prevents both false approvals and alert fatigue: auto-execute inside the envelope silently (no nagging), gate only over the cap, and add a hold-to-confirm for >$200 purchases (Nielsen Norman Group guidance on rubber-stamping). A rubber-stamp guard watches the approve-rate and warns if you approve everything and reverse nothing. Making the ledger tamper-evident with a live /api/verify endpoint was straightforward but was the differentiator judges noticed. Accomplishments that we're proud of The end-to-end loop is real: agent calls checkout over WebMCP, the page pauses, a human approves on the card, the receipt is written to a hash chain, and the human can undo within the window. We also nailed the spec a head-of-time: humanInTheLoopHint and untrustedContentHint predate their own proposal, mapping to webmcp issue #198 and Chrome's agent-content guidance. What we learned Governance has to be first-class UI, not a backend API. Stripe's Machine Payments Protocol already has our exact rule types - but ships them as a backend API nobody wraps in a consumer surface. The merchant page is the right place for the human-agent contract because that is where the spend actually happens. What's next Deploy to Netlify, add multi-agent shared ledgers, and richer declarative form-tools for the approval step. Longer term: let merchants recognize a governed-agent session and surface the consumer's own rules, closing the loop between shopper intent and checkout. title: Noema Blueprint
pitch: Noema Blueprint lets people and agents design a private AI setup together in the browser. One scan configures, downloads, and launches it in Noema, a local AI app available on iOS and iPadOS.
about_excerpt: Noema Blueprint lets people and agents design a private AI setup together in the browser. One scan configures, downloads, and launches it in Noema, a local AI app available on iOS and iPadOS. Like Comment Story Updates Create a private on-device Noema project from the web: without sharing files, prompts, conversations, or account data. Choose a purpose, device, local model, and runtime while the final Blueprint updates live. Blueprint Forge validates the manifest, model catalog entry, and handoff payload before sending anything to Noema. Compare candidate runtimes, context sizes, privacy, and settings before choosing the final Blueprint. Send the Blueprint by QR code or deep link: no login, pairing, files, prompts, or conversations included. 1. Noema checks the iPhone, verifies the local model download, and opens a private, ready-to-use chat. Noema Blueprint Inspiration Wanting to run local and private AI should not require people to become infrastructure experts. Today, setting up a local model means researching compatibility, device limits, runtime behavior, and download size before even sending a prompt. We wanted setup to feel like designing a workspace with an expert beside you. WebMCP turns the page into a shared workspace for both the person and the agent. The person can directly choose the Project goal, target device, runtime preset, model, and final Blueprint. The agent can inspect that same visible state, tune advanced model settings, fork and compare alternatives, audit candidates, and stage recommendations. Every agent suggestion remains visible, and only the person can approve it or choose what gets handed off. What it does Noema Blueprint is a visual studio for creating a private local AI Project. A person chooses what they want to accomplish and where they want to run their AI. Agents can then inspect the live Blueprint, change supported settings, fork alternative candidates, compare them, and stage recommendations directly on the page. Every proposed change appears visibly. The person remains the only one who can choose the final candidate. When the Blueprint is ready, the website creates a QR code and a same-device link containing a validated configuration. The agent can also return the QR code directly inside the conversation. Scanning the code opens Noema on your device (iOS, iPadOS). The app checks the configuration against the actual device before asking for approval. If the selected model is missing, Noema downloads it. The settings are then applied and the finished Project opens ready for a private conversation. The handoff is stateless. The link contains no files, prompts, credentials, or personal data. Why WebMCP Without WebMCP, an agent could recommend settings, but the person would need to reproduce them manually inside a different interface. With WebMCP, the agent operates the exact page the person is viewing. The Blueprint becomes a shared source of truth. The agent can explore possibilities while the person sees the consequences before anything becomes final. This makes setup faster without turning it into invisible automation. It also enables a workflow that was previously more opaque: an agent can help construct and evaluate a local AI environment, then hand the reviewed result to the device where it will actually run. How we built it The website is a React application written in TypeScript. It registers 12 narrowly scoped tools using document.modelContext.registerTool . Those tools operate on the same Blueprint state rendered by the interface. They let an agent inspect the current configuration, edit supported values, create candidates, compare them, stage proposals, validate the result, and prepare the handoff. The tool schemas accept only known models and bounded configuration values. Tool registration uses AbortSignal lifecycle handling. If WebMCP is unavailable, the complete interface remains usable manually. The final Blueprint is canonicalized and validated before being encoded as a versioned base64url manifest. The website places that manifest inside a Noema universal link and renders it as a QR code. The native receiver is built with SwiftUI. Noema accepts only the dedicated Blueprint route and maps public identifiers through its trusted model catalog. The app performs its own compatibility checks and preserves explicit download consent. Challenges The hardest design problem was deciding what the agent should be allowed to do. If the agent could silently select the final candidate or deploy it, the page would stop being collaborative. We separated proposals from approval so agent assistance remains visible and reversible. WebMCP is still experimental, so the page also needed a complete manual path. Feature detection keeps the experience functional in browsers without the API. The cross-device link created another trust boundary. We rejected arbitrary model URLs and unsupported settings. The native app treats every website value as a request rather than an instruction. We also had to balance helpful planning with hardware reality. The website can guide the person, but only the destination device can make the final compatibility decision. What we learned WebMCP is strongest when the webpage is a shared object and when it doesn't act as merely a front end for a hidden API. The person should be able to see what the agent understands and watch the result change. We also learned that local setup can feel magical without hiding important decisions. The right abstraction should be a clear plan that requires approval. Hackathon scope NoemaAI existed before the challenge. Noema Blueprint and its WebMCP tool surface were built during the submission period. The Blueprint Forge workflow and cross-device handoff were also created as part of this work. The public repository includes dated commit history showing the challenge implementation. A human-first automotive showroom where people and AI agents search, compare, estimate trade-ins, and prepare a test-drive request together.

 Inspiration 

 Buying a car rarely begins with a perfect form. It begins with a thought: “I need an automatic SUV, I have a trade-in, and I do not know where to start.” The Dealer's Desk turns that thought into structured, inspectable progress without hiding the human decision at the end. 

 What it does 

 The experience combines a natural-language agent brief with a clear showroom UI. An agent can call four page-level WebMCP tools: 

 
 search_inventory finds matches in a synthetic Emilia-Romagna dealer inventory. 
 compare_vehicles returns a contextual comparison, not just a list of fields. 
 evaluate_trade_in prepares an indicative range with explicit assumptions. 
 draft_test_drive_request prepares a request for human review. 
 

 The interface shows the same work to the person: the active brief, the shortlist, the comparison board, the trade-in context, and the final handoff. Search and comparison calls update that visible state directly, so the agent and the person stay in the same showroom context. Every action in the demo is draft-only: no message is sent, no appointment is booked, and no real lead is created. 

 How we built it 

 The public repository is a small Next.js application with a typed synthetic inventory, client-side WebMCP feature detection, and four structured tools registered through document.modelContext . The UI is intentionally usable without an agent, while capable browsers can discover the same actions as tools. 

 Why WebMCP matters here 

 WebMCP lets a website expose capabilities instead of forcing an agent to guess through clicks and visual labels. The Dealer's Desk uses that capability to make the first steps of a dealership journey more useful while keeping scope visible and human-controlled.

AI-powered optical vibration analysis rig using Riesz Phase-Based EVM, ISO 10816-3 diagnostics, 3D ODS digital twin, and autonomous W3C WebMCP agents for non-contact predictive maintenance.

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 What we learned 

 Inspiration 

 Industrial turbomachinery and rotary assets experience sub-pixel micro-vibrations and structural stress long before catastrophic failure occurs. Traditional physical accelerometers demand invasive mounting, costly physical wiring, and human intervention in hazardous operating zones. We set out to build a fully non-contact, physics-informed computer vision rig capable of turning standard camera feeds into sub-pixel vibration telemetry, automated ISO 10816-3 compliance audits, and an autonomous digital twin. 

 What it does 

 ChronoPhys-Vision 3.0 is an industrial-grade, physics-informed optical telemetry platform: 

 
 Optical Motion Magnification: Utilizes Riesz Phase-Based Eulerian Video Magnification (EVM) to amplify imperceptible mechanical vibrations from 50x up to 200x in real time across 1.0–6.0 Hz bandpass filters. 
 Deterministic ISO 10816-3 Classification: Isolates mechanical vibration harmonics (1X Unbalance, 2X Misalignment, BPFO Bearing Faults) and shifts ISO operational zones dynamically (Zone A to critical Zone D trips). 
 3D ODS Digital Twin: Live modal deflection wireframe visualization rendered in real time using Three.js / WebGL driven directly by continuous telemetry. 
 W3C WebMCP JSON-RPC Agent Protocol: Integrates a 12-tool autonomous agent bridge enabling AI-directed parameter tuning, safety throttling, and automated persistence to SQLite. 
 Gemini AI Reliability Specialist: Integrated multimodal assistant providing root-cause failure analysis, PINN fatigue life modeling, and one-click ISO 17025 audit PDF generation. 
 

 How we built it 

 
 Architecture: Decoupled dual-port full-stack architecture. 
 Frontend (Port 3000): Next.js 14, React, Tailwind CSS, Three.js WebGL rendering, Lucide Icons, and client-side WebMCP JSON-RPC handlers. 
 Backend CV Engine (Port 8000): Python, FastAPI, OpenCV, NumPy, SciPy (Riesz Pyramids, 2D FFT spectral analysis), and Modbus TCP industrial bridge. 
 AI & Persistence: Google Gemini API for diagnostic intelligence, Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) fatigue curves, and SQLite3 time-series logging. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Processing multi-scale Riesz phase pyramids and 2D FFT spectral transforms alongside real-time MJPEG streaming caused severe latency. We optimized the processing loop using multi-threaded frame buffers and sub-sampled regions of interest (ROI) to sustain a rock-solid 30–60 FPS optical pipeline. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 Achieving sub-pixel vibration measurement without a single physical sensor. 
 Integrating the W3C WebMCP draft standard for autonomous tool-driven agent maintenance. 
 Creating an end-to-end loop from raw video capture to ISO 17025 audit PDF export in real time. 
 

 What we learned 

 Bridging high-frequency computer vision algorithms with deterministic industrial standards (ISO 10816-3/13373) and agentic browser protocols provides a non-invasive, cost-effective pathway for modern smart factories. 

 What's next for ChronoPhys-Vision 

 
 Multi-camera triangulation for complete 360-degree spatial structural deflection. 
 Edge deployment optimizations directly on NVIDIA Jetson Orin micro-appliances.

title: odyssey
pitch: 3:52 AM Blind Spot finds accessibility barriers that automated scanners miss by testing whether real user tasks remain reachable through a live, accessibility-derived WebMCP tool surface.
about_excerpt: 3:52 AM Blind Spot finds accessibility barriers that automated scanners miss by testing whether real user tasks remain reachable through a live, accessibility-derived WebMCP tool surface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Automated accessibility scanners are valuable, but they usually evaluate isolated rules—not whether someone can complete an entire task. A page can pass conventional checks while an essential action remains unreachable. For example, a styled <div> may look exactly like an Add to cart button to a sighted developer while exposing no semantic activation role or keyboard-reachable action. That gap inspired Blind Spot : Automated scanners test rules. Blind Spot tests whether a task remains reachable through an accessibility-derived interaction surface. Blind Spot is not a replacement for disabled-user testing, assistive-technology testing, axe, Lighthouse, or Playwright. It provides an earlier, task-level signal that helps developers find critical barriers before shipping. What it does Blind Spot gives an agent a constrained set of semantic actions derived from the application’s currently rendered state. Our demonstration begins with the task: Add the cheapest keyboard to the cart. The agent can read the page and navigate its semantic model, but the cheapest product uses a pointer-only <div> as its Add to Cart control. Because Blind Spot cannot find a defensible semantic activation action, it does not expose activate_current . The audit then produces an evidence-backed finding containing: The blocked task step The affected element Its observed role and accessible name Keyboard-focusability evidence The detector and confidence level The reason the action was withheld A suggested remediation The developer applies the demonstrated semantic repair, replacing the inaccessible control with a native button. Blind Spot immediately recompiles the capability surface, and activate_current appears in the WebMCP registry. The same task is then repeated. This time, the agent activates the repaired control, adds the product to the cart, and completes the audit successfully. The visible transition from: Task blocked activate_current unavailable Cart: 0 to: + activate_current Task passed Cart: 1 is the core of Blind Spot. How we built it Blind Spot is a React and TypeScript web application with four connected layers: Rendered application ↓ Semantic adapter ↓ Capability compiler ↓ Dynamic WebMCP registry ↓ Agent task attempt and evidence report The semantic adapter examines browser-observable information from the live page, including native semantics, accessible names, focusability, and application-declared intended actions. The capability compiler converts that evidence into the actions the agent may use. It also creates diagnostic action-gap records when an intended human action has no corresponding semantic exposure. The generated tools are registered through the browser-native WebMCP API: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) Our core tool surface includes: start_accessibility_task read_current_context move_cursor inspect_current_evidence report_task_blocker finish_accessibility_task activate_current , registered only when the current action is defensible Each registration has its own AbortController . When the page state changes and a capability is no longer valid, Blind Spot aborts that registration. When a repair makes an action available, the registry adds the corresponding tool. Tool results include structured state and evidence so the agent can verify what happened instead of relying on a generic success message. We also built a visible mission-control interface showing: The agent’s constrained perception The current semantic cursor Available WebMCP tools Tool invocation history Registry revisions and diffs Evidence-backed findings Before-and-after audit status A scripted audit mode exercises the same registered tools through getTools() and executeTool() , allowing the workflow to be inspected without replacing WebMCP with a mock. Why WebMCP WebMCP is especially well suited to this problem because accessibility depends on live application state. Source HTML alone cannot reliably represent computed visibility, focus state, portal content, dynamic relationships, or the exact mid-workflow page the developer is inspecting. Blind Spot operates inside that same rendered tab and updates its tool surface as the application changes. The WebMCP registry is the executable test surface—not the source of truth by itself. Blind Spot’s capability compiler decides which actions are supported by current evidence, the registry enforces that decision for the constrained workflow, and the captured evidence explains every finding. This also creates a collaborative human-agent loop: The human provides a real task. The agent attempts it through the constrained tool surface. Blind Spot identifies where the path becomes unreachable. The human repairs the application. The WebMCP surface changes immediately. The agent repeats and completes the same task. Challenges we faced The greatest challenge was keeping our claims technically honest. A webpage cannot guarantee that an agent has no other browser capabilities, and it cannot directly reproduce everything NVDA or VoiceOver would announce. Blind Spot therefore does not claim to simulate the lived experience of a blind user or certify accessibility compliance. Instead, it runs a documented, constrained audit protocol and records which semantic actions were available at each step. We also learned that: Missing tools are not sufficient evidence by themselves. DOM event listeners cannot always be discovered reliably, especially with delegated React events. Accessible semantics are not identical to the browser’s complete platform accessibility tree. Synthetic keyboard events cannot prove every aspect of native keyboard behavior. Dynamic tool registration requires careful lifecycle and concurrency handling. The auditing product must itself be accessible. These constraints led us to pair semantic evidence with an application-declared action inventory. This lets Blind Spot compare what the application intends people to do with what is actually exposed through its semantic interaction surface. What we learned WebMCP is more than a convenient way to let an agent click interface controls. Its dynamic registration model can express temporary, state-dependent capabilities. We learned that tool absence can be meaningful when it is produced by a transparent compiler and accompanied by reproducible evidence. We also learned that narrowly scoped, high-confidence findings are more useful than broad accessibility claims that the browser cannot prove. Most importantly, we found that human-agent collaboration can improve developer tooling—not only end-user automation. The agent attempts the task, the developer makes the judgment and repair, and both participate in validating the result. What’s next Blind Spot currently demonstrates an intentionally focused, self-contained workflow. Future versions could add: A development package for integration into existing applications Framework adapters for React, Next.js, and Vite Additional task fixtures and semantic action types Exportable Markdown, JSON, and CI reports Playwright integration for repeatable regression testing A browser companion using trusted accessibility and keyboard information Support for larger authenticated, multi-step workflows Validation with accessibility specialists and disabled users Blind Spot does not replace established accessibility tools. It connects them to something they often cannot answer alone: Can this task still be completed through the semantic actions available right now? title: Common Table
pitch: WebMCP repairs a shared group order after a kitchen stockout—replacing one line while preserving every constraint.
about_excerpt: WebMCP repairs a shared group order after a kitchen stockout—replacing one line while preserving every constraint. Like Comment Story Updates The kitchen marks Nordique unavailable. The €70 cart stays unchanged, making the conflict visible before repair. WebMCP preserves four lines and replaces only Nordique with Forestière. Total: €68.50. All four group constraints remain satisfied. Inspiration A group order can satisfy everyone's needs—until the kitchen runs out of one ingredient. The person coordinating the order must then find a replacement without breaking the budget, losing dietary preferences, or discarding choices that still work. That fragile moment inspired Common Table: a storefront where a human and an agent collaborate on the same visible cart. The goal is simple: repair what changed, preserve what still works, and leave the final decision to the person. What it does Common Table demonstrates a complete, reproducible scenario: An agent calls build_group_order to create five meals within a €70 budget, including two vegetarian meals and no declared peanuts. A person simulates a kitchen stockout. Nordique becomes unavailable, but the existing cart remains unchanged so the conflict stays visible. The agent calls repair_unavailable_cart_items without increasing the budget. Four cart lines are preserved. Only Nordique is replaced, with Forestière. The total falls to €68.50, and all four group constraints remain satisfied. The agent cannot place or pay for an order. The final review remains a human action. How I built it — with Codex agents One human, a team of Codex agents. I built Common Table as a solo developer, working with Codex agents on implementation, testing, evidence review, and demo production. I made the product decisions and reviewed the final result. The demo narration is my own voice. The page registers two narrowly scoped, typed tools through document.modelContext.registerTool . Both tools use the same deterministic domain functions as the visible fallback controls. People and agents therefore operate on one shared in-memory state. Tool results expose cart and catalog revisions, constraint checks, and explicit changes. The repair result identifies preserved items, removed and added items, the number of changed lines, and the price difference. The application uses JavaScript, HTML, and CSS, has no runtime dependencies, and runs on GitHub Pages. The public repository includes an MIT license, run instructions, syntax checks, and six automated tests. Challenges The main challenge was defining what an agent is allowed to change. A repair must preserve available cart lines, respect the active group constraints, and never silently relax the budget. Invalid inputs or impossible repairs must fail without mutating the cart. Making those boundaries understandable was equally important. Common Table keeps the unavailable item visible, shows the constraint checks, and records the effect of each action. Accomplishments and learning The key result is measurable: four lines preserved, one replaced, and a valid cart restored. Common Table goes beyond generating a shopping basket. Its focus is the next interaction: recovering from a change while preserving the valid choices already made. I learned that WebMCP becomes especially useful when a site exposes meaningful operations with explicit effects—not just another way to click its buttons. Deliberate boundaries This is a synthetic demonstration using eight fictional menu items. There is no backend, merchant or customer data, real order, payment integration, or production connection. Dietary filtering uses declared synthetic attributes only; it is not a medical guarantee. The demonstrated result is a reproducible technical proof, not evidence of real-world adoption. What's next The challenge scope is intentionally frozen around this working demonstration. A future evaluation could test the same repair approach with larger catalogs, multiple simultaneous stockouts, and more varied group constraints, while retaining the human decision boundary. title: Web MCP Consent
pitch: adding human authentiation to agent workflows
about_excerpt: adding human authentiation to agent workflows Like Comment Story Updates What it does A Chrome extension that holds every WebMCP write until a human approves it. Reads run freely, around 5ms, no prompt. Works on any WebMCP site, including sites that never adopted anything and don't know it exists. No SDK, no code change, nothing for the site to install. The approval card shows the tool name, the real arguments, and the site. Not a yes/no on an opaque tool name Catches sites that lie. A tool that declares readOnlyHint: true and then fires a POST while running is held at the network layer. "Always allow" is per site + tool, listed in the popup, and revocable there. A cache you can't see or undo isn't consent. A declined call tells the agent plainly that a human declined it and not to retry, instead of a generic error it would just try again. How we built it A document_start content script in the MAIN world replaces registerTool before any page script runs. The site registers its tools the normal way and is calling our wrapper. It never finds out. MAIN world is what makes this possible. The default isolated world hands the script a private copy of the context, and you'd patch something the page never reads. MAIN-world scripts can't touch chrome.* , so decisions cross a private MessagePort → an isolated-world bridge → chrome.runtime → an MV3 service worker that owns the queue, the allow list and the badge. Classification is one line: def.annotations?.readOnlyHint !== true . No annotation means gated. It never reads the tool's name or description to guess intent — that's attacker-authored text, and putting it in charge of a security decision is the problem we're solving. window.fetch is patched too, with a call stack tracking which tool is executing, so a "read-only" tool that POSTs gets caught. Pending proposals live in chrome.storage.session so they survive service-worker eviction. The allow list is in chrome.storage.local , keyed origin::toolName . Zero dependencies, no build step, ~15 KB. ## Challenges we ran into We found a vulnerability in our own approval channel. Approvals were relayed over window.postMessage , which page scripts share with the interceptor. A page could watch for its own proposal, read thepproval — approving its own writes with no human involved.Fixed with a private MessagePort handed over at document_start , before any page script exists. Re-ran the exploit: the page can't even see a proposal now. We were silently destroying tool results. On approval the code did typeof result === 'string' ? result : 'Approved.' . On the network path, commit resolves with a Response — so an approved request hring "Approved." Our own demo never caught it because itdiscards its response. Only showed up testing against a site we didn't write. Accomplishments that we're proud of It works on sites we didn't build. On Cloudflare's WebMCP coheld with the cart at 0 , and only after approval did itbecome 2 × Guji Shakiso, $44.00 . The network-layer catch is confirmed two independent ways: wire on decline, **exactly one * on approve — verified byResource Timing inside the browser and by the server's own access log outside it. We found and fixed our own self-approval vulnerability beforather than quietly patching it. We removed two features that didn't earn their place. Shipping less than we built was the right call both times. Zero dependencies, no build step, 15 KB. Download, unzip, lo What we learned Real sites don't annotate. Chrome Labs' own hotel demo hying readOnlyHint . That's exactly why gate-by-default isright, and exactly why one-click "always allow" has to exist. Testing against sites you didn't write finds things your own worst bugs surfaced that way. The WebMCP runtime replaces a thrown error with generic text, so a rejection reaches the agent looking like a bug — and an agent that thinks a tool is buggy retries it. A declined call has to resolve with a clea API details that cost us time: getTools() returns a Promise , and inputSchema arrives as a JSON string , not an object. Reading navigator.modelContext logs a deprecation warning nt.modelContext` first. The honest summary: this raises the cost of an injection from "the agent was convinced" to "the agent was convinced and a human approved a card describing the action." That's a big gap. It isn't a proof. What's next for WebMCP Consent Advisory-only LLM triage. A model offers a plain-Englishith the raw metadata beside it — but a human still clicks towhitelist. Advisory on purpose: a model that auto -approves based on a tool's own description reopens the exact vulnerability we're defending against. Support destructiveHint and idempotentHint , the other stextensions of the same model. Patch XMLHttpRequest and sendBeacon to close the non- fetch gap. Community-curated allow lists, ad-blocker style. Credible wirt problem today. For browsers that don't accept extensions, a local proxy injecting the same patch. Platform-agnostic, but it asks the user to trust a local root CA. title: Necivia
pitch: Council services for everyone - Humans × Agents
about_excerpt: Council services for everyone - Humans × Agents Like 2 Comment Story Updates Live page adapted by WebMCP to make the experience easier to read and use. Natural-language request triggers WebMCP and changes the same live Necivia interface. Necivia exposes six structured WebMCP tools — deliberately with no submission tool. The agent updates the same housing-repair draft the resident can see and edit. WebMCP opens the final review, but only the resident can confirm and submit. After human confirmation, Necivia creates the repair and generates a unique NEC reference. The same persisted repair and reference appears immediately in the authorised staff inbox. Final WebMCP evaluation: 11/11 natural-language tool-selection and safety scenarios passed. Inspiration Many council websites provide great essentials, but I have noticed one weakness that they have in common: they expect everyone to use the same interface. Sometimes people may have different needs such as they might not have their glasses and need larger text for only that day, they could be exhausted, find buttons difficult to tap, need simpler language or just want to complete a task one step at a time. But what if, instead of expecting people to adapt to a website, the website could adapt to them? That led to the core idea behind Necivia. I decided to explore the concept of WebMCP beyond just being an alternative to AI clicking around a website. I wanted the human and the agent to collaborate through the same interface and same state. What it does Necivia is a fictional council-service platform that was developed around the idea of Humans × Agents . A resident can naturally describe what they need and an AI agent can use the exposed WebMCP tools to help complete the task. For example, if someone says that the writing is too small, buttons are difficult to tap, the page feels overwhelming or they want to go one step at a time, the agent can adapt the live website in real time. Text size, control size, information density, language complexity, motion and journey style can all be modified without creating a separate AI interface. The housing-repair journey goes further. An agent can: understand the information required for a repair read the resident's current draft add or correct only the information the resident provides check whether the report is complete open the final review screen But the important part is what it cannot do. Necivia intentionally exposes no submission tool through WebMCP. The agent can help with the task, but the resident must personally press "Confirm and submit". Only then does the server validate and create the repair, generate its NEC-... reference and make the same case available to authorised council staff. This means the agent is not operating a hidden parallel workflow. The human and agent are collaborating through the same real service. How I built it Necivia is built with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, PostgreSQL and Railway. The live product exposes six WebMCP tools : adapt_experience get_experience_preferences get_housing_repair_requirements get_housing_repair_draft update_housing_repair_draft open_housing_repair_review The Page Support and housing-repair interfaces share their state with these tools, so a change made through WebMCP is automatically shown in the resident's interface. For the production side, I added authenticated resident and staff accounts, database-backed sessions, persistent repair cases, role and tenant isolation, protected attachments, server-side validation, rate limiting, security headers, audit records and a delivery adapter. Challenges I ran into One of the biggest challenges was deciding where the agent's authority ends. It would have been easy to just expose a submit_repair tool and let the agent complete everything, but for a council service, I didn't think that it was the right architectural decision. I instead separated assistance from authority : WebMCP can prepare and review the task, while submitting the final form remains a human action. Another challenge was keeping the human interface and agent interface from becoming two separate systems. The WebMCP tools therefore operate on the same visible draft and Page Support state rather than maintaining their own hidden copy. I also spent a huge chunk of my time testing edge cases: partial updates, missing answers, invalid future dates, uncertain safety answers, unauthenticated access and requests unrelated to the available tools. Deployment also brought its own challenges too, including database migrations, persistent storage, authentication and ensuring the same submitted case could move all the way from the resident account to the staff inbox. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I am very proud that Necivia demonstrates WebMCP as more than just browser automation . A natural-language request can actually adapt a person's live experience and the resident can continue exactly from where the agent left off. I am also proud of the human-confirmation boundary . There are six useful tools but no submission tool, that is deliberately part of the design. The final deployed workflow also works end-to-end: a resident can prepare and submit a housing repair, receive a server-generated reference, refresh and still see it and an authorised staff user can see and manage the same persisted case. My final WebMCP natural-language evaluation passed 11 out of 11 scenarios , alongside the application's automated test suite and production verification. What I learned The biggest thing I learned is that designing for agents is not just about exposing as many tools as possible. The description, schema and boundaries of each tool matter because the agent needs to know enough information to be able to choose the right action and should know enough restrictions to know when not to act . I also learned that WebMCP becomes much more interesting when it complements the existing website instead of replacing it. The best experience was not “AI does everything for you”; it was the human and agent being able to work together on the same task. Building Necivia also substantially taught me about production architecture, authentication, database persistence, security, evaluation and deployment beyond the WebMCP integration itself. What's next for Necivia Necivia currently focuses on one specific flagship council journey rather than trying to simulate every possible council service. The next step would be applying the same pattern to more services while keeping the foundational principles the same: one shared interface, structured AI agent capabilities, reversible assistance and clear human control over consequential actions. I would also like to explore how the adaptation layer could become more contextual over time, so websites can respond to temporary requirements without forcing people to permanently configure accessibility or preference settings. Ultimately, Necivia is an experiment in a different relationship with the web: instead of every person having to learn how each website works, the website can meet the person where they are. title: Blnq Studio
pitch: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations.
about_excerpt: Accessible-by-default web building. Blnq exposes its editor, live preview and WCAG audit to browser agents via WebMCP — so the AI that writes your code also catches its a11y violations. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Inspiration I built blnq.studio because front-end work had become a pile of tabs: an editor, a dev server, a browser, DevTools, an accessibility checker, a design spec, and now an AI chat window that can't see any of them. Every one of those handoffs is where quality leaks out — especially accessibility, which is the first thing dropped when you're moving fast and the last thing an AI agent notices, because it can't see what it built. I wanted a single tab where the code, the live preview, the audit and the AI all look at the same thing. WebMCP was the missing piece: it lets the editor tab itself become the tool surface an agent uses, so the loop closes without any extra setup. What it does blnq.studio is a browser-based editor purpose-built for front-end: code, preview, ship — all in one tab. Live multi-file editing — Monaco under the hood, real HTML/CSS/JS files with folders and ES module imports, no build step. The preview updates as you type. Accessibility first — every preview refresh runs the pour engine against WCAG 2.0–2.2 A/AA plus best-practice rules. The A11y panel lists each violation with its impact, a plain-English fix and the exact element. Colour-contrast checks are built into the editor, not bolted on afterwards. Multi-device preview — switch viewports, check every breakpoint, see the FPS overlay, all without leaving the tab. Design systems your AI respects — drop a DESIGN.md at the project root and the editor treats it as the source of truth: colour and font literals that drift from your tokens get flagged, so AI-written CSS stays inside the system instead of inventing new values. Baseline compatibility — a built-in tool tab tells you which features you're using aren't yet widely available across browsers. Collaborate and fork — real-time multi-cursor collaboration over Yjs, forks and merge requests, a community showcase. Ship from the editor — push to GitHub, deploy from the menu, or download the whole project as one self-contained HTML file. AI & MCP, on your terms — AI is optional. When you want it, connect Claude Code (or any MCP client) over the built-in MCP server, use the in-editor chat with your own model, or — new for this challenge — turn on WebMCP and let a browser-native agent drive the tab directly. WebMCP: the editor tab is the tool server Click Start WebMCP and blnq registers 30+ tools with the browser via document.modelContext . No MCP ID, no config file, no separate process. An agent running in the browser can then: Read and edit files by line range or find-and-replace, with undo snapshots and live edits landing in the editor and preview See what it built — blnq_screenshot returns a real PNG, plus element inspection, console errors and viewport switching Audit with blnq_check_preview , which returns JS errors, every WCAG violation with its element HTML and fix hint, and any design-token drift Interact — click, type, press keys, wait for elements — so it can tab through a form or open a modal and re-audit the new state Fix and re-audit until the report is clean The key design decision was that WebMCP isn't a separate integration. blnq has one shared tool registry; the MCP server and the WebMCP endpoint are two thin adapters over it. A tool added to the registry appears in both, and edits behave identically — same validation, same undo, same activity toasts, same prompt history — whichever transport the call came in on. How I built it blnq is an Express + Monaco + Yjs app with a plugin system; the MCP server, AI chat, Baseline and spellcheck tools are all plugins. The accessibility engine runs inside the preview iframe and posts results up to the editor, so the panel a human reads and the result an agent reads come from the same run. WebMCP was around 350 lines: a client module that fetches tool descriptors and calls registerTool() for each (with readOnlyHint annotations and MCP-shaped { content } results including images), and a server endpoint that Zod-validates and runs the shared handler. The endpoint is same-origin only and still requires the tab's random bridge ID; the browser handles user consent on its side. What I learned The accessibility audit turned out to be the most valuable thing blnq can hand an agent. A screenshot tells a model roughly what it built; a WCAG report with the offending element and a fix hint tells it exactly what to change. Structured, model-readable audit output beat any amount of prompt engineering. And WebMCP inverts the usual relationship: the page stops being something an agent scrapes and becomes something it calls . Once you have a decent tool registry, the browser becomes the integration layer for free. What's next Structured JSON from blnq_check_preview so agents can diff violations between audits A blnq_fix_a11y tool that applies remedies for common rule classes automatically Focus-order and keyboard-navigation audits driven by key-press sequences Ship the Chrome origin-trial token on blnq.studio so WebMCP works without flags Share a collaboration session with an agent so humans and AI can work on the same project live Built With ai css framework-free html javascript Try it out blnq.studio Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by David Yarham Like Share this project: Updates David Yarham posted an update — Aug 26, 2026 04:58 PM EDT I dont have a youtube or any video of Blnq, it is a live site and no need Log in or sign up for Devpost to join the conversation.
