title: StagePair
pitch: StagePair is a small experiment in co-directing. You move the performer, the agent finds the camera, and both of you work from the same changing scene.
about_excerpt: StagePair is a small experiment in co-directing. You move the performer, the agent finds the camera, and both of you work from the same changing scene. Like 1 Comment Story Updates StagePair Why I made StagePair I kept thinking about a small problem in AI creative tools. When I change my mind about a shot, the usual answer is often to generate something again. But on a real set, changing the camera does not mean rebuilding the room or asking the actor to perform the scene from scratch. So I wanted to try something simpler. What if a person and an agent could work inside the same scene? In StagePair, I move the performer and decide the blocking. The agent reads the stage as it exists right now, evaluates camera positions, moves the camera, and can save the resulting frame to a contact sheet. The scene is deliberately small. There is one performer, a table, a door, and a camera. I wanted the collaboration itself to be easy to see. The part I cared about most The interesting problem was not getting an agent to move a camera. It was what happens when the person changes something while the agent is working. StagePair gives the shared scene a revision number. If the agent inspects revision 1, and I move the performer before the agent changes the camera, the scene becomes revision 2. A camera move based on revision 1 is then rejected. The agent has to inspect the page again and continue from what is actually there now. That small rule became the part of the project I liked most. It makes the collaboration feel less like sending commands to a remote service and more like two people taking turns working on the same thing. How WebMCP fits The page exposes five WebMCP tools. inspect_stage reads the current performer, camera, props, locks, and revision. inspect_camera reads the current shot. evaluate_camera checks a possible camera position without changing the scene. set_camera moves the camera, but only when it is based on the latest stage revision. capture_take saves the current viewfinder image to the contact sheet. Because these tools come directly from the live page, the agent is working with the same state I can see and edit in the browser. Building it StagePair is built with React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, and the WebMCP imperative API. I kept the stage procedural instead of using downloaded 3D assets. That gave the project a simple model-making quality that felt closer to blocking a scene on a director's table than trying to imitate a finished film set. I also wanted the interface to feel like a small editorial object rather than a generic AI dashboard, so the visual language borrows from contact sheets, camera markings, printed production notes, and Swiss editorial design. What I learned My first instinct was to think about the agent as another tool user. After building StagePair, I became more interested in the handoff itself. If people and agents are going to work in the same interfaces, it matters whether both sides know what changed, which version they are acting on, and when an old decision should no longer be valid. StagePair is only a small experiment, but that is the question I wanted it to make visible. title: SciStudio-web
pitch: Scientific data workbench with your AI partner.
about_excerpt: Scientific data workbench with your AI partner. Like 1 Comment Story Updates AI help you build and run data analysis workflows A workflow can pause in the middle for your decisions with interactive blocks! Just ask AI to make one! We have great and fun tutorials like a video game! Editing codes for blocks with your AI partner! Our branding Inspiration I built SciStudio because I wasn't satisfied with scientific agents like Rosalind or Claude Science. Scientists find them hard to use because they are AI-chat centered. But scientists want to see the data the whole way through — every intermediate step, all the way to the result. Sometimes interacting with data with a GUI is also important. And I throw away the analysis script every time a session ends, because I have no good way to reuse or automate it. As biological research moves toward multimodality, this shape makes cross-modal data analysis difficult. This made me want to build SciStudio: a standardized workflow system for multimodal data analysis that integrates the capabilities of AI agents. You, and your agent, work together. For AI integration, SciStudio's solution before this hackathon was a desktop application plus a PTY running the codex CLI. But for wet-lab scientists, CLI tools are quite off-putting — I watched them struggle with the various buttons on top, not knowing that it can only be operated with the keyboard, and so on. Another problem is that users (I wish I had...) tend to stick with what they know; therefore, an AI interaction system they're already familiar with would greatly increase the product's appeal. Apps like ChatGPT are the perfect choice. After seeing WebMCP, I realized that our current AI system and prompts could be easily migrated to WebMCP and would naturally gain the ability to integrate the various scientific tools that ChatGPT has. After I ran the protein design tool with my data analysis workflow together within the same session with AI, Bang! That is why I chose to join this hackathon. What it does SciStudio-web is an interactive workflow orchestration system for multimodal scientific data analysis. The unit of data processing here is the block; scientists can get hands-on and use building blocks to create workflows, make plots, and automate their data-analysis work. Combined with a powerful AI agent, they can build workflows, carry out the steps of data analysis, and work through an interactive data-analysis interface, turning it all into assets that individuals and labs can reuse. We hope SciStudio has the chance to become the running partner of AI agents. The scenario I hope to see is one where the user prompts, and ChatGPT, through WebMCP, works together with the user to process data — combining all the other powerful biology tools — and ultimately delivers data visualization, interactive analysis, and a personal/lab asset system. How we built it It's a long story, and I can't believe I could go this far. I'm good at coding in data science, but I actually know nothing about software engineering (I'm a biologist). I started with an idea and asked AI agents to build it directly, then realized it didn't work. I asked why, and the AI told me we needed an architecture. So I wrote the architecture file and let the AI build it, only to realize it still didn't work... This happened for several rounds until I had built a robust software-engineering system for AI coding: architecture, specs, implementation, testing, documentation maintenance, and CI/build QA tools to maintain code quality. Honestly... I learned a lot. Challenges we ran into Failed to deploy, lots of frontend troubles, submission documents (hate it!) Accomplishments that we're proud of The old SciStudio called ChatGPT agents by providing an MCP server and a PTY for CLI apps to run in. During the submission period, I migrated our MCP server system to WebMCP, enabling us to run SciStudio's agentic features directly inside ChatGPT. I also optimized the frontend for a better user experience in ChatGPT. Finally I explored and built some demo projects to show the power of SciStudio. This gives me the benefits of modern scientific agent harnesses and the integration of other agentic tools, plus our reproducible workflow runtime and data-interaction capabilities. SciStudio will surface the hardest question of working with AI: "What did the AI do to my data???" This change is groundbreaking to me, honestly. I struggled with the limited resources I could access as a solo developer. I thought SciStudio was limited because I lacked access to big-data resources and collaborations with other tools and apps. The WebMCP integration changed everything. (I'm also proud that my old SciStudio migrated pretty easily.) What we learned Finding people to use a product is more difficult than building it. What's next for SciStudio-web I don't know, let me get some users first... New & existing work SciStudio is a pre-existing open-source project (desktop app, workflow runtime, MCP server). Everything in this submission repo was built during the WebMCP Challenge submission period: the MCP→WebMCP bridge, the Docker/Cloudflare public deploy, the ChatGPT-facing frontend rework, and the demo case. The full scope is visible in this repo's git history (jiazhenz026/scistudio-web-demo), which starts at the time I joined the hackathon (Sept.3!! Almost missed it!!). title: Counterparty
pitch: Let AI agents negotiate with competing sellers—while humans control the final deal.
about_excerpt: Let AI agents negotiate with competing sellers—while humans control the final deal. Like Comment Story Updates homepage Inspiration Most shopping assistants stop after recommending a product. But for many purchases, finding the product is only the beginning. People compare several sellers, look at price, warranty, delivery, and reputation, and sometimes negotiate for better terms. This work is repetitive, so it is a good fit for an AI agent. But the final purchase is still an important human decision. That led me to one question: What if an agent could handle the negotiation, while the person stayed in control of the deal? That is why I built Counterparty. What it does Counterparty is an agent-native marketplace where an AI agent can: search for products using structured requirements; open negotiations with multiple sellers; submit counteroffers for price, warranty, and delivery; compare the latest offers; respond when the human changes their priorities; prepare an agreement for review. The agent cannot complete a purchase by itself. When it tries to commit an agreement before approval, Counterparty returns HUMAN_APPROVAL_REQUIRED . The human must review and approve the exact terms before the transaction can succeed. In the demo, the agent initially recommends GearFrame because it has the lowest price. The human then changes the priority to warranty. The agent compares the same offers again and recommends ForgeBook instead. This is the main idea behind Counterparty: the agent does the repetitive work, while the human provides judgment and authority. Why WebMCP Negotiation is stateful. The agent needs to understand products, sellers, offers, negotiation rounds, accepted terms, and approval status. Trying to infer all of this from buttons and page structure would be unreliable. Counterparty exposes six semantic tools through WebMCP: search_products start_negotiation submit_counteroffer get_negotiations prepare_agreement commit_agreement These are real product capabilities, not instructions for clicking the interface. Each tool uses a strict JSON Schema. Tool calls update the same application state shown in the human interface and activity feed. How I built it I built Counterparty with Next.js, React, and TypeScript. The application has three main domain layers: A catalog service for products and public seller information. A deterministic negotiation engine for offers, counteroffers, acceptance, rejection, and negotiation rounds. An agreement service for preparation, approval, integrity checking, and commitment. Each seller has a different private negotiation policy. This creates meaningful tradeoffs between price, warranty, delivery, and reputation. The human interface and WebMCP tools use the same domain services. This means an action performed by the agent immediately appears in the interface. For the approval boundary, Counterparty creates a fingerprint of the exact agreement terms. If those terms change after approval, the approval becomes invalid. The marketplace data and final transaction are simulated so the demo remains reliable. The WebMCP tools, negotiation flow, shared state, recommendations, and approval checks are real. Challenges I faced The hardest challenge was deciding what the agent should and should not be allowed to do. I wanted the agent to be useful enough to negotiate independently, but not powerful enough to make an important purchase without the user. Another challenge was keeping the human interface and WebMCP actions synchronized. I solved this by making both surfaces use the same catalog, negotiation, recommendation, and agreement logic. I also needed the demo to be reproducible. Real seller integrations could fail or return unpredictable results, so I created deterministic seller strategies that still produce different and meaningful outcomes. Finally, I had to design tools around business actions instead of page actions. A tool such as submit_counteroffer is much more useful to an agent than a tool such as “click the counter button.” What I learned Building Counterparty changed how I think about web applications. A website designed for agents needs more than a good visual interface. It also needs a clear capability interface, structured state, useful errors, and explicit authority boundaries. I also learned that human-agent collaboration becomes more valuable when the two participants have different responsibilities. The agent is good at repeated comparison and negotiation. The human is better at deciding which tradeoff matters and whether the final deal should happen. Accomplishments I am proud of Six working semantic WebMCP tools Parallel, stateful seller negotiations Recommendations that respond to human preference changes A visible activity trail for agent and human actions Human approval required before commitment Approval invalidation when terms change A complete deployed product rather than only a technical demo 18 automated tests covering the critical flow What's next The next step would be connecting Counterparty to real businesses that expose negotiation capabilities through WebMCP. The same model could eventually support electronics, travel, vehicles, freelance contracts, subscriptions, and business procurement. A production version would also add authenticated users, durable server-side state, real seller integrations, inventory reservation, and payment processing. title: Pillbox
pitch: A caregiver and a pharmacist each get an agent on one medication list, every flag quoting the FDA label.
about_excerpt: A caregiver and a pharmacist each get an agent on one medication list, every flag quoting the FDA label. Like 1 Comment Story Updates This image is currently processing. Please be patient... Every Sunday I photograph the grid on my dad's fridge and text it to myself. Eleven prescriptions, four doctors, his handwriting. He is 78 and I live in another city. When a fifth doctor added ciprofloxacin last week, nobody checked it against the warfarin. The interaction checker I found online said "moderate." That was the entire explanation. Pillbox is my answer to "moderate." One list, two links. I open the medication list with my link and get 12 WebMCP tools. His pharmacist opens the same list with a different link and gets 9. Same page, same origin. add_medication , accept_change , print_round_card and the side-effect form only exist in my window. propose_change and add_counsel_note only exist in the pharmacist's. If you open DevTools, Application, WebMCP in each window the lists disagree, and that disagreement is the product. The label, verbatim. I tell my agent "he started ciprofloxacin yesterday." It calls check_interactions with add: "ciprofloxacin" , so the new drug is checked against the list before it is added. Two rows go red. Each flag shows the exact sentence from the FDA label that triggered it, the label's set_id , the openFDA URL, and a severity taken from which section the sentence lives in (boxed warning, contraindication, warning, interaction). Nothing is rephrased. Click the set_id and read the label yourself. That rule cost me most of the data work. openFDA hands you combination products first, so the label for "Amlodipine and Atorvastatin" would have stood in for atorvastatin and given it no pharmacologic class at all. The index now aggregates brands, classes and section text across every prescription label for a generic instead of trusting the first hit. 64 drugs, 1,012 interaction sentences, 497 geriatric-use sentences, each tied to its set_id. The seed set is printed on the page; it is not the whole formulary. openFDA labels become a sentence index keyed by every drug each sentence names; check_interactions returns the sentence, the set_id and a severity; the page registers tools per link and the server re-checks every write. Who gets to say yes. The pharmacist's agent calls propose_change , hold warfarin until the INR is rechecked. It pauses in a confirmation card until the pharmacist clicks Confirm, then shows up in my window over a live stream, no reload, with Accept and Reject buttons the pharmacist never sees. My agent calls accept_change ; I press Confirm; warfarin flips to held and the flags recompute against what is actually active. If the pharmacist's agent tries to accept its own proposal, the server answers 403: "Only the caregiver can accept change. You are the pharmacist: propose a change instead and the caregiver confirms it." The role comes from the capability key in the URL, re-derived on every write. Hiding a tool is not the boundary; the server is. Two things only a person can do. The side-effect report is a real <form toolname="report_side_effect"> with toolparamdescription on each field and no toolautosubmit ; the agent fills it, a human presses Send. print_round_card snapshots the list into a grid by time of day, which is the thing that actually replaces the photo on the fridge. The caregiver's window and the pharmacist's window on the same list. The pharmacist can propose; only the caregiver can accept, and the server enforces it. Under the hood. document.modelContext.registerTool , native first, @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill behind it, a badge on the page saying which is live. Fourteen tools with strict schemas and readOnlyHint . untrustedContentHint is true on lookup_label_section and check_geriatric_warnings because label prose is third-party text; it is wrapped in <untrusted-user-text> on the tool, REST and SSE paths alike. Descriptions change with state: accept_change says how many proposals are pending. Confirm gates live inside each mutating tool's execute . Seventeen eval fixtures, the negative ones asserting the denied tool is absent from that session's toolsForRole ; 132 tests. Versioned writes (409 after four losing retries) and a rate limit of 60 per minute per IP and per list (429 with Retry-After), which I burst-tested against the live deploy with 70 concurrent requests. What I got wrong. The first deploy passed reportForm={false} to the tools panel, so the side-effect form never registered. Five of the seven review passes I ran caught it. It is mounted now. The footer carries openFDA's disclaimer. This is label text for discussion with a pharmacist, not a diagnosis, and nothing on the page says otherwise. Everything here was written on 4 September 2026 with Next.js 16, TypeScript, Tailwind 4, Upstash Redis, Vitest and openFDA. The build script, every openFDA query URL and the eval fixtures are in the repo. title: webMC(P)
pitch: genMC(P) turns Minecraft skin creation into human–AI collaboration. With WebMCP, agents edit real pixels while you guide them through messages and visual masks—all in a shared 3D studio.
about_excerpt: genMC(P) turns Minecraft skin creation into human–AI collaboration. With WebMCP, agents edit real pixels while you guide them through messages and visual masks—all in a shared 3D studio. Like Comment Story Updates skin gallery manual skin creation shimmering while agent is working on the skin Inspiration Creating Minecraft skins has always been a personal benchmark for AI model performance—especially spatial reasoning. A model must understand how a flat texture wraps around a 3D character, not just produce a convincing front view. With genMC(P), I wanted to turn that benchmark into a shared workspace where humans and agents create and refine skins together. How I built it I built the editor with React, TypeScript, and Three.js. WebMCP gives agents structured tools to inspect skins, edit pixels, and respond to user instructions. Users can paint directly, mark areas, and send messages while the agent works. Each skin has its own session. Gallery skins open as private copies, and publishing requires human confirmation. The backend uses Cloudflare Workers, D1, and R2, deployed through ChatGPT Sites. Challenges The biggest challenges were mapping 2D textures correctly onto 3D body parts and keeping human and agent edits coordinated. Session and revision checks prevent stale edits. Message tracking distinguishes “read” from “completed.” I also learned that a marked area should be guidance by default—not a restriction that prevents the agent from completing the task. What I learned Good agent integration needs more than tools: it needs clear state, visible feedback, and human control. Minecraft skins remain a surprisingly demanding spatial-reasoning test. WebMCP turns that test into an interactive creative process, where users can guide the model and improve the result together. title: Flowline
pitch: A shift-scheduling game where an agent reads your live plan through eight WebMCP tools, stress-tests it, and proposes a better order — and only your click can commit one.
about_excerpt: A shift-scheduling game where an agent reads your live plan through eight WebMCP tools, stress-tests it, and proposes a better order — and only your click can commit one. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration I wanted to build the thing I keep failing to get out of a chatbot: help with the work already on my screen. Every scheduling tool I have used either decides for you or leaves you alone with a number that does not say why. So I built a small operations floor — one prep lane, two dispatch berths, four jobs, one deadline that matters — and gave the page an agent that can see it, argue with it, and be unable to touch it. Whose problem this is: the person who owns a running order. A shift scheduler, a dispatcher, a floor lead — someone handed a board that is already tight before anything goes wrong, who has to resequence it while the shift is running and be accountable for the result. The cost of the wrong order is not abstract. A load misses its window. A berth stands idle mid-shift while work queues behind it. A job that had to be out by slot 6 finishes at 7, and the reason is three decisions back. That is a decision made under time pressure by someone who will answer for it, which is exactly why the assistant here is allowed to propose and not to commit. The reason this had to be WebMCP and not a chat integration is the state. What the agent needs here is live page state — which shift is open, the current board revision, which berth is free at slot 3, how much slack a job has left. All of it moves every time you drag a card. Paste it into a transcript and it is stale before the model finishes reading it. A tool call is the only way to ask a page what is true now . And the inversion is the point. When the model holds the whole task, every safeguard is an instruction it may or may not follow. When the page holds the task and publishes named tools, the safeguard is code. So the agent here gets everything it needs to reason about a schedule and nothing it needs to commit one. What it does One board, four jobs, three shifts of escalating difficulty. You order the jobs; the page simulates the shift and scores it against the deadlines. Then a disruption lands — a berth goes down, a job arrives late — and your order has to survive it. The three shifts are not one board with different numbers: an eight-slot last dispatch that loses a berth after the start, a ten-slot rolling intake that loses one while work is still arriving, and a ten-slot night handover where nothing is lost at all except a head start — the critical transfer clears customs three slots late. Each has its own objective, its own disruption and its own grade, and the campaign rail keeps the result of each. Any station opens into a 3D floor built from the same evaluation the 2.5D board is: the stand, the handoff, the deadline and the disruption magnified, four camera presets, five zoom steps, and the shift walked slot by slot. three.js is imported only when you open it, and when WebGL is unavailable the floor degrades to a labelled text floor while the plan stays playable and the tools keep answering. The board is arranged by a human first. You build the running order yourself: drag a card onto the job whose queue slot you want, or move it with the arrow keys — Home and End send it to either end — from the queue rail or from a stand on the 2.5D floor, and a drag can cross from one surface onto the other. The human review gate takes your arrangement exactly as it takes an agent's proposal: it asks for a written reason and keeps it on the receipt. The agent is optional here. The person is not. The agent works the same board through eight tools. It reads the layout, finds the bottleneck, compares two candidate orders under the same disruption, and stages a proposal with its reasoning attached. Staging is the most any tool can do. There is no tool that starts a shift and no tool that commits a plan — you press those, or they do not happen. The eight tools, by what they can touch. Six only read: inspect_board (board, phase, revision, the receipt of the last confirmed plan), list_shifts (the campaign), find_bottleneck (where the order is tight), simulate_disruption (normal against one berth offline), compare_plans (weigh an order without committing it), review_shift (a closed shift's card). Two write, and only into a pending slot: stage_schedule proposes an order, undo_schedule prepares an exact rollback from the receipt id inspect_board reports. Every value a write needs can be learned from a read, and neither write commits. None of the eight claims to be read-only. All eight register readOnlyHint: false , the six reads included, because all eight write something a person can see — they move the shared focus the timeline and the floor highlight, and every call, refusals included, appends a line to the on-screen audit trace. A host may use a read-only hint to skip its confirmation prompt, so the narrower claim stays internal: it lives on the spec as boardReadOnly , is asserted in the tests, and is never sent to a client. What that changes: you never leave the board. No pasting a state dump, no composing a prompt describing your own screen, no reading a reply that refers to a version of the plan you have already changed. You ask in your own words; the work arrives as tool calls and the board updates around them. The proposal shows up as a stageable order with a written reason , not as a paragraph you have to translate back into drags. And because every write quotes the revision it was built from, a proposal composed against a board you have since changed is refused rather than silently applied. The part I did not expect to have working: a model that in a fresh model session, Claude Opus 5 chose these tools on its own. chose these tools on its own. Given only "the disruption has landed, work out what actually protects the deadlines" — no tool named in the prompt — claude-opus-5 made ten calls across two turns, every one of them a page tool , with 25 built-in tools also on offer and none of them used. It hit a refusal on its own — it tried to stage before comparing against the current revision, got precondition_failed , ran the comparison, and staged successfully — then wrote its reason: "BEACON first so it clears prep at 1 and dispatches 1-3, finishing 3 slots inside its D6 even with only one berth… cutting intake wait 9 to 6. Stress: 4/4 on time, score 93 vs 28." It committed nothing. The two clicks that started the shift and accepted the plan were pressed outside the tool surface, because there is no tool that reaches them. That is a bounded proposal loop: the machine does the search and the argument, the person keeps the commit. Six sessions later that came to 51 tool calls, and the revision has still never moved from a tool call. Every plan commit in the application was made through a human UI click. The pattern is not about scheduling. A staged proposal, plus the revision it was built from, is what any page needs if an agent may propose and only a person may commit; the board here is the example, not the claim. And the boards are data: src/data/fixtures.ts exports the three shifts and a lookup by id, at two different horizons, so bringing your own floor is a fork, one file and pnpm dev — no new code, and no tool that can write a board definition. How we built it React 19.2.8 and TypeScript on Vite, no backend, no network calls, no persistence. The scheduling simulation and the scoring live in the page's own domain code; the agent surface is a thin registration layer over it. Eight tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool , with a fallback to the navigator.modelContext surface Chromium has deprecated. Six leave the board of record untouched; two write, and neither of them commits. The six read the board, the shift list, the current bottleneck, the shift's shock test and a closed shift's result card, and compare a candidate order against the active one under both normal and disrupted conditions. The two writes stage a proposed order with a written reason, and prepare an exact rollback of a confirmed plan from its receipt id — both of them for a human to review. Every write quotes an expectedRevision , so a call composed from a stale read is refused precondition_failed or stale_revision instead of overwriting work the agent could not see. The refusal carries a sentence saying what to do next, which is how the model recovered without being told. One detail I would defend in a code review: not one of the eight advertises readOnlyHint: true , on purpose. Six are read-only about the schedule , but every tool here writes something the player can see — the audits move focus and file their own finding, the comparison stores its result. Claiming read-only would be a bid to be called silently, so all eight ship readOnlyHint: false with destructiveHint: false , which is the honest pair. title: LingoMargin
pitch: LingoMargin turns any text into a personalized language lesson where learners and agents collaborate through contextual annotations, grammar missions, and review practice powered by WebMCP.
about_excerpt: LingoMargin turns any text into a personalized language lesson where learners and agents collaborate through contextual annotations, grammar missions, and review practice powered by WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Language learners increasingly use AI to understand given texts, but the usual workflow is fragmented: read in one place, copy a confusing sentence into chat, receive an explanation elsewhere, and manually save useful vocabulary. I wanted to explore a more natural model where the learner and agent share the same reading workspace. The learner stays focused on the text while the agent understands the current passage, proficiency level, annotations, exercises, and learning progress. What LingoMargin does LingoMargin turns any passage into an interactive, level-appropriate language lesson. Learners can paste their own text or request a new passage by specifying a language, level, length, and topic. They can select unfamiliar phrases, save vocabulary, inspect contextual explanations, complete Grammar Detective missions, review mistakes, and export learning material. The agent can directly update the workspace by: Adding selective vocabulary, grammar, and cultural annotations Creating hidden-answer Grammar Detective missions Generating contextual review activities Leaving feedback in the margin Producing new level-appropriate passages Every agent action creates a visible change in the interface. The learner decides what to study and can undo passage replacements when needed. How I built it LingoMargin is built with React, TypeScript, Vinext, and WebMCP, and is deployed using ChatGPT Sites. The application registers six tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() : get_learning_context annotate_text create_grammar_mission create_activity add_feedback create_generated_passage These tools give the agent structured access to the current lesson and allow it to make precise, verifiable updates. Mutating tools return confirmation describing what changed, while the learner immediately sees the result in the passage or margin. The workspace is stored locally in the browser. Passage content and learning state are shared with an agent only when the learner asks for help through a WebMCP tool. Challenges The main challenge was designing genuine human-agent collaboration instead of attaching a chatbot to a reading app. Annotations had to remain anchored to exact character ranges while preventing duplicates and overlaps. Grammar missions needed to accept the complete intended phrase without incorrectly accepting tiny fragments. Agent-generated activities also required validation so malformed exercises could not enter the interface. Another challenge was preserving learner control. Replacing a passage clears lesson-specific state, so I added confirmation, recovery, and one-step undo. I also had to make the relationship between the page and adjacent agent chat understandable without filling the interface with technical WebMCP terminology. Finally, the workspace needed to remain usable on mobile, where the mission must appear before a potentially long passage. What I learned WebMCP changes interface design, not just integration code. A useful agent-native application needs carefully scoped tools, observable outcomes, reliable validation, and clear boundaries between human and agent responsibilities. The best result came from giving each participant a distinct role: the agent analyzes and adapts the lesson, while the learner notices, selects, answers, and decides what becomes knowledge. title: Lockshot
pitch: Drop iOS screenshots. ChatGPT writes and localizes App Store overlay copy in the page via WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Drop iOS screenshots. ChatGPT writes and localizes App Store overlay copy in the page via WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Studio template: ChatGPT-written headline and subhead overlays on iOS screenshots. Lockshot is an App Store screenshot localization desk. Open the live demo and the desk is already loaded with 3 sample iOS screens (sc1-sc3), so ChatGPT can call the tools on the very first visit with no login and no setup. ChatGPT writes headline and subhead overlay copy, switches locales, measures overflow against the real 1320x2868 export, and exports a ZIP of production PNGs. Templates are Studio, Campaign, and Poster. The Campaign template can generate a 9:16 marketing graphic whose type is inferred from the product-slide copy. Click "Add yours" any time to swap the samples for your own screenshots. Why WebMCP Localization is a two-player job. The human owns pixels, lock, and ship. The agent owns copy, translation, and overflow. WebMCP lets ChatGPT call real tools on the live page (get_page_state, set_overlay, set_template, add_locale, check_overflow, export_zip) instead of guessing at the UI. There is no extra API key and no backend agent loop. Better UX One desk, one ChatGPT chat. Because samples are already on the canvas, the agent can write headlines, add German, fix overflow, and export immediately. Locked slides return an explicit error so the agent cannot overwrite a frame you approved. What humans and agents can do together Humans: click "Add yours" to add or replace screenshots, pick a template, lock the slides they approve, and download the ZIP. Agents: read the desk with get_page_state, write copy with set_overlay, switch templates, add locales and translate, check overflow against the real export canvas, and export_zip - respecting every human lock. What was hard before People paste screenshots into Figma, rewrite copy by hand for every language, and find out text overflows only after App Store Connect rejects the asset. Agents that only see pixels cannot measure type against the real export canvas or respect a human lock. How we implemented WebMCP @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill plus document.modelContext.registerTool on the top-level page (no iframes). ChatGPT Desktop and Chrome with WebMCP testing can call the tools. Image upload is intentionally human-only because WebMCP cannot attach files, which is why the desk ships with sample screens so agents are never blocked. title: Janux
pitch: The fullstack framework for the Agentic Web. Every Janux app ships a WebMCP surface by default, so agents use your real UI tools instead of scraping it. Bun-native, React-ecosystem compatible.
about_excerpt: The fullstack framework for the Agentic Web. Every Janux app ships a WebMCP surface by default, so agents use your real UI tools instead of scraping it. Bun-native, React-ecosystem compatible. Like Comment Story Updates One component, two faces: write one definition and ship a live UI for humans plus typed MCP tools for agents. A real tools/list from the live site. Nobody wrote an MCP server: these are the app's own functions, published by the framework. The live playground: component source, rendered UI, and what the agent sees - the same intents published as tools, with guards. guard: 'confirm' - the agent asked to run counter.reset. Nothing happens until a human approves it. A bolted-on agent surface is a copy, and copies rot: drift, unclear authority, nothing you can gate in CI. GIF An agent driving a real Janux app: it calls the app's own intents and the UI glows on whatever it touches. Inspiration Watch an AI agent use a website today and it is doing an impression of a person. It screenshots the page, guesses which pixels are a button, clicks, and hopes nothing moved. We built a GUI-agent demo ourselves and the lesson was blunt: the agent was not slow because the model was weak. It was slow because the app refused to tell it anything. Every capability the app already had — typed, validated, permission-checked on the server — was hidden behind a rendering of itself. WebMCP inverts that. The page stops being a picture to be interpreted and starts being a host that hands the agent real tools. Once we saw that, the question stopped being "how do we automate the browser better" and became "what would a fullstack framework look like if agents were a first-class audience from line one?" That framework is Janux. What it does Janux is a fullstack framework for the Agentic Web. You write your app once; humans get a UI and agents get tools, from the same definitions. An action you already wrote for a form is published three ways with no extra code: as the UI handler, as a WebMCP tool inside the browser session, and as an MCP tool over the wire for out-of-page clients. Same types, same auth, same permission checks. The framework also ships the rest of the stack the Agentic Web needs — llms.txt so an agent can discover what your site does, and Web Bot Auth so it can prove who it is — plus the safety layer that opening this surface demands. And you do not have to bet your stack on it: Janux runs the React ecosystem through a compatibility layer, so it can be adopted page by page. How we built it The framework is Bun-native. The agent surface is not a plugin bolted on top; it is derived from one place. A single server-side manifest describes every tool, its schema, its guard level and whether it can touch untrusted content — the browser bridge, the MCP endpoint and the security pipeline all read from that one description rather than each maintaining its own idea of what exists. Every tool declares a guard. auto runs on the agent's word. confirm produces a signed proposal a human has to approve. Tools can also declare effect: 'irreversible' , which changes how the pipeline treats them under pressure. Our hardest rule was a process one: zero workarounds in the example app . Every time building a demo required a hack, the hack was banned and the friction became a framework change with a test written first. That is where most of the real API came from — event-based tool targeting, keeping runtime nodes alive across SPA navigation, resolving highlight targets for DOM the tool itself creates, disambiguating controls that share an intent. Challenges we ran into Exposing your app's real capabilities to an untrusted caller is a security project wearing a DX project's clothes. Four things we did not see coming: The worst hole was a GET. Our API handler never looked at the HTTP method — it parsed the body and ran the tool. So GET /_janux/api/payments.transfer executed with the defaults from the input schema . That is an tag on any website in the world, no JavaScript, no CORS preflight, nothing. Invocation endpoints now return 405 for read-only verbs: they have no reads to offer. Sec-Fetch-Site: same-site is not a defense. Measured in real Chrome: two different ports on localhost are same-site. Trusting that header would have left the actual attack open, and in production it is the shape of a subdomain takeover. It falls through to an origin comparison like cross-site does. Computing a preview can be the side effect. Our proposal flow shadow-runs an intent to show the human a diff. When we made tainted irreversible tools downgrade from auto to confirm , we routed exactly the most dangerous operations through the path that runs their body before anyone approves. The shadow only shadows state — an outbound call still really happens. Caught reading our own diff, not by a test. Machine output was wearing the human's role. For compatibility with OpenAI-shaped APIs, tool results came back into the conversation as role: 'user' . Our injection guard was faithfully classifying scraped third-party content as "the last thing the human said." Untrusted content is now fenced with a per-call random nonce — without the nonce, a payload can simply close the fence itself and continue as trusted prose. What we learned Green tests were not enough for any of this. What convinced us was mutation: delete a rule, and watch the exact rows of the attack corpus that rule exists for turn red. If nothing goes red, the rule was decoration. The deeper lesson is that WebMCP is not a transport problem, it is a trust-boundary problem. Handing an agent a tool is the easy half. The hard half is that your app now has a caller that can be persuaded by a web page it read a second ago — and the framework, not each app author, should be the one holding that line. What's next More of the standard surface, adoption paths from existing React apps, and pushing the security defaults further so that being agent-ready is the boring default rather than a feature you have to remember to turn on. Try it: bunx create-janux my-app (requires Bun >= 1.3) — https://janux.build Built With ai-agents bun cybersecurity huggingface javascript jsx llms.txt mcp mdx node.js opentelemetry playwright postgresql react redis sqlite tailwind-css typescript vercel vercel-ai-sdk vite web-bot-auth web-components webmcp websockets Try it out janux.build janux.build github.com janux.build janux.build www.npmjs.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Aral Roca Gomez Like Share this project: Updates Aral Roca Gomez started this project — Aug 31, 2026 08:38 AM EDT

title: Chalkboard
pitch: Chalkboard is an AI-powered collaborative classroom where humans and autonomous teaching agents think, draw, and learn together in real time, making AI an active teaching partner.
about_excerpt:
Chalkboard is an AI-powered collaborative classroom where humans and autonomous teaching agents think, draw, and learn together in real time, making AI an active teaching partner.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Chalkboard Logo 
 
 
 
 
 

 GIF 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Chalkboard Logo 
 
 
 
 
 

 GIF 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 



 
 Inspiration 

 The idea for Chalkboard came from a simple problem: online collaboration often feels disconnected from the way we naturally think and communicate in person. 

 In a physical classroom, someone can walk to a board, draw a diagram, point at a specific part of it, explain an idea, ask a question, and immediately see how other people respond. The board becomes more than a place for writing. It becomes the shared context for the entire conversation. 

 Online, that experience is usually fragmented across multiple tools. A video call handles communication, a whiteboard handles diagrams, a document contains notes, chat contains links and messages, and another application might be needed for specialized activities such as mathematics or technical diagrams. 

 I wanted to bring those interactions together into one shared space. 

 The inspiration came from the traditional classroom chalkboard. There is something remarkably intuitive about standing in front of a board and explaining an idea visually. Rather than building another generic digital whiteboard, I wanted Chalkboard to preserve that feeling while adding the capabilities that are possible with modern web technology. 

 That led to the idea of Chalkboard: a real-time collaborative space for teaching, learning, brainstorming, explaining, and creating together. 

 What I Built 

 Chalkboard is a real-time collaborative canvas designed around the idea of a shared classroom or workspace. 

 Users can create rooms and invite other people to collaborate on the same board. Once inside a room, participants can draw together, write notes, create shapes, move objects, add links, react to each other, raise their hands, and communicate through voice. 

 The important part is that everyone is interacting with the same live canvas . 

 When one participant draws something, other participants see it appear in real time. When someone moves an object, changes the board, reacts, or joins the room, those changes become part of the shared experience. 

 This makes Chalkboard useful for much more than traditional online classes. 

 A room can become: 

 
 A classroom where an instructor teaches students 
 A workshop where participants work through an exercise 
 A brainstorming space for a team 
 A technical architecture board for developers 
 A planning space for a project 
 A collaborative design surface 
 A mathematical workspace 
 A creative studio 
 

 The underlying idea is that the board should adapt to the activity rather than forcing every type of collaboration into the same workflow. 

 The Collaborative Classroom 

 I designed Chalkboard around the concept of a room rather than simply a canvas. 

 Each room has its own participants, permissions, presence, activity, canvas state, and history. 

 Participants can see other users' cursors and activity, allowing the board to feel more like a physical room where everyone is present rather than a collection of isolated users editing the same document. 

 Rooms can also have different access models, including open rooms, approval-based rooms, and password-protected rooms. 

 Different roles can be assigned to participants, including owner, instructor, and viewer , allowing Chalkboard to support situations where an instructor controls the lesson while students participate. 

 This room-based architecture became important because it allowed me to think about Chalkboard as an actual digital classroom environment , not just a drawing application. 

 The Canvas 

 At the center of Chalkboard is its interactive canvas. 

 I wanted the canvas to retain the simplicity of a physical chalkboard while supporting the capabilities users expect from modern collaborative software. 

 Users can: 

 
 Draw freehand with chalk-style strokes 
 Create shapes 
 Add text and notes 
 Select and transform objects 
 Move and resize content 
 Copy and paste objects 
 Group elements 
 Zoom and pan around the board 
 Add links 
 Undo and redo actions 
 Interact with mathematical visualization tools 
 

 Rather than treating the canvas as a static image, Chalkboard maintains a structured representation of the objects and actions taking place on the board. This becomes especially important for collaboration, plugins, and eventually AI agents because the system can understand that something on the board is a circle, text element, arrow, diagram, or other object , rather than simply seeing pixels. 

 Real-Time Collaboration 

 One of the most important engineering challenges was making the collaboration feel immediate. 

 A collaborative canvas generates a continuous stream of events. A user might draw a stroke, move their cursor, move an object, react to another participant, or change something on the board — all within a few seconds. 

 I therefore designed Chalkboard around real-time events rather than treating the canvas like a traditional CRUD application. 

 The real-time system synchronizes things such as: 

 
 Canvas changes 
 Drawing strokes 
 Object transformations 
 Cursor positions 
 Participant presence 
 Reactions 
 Raised hands 
 Room activity 
 Collaboration state 
 

 This also introduced another challenge: connection reliability . 

 Users can temporarily lose their connection, refresh their browser, or reconnect from another device. I had to design the presence and synchronization system so that short network interruptions would not make the classroom feel unstable. 

 A short presence grace period helps prevent users from constantly appearing and disappearing when they briefly disconnect. 

 How I Built It 

 I built the frontend using React, TypeScript, Vite, HTML5 Canvas, and Zustand . 

 Rather than relying entirely on a canvas abstraction, I implemented much of the canvas interaction and rendering logic myself. This gave me more control over how strokes, objects, selection, transformations, zooming, and the chalkboard visual experience behave. 

 The backend is built with Node.js and Hono , with Socket.IO providing the real-time communication layer. 

 For persistent application data, I use PostgreSQL with Drizzle ORM . PostgreSQL handles durable data such as users, rooms, memberships, permissions, plugins, and other application records. 

 For fast-changing collaborative state, I use Redis . This allows active room state, presence information, real-time coordination, and other ephemeral data to be handled without constantly writing every interaction to the primary database. 

 I also use BullMQ for background jobs and cleanup tasks, while the Socket.IO Redis adapter allows the real-time architecture to work across multiple backend instances. 

 Authentication is handled through Google Identity Services , with the backend verifying authentication and creating secure sessions. 

 I also integrated LiveKit to provide voice communication inside rooms, allowing Chalkboard to combine the visual collaboration experience with real-time conversation. 

 The Plugin System 

 As I built Chalkboard, I realized that a collaborative canvas becomes much more powerful when developers can extend what can happen inside it. 

 Instead of putting every possible feature into the core application, I designed a plugin system that allows developers to create new tools and experiences for Chalkboard. 

 A plugin can introduce new capabilities to the board while remaining separate from the core application. 

 For example, Chalkboard can have plugins for: 

 
 Mathematics 
 Diagrams 
 Notes 
 Data visualization 
 Learning activities 
 Technical architecture 
 Games 
 Productivity tools 
 

 I have already experimented with mathematical capabilities that can generate things such as Venn diagrams, number lines, coordinate grids, and set visualizations directly on the canvas. 

 The plugin architecture also introduces a path for third-party developers to contribute to Chalkboard. Plugins can have their own identity, ver

title: NapkinLab
pitch: Sketch UI flows with your AI agent on the same live canvas through native WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt: Sketch UI flows with your AI agent on the same live canvas through native WebMCP tools. Like Comment Story Updates Product ideas usually start visually: a rough layout, a screenshot, a few boxes, or a hand-drawn flow. But when an AI coding agent joins the process, that visual context gets flattened into prompts and descriptions. The person can see what they mean, while the agent receives an incomplete or outdated translation. I wanted a workspace where the person and the agent could collaborate on the same live artifact. The human should be able to think spatially and direct the product visually; the agent should be able to inspect the actual structure, make precise changes, and immediately return control to the human. That is what Napkin Lab is designed to do. What it does Napkin Lab is a browser-based visual UI-flow sketcher. It helps people turn rough product ideas into structured, testable flows before committing to production code. The studio has three connected views: IdeaFrame for arranging Frames and reusable interface blocks. FlowMap for connecting navigation and understanding the journey between Frames. RoughDraft for clicking through the planned experience like a lightweight prototype. Napkin Lab also supports browser-local autosave, .napkin import and export, annotations, visual tracing, temporary agent handoffs, and snapshots of eligible public URLs. The important WebMCP addition is that an AI agent no longer has to infer the sketch from a screenshot or wait for the user to export a file. In a WebMCP-capable browser, the agent can work with the sketch that is open right now. How WebMCP is used Napkin Lab exposes two native WebMCP tools: napkin_describe This read-only tool returns a compact, structured description of the active sketch, including its Frames, interface elements, notes, navigation flows, canvas items, and current selection. It intentionally does not expose the application’s raw state store or embedded image data. The agent receives the information it needs to understand the product flow without receiving unrelated internal state. napkin_apply_operations This tool lets an agent apply a validated batch of document operations to the live sketch. The operation input is treated as untrusted data and parsed at runtime. Napkin Lab validates the entire batch before applying anything. If one operation is invalid, the whole batch is rejected and the document remains unchanged. A successful batch: Appears immediately on the visible canvas. Can contain between one and 100 operations. Supports references to objects created earlier in the same batch. Produces an updated structured description for verification. Is recorded as one Undo step. Napkin Lab also rejects agent writes while the person is in the middle of a canvas gesture. This creates a clear coordination boundary: the agent cannot race the human while they are dragging, resizing, or editing something. The result is a genuine shared-canvas workflow. A person can sketch or select something, ask the agent for a change, watch that change appear in the real document, and undo the entire agent action once if it is not what they wanted. What was added during the challenge Napkin Lab existed before the WebMCP Challenge. The pre-existing product already included the visual editor, FlowMap, RoughDraft, import and export, browser-local autosave, an optional stdio MCP server, and hosted handoff infrastructure. During the challenge submission period, I added and refined the native in-page WebMCP implementation. That work included: Native discovery of napkin_describe and napkin_apply_operations. A shared compact description layer used by the browser and stdio transports. Runtime parsing of untrusted operation input at the document-store boundary. Atomic operation batches with one-batch/one-undo behavior. References to objects created earlier in the same batch. Rejection of writes during an active human gesture. Safe registration and cleanup across React StrictMode remounts. Serialized registration and duplicate-name retry behavior. Selection cleanup after mutations. Updated agent guidance and WebMCP-specific regression tests. Validation in ChatGPT’s WebMCP-capable in-app browser. The WebMCP layer is intentionally thin. It does not create a second, agent-only editing engine. Both the person and the agent operate on the same underlying document model. How I built it Napkin Lab is built with React, TypeScript, Vite, and Zustand. The application detects document.modelContext or navigator.modelContext and registers its tools only when WebMCP is available. Browsers without WebMCP still receive the normal visual editor. The public application is hosted on Cloudflare Pages. Temporary relay sessions use Workers KV, while Snapshot from URL uses a service-bound Cloudflare Worker with Browser Rendering. The core editor does not require an account. OpenAI Codex helped me implement and review the WebMCP transport, refine the tool schemas and descriptions, test runtime validation and atomic behavior, diagnose registration lifecycle issues, and verify the native tools in the in-app browser. I also used Codex to run the automated test, lint, type-check, and production-build gates; audit the repository before publication; prepare a history-free public contest snapshot; and verify the deployed site, relay, snapshot service, license, and native WebMCP discovery. Challenges The hardest part was not simply registering a browser tool. It was making agent edits behave like trustworthy product interactions. That meant handling partial failures, malformed operation input, React registration lifecycles, duplicate tools, human-agent editing conflicts, selection state, and undo history. A tool call returning successfully was not enough: the visible canvas, structured result, and document history all needed to agree. Another challenge was preserving the value of an existing product while being transparent about what was specifically built during the challenge. The public repository therefore includes a dedicated contest-period document that separates the original editor from the new WebMCP work. What I learned The biggest lesson was that useful agent integration is as much about boundaries as capabilities. Giving an agent permission to mutate a document is easy. Making that mutation understandable, validated, atomic, reversible, and coordinated with the person is the real work. WebMCP makes it possible for the webpage itself to define those boundaries. Napkin Lab can expose a small, intentional interface instead of handing an agent unrestricted application state or forcing it to interpret the UI through screenshots alone. Why it matters Napkin Lab explores a different relationship between visual tools and coding agents. The agent is not replacing the canvas, and the canvas is not merely producing a prompt for the agent. They are sharing one working model. That makes it possible for product owners, designers, developers, and small teams to communicate product structure more directly, make changes with less translation, and keep a human-visible, reversible record of what the agent did. title: Countersign
pitch: Working Together Under Writer and Agents. AI reads your live underwriting case, catches what you'd miss — fraud patterns, over-insurance, non-disclosure. Proposes. Waits. Nothing binds without you.
about_excerpt: Working Together Under Writer and Agents. AI reads your live underwriting case, catches what you'd miss — fraud patterns, over-insurance, non-disclosure. Proposes. Waits. Nothing binds without you. Like Comment Story Updates Agent can take action on behalf of Underwriters proposing exclusion clauses Inspiration I am working in insurance industry for 20 years and is one of the slowest moving industry when it comes to tech . Underwriting is still done the way it was 20 years ago: an underwriter alone in a tab, manually cross-referencing claims history, other policies, and disclosure forms that live in different systems. The risk factors that matter most — a second policy on the same address, a claim filed right before renewal, a "no prior claims" answer that doesn't match the file — aren't hard to catch, they're just easy to miss when you're moving fast through a queue of files. We wanted to see if WebMCP could let an AI agent sit inside that same case file, alongside the underwriter, and catch what a tired reviewer on their tenth file of the day might not. Not an agent that decides. One that notices, and says so. What it does Countersign is a shared underwriting workspace. The underwriter reviews a live policy application — applicant details, requested sum insured, policy terms. An AI agent, connected through WebMCP tools registered directly on the page, can read the same case data (claim history, other active policies) and propose changes: a risk flag, a premium loading, a change to the excess or an exclusion — each with a plain-language reason citing the specific data behind it. Every proposal lands in a queue, clearly attributed to the agent, and does nothing to the actual policy until the underwriter accepts or rejects it. Nothing binds without a human. Every action — human or agent — is timestamped in an activity log, so the final policy comes with a defensible trail of who decided what, and why. Working together. Underwriter and agent. AI reads your live underwriting case, catches what you'd miss — fraud patterns, over-insurance, non-disclosure. Proposes. Waits. Nothing binds without you. How we built it The app is a single-page React + Vite frontend, no backend — WebMCP tools run entirely client-side against in-memory state. We registered five tools via navigator.modelContext.registerTool : Two read-only tools — check_claim_history and check_other_policies — that return structured data plus computed signals like aggregate exposure across policies Three propose-only write tools — propose_risk_flag , propose_loading , propose_field_adjustment — that never mutate the policy record directly; they push into a pending-proposals queue that only a human accept/reject action can resolve We modeled the mock case data around real underwriting fraud patterns rather than generic risk scores: claims frequency thresholds, sum-insured-vs-declared-value mismatches, and same-address aggregate exposure across multiple insurers. We tested tool discovery and invocation in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, then verified the full flow again through ChatGPT's desktop browser Site Tools before finalizing. Challenges we ran into Getting the human-in-the-loop boundary right took more iteration than the tools themselves — it was tempting to let "safe" proposals auto-apply, but any auto-apply path undermines the audit story that makes this credible for a regulated workflow, so we held the line at approval-gated everything. We also hit the classic stale-closure bug with tool execute callbacks holding onto old state snapshots when the active applicant changed, which we fixed by reading current state through a ref instead of a captured value. Getting WebMCP tool descriptions specific enough that the agent reliably called the right tool with the right applicant ID — rather than guessing or hallucinating case data — took several rounds of tightening the schema and description wording. Accomplishments that we're proud of We're proud that the propose-only architecture isn't just a safety feature bolted on — it's the actual product insight: an LLM in a regulated decision workflow shouldn't want authority, it should want to be legible. Every accepted or rejected proposal, plus the reasoning behind it, is captured automatically, which means the audit trail underwriting teams need for compliance falls out of the design instead of being built as an afterthought. We also managed to build tools that reflect how underwriters actually think — loading vs. excess vs. exclusion as distinct levers, aggregate exposure as a first-class concept — rather than a generic "risk score" that wouldn't hold up to anyone with real domain knowledge. What we learned WebMCP's biggest value isn't letting an agent do more — it's letting an agent act inside a shared object both parties can see and trust, instead of narrating actions in a chat window disconnected from the real record. We also learned how much of "trust" in a human-AI collaboration tool comes from what the system refuses to do automatically, not what it can do. On the technical side: closures over live app state are the easiest way to introduce subtle bugs when wiring WebMCP tools into a React app, and it's worth designing state access through refs from the start rather than retrofitting it. What's next for Countersign Near-term, we'd add a referral tier — when proposed changes cross an underwriter's authority limit (e.g. aggregate exposure above a threshold), Countersign would route them to a senior underwriter instead of a simple accept/reject, matching how real underwriting authority limits work. We'd also like to make agent reasoning traceable at the data level — clicking a proposal highlights the exact claim or policy row it's citing, so nothing the agent says is a black box. Longer-term, the same propose-and-approve pattern applies well beyond underwriting — claims adjudication, loan structuring, compliance review — anywhere a human needs to stay the final signature on a decision an AI can help inform but shouldn't make alone. title: Hearthkeeper
pitch: One care plan for an aging parent, shared by the family and their agents. Mom says how she feels; the agent acts on the real plan; the family sees it.
about_excerpt:
One care plan for an aging parent, shared by the family and their agents. Mom says how she feels; the agent acts on the real plan; the family sees it.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 What it is 

 Margaret is 78 and lives alone. Her daughter Alex and her son Sam help look after her from two different cities. Hearthkeeper is the one care plan they all share : medications and today's doses, appointments, who is doing what, a symptom journal, and a family feed. Margaret talks to the care agent by voice or text. The agent edits the plan through WebMCP, and the family's screens update. 

 Live: https://hearthkeeper.vercel.app · Code: https://github.com/chinesepowered/hearthkeeper 

 The moment it is built for 

 Margaret says: "I've been dizzy since I started the new blood pressure pill on Monday." 

 The agent reads the plan, logs the symptom, checks Amlodipine against her Metoprolol (an additive blood-pressure effect, dizziness on standing is a known early side effect), adds a note to the medication card, books a phone call with the pharmacist for tomorrow, gives Alex a concrete job tonight (blood pressure sitting and standing), and sends the family an urgent update. Switch to Viewing as Alex and it is all there: the alert at the top of the feed, the task in her list. She asks "did Mom take her morning pills?" and gets an answer from the live plan. 

 No forms. No phone tree. Mom just said how she felt. 

 Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP 

 Caregiving is coordination: a dozen small facts scattered across text threads, pill bottles and fridge notes. An agent can only help if it can act on the real plan, not a screenshot of it, and not a copy that drifts. Hearthkeeper exposes the plan as twelve structured tools registered with document.modelContext.registerTool : 

 get_care_plan , log_symptom , check_interactions , add_medication , update_medication , mark_dose_taken , add_appointment , reschedule_appointment , cancel_appointment , assign_task , complete_task , notify_family 

 Any WebMCP-capable agent, whether ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with WebMCP enabled, or the built-in Gemini care agent, reads and updates exactly what the family sees. Tool descriptions carry the guardrails (the agent may move a dose time but never change a dose; dose changes come from the prescriber), and every write posts to the shared feed so nothing an agent does is invisible. 

 How it creates a better experience 

 
 For the parent: talk, don't navigate. Voice input, plain-language replies, and the agent takes the follow-up steps instead of handing back a to-do list. 
 For the family: one plan instead of a group chat. Every agent action lands in the feed with who it was sent to. Tasks are concrete and assigned. Perspective switching shows the same plan from each person's side. 
 For safety: the interaction check is a read-only tool with a small reference table, and the prompt escalates red-flag symptoms to emergency services rather than trying to be a doctor. 
 

 What people and agents can do together that was hard before 

 Before: Mom mentions dizziness on the phone, Alex googles it at work, Sam doesn't hear about it until Sunday, nobody calls the pharmacist. Now: Mom says it once, the agent does the coordination in seconds, and the family corrects or extends it on the same board. The human keeps judgment and relationships; the agent keeps the plan in sync. 

 How WebMCP is implemented 

 
 lib/webmcp.ts : tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool(..., { signal }) and unregistered via AbortController on unmount. Native calls from the browser agent and calls from the in-page agent share one execute path and one activity log. 
 lib/tools.ts : the twelve tools with JSON Schema inputs, natural-language descriptions and read-only / destructive annotations. 
 lib/care.ts : the shared store. The UI's checkboxes and the tools mutate the same state, so agent edits appear instantly for every viewer. 
 components/AgentPanel.tsx + app/api/agent/route.ts : a Gemini function-calling loop that discovers the registered tools and dispatches through WebMCP, with Web Speech API for voice in and out and a model fallback chain for free-tier limits. 
 

 Tested in Chrome 153 with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing (DevTools → Application → WebMCP lists all twelve tools) and with the in-page Gemini agent. 

 Demo data only. Not medical advice. 

 Stack 

 Next.js 16 · Tailwind 4 · Web Speech API · Gemini function calling · WebMCP · Vercel

 gemini next.js react tailwind typescript vercel web-speech-api webmcp
