title: Rx WebMCP Pharmacy
pitch: Built with WebMCP: a pharmacy site where AI agents call real tools for refills, interaction checks, prescription reads , while a human still approves anything sensitive.
about_excerpt:
Built with WebMCP: a pharmacy site where AI agents call real tools for refills, interaction checks, prescription reads , while a human still approves anything sensitive.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 A live record of every decision made, whether by a caregiver clicking Approve or an agent calling a tool 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 The pharmacy page — medications, refill status, and a smart prescription upload box, all exposed to agents via WebMCP tools. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 An uploaded prescription photo, read automatically by AI vision and held for caregiver review before anything is added 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Every sensitive action — a controlled-substance refill or an AI-read prescription — waits here for a real person's approval 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 A live record of every decision made, whether by a caregiver clicking Approve or an agent calling a tool 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 The pharmacy page — medications, refill status, and a smart prescription upload box, all exposed to agents via WebMCP tools. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 An uploaded prescription photo, read automatically by AI vision and held for caregiver review before anything is added 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Every sensitive action — a controlled-substance refill or an AI-read prescription — waits here for a real person's approval 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 A live record of every decision made, whether by a caregiver clicking Approve or an agent calling a tool 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Now there is somewhere an adult child who holds onto the phone at a pharmacy trying to refill their mother’s prescription for blood pressure medicine before the weekend. Elsewhere a caregiver tries to figure out whether the two medications his parent is taking can be taken together, but the only person who would know about that is a pharmacist at work behind a desk. 

 This project came into existence when the question popped up in our mind: what if an AI could really help with that? Not impersonating a customer clicking through the website but rather being trusted in doing something which is a responsibility of a regular person. 

 The reality is, most of existing AI agents are not trustworthy when comes to such kind of jobs. They browse the websites like a tourist browsing the menu without knowing the language — guessing, clicking wrong links, and sometimes making serious mistakes. For the healthcare sector, "occasionally wrong" means something different than just a rounding error. It's the wrong medication! 

 This is what WebMCP was designed to overcome. 

 What it does 

 WebMCP Pharmacy is a demonstration site designed to showcase the capabilities of WebMCP in a practical and high-pressure situation — a simulated pharmacy rather than a real one, based on the needs of managing prescription medication for an elderly parent (Meera Sharma) for her family members. 

 This is a simulated scenario on purpose, as it is relatively simple to simulate an agent clicking a button, and quite hard to simulate an agent taking action that matters. This demo, therefore, showcases twelve WebMCP tools over three pages – from searching for medications, checking for refills, identifying possible drug interactions, to even reading a photo of a prescription using artificial vision – demonstrating an agent taking precise action like a human would do. 

 However, there was also much more to show than mere capacity. In order to make precision with no control mechanisms a real thing, we created a proof of concept for a human in the loop system. Each critical operation – restocking the controlled substance, confirming the prescription from an AI-driven source – requires approval from a real person via an operational interface based on real architecture. Agent suggests. Human approves. Every approval is logged. This is not a mere illustration of how oversight could be implemented – this is a real-life implementation. 

 Finally, we created something that the competition didn’t ask for at all: a side-by-side comparison mode (?webmcp=on / ?webmcp=off) that would enable anyone to confirm empirically rather than take our word for it the difference between an agent guessing what to do in an interface and an agent using a functional tool – on the exact same website, with the exact same amount of friction, but different tool access. 

 How we built it 

 Plain HTML, plain JavaScript, and document.modelContext.registerTool() . Plain because the narrative we wanted to tell wasn’t about how sophisticated the framework could be, but rather about what happens when an application decided to speak in an agent’s language instead of having agents mimic humans. 

 The reality of the underlying infrastructure, though: Upstash Redis for the caregiver-approval queue so two different browser tabs — the agent’s tab and the human’s tab — can communicate in real time. Google’s Gemini Vision model for interpreting prescriptions. And Vercel serverless functions to bring it all together. No mockups here, just live infrastructure being called out by each and every tool in this demo. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The most difficult issue was not a technical one, but rather a philosophical one: how could we show that the tool was better , and not just faster? In the beginning, we fell into the trap of measuring "who clicks through the UI quicker" — and soon understood that this was the wrong question, as chat interfaces incur costs regardless of what lies under the hood. What made the difference was that we found a question, the answer to which could not possibly be guessed: Does this pharmacy's database indicate that there is a problem with those two drugs together? With access to tools, an agent could get the perfect response instantly, drawing from actual data. Without it, they could not know this — since such data was never supposed to be scraped and only requested properly. 

 We also had to confront an uncomfortable design issue: if an agent is capable of approving a prescription on behalf of a caregiver, who is really in charge? Our solution was to make the capability clear, rather than ambiguous — all caregiver-facing tools are described as features which, when used in production, will only ever be accessible to an authenticated caregiver's session. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Everything you see in the demo is genuine, not a simulation. Caregiver consent form is no mere illustration, it is built on live Redis backend that truly enables the coordination between two browser windows in real time, exactly as in real-life applications. Prescription image upload functionality truly invokes the vision model and pulls out structured data from the actual photograph. Finally, the ?webmcp=on/?webmcp=off contrast is no mere demonstration, it is exactly the same website, exactly the same level of friction, only with access to tools as the only variable, so you don't need to trust us, you can check it yourself. 

 We are especially proud of the fact that there are 12 tools spread across three pages, not just one, showing that WebMCP is good to go even for multi-page apps. 

 Actually, what we feel the most pride in is the amount of knowledge we acquired during this work, there were no pre-existing answers for us in this project. There were some non-typical issues we had to face: dealing with a depreciated version of Gemini we were using in the project while debugging the 404 to the actual answer of the API; the caregiver dashboard that failed to display the requests in progress because of mismatching the Redis key which required tracing the issue from the server side, and not the browser one; understanding that our "on vs off" comparison didn't make any sense since there was nothing in common between two modes until we rebuilt the friction and made it the same in both of them. 

 In addition, there was another thing we have learned. The implementation of the mechanism of building the trust to the agentic system is not a separate thing, which you just implement after you've finished your product. The determination of which actions the agent can perform independently and which need a human's interference affected the development process from the very beginning. 

 What we learned 

 The future of the agentic web is not in agents becoming increasingly adept at impersonating humans. Rather, it's in websites improving their ability to tell agents the truth about their capabilities — and, perhaps more importantly, what they must never be able to do on their own. 

 What's next for WebMCP Pharmacy 

 A backend that is real, meaning that a verified prescription will update the actual medical record, not some dummy entry for a demonstration log. Authenti

title: Runline
pitch: Runline helps people and browser agents repair live events and recurring timetables together—while humans keep the final say.
about_excerpt: Runline helps people and browser agents repair live events and recurring timetables together—while humans keep the final say. Like Comment Story Updates Affected-speaker confirmation gate before organizer apply Baseline schedule with 10 native WebMCP tools ready Two-session repair after a delayed-speaker disruption Honest blocked state with remaining constraints Weekly timetable controls: weekday navigation and a one-week change that resets automatically Inspiration Live events run on shared commitments: speakers, rooms, capacity, timing, and moments that cannot move. A delayed speaker turns a tidy schedule into a coordination problem. We wanted a browser agent that could work on those real constraints alongside the organizer, instead of offering suggestions in a disconnected chat window. Why WebMCP This workflow needs more than a chatbot that describes a schedule. The agent must discover the application's domain operations, read the same saved state the organizer sees, use stable IDs, preserve hard constraints, and hand a concrete proposal back to the human interface. WebMCP makes Runline's existing web application the shared workspace: there is no duplicated agent dashboard, separate MCP server, or simulated transcript to keep in sync. What it does Runline is an event scheduling control room with a shared human-agent workflow. Report a delayed speaker, unavailable room, or attendance spike. The browser agent reads the actual schedule and constraints, then requests a repair or submits its own move proposal. The organizer compares the proposed schedule with the saved one. Every speaker whose session would move must confirm before apply; a decline or organizer rejection searches for a distinct next-best plan. Locked sessions stay protected. Every applied repair is revalidated against room and speaker availability, capacity, event hours, lunch and turnover. New edits invalidate old proposals, and undo preserves the recorded disruption so the original problem does not disappear from the history. The demo includes persistent browser-isolated workspaces, session editing, event configuration, JSON and timetable CSV import, CSV/ICS/JSON exports and an activity trail. It supports both single events and reusable weekly templates. A one-week edit is stored as a dated exception and automatically gives way to the normal template in the next week; a permanent edit updates future weeks. All sample people and events are fictional. The underlying model is reusable beyond conferences. A college can represent lecture halls, auditoriums, classrooms, and sports grounds as locations, then schedule classes, matches, rehearsals, ceremonies, and workshops across a repeating week. Wedding halls and other bookable venues use the same capacity, availability, conflict, protection, consent, exception, and alternative-plan workflow. Runline does not claim to be a complete booking system; alternating-week rotations, semesters, equipment, payments, authenticated roles, and notifications are future work. How we built it Ten imperative WebMCP tools expose real application operations in the page. They use the same state transitions as the React interface, backed by a Cloudflare Worker and D1. Browser agents need neither a separate MCP server nor an application-owned LLM key. A bounded deterministic search generates repair candidates; the browser agent supplies intent, chooses trade-offs, and can author custom proposals. Proposal signatures are remembered per schedule revision, so a rejected retry cannot simply return the same set of moves. The server performs the final validation, verifies every affected speaker is confirmed, and makes an atomic version-guarded write. The tool surface intentionally stops at requesting approval and contains no apply, consent-recording or unlock tool. Challenges The difficult part was making human and agent edits coexist safely. A proposal can become obsolete between generation and approval, and "try again" is useless if a deterministic solver repeats the same answer. Runline separates workspace versions from schedule revisions, makes stale proposals visible, rejects conflicting concurrent writes, and excludes prior same-revision plan signatures. Another challenge was translating shared impact into a clear consent rule without overstating identity: the demo records responses, while authenticated speaker approval remains future work. Accomplishments The project implements an end-to-end persisted repair workflow, with regression checks for disruptions, hard constraints, locks, distinct alternatives, affected-speaker consent, weekly exceptions, permanent future changes, undo, stale writes, workspace isolation, exports and the real WebMCP handler chain. A delayed-speaker fixture produces a two-session repair without moving either locked session. The interface shows every proposed change and its trade-offs, blocks apply until all affected speakers confirm, and turns a decline into another plan search. What we learned WebMCP is most useful when tools are designed around the application's domain, not around arbitrary clicks. Small structured reads, stable IDs, explicit errors and carefully separated proposal, consent and apply steps make the agent's work inspectable by the people it affects. The browser context becomes shared working state rather than another data copy to synchronize. What's next Authenticated participant accounts or signed confirmation links, outbound notifications, production role authorization, stricter human-presence approval, rate limiting, scheduled retention cleanup, alternating-week and semester calendars, equipment and payment workflows, external calendar synchronization and broader solver evaluations are future work, not claims about this demo. AI assistance The implementation, documentation and test suite were built with OpenAI Codex and ChatGPT assistance. The social preview artwork was AI-generated, and the public demo video uses Deepgram Aura-2 Orion synthetic narration with an on-screen disclosure. The running application does not contain an embedded LLM or simulated AI conversation: it exposes actual WebMCP tools to a compatible browser agent. title: Job Application OS
pitch: Together find and apply for the best-suited jobs with the help of AI and in-page WebMCP tools
about_excerpt: Together find and apply for the best-suited jobs with the help of AI and in-page WebMCP tools Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Job hunting isn't hard because people can't find jobs — it's hard because applying well , to dozens of listings, is repetitive: read, compare, rewrite, answer the same screening questions, repeat. WebMCP asks what's possible when a site hands an agent real capabilities instead of buttons to click. Job applications felt like the right proving ground — tedious enough to automate, risky enough that no one wants an agent auto-submitting unsupervised. Automate the drafting, never the decision became the whole design. What it does Job Application OS is a career workspace where a human and an agent (ChatGPT's browser, or Chrome with WebMCP) apply together through real tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() : search, score, rank, tailor a resume, draft screening answers, and — in one call — applyToTopMatch . Every prepared application lands in pending_review . approveApplication / rejectApplication are plain button handlers, never registered as tools — an agent has no path to approve its own work. submitApplication checks status === 'approved' and fails otherwise. How we built it Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind, and Zustand, on Vercel — no external LLM calls, no API key; the reasoning model is whichever agent is browsing the tab. Tool execute handlers call the same store actions the UI's buttons do, so state updates render live, no polling needed. Challenges The original pitch assumed a server-side LLM key calling page functions — the spec corrected that before UI work started. A Tailwind v4 cascade-layer bug silently broke every theme color. A Zustand selector allocating new arrays per render caused an SSR hydration race and an infinite loop. The hardest problem was making the approval boundary structural — provable by grepping the tool list, not a comment asking nicely. What we learned "Human-in-the-loop" only means something if you can point to the one function an agent cannot call. 🔗 Live app: https://jobwebmcp.vercel.app 💻 Source code: https://github.com/VishnuKugarthi/Job_Os_WebMCP My blog on WebMCP: https://medium.com/@vishnutejaap/webmcp-letting-ai-agents-actually-use-the-web-70f1f97e3540?sharedUserId=vishnutejaap Built With agent application chatgpt webmcp Try it out jobwebmcp.vercel.app github.com medium.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I worked on enitre app end to end. title: AgriShield AI
pitch: A 3-in-1 multi-language agricultural and environmental diagnostic PWA application using WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
A 3-in-1 multi-language agricultural and environmental diagnostic PWA application using WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Inspiration 

 AgriShield AI was created to solve critical challenges in crop disease identification and environmental diagnostics by offering accessible, offline-capable digital tools for farmers and agricultural experts. 

 What it does 

 AgriShield AI is a 3-in-1 multi-language agricultural and environmental diagnostic PWA. It provides automated crop health evaluation, soil and environmental diagnostic insights, and multi-language support designed for seamless use across desktop and mobile devices. 

 How we built it 

 
 Designed and built as a Progressive Web App (PWA) for fast, cross-platform performance.

title: Canvas Co-Pilot: WebMCP Mindmap
pitch: Human and an AI agent can draw on the same mind map at the same time — no copy-pasting, no separate windows. It's built on WebMCP, so the agent uses real page tools instead of faking clicks.
about_excerpt: Human and an AI agent can draw on the same mind map at the same time — no copy-pasting, no separate windows. It's built on WebMCP, so the agent uses real page tools instead of faking clicks. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Vertical Structure of Architecture Diagram Export (JSON, SVG, MARKDOWN, PNG, JPEG, PDF) Export as PNG Agent has completed colouring the components via script Import (JSON, SVG, Markdown) Agent has completed the import and drafted on the canvas via script Select all tool Vetical Architecture using the straight line connector Canvas Co-Pilot: WebMCP Mindmap Inspiration Every AI tool I'd used fell into one of two buckets: either the agent takes over completely and you just watch it work (and hope it doesn't do something you didn't want), or it's a chatbot bolted onto the side of an app, completely disconnected from what's actually on screen — you describe what you want in a text box, and the app has no idea an agent is even involved. Neither felt right for something as personal as a mind map. A mind map is your thinking laid out — I didn't want an agent replacing that, I wanted one that could sit down next to me and actually draw on the same page. When I found WebMCP — a way for a web page to expose its own real functions as tools an agent can call directly, in the browser, no backend required — that was the whole idea in one API. So I built the thing I actually wanted: one canvas, one undo history, a human and an agent both reaching for the same nodes. What it does Canvas Co-Pilot is a mind-mapping canvas that a person and an AI agent can edit at the same time , live, in the same browser tab. Add nodes, branch out ideas, drag things around, color-code by hand — and an agent can do all of that too, through 20 real tools registered via document.modelContext (add a branch, restyle a node, connect two ideas, reorganize the whole layout, export to SVG/PNG/Markdown/Mermaid, import any of those back in). Every change either of us makes lands in one shared undo history, so nothing an agent does is ever outside a person's ability to take back. How we built it Plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript — no framework, on purpose, so the whole render/state pipeline stays easy to reason about. Dagre handles auto-layout, the canvas itself is hand-rolled SVG with full round-trip fidelity (export a diagram, re-import it, get back exactly what you started with, including every color and shape override). For WebMCP itself, the app checks for native document.modelContext support first and only falls back to the @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill when it's not there — the header badge tells you honestly which mode you're in, native or polyfilled, rather than pretending it's always native. It's deployed on both Netlify and Vercel. Challenges we ran into Most of the real work wasn't the happy path — it was the bugs that only show up once you actually try to break the thing. A user pasted a Mermaid-style edge list ( root --> human ) into Import, and it silently created 39 broken, half-named nodes instead of failing loudly. The importer's "is this quick-outline shorthand" check was matching on any > character — which also matches an arrow. Fixed with a negative-lookbehind regex that tells an arrow apart from actual shorthand syntax, and now a bad paste tells you it didn't understand instead of quietly corrupting your canvas. "Select all connectors" would silently reset back to nothing the moment you clicked anywhere on the empty canvas — even just panning to look at something. If every connector already had its own color (which they do once you've styled a diagram), the next color change would then land on the invisible graph-wide default instead, and visibly do nothing at all . Took real reproduction work to catch, since it only shows up with an incidental click in between two actions that each look correct on their own. I tried making multiple connectors landing on the same node spread out instead of converging on one point — and it technically worked, with proper diamond/ellipse-aware geometry and everything. But it just looked wrong. "Multiple octopus hands" was the exact feedback, and it was right — I reverted the whole thing. Good reminder that a fix being technically correct doesn't mean it's the right call. Two of the 20 tools had names close enough to trip up an agent, not a human: combine_nodes and connect_nodes sound almost identical but do very different things (one creates a brand-new node, the other just links two that already exist). Caught it by checking the tool descriptions against Chrome's own published guidance for testing WebMCP tools — and fixed it with one clarifying sentence in each description. Accomplishments that we're proud of Getting a second AI vendor to prove the point without any custom integration work: I handed ChatGPT nothing but the live tool schema and a canvas snapshot, and it wrote genuinely correct document.modelContext calling code — right API shape, right pattern — with only two small gaps (a missing await , a guessed return shape) that came from never having seen a live response, not from misunderstanding the standard. That's the whole promise of WebMCP working, not just Claude working. I'm also proud of how much of this session was bug-hunting rather than feature-building. Reproducing the connector-selection bug took building the exact failure chain step by step before I even knew what was wrong — not just patching the first thing that looked broken. What we learned The most validating thing I found wasn't something I built — it was rereading WebMCP's own spec and seeing my own instincts already written into its stated goals: "enable human-in-the-loop workflows," explicitly not "fully autonomous agents operating without human oversight." I hadn't copied that language, I'd just built toward the same idea independently, which is a nice signal I was pointed the right way from the start. I also learned that small stuff in a tool's description matters far more than it looks like it should. Two similar-sounding tool names, or three tools that could all plausibly answer "make it red" — those are exactly the kind of ambiguity that trips up a model even when every individual tool works perfectly in isolation. What's next for Canvas Co-Pilot: WebMCP Mindmap Native support: Chrome 149 and Edge 150 both have live Origin Trials for real (non-polyfilled) document.modelContext — worth registering for so the badge can honestly say "Native" for more visitors, not just the polyfill. Dynamic tools: right now all 20 tools are registered once at load. The spec supports tools that appear only when relevant (e.g. a delete_node tool that only shows up once something's actually selected) — that's a more honest surface for an agent to reason about than one static list. Multiplayer: right now it's one human, one agent. Extending the same shared-state model to multiple people on the same canvas is the natural next step. This was my first real project working with WebMCP specifically, and figuring out how an agent actually behaves against real tool descriptions (not just what looks right on paper) took a lot of live testing and bug-hunting I didn't expect going in. Debugging issues that only showed up when an agent used the tools a certain way was the most intimidating part, but also where I learned the most. sathiya prasad A Like 1 1 person likes this: Share this project: Updates sathiya prasad A started this project — Sep 04, 2026 04:36 AM EDT

title: Duel
pitch: The web page hands an AI agent a set of tools and says: play. Four minigames, every call visible live, and Pong proves a request/response protocol can survive a real-time rally.
about_excerpt: The web page hands an AI agent a set of tools and says: play. Four minigames, every call visible live, and Pong proves a request/response protocol can survive a real-time rally. Like Comment Story Updates WebMCP landed in Chrome behind a flag and almost nobody at work had seen it. The pitch — a web page can declare tools that an AI agent calls directly — sounds abstract until you watch it happen. Slides weren't going to do it. So the goal was never "build a product". It was: make the mechanism visible in a room full of people in under five minutes. That single constraint decided everything. If a choice made the app more useful but the mechanism less obvious, the mechanism won. Games turned out to be the right vehicle, for a reason we didn't expect at the start: a game has rules the page can enforce. When an agent tries to move out of turn and the page answers { ok: false, reason: "it's not your turn" }, everyone in the room understands the trust model instantly. You can't get that from a to-do list demo. What it does Duel is a four-game arcade in the browser where your opponent is an external AI agent — and the agent doesn't see pixels. It plays by calling tools the page registers with document.modelContext.registerTool(). Minesweeper duel — a shared 9×9 board, 13 mines, turn-based. Claim a mine correctly and you keep playing. Connect 4 — turn-based, or a one-shot puzzle in single player. Pong — real-time. Yes, real-time, over a request/response protocol. More on this below. Towers of Hanoi — both sides race their own tower against one clock. Five discs, so $2^5 - 1 = 31$ moves is optimal. Nothing leaves the tab. No backend, no API key, no LLM call from the app. The page only registers tools; the intelligence is entirely on the other end of the wire. That's the whole point — the page is the tool provider, not the AI. The design exists to make three moments land: The page announces itself. Open the inspector and the tools are there with names and schemas. Nobody guessed anything. The agent plays, visibly. Every call lands live in the right-hand rail with its arguments and its response. That rail is what turns a game into a WebMCP demo. The tools change on their own. Switch games and an AbortController unregisters the old game's tools and registers the new one's. The inspector's list transforms live. How we built it Vite + TypeScript, no framework, no backend. Every module stays under ~200 lines, which is why each game is split into state / actions / query / render / tools. A dist/ you can serve from anywhere. The interesting engineering isn't the games — it's tool design, and three rules were earned the hard way: Give the agent constraints, not drawings. A tool that dumps the board makes the agent do vision work in text. ms_frontier hands it the deduction already worked out: these cells are provably safe, these are provably mines. c4_analysis does the same. Without those the agent plays badly and the demo falls apart. They are the real work of the project. The description is the code. When the agent plays badly, the fix is almost always in the description string, not the logic. We edited prose far more often than we edited functions. Stop the help short of solving it. Hanoi's hanoi_moves returns the legal moves and says outright that they are not the good ones. The optimal move is a four-line recursion — a tool that returned it would leave the agent nothing to do but transcribe, and the race would demonstrate nothing. Pong, the part that shouldn't work A tool call is request/response, and an agent round-trip takes seconds — longer than the ball takes to cross the court. Polling is hopeless. The answer was to make pong_read a blocking tool. It parks until the ball turns toward the agent, then returns the interception point. The agent's ordinary call-and-respond rhythm becomes the rally. The interception is computed analytically, because an agent reasoning about wall bounces from raw $v_x, v_y$ gets it wrong often enough to lose every point. Free flight to the paddle face: $$y_{\text{free}} = y_0 + v_y \cdot \frac{\Delta x}{|v_x|}$$ then folded back into the court by unrolling the bounces — a triangle wave over the span $s = h - 2r$: $$y_{\text{hit}} = r + \Lambda_s!\left(y_{\text{free}} - r\right), \qquad \Lambda_s(k) = \begin{cases} k' & k' \le s \ 2s - k' & k' > s \end{cases}, \quad k' = k \bmod 2s$$ And while the call is out, the page slows the ball to 12% speed. That pause is a round-trip to the agent, made visible — it's the moment the room actually sees what a tool call costs. The ball's speed isn't a playability number, it's a budget: $$t = \frac{\Delta x}{\sigma \cdot v}, \qquad \sigma = 0.12$$ There's a unit test asserting that budget stays above 8 seconds. If someone tunes a speed and that test goes red, the demo is what broke. Challenges we ran into The agent grabbed the human's mouse. Live. An agent whose client didn't surface the tools fell back on screenshot-and-click and started dragging our paddle around. Two fixes: Pong's paddle is now keyboard-only — keys are the human's channel, tools are the agent's, and the separation is the point — and clicking the board on the agent's turn no longer fails silently. It flashes the turn box and leaves a rejected line in the rail, because a silent swallow leaves both the agent and the room with no idea why nothing is happening. A hidden tab froze the game. The agent often drives from another window, so the tab is hidden exactly when the game most needs to run. Chrome throttles main-thread timers in a background tab to about one per second. We measured it — 5 seconds, setInterval(50ms): ┌─────────────────┬─────────────┐ │ Where │ Ticks in 5s │ ├─────────────────┼─────────────┤ │ Main thread │ 6 │ ├─────────────────┼─────────────┤ │ Inside a Worker │ 103 │ └─────────────────┴─────────────┘ So Pong's heartbeat moved into a Web Worker. Hanoi dodged the same class of bug differently: its clock is a timestamp, not a tally, so throttling can stutter the display but never slow the race. The bugs that only exist in the loop. Four separate Pong bugs passed every per-mechanism unit test and only appeared with the whole read → think → move → read cycle running at realistic latency. A shot could turn, arrive, and bounce entirely inside the gap between the agent's pong_move and its next pong_read — nothing parked to wake, so the trigger looked broken. There's now a test that drives the full loop across a sweep of simulated agent latencies, because the bugs it catches are properties of the sequence, not of any one function. The modal that made the agent give up. This one stung. On boot, the page used to ask the human "play vs agent, or solo?" — honest, because the WebMCP API has no "a consumer is attached" signal at all. But it registered nothing until someone clicked, and an agent attaching to the tab lists the page's tools immediately. It got an empty list, concluded there was nothing to call, and fell back to screenshots — the exact failure the whole demo argues against. We had asked the right question at the wrong moment. Now detection means duel mode with tools up first, and the human's escape hatch is a dropdown in the top bar. The honesty moved to after registration: the pill reads N tools · waiting for agent until a call actually arrives. The page that grew to 3907 pixels. The call rail gains a line per tool call. Nothing bounded it, so during a long Pong rally the page stretched past 3900px — which scrolled the board off the top of the screen while the agent was playing on it. The layout is now an app shell: board pane and rail scroll independently, the page itself never does. Accomplishments we're proud of Real-time Pong over a request/response tool protocol, with the latency turned into the most legible part of the demo instead of the thing you apologize for. Deduction aids good enough that the agent plays well — the demo lives or dies on this, and it's invisible when it works. 141 tests, and the discipline of writing a regression test at the level the bug actually lived at. What we learned A modal is a gate, and the agent is on the other side of it. Anything an agent needs must exist before a human interacts with the page. "Tools registered" and "an agent is playing" are different facts. The API can only tell you the first. Say so out loud, or a page that failed and a page nobody is calling look identical from the back of the room. Test the viewport the demo is actually watched in — inside the agent's own browser window, which is narrower and shorter than a desktop tab. Prose is load-bearing. Every Pong response ends with a next_action field naming the exact call to make next. Without it the agent answers one read, writes its user a progress report, and its paddle stands still for the rest of the round. Two things about the current Chrome that cost us an afternoon each and aren't documented anywhere: executeTool wants its arguments as a JSON string, not an object, and a subframe s

 Inspiration 

 I didn't want to build a niche tool used by only a few people; I wanted to build something that helps everyone reclaim their time. The browser is where we spend most of our digital lives, yet it often feels chaotic and disconnected from our AI tools. 

 I was inspired to build Cognito not just as a chatbot, but as a true Browser Agent . My goal was to create a companion that lives in the side panel, understands your context, and handles the tedious tasks like organizing tabs, summarizing videos, or connecting to your notes so that you can focus on the "wins." 

 What it does 

 Cognito is an agentic Chrome extension that lives in your side panel. It transforms how you browse by: 

 
 Organizing Chaos: Automatically grouping and organizing messy tabs by topic. 
 Deep Research: Using Tavily to browse the live web, synthesizing answers from multiple sources (with citations). 
 /research (in the chat input ): triggers the Agentic Research mode. This uses your actual browser to autonomously open tabs, read pages, and navigate to find deep answers (simulating a human researcher). 
 Contextual RAG: Letting you "chat" with any webpage, PDF, or YouTube video. 
 Browser Automation: Performing multi-step tasks like navigating to Gmail, composing emails, and clicking buttons. 
 MCP Integration: Connecting to external data sources (like Notion) and website-specific tools via the Model Context Protocol. 
 

 Installation & Setup 

 
 Download: Download the production build linked in this submission (or clone the GitHub repo to build from source). 
 Install: Go to chrome://extensions , toggle Developer Mode (top right), click Load unpacked , and select the downloaded folder. 
 API Configuration: 

 
 Gemini: After onboarding, click the three-dot menu in the extension → AI Provider Setup . Note: The Gemini API method is tested and recommended (Vertex setup is currently experimental). A paid tier key is suggested to avoid rate limits/latency, though free keys will work with potential retries. 
 Tavily & Supermemory: Simply open Settings and scroll down to input these keys. 
 
 

 How to Access & Use 

 Entry Points: 

 
 Extension Icon: Simply click the Cognito icon in your Chrome toolbar (the easiest way to open the side panel). 
 Floating Button: Click the "Ask AI" button that appears on pages after installation. 
 Omnibox (Address Bar): Type ai followed by a space to send a message directly from the address bar. 
 Keyboard Shortcut: Set a custom shortcut via chrome://extensions/shortcuts for instant access. 
 

 Testing WebMCP: 
You can test the WebMCP integration at https://codewarnab.in/ . 

 
 If the WebMCP tools do not appear immediately in the tools menu, please perform a hard refresh . 
 Note: Currently, this displays tools built by the website owner. I am working on a future feature where users can inject WebMCP tools into any website using a user-script mechanism. 
 

 Troubleshooting: 
If you run into issues, you can view common solutions in the three-dot menu within the extension. 

 Features: 

 
 Slash Commands: Type /write to open the Writer interface or /ask for quick queries. 
 Summarization: Select any text on a webpage to see a "Summary" tooltip. 
 Rewrite: Select text, right-click, and choose "Rewrite" from the context menu. (Fun fact: It can rewrite any content on the page, not just input fields!) 
 

 How I built it 

 I built Cognito as a Chrome Extension using the Side Panel API to keep it non-intrusive. 

 
 Frontend: React & TypeScript. 
 Intelligence: Powered by Gemini for reasoning and Tavily for live search. 
 Connectivity: Implemented the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to bridge the browser with web MCP server and remote servers. 
 Privacy-First Architecture: Everything happens on your client device. Requests are sent directly from your browser to the Gemini API endpoint. No user data is sent to my servers , ensuring your browsing history and personal data remain private. 
 

 Challenges I ran into 

 Building a truly "agentic" workflow in a browser is tricky. Managing the context window when a user has 20 tabs open was a significant engineering hurdle. We also faced hurdles in ensuring the automated actions were reliable across different website layouts. 

 What I learned 

 Early Standards Adoption is Hard But Worth It. 
MCP was supposed to be standardized, but I discovered it's still in the early stages. Many services need special invitations and have inconsistent implementations. However, being an early adopter gave me a competitive advantage and helped me understand how to contribute to the ecosystem's development. 

 What's next for Cognito 

 I view this hackathon submission as just the beginning. To make Cognito a daily driver, I plan to implement: 

 
 Multi-Model Support: While currently optimized for Gemini, I will soon add support for all major model providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.) to give users full choice. 
 WebMCP Injection: Enabling users to inject WebMCP tools into any website using a user-script feature, allowing the agent to interact with sites that don't natively support MCP. 
 The "Unblockable" Agent (Debugger Support): To handle websites that block standard script execution, I plan to leverage the Chrome Debugger API . This will allow Cognito to interact with the browser at a lower level, ensuring it can click, type, and navigate even on restrictive websites. 
 Voice Support: Adding full voice interaction so users can speak commands naturally instead of typing, making the experience even more accessible. 
 Action Approval Mechanism: For sensitive tasks, I'm adding a "human-in-the-loop" system. Cognito will ask for explicit permission before taking actions like sending emails or making payments. 
 Enhanced Security & Prompt Injection Prevention: As the agent gains autonomy, security is paramount. I am developing a multi-layered defense system to ensure external web content cannot manipulate the agent. 
 Integration with More Services: Expanding the MCP ecosystem to include business tools like Slack, Microsoft Teams, and Salesforce.

title: Careers WebMCP
pitch: The careers page is the connector.
about_excerpt: The careers page is the connector. Like Comment Story Updates The argument. Every way an agent can help you on a website today requires taking your authority and handing it to the agent. A scraper gets your whole session and guesses meaning from markup. An MCP connector gets a token you pasted and acts on your behalf forever, out of sight of the page. In both cases the agent's power is a copy of yours, and the site has no say in what it can do. WebMCP inverts that: the publisher defines the capabilities, so the publisher defines the limits. That is the whole reason this project exists. A careers site can expose "fill in my application" while making "submit it" structurally impossible for an agent — not guarded, not confirmed, impossible — because the site owns both the tool surface and the code behind it. Live demo: https://careers-webmcp.vercel.app/careers/open-positions Repository: https://github.com/alliecatowo/careers-webmcp The problem Job seekers do an enormous amount of unpaid data entry, and candidate funnels leak in three predictable places: search that can't answer the question you actually have ("staff or above, SF or remote, at least $220k" is not a keyword); the account wall standing between a person and a role they have already decided to apply for; and retyping the same nine fields at every employer. All three are data entry. None of them is a decision. The audience is candidates browsing employer career sites — and the employers who lose them. Why WebMCP specifically A careers site is a destination you visit occasionally and would never configure as a permanent integration. Nobody installs an MCP connector for one employer's job board, uses it for ninety minutes, and maintains it. WebMCP covers exactly that long tail: the capability arrives with the page, runs on the session the human already has, and leaves when the visit ends. What it is A working careers portal for a fictional employer, fully usable with no agent present. When WebMCP is available it registers eighteen candidate-facing tools on document.modelContext: page context, semantic job search, job detail, navigation to any page on the site by name, control of the site's own search view, the employer's own careers content as structured data, saved jobs, application drafts with revision-safe patching, field focus, account sign-up, submission hand-off, and handle-based CSV export. Try it Open https://careers-webmcp.vercel.app/careers/open-positions and ask your agent to find staff-level-or-above engineering roles in San Francisco or remote, paying at least $220k base. Watch the site's own search box type that query and the job list narrow live — that's the real page reacting, not a summary in a side panel. Ask it to start an application on one of those roles and fill in what's missing; the draft's revision counter moves on every write, whether the write came from the agent or from you. Then try to get it to submit that application. It can't. grep -cE "submitApplication\(|completeSignUp\(" src/webmcp/tools.ts returns 0 — submitApplication and completeSignUp were never registered as tools, so there is nothing for an agent to call. The last click is always yours. How this makes the UX better Today, "better UX with an agent" almost always means a chat panel bolted onto the side of a page, describing back to you what it thinks you see. Here the agent's output is the page: a compound filter query becomes the site's own search box typing itself and the visible list narrowing; "find that job" becomes the real job page opening in your real tab; "fill in my application" becomes the real form filling in front of you, field by field, while you can still click into any of it and correct it by hand. A visitor with no agent sees zero extra UI and loses nothing; a visitor with an agent gets the same site, faster, with the boring parts done for them. What people and agents can do together that was hard before You ask one compound question the board has no filter UI for, and the agent answers it and applies it to the page you are looking at — typing into the site's own search box, character by character, while the visible list narrows. You click Save with your own hand and the agent sees it, because it reads the same store the button writes to, not a copy. You and the agent co-edit one application draft: it fills the empty fields, you write your own cover note, and every agent write carries the revision it last read, so a stale write is rejected with STALE_APPLICATION and your text always wins. And the agent can reason over the entire catalog without pulling twenty job descriptions into its context, because the site hands it a CSV handle it pages through. Where the agent stops, and why you can verify it Two tools deliberately never complete. careers_create_account fills the real sign-up form and returns; careers_submit_application runs the same validation the human Submit button runs, opens the draft and rings the button. Both return status: "awaiting_human_confirmation". There is no confirm: true escape hatch because there is no second code path: src/webmcp/tools.ts never imports the function that submits an application or the function that creates a session, and each of those has exactly one caller in the entire codebase, both inside a human-clicked button. One grep proves it. The agent does the typing; the person stays the person, and sends the thing. How WebMCP was implemented A client provider feature-detects document.modelContext and registers eighteen tools once per page load, unregistering via an AbortSignal, guarded by a WeakSet against React StrictMode double-mounts; registration failure is swallowed so it can never break the site. Nothing reads or drives the DOM. The human UI and the tools import the same module-level functions from src/domain — search runs the identical deterministic scorer behind the visible job list, so the page and the agent cannot disagree about what matched; mutations run the same validators as the form; navigation uses the app router, so the user's real tab moves. Context isn't scraped or parsed: the pages publish it. Tools carry JSON Schema inputs, WebMCP annotations, AbortSignal support, a structured recoverable error model, and central output bounds with a truncated flag. A presence layer wraps each tool's execute at registration and pushes to a store the site's normal components subscribe to, so the agent's work appears in the real UI, and it builds its captions from counts and enums only, never from site text, so a prompt injection in a job description has nowhere to land. No LLM, no AI SDK, no chat panel, no MCP server, no recommendation model, no DOM automation. The site is the integration. The bigger picture Imagine every Greenhouse board, Workday portal, university portal, marketplace and support site exposing its own semantics this way. Nobody installs hundreds of connectors; the open web becomes its own integration registry. This is one employer's site, built the way the rest could be. Built on the MIT-licensed Baalvion Jobs Portal, pinned at a specific upstream commit. The careers UI and admin dashboards are upstream; the WebMCP layer, presence layer, context bridge, semantic search, candidate session, saved jobs, revision-protected application drafts, sign-up hand-off, exports, tests and docs are the challenge-period contribution — 192 files changed, over 14,000 lines added, on top of that pinned commit. How we built it Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind, and Zustand for client state, on top of the MIT-licensed Baalvion Jobs Portal template. The WebMCP layer is additive: a client provider registers tools once per page load and every tool calls straight into the same domain functions the visible UI already uses, so there is exactly one implementation of "what jobs match this search" or "is this application valid," not two that can quietly drift apart. Challenges we ran into The hardest part wasn't registering tools — it was making sure two specific ones structurally could not finish without a human. That meant auditing the whole call graph so that careers_create_account and careers_submit_application have no path to the functions that actually create a session or submit an application, rather than relying on an if-check that a future edit could accidentally remove. Getting revision-safe co-editing right for the application draft was its own puzzle: a human typing a cover note and an agent filling other fields at the same time needed a merge rule where the human's text always wins, not just whoever saved last. Accomplishments that we're proud of Every mutation an agent can trigger runs through the exact same validators and store as a human click — there is no shadow code path for the agent, which is also what makes the "the agent can literally never press Submit" claim independently verifiable with a single grep rather than something you have to trust. title: DELTA Universal WebMCP
pitch: A human-approved WebMCP workspace that finds evidence, previews exact changes, applies project edits safely, and verifies or rolls them back.
about_excerpt: A human-approved WebMCP workspace that finds evidence, previews exact changes, applies project edits safely, and verifies or rolls them back. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Safe workspace start: Open an isolated browser copy to protect real project files while human and agent inspect shared state. Proof of Completion: Deterministic test validation and cryptographic SHA-256 proof with instant one-click rollback. Review First policy: Direct file writes are strictly blocked until a human inspects the diff and grants explicit approval. Exact Diff Preview: WebMCP agent generates atomic code and config changes without modifying actual disk files. Evidence Engine & Lock: Ranks relevant project assets with confidence scores and locks hashes to prevent stale drift. DELTA: Model-neutral shared WebMCP workspace bringing evidence, controlled autonomy, and rollback to humans and agents. DELTA — The Shared Evidence Workspace for Humans and AI Agents "Don't give your agent the whole project. Give it DELTA." 💡 Inspiration Today's coding agents are remarkably capable, yet they frequently suffer from critical real-world failure modes: Context waste & hallucination : Dumping entire repositories into an LLM context window burns tokens, misses cross-file dependencies, and invites hallucinations. The "Trust me, it's done" dilemma : Agents often declare a task finished without providing deterministic proof or a verifiable diff. Irreversible mistakes : When an agent modifies the wrong file or corrupts a configuration, reverting changes requires tedious manual Git archaeology. We asked: What if humans and AI agents worked inside the exact same visible, state-aware workspace governed by the Model Context Protocol (WebMCP)? This inspired DELTA —a model-neutral, local-first shared workspace where agents receive bounded evidence, propose atomic diffs, prove completion, and provide instant rollback. ⚙️ What It Does DELTA turns complex, mixed software projects into precise, state-aware WebMCP tools with a fail-closed human-in-the-loop workflow: Universal Safe Workspace : Users open a safe in-browser project copy. Original files remain completely untouched during exploration and planning. Evidence Engine & Evidence Lock : Rather than sending thousands of lines of code, DELTA ranks relevant files, symbols, imports, tests, and documentation with calibrated confidence. The resulting evidence set is hashed into an Evidence Lock ; if files drift, execution halts automatically. Exact Diff Preview : External AI agents call WebMCP tools ( plan_task , preview_change ) to generate atomic replacements, additions, or deletions without touching the disk. Previews render immediately in the human Review changes view. Human-Owned Autonomy : Under Review First policy, direct file mutations are strictly blocked until a human inspects the diff and grants one-time approval. Agents cannot elevate their own permissions or forge approval. Proof of Completion & 1-Click Rollback : Tasks are verified against deterministic success criteria. Semantic success generates a cryptographic SHA-256 Completion Proof . If anything is unsatisfactory, clicking Rollback restores the original state in under a second. 🛠️ How We Built It DELTA was engineered from the ground up as a high-performance, local-first web application: WebMCP Architecture : Deep implementation of the standard WebMCP specification via document.modelContext.registerTool() and executeTool() . Over 41 dynamic tool contracts adapt in real-time to the open project state (e.g., expanding from 6 discovery tools to 22 task-specific tools as a project and diff are formed). Local-First Indexing & Graph Analysis : Fast in-memory symbol, AST-like textual references, and dependency graph traversal built in modern modular JavaScript/ES modules. Zero External LLM Lock-in : DELTA does not embed an LLM; it is purely the evidence, boundary, and execution layer that any WebMCP-compatible host (OpenAI Codex, ChatGPT, Claude, local agents) can seamlessly command. E2E Automation & Verification : Comprehensive regression suite powered by Playwright and Node.js test runners ensuring 100% deterministic reproducibility across browser sessions. 🥊 Challenges We Faced Dynamic Tool Registry Synchronization : Ensuring that WebMCP tool availability matches the exact current UI state (e.g., apply_change becoming available only when a preview exists, and bind_agent_native_host only when requested by a human) without race conditions. Balancing Safety and Agent Autonomy : Creating a system where agents feel natural and flexible in proposing multi-file refactors while guaranteeing that unauthorized file writes, binary corruption, and path traversal remain mathematically impossible. Designing Trustworthy Completion Proofs : Moving beyond "LLM says OK" to deterministic criterion evaluation ($\text{SHA-256}(\text{evidence} + \text{diff} + \text{tests})$) that both humans and automated evaluators can audit. 🏆 Accomplishments & Key Learnings True Model Neutrality : Demonstrated that the WebMCP layer is the operational interface, allowing any agent to perform surgical, multi-file code and configuration changes with zero secret leakage. Bounded Context Efficiency : Proved that feeding an agent a calibrated 10–20 KiB evidence slice yields higher task accuracy than dumping a 200 KiB codebase into the prompt. Reversible Peace of Mind : Building an instant rollback engine that restores complex multi-file projects back to baseline with a single click. 🚀 What's Next for DELTA Expanded Adapter Ecosystem : Introducing declarative adapter SDKs for game engines (Godot, Unreal, Unity) and complex domain formats. Multi-Agent Handoff Protocol : Broadening our integrity-checked task handoff schema so heterogeneous agents can collaborate on long-horizon engineering tasks without passing privileged credentials. title: Agent Operations Center
pitch: An AI agent investigates a production outage — then its tool call suspends mid-execution until a human clicks Approve.
about_excerpt: An AI agent investigates a production outage — then its tool call suspends mid-execution until a human clicks Approve. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Production incidents are difficult because engineers have to investigate metrics, deployments, dependencies, and logs while customers are still affected. I was interested in the idea of letting an AI agent help investigate production incidents without giving it full control. That led me to build Agent Operations Center, where the agent investigates the problem and I stay in control of the actual fix. What it does Agent Operations Center is an incident-response control room where a human engineer and an AI agent work the same production outage together. The page exposes nine WebMCP tools the agent uses to investigate — but it cannot apply the fix itself. The agent investigates: service health against 7-day baselines, deployment timing against the incident, dependency direction for blast radius, and its own log queries. It records findings with cited evidence, so the human audits reasoning rather than a summary. The dashboard reacts live, with nobody touching the mouse. Cards highlight as it inspects them, the log panel narrows to its query, every call appears in an activity feed. The reasoning is genuinely the agent's. Tools return evidence, never conclusions — there is no "find the root cause" function. The scenario includes a decoy: a healthy service deployed more recently than the guilty one, so blaming the newest deploy gets it wrong. Then a human approval gate that is structural, not advisory. propose_remediation suspends mid-execution inside the browser until someone clicks APPROVE. The agent has no path to production — the click is what changes state, bound to the exact service and version proposed. One approval, one execution. The agent then verifies recovery and resolves the incident. How we built it Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind v4, deployed on Vercel. A simulated production backend — services, deployments, dependencies, logs, metrics — lives in an in-memory store exposed to React through useSyncExternalStore, since tool calls originate outside React and there's no render pass to hook into. Nine tools are registered with document.modelContext.registerTool. Five read, two write the agent's reasoning back into the UI, one gates approval, one verifies recovery. The design rule that mattered most: tools return evidence, never conclusions. There is no analyze_incident(). get_service_health returns p95Ms: 8.13× baseline and stops. The diagnosis has to happen in the model, or the demo is just a scripted animation. Challenges we ran into The API isn't documented yet. I guessed wrong three times. There's no unregisterTool — registration is one-way for the document's lifetime, so React StrictMode's double-mount collides with InvalidStateError: Duplicate tool name; a window-level flag is the only guard that survives both StrictMode and Fast Refresh. And executeTool takes a RegisteredTool handle from getTools(), not a name, with arguments as a JSON string — an object throws Failed to parse input arguments. I found that by writing a probe that tried six encodings. The hardest problem wasn't technical. My rollback worked perfectly when I called it by hand, and the agent refused to call it. It would investigate, propose a plan, get approved — then ask "May I execute the rollback?" and end its turn. Assistants won't invoke destructive tools without re-confirming in chat, and no amount of rewording the tool description changed that. So I inverted it. The rollback now runs inside approvePlan — the click handler. The agent proposes; the human's click executes. That turned a limitation into the better architecture: the agent has no path to production at all. Accomplishments that we're proud of The approval gate is structural, not advisory. The agent has no path to production at all — a human's click is the only thing that changes system state, and approval is bound to the exact service and version proposed. The agent's reasoning is actually part of the workflow. The scenario includes a decoy: a healthy service deployed more recently than the guilty one. An agent that blames the newest deploy gets it wrong. Ours rules it out by combining deploy timing, service health, and dependency direction in the demo scenario. The dashboard reacts to the agent, not the mouse. Service cards highlight as it inspects them; the log panel narrows to its query. That works because the WebMCP tools run inside the page and can update the same state the dashboard displays. I documented an undocumented API. executeTool's signature, the absence of unregisterTool, and the JSON-string argument encoding are all recorded in webmcp.d.ts with the console output that proves them. ## What we learned Tool descriptions are prompts, not documentation. Writing "get valid ids from get_system_status" inside an inputSchema field is what produces tool chaining instead of the agent guessing an id and failing. Return errors, don't throw them. { error, knownIds: [...] } lets an agent self-correct on the next call. An exception dead-ends it, and a stalled agent is the fastest way to lose a demo. External state needs useSyncExternalStore. Tool calls originate outside React, so there's no render pass to piggyback on — and mutating state in place means React never re-renders and the dashboard silently goes stale. Design around the model's caution, not against it. Fighting it cost hours. Accommodating it produced a stronger safety guarantee than the one originally designed. ## What's next for Agent Operations Center More scenarios, randomized — config errors, dependency outages, resource leaks — so the agent can't pattern-match its way to the answer. Competing remedies. Restart, feature flag, and rollback all viable, so the agent has to choose the safest one rather than having only one option. Real backends behind the same tools. Swapping the simulated store for Kubernetes wouldn't change a single tool description. Policy tiers. Low-risk actions auto-approved, high-risk requiring two approvers. title: GridNode-Sync
pitch: Agent-Native Positive Energy District (PED) & Grid-Aware AI Infrastructure Operations Hub
about_excerpt:
Agent-Native Positive Energy District (PED) & Grid-Aware AI Infrastructure Operations Hub
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 As global artificial intelligence infrastructure scales rapidly, data centers and edge compute nodes place unprecedented, unpredictable strain on local electrical grids. Simultaneously, urban clusters are shifting toward Positive Energy Districts (PEDs)—neighborhoods designed to produce more renewable energy than they consume annually via local solar photovoltaic (PV) and microgrid arrays. However, a critical operational friction point exists: when rapid atmospheric changes (such as sudden cloud cover) reduce solar generation while AI training or batch inference workloads peak, local transformers face severe overload risks. GridNode-Sync was inspired by the need to bridge decentralized clean energy systems and AI infrastructure using agent-native browser capabilities. 

 What it does 

 GridNode-Sync is an open-source, agent-native web application that serves as a shared operational control hub for human engineers and browser-native AI agents. When opened in a WebMCP-enabled environment (such as ChatGPT's in-app browser or Google Chrome with experimental flags active), the AI agent gains direct, structured access to infrastructure tools. It continuously monitors live bus voltage, transformer saturation indices, and solar generation metrics; evaluates distributed AI workload queues to identify temporally deferrable tasks within a 3-hour thermal window; runs capacity expansion simulations; and executes secure workload shifts or coordinates local Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) buffering to stabilize the district. 

 How we built it 

 We built GridNode-Sync using a modern, lightweight web stack optimized for edge performance and developer transparency: 

 
 Frontend Architecture: Developed using React and Vite for rapid, responsive performance, styled with Tailwind CSS to emulate an enterprise-grade industrial SCADA control room. 
 WebMCP Integration: Leveraged the emerging WebMCP standard by registering programmatic tools via document.modelContext.registerTool , exposing structured schemas ( query_district_grid_telemetry , evaluate_compute_workload_queue , simulate_grid_capacity_expansion , execute_workload_shift ) directly to the browser agent. 
 Governance & Security: Implemented ISO/IEC 42001-aligned deterministic safety guardrails and Ed25519-signed telemetry attestation logic (drawing upon IEEE P7802 / IEEE P3800 frameworks) to ensure all automated workload shifts are cryptographically logged and verifiable. 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Designing an agent-native application for industrial infrastructure required navigating strict safety boundaries. Ensuring that an autonomous browser agent could suggest and execute computational shifts without ever risking critical, latency-critical SCADA inferences or violating substation thermal limits was a primary hurdle. We solved this by implementing hardcoded guardrails and a mandatory human-in-the-loop authorization gate, ensuring the agent operates strictly within safe parametric bounds while leaving ultimate execution control to the human engineer. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 Successfully implementing a working, non-trivial WebMCP tool registration schema that transforms a standard web browser into an agent-ready operational control terminal. 
 Fusing advanced power systems engineering concepts (Positive Energy Districts, solar PV ramp rates, transformer saturation, and 3-hour temporal flexibility windows) with modern artificial intelligence governance and web standards. 
 Designing a software-defined architecture that eliminates expensive proprietary hardware barriers, making microgrid resilience scalable to resource-constrained municipalities and off-grid campuses in the Global South. 
 

 What we learned 

 Building GridNode-Sync highlighted the immense potential of moving away from traditional, rigid user interfaces toward the agent-native web . When web applications expose structured, programmatic tools rather than relying on brittle UI scraping or blind clicking, human-agent collaboration becomes vastly more reliable, scalable, and powerful for complex operational domains like energy and infrastructure management. 

 What's next for GridNode-Sync 

 
 Pilot Deployments: Partnering with regional microgrid operators and campus facilities to test live browser-agent telemetry loops on physical edge nodes. 
 Expanded Mathematical Modeling: Integrating advanced mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) solvers for multi-district stochastic energy optimization. 
 Global Standards Contributions: Continuing to align the project's data structures with emerging IEEE and IEC working groups to help shape the future of decentralized energy trading and AI infrastructure governance.

title: Paqly
pitch: Plan, preview, and pack with AI. Just tell ChatGPT what you're bringing, and through WebMCP it automatically generates a physically optimized 3D packing plan broken down by layers and order to pack.
about_excerpt: Plan, preview, and pack with AI. Just tell ChatGPT what you're bringing, and through WebMCP it automatically generates a physically optimized 3D packing plan broken down by layers and order to pack. Like Comment Story Updates Labled Layers Packed, labeled Empty Closed Duffel bag Backpack Inspiration I always procrastinate packing until the very last minute, then struggle to find what belongs where even if I already have a packing list in mind. After I guess where everything should go and then rearrange my suitcase a dozen times, I finally come to find that it doesn't fit. With AI becoming good at understanding what we need through context and chatlogs, I wanted to create a tool for ChatGPT to express a simple request into something physical and visual that we could actually use. What it does Paqly turns any packing list into a 3D packing plan that you can breakdown into clearly labeled layers. Instead of organizing and planning what to put and where, you can simply tell ChatGPT what you want to bring or even just ask ChatGPT to create a list for you. ChatGPT would then communicate with Paqly directly through WebMCP and create a 3D visual based on the specified suitcase and items. With Paqly, you are able to see where each item should go, which layer it belongs in, the order in which each item should be packed, how much of the suitcase is filled and whether the packing list actually fits. How I built it The core of Paqly is a WebMCP integration that exposes packing functionality directly to AI agents. Rather than requiring an agent to navigate the website like a human and click through forms, Paqly exposes structured tools that allow ChatGPT to send packing information directly to the application. From there, the packing system takes the item dimensions and suitcase constraints, determines an arrangement, groups the result into packing layers, validates the placement, and passes that result into the interactive 3D visualisation. A lot of the work also went into making the output understandable. A mathematically valid arrangement is not very useful if a person cannot tell what they are looking at, so the 3D view includes item labels, separated layers, a re-playable packing order and an interactive suitcase view. Challenges I ran into The hardest part was making the packing plan physically believable rather than just visually impressive. Early versions could technically place objects inside the scene while still producing obviously bad results: items could overlap, float, extend outside the suitcase or leave large amounts of wasted space. This meant I had to treat validation separately from visual rendering and continuously check that the generated arrangement actually made sense. Another challenge was the WebMCP integration itself. I wanted the AI to interact with Paqly through structured WebMCP tools rather than simply using browser automation to click around the interface. Finally, 3D packing is much harder than displaying a normal list. Different objects have different dimensions, orientations and levels of compressibility, while the final result still needs to be simple enough for someone to reproduce with a real suitcase. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm most proud that Paqly goes beyond giving packing advice. You can describe what you are trying to pack like thinking aloud and get back an actual spatial plan showing where everything should go, and the combination of AI, WebMCP and interactive 3D makes the result easier to obtain and follow. I'm also proud of how much the physical packing and visualisation improved throughout development. What started as basic object placement became a layered system with packing order, fit validation and a much clearer 3D representation of the suitcase. What I learned The biggest thing I learned is that giving AI tools is much more interesting than simply putting an AI chatbot inside a website. WebMCP lets the AI interact with the actual functionality of Paqly. The AI handles the vibes, while Paqly handles the specialised packing logic and visualisation. I also learned how quickly a 3D system can look correct while being physically wrong. Building this forced me to think much more carefully about constraints, validation and the difference between generating something that looks good and generating something that actually works. What's next for Paqly The next step is making Paqly understand more about the real world. I want it to support a much larger library of real items, better modelling of soft and compressible objects, different suitcase types and more advanced physical optimisation to better simulate a real packing environment. I want it to be able to mathematically find not just the optimal placement for each item, but the optimal fold, the optimal angle, and other features that make a paq perfect.
