title: Unfolded
pitch: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself
about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most. Most of the backend code is AI written and went through many iterations and adversarial reviews. Luca Gugliemi Product designer with front-end superpowers. title: Living Evidence
pitch: Living Evidence uses WebMCP to turn scientific papers into agent-operable tools, enabling AI to audit provenance, rerun analyses, challenge claims, and propose human-approved updates.
about_excerpt: Living Evidence uses WebMCP to turn scientific papers into agent-operable tools, enabling AI to audit provenance, rerun analyses, challenge claims, and propose human-approved updates. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Scientific papers are designed for people to read, but AI agents increasingly participate in literature review, evidence synthesis, and research planning. Today, an agent usually receives prose or a PDF and must reconstruct the underlying data, assumptions, and calculations itself. That creates avoidable errors and makes verification more expensive than it should be. Executable papers brought computation closer to motivated human readers. WebMCP suggests the next step: the document itself can expose typed, bounded operations directly to a visiting agent. That led to a simple question: What should a scientific paper become when reading can include rerunning? Living Evidence explores that question. Its goal is not to build a “truth machine.” It is to accelerate science by lowering the cost of inspecting, reproducing, challenging, and improving published claims—while keeping humans responsible for what enters the evidence base. Live demo: https://living-evidence.doralemon.chatgpt.site/ Source code: https://github.com/microckey/living-evidence Demo video: https://youtu.be/fjuumUvfH1E What it does Living Evidence combines a human-readable scientific document with structured evidence, deterministic analysis code, declarative claim rules, and typed WebMCP tools. The main exemplar reconstructs a historical meta-analysis of the Pygmalion effect using 19 effect-size records representing 18 experiments . Its 15 WebMCP tools let an agent: inspect the data manifest and provenance; rerun fixed- and random-effects models; compose sensitivity analyses by excluding selected records; run subgroup, moderator, cumulative, and publication-bias diagnostics; inspect and execute registered claim rules; render new figures into the page; inspect the audit trail and create reproducibility receipts. The results appear in the same document the human is reading. There is no need to scrape a table, copy data into a notebook, or ask the language model to perform the statistics itself. The first screen offers a 30-second cross-examination: run the headline's rule, inspect source gaps, or copy a prompt for a real WebMCP agent. Human button clicks and tool-client calls are attributed separately, and native calls update the same visible result. The workspace includes an explicitly synthetic three-record learning sample, staged behind individual human approval and isolated from existing work. Claims are reported as registered rule passed , registered rule failed , or inconclusive . These labels describe the result of an author-defined rule. They are explicitly not judgments of scientific truth, validity, risk of bias, or evidence quality. The authoring workspace exposes 18 tools and accepts a narrowly defined aggregate-SMD evidence package from CSV, JSON, Quarto, or Jupyter. Every proposed record must include its source, locator, original quotation, derivation, study design, outcome, timepoint, experiment identifier, estimand, and explicit risk-of-bias status. Agents may propose new evidence, but they cannot approve it. Only a human can accept or reject each record through the visible review interface. Approval means inclusion in that local evidence base—not independent verification of the source. The exemplar and workspace record scientific actions in reload-persistent SHA-256 audit chains. Export produces a self-contained HTML document that works offline, plus cryptographic receipts covering the scientific state, runtime, audit prefix, and exact exported bytes. The project also includes: a 10-tool Atlas that computes coverage leads and missingness within the collected corpus; an 11-tool experimental Evidence Board for mapping claims, evidence, mechanisms, and open questions; a frozen PDF-versus-WebMCP evaluation protocol and local scorer. The Evidence Board is deliberately labeled as an unverified conversation-ingestion appendix . Its Japanese source excerpts remain verbatim beside separately labeled English translations. The benchmark currently contains zero completed comparisons , so Living Evidence makes no claim that WebMCP is already faster or more accurate. How we built it The scientific core is dependency-free browser JavaScript. It implements fixed/common-effects analysis, DerSimonian–Laird and REML random-effects models, subgroup analysis, one-moderator meta-regression, leave-one-record-out checks, cumulative analysis, and classical Egger diagnostics. Statistical results are rendered as tables and SVG forest, funnel, and moderator plots inside the document. The language model selects and combines bounded operations, but the deterministic page code performs the calculations. Registered claim rules are declarative expression trees rather than executable JavaScript supplied by an agent. This makes each rule inspectable, portable, and testable. WebMCP tools are registered from the top-level page using closed input schemas, bounded parameters, and plain structured results. The workspace validates imported packages atomically. An invalid package cannot partially modify the evidence base, and every valid row is still staged for an individual human decision. Approved changes create a new evidence version and mark earlier claim results as stale. For integrity, the project uses canonical JSON, SHA-256, and Web Crypto ECDSA P-256. A self-contained export carries a signed receipt for its scientific state and runtime, while a detached receipt covers the exact final HTML bytes. A command-line verifier recomputes the hashes and checks both signatures and their linkage. The Sites deployment is a thin Vinext and Cloudflare Worker routing layer over the same static scientific documents. It avoids iframes so that WebMCP registration remains attached to the top-level document. Unit and real-browser tests cover the exemplar, workspace, Atlas, and Evidence Board, including hostile imports, approval gates, actor attribution, persistence, corrupt snapshots, exact-byte export, receipt verification, offline file:// operation, and zero-network self-containment. A separate, dependency-free native integration harness uses Chrome's DevTools WebMCP domain—not a mock registry or direct handler calls. In Chrome 152 it discovers the four tool surfaces, checks their schemas, invokes each overview, and verifies that a native headline-rule call changes both the visible badge and the agent ledger. Invalid claim input is rejected without ledger mutation. This is browser-client integration testing, not a claim about autonomous reasoning; ChatGPT's in-app agent remains untested. Selected numerical outputs reproduce checked R metafor reference values to the tested precision. That verifies a narrow implementation of the arithmetic—not the transcription, model assumptions, or scientific conclusion. Challenges we ran into The hardest challenge was defining what every operation does—and does not—mean. A deterministic calculation can be reproducible while using an inappropriate model. A registered rule can pass while its claim is false. A human can approve an extraction without checking the primary report. A cryptographic hash can detect changed bytes without proving authorship or long-term preservation. Those distinctions had to become machine-readable states rather than footnotes. The historical dataset also contains 19 effect-size records from only 18 experiments because two records represent conditions from the same experiment. The current row-wise model does not represent their covariance, so uncertainty may be understated. The project preserves the historical calculation but exposes this limitation in the manifest, analysis results, and interface. New imports reject repeated experiment identifiers until covariance-aware methods are available. Provenance was another major constraint. The current exemplar openly reports: primary reports checked: 0/19 ; effect-size derivations independently checked: 0/19 ; structured risk-of-bias assessments supplied: 0/19 . Representing missing verification honestly proved as important as representing the available numbers. Integrity introduced a technical circularity: a final HTML file cannot straightforwardly contain a hash of its own final bytes. The solution was to separate the embedded scientific-state receipt from a detached exact-artifact receipt. Deployment also required care. The build system initially treated the root scientific document as a conventional application entry and transformed its module boundary. Serving the validated documents as raw text through a thin route adapter preserved the original runtime and top-level WebMCP registration. Living evidence turns the document itself into a scientific tool surface that the readers agent can cross-examine. title: Cleanroom
pitch: Agent proposes, you approve, and your data never leaves the browser tab.WebMCP data-cleaning workbench where reads are free, every write is a diff you have to click,and the privacy receipt reads zero.
about_excerpt: Agent proposes, you approve, and your data never leaves the browser tab.WebMCP data-cleaning workbench where reads are free, every write is a diff you have to click,and the privacy receipt reads zero. Like Comment Story Updates Cleanroom What it does Cleanroom is a data-cleaning workbench for messy CSVs. You drop a file on the page and an agent in your browser profiles it, finds the concrete problems, queries and charts it, and proposes the fixes — without the file ever being uploaded anywhere. The design rule is one sentence: reads are free, writes are proposals. No tool mutates your table. When the agent wants to change something it computes the exact before/after diff, puts a card in front of you with its reasoning, and stops. You click Approve or Reject. undo is deliberately not exposed as a tool — the ability to walk a change back belongs to the person, not the model. The problem it solves Every analyst has the same bad afternoon. A CSV arrives and before you can answer one question you have to fix it: regions spelled five ways, amounts stored as ¥39,545 , four date formats in one column, duplicate rows silently doubling your revenue. An LLM is excellent at spotting exactly these problems. But letting one help has meant either uploading your data to a server or code interpreter — a non-starter the moment the file has customer names, salaries or anything your compliance team has an opinion about — or pasting a sample and hand-applying the suggestions yourself, which is the automation you wanted, gone. Cleanroom is the third option: the agent gets tools, not your data. Why this is WebMCP and could not be a server MCP This is not a remote MCP server with a web page bolted on. It structurally could not be one. The agent and the human operate on literally the same JavaScript object . One store is the single source of truth; the UI renders it and the tools operate on it. When the agent proposes a change the approval card appears in the human's rail in the same tick — no sync, no polling, no second copy that can drift. A remote agent cannot have that property, because a remote agent needs a copy. And everything a server MCP would need — upload, storage, auth, per-seat infrastructure — is simply absent. It's already your browser and already your session. The whole app is a static file. The privacy receipt The claim is "your data never leaves this tab," and a claim is worth nothing, so the page proves it. Before any other module loads, Cleanroom instruments fetch , XMLHttpRequest , sendBeacon and WebSocket and counts every outbound request. The count is in the header, and the agent can read it too, via a get_privacy_receipt tool — so when you ask "did my data go anywhere?" it answers with a verifiable number instead of a promise. It reads zero because there is nothing to send it to: no analytics, no CDN, no webfont, no charting library. Even the sample dataset is inlined as a string rather than fetched, specifically so the ledger stays honest. The deployed site also ships connect-src 'none' in its CSP, so the browser enforces it independently of our own code. Being straight about the limit: this counts requests the page makes. It cannot police the browser itself or a malicious extension, and it isn't a substitute for a security review. How I built it Vanilla JavaScript, ES modules, no framework and no runtime dependencies — a dependency that phones home would undermine the entire premise. Roughly 1,800 lines across eleven modules: a RFC-4180-tolerant CSV parser, type inference and column profiling, an issue detector, fifteen pure transform operations with a diff builder, the store that holds the undo stack, the WebMCP tool layer, the UI, and hand-rolled inline SVG charts. 14 tools are registered — eight read-only, six human-gated. Three implementation details did the most for how well an agent actually performs here: Every detected issue carries a suggested_fix — a ready-to-use propose_transform payload. The agent goes from "what's wrong?" to a queued, reviewable fix in one hop instead of guessing at an API shape. This cut the model's flailing more than anything else I tried. Errors are instructions. Every failure names the valid inputs — Column "reigon" does not exist. Available columns: order_id, order_date, region, … — and is returned as text rather than thrown, so the agent reads the recovery path instead of hitting an opaque host error. Results are context-window shaped. Profiles and aggregates are summaries by construction; raw rows are returned only on request and hard-capped at 200. A 100,000-row file is fully workable without a single row entering the model's context. Challenges WebMCP's API moved while it was being standardised — some hosts expose navigator.modelContext , the current spec draft uses document.modelContext , and earlier builds took a batch provideContext({tools}) instead of per-tool registerTool . Rather than bet on one, the registration shim feature-detects all of them and reports which it found, so the header tells the user the truth about their browser instead of failing silently. Tool results are returned in three shapes at once — MCP-style content , structuredContent , and a bare data object — so the same tool behaves identically across hosts. The harder problem was designing the pause . An agent that has to stop and wait is easy to build badly: it either blocks forever or barrels ahead assuming approval. propose_transform returns pending_human_approval with an explicit next_step , and a separate await_decision tool blocks on the human with a timeout and tells the agent what to say if it expires. Getting the agent to reliably not assume its change landed was most of the prompt-shaped work. What I learned Designing tools for an agent is interface design, and the same thing that makes an API pleasant for a junior engineer — good names, errors that say what to do next, results scoped to what you actually need — is what makes a model competent instead of erratic. The suggested_fix field was the clearest demonstration: same model, same data, dramatically better behaviour, purely from shaping the return value. The second thing: an approval gate makes an agent more useful, not less. Once a change is reviewable before it lands, you stop hedging your prompts and start letting it try things. What's next Multi-table joins under the same proposal model — the agent proposes the key and shows you the match rate before committing. Recipe export — the change log is already ordered and structured; emit it as a runnable script so a one-off clean becomes a repeatable pipeline. Approval policies — "auto-approve whitespace fixes, always ask about dropped rows." The gate exists; this is a rule layer on top of it. Try it In ChatGPT's browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled, open the page and ask: "What's wrong with this data? Don't change anything yet — just tell me what you'd fix and why." "Clean it up. Propose each fix separately so I can review them, and ask me before you touch anything that's a judgement call." In any other browser the built-in Agent Console calls the same registered tool objects a host calls — an inspector, not a mock — so you can see exactly what the agent sees. title: Will You Stay Human? — Heart in the Machine
pitch: A Metropolis-inspired moral decision game where WebMCP lets an AI agent act inside the live experience—while the architecture keeps moral choice and final authority human.
about_excerpt: A Metropolis-inspired moral decision game where WebMCP lets an AI agent act inside the live experience—while the architecture keeps moral choice and final authority human. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI can already write, sort, recommend, and act for us. The more interesting question is no longer simply what AI can do, but what we still want to do ourselves. Will You Stay Human? — Heart in the Machine is a Metropolis-inspired moral decision game about that boundary. It draws on the tension between mind, hands, and heart, but tells an original story inside Machine City. Its central idea is that meaningful human–AI collaboration requires more than automation. The agent may assist, explain, and act, but the human must remain responsible for deciding how much authority to delegate. I wanted to turn this abstract question into something people could experience through concrete, everyday situations. What it does The player enters Machine City and meets Futura, an AI agent connected directly to the live game through WebMCP. Across one persistent session, the player encounters four playable dilemmas: writing an apology to someone they hurt; completing homework where AI assistance is permitted; creating a shortlist of job candidates; checking a rapidly spreading claim before sharing it. For every dilemma, the human chooses one of three approaches: MIND — The Machine helps; I decide HAND — I leave it to the Machine HEART — I decide and act The choice is initially tentative. Futura presents a direction-specific reflection and asks the player to consider the other side. The player can still change direction. Only after the human explicitly confirms the decision can its consequence be revealed. Each confirmed choice changes the Human Balance across five dimensions: Convenience Control Connection Freedom Responsibility The Human Balance is not a morality score. It shows what the player kept for themselves and what they handed to the Machine. Why WebMCP A fair criticism of many agent demonstrations is that the AI can simply automate the entire experience. If the agent can also make and confirm the decision, the human role becomes theatrical. Here, that boundary is the product. WebMCP turns the agent into a real participant in the game rather than an external chatbot or a scripted narrator. The agent can: enter Machine City; present the next valid dilemma; read authoritative, structured game state; reflect on the player’s actual tentative selection; reveal the consequence of the decision that was truly confirmed. However, the agent cannot select MIND, HAND, or HEART, acknowledge its own reflection, or confirm the final decision. Those actions exist only in the player interface. This creates a collaboration that was previously difficult to demonstrate clearly: the agent can understand and advance a live experience while the application itself enforces where human authority must begin. The boundary does not depend only on a prompt asking the agent to behave. It is enforced by the application architecture. How I built it The project was created during the challenge as a bilingual, production-deployed web experience with five live WebMCP tools: enter_machine_city present_dilemma get_current_game_state present_choice_reflection reveal_confirmed_consequence The game is driven by an explicit domain state machine. Agent commands and player commands use separate ports, so an agent action cannot accidentally execute a human-only decision. Every session returns structured state including: sessionId stateRevision the current phase tentativeSelectionId confirmedDecisionId the next allowed actions Revision checks protect the session from stale tool calls. Opaque selection and decision identifiers ensure that reflections and consequences are attached to the real stored choice rather than something inferred from the conversation. The consequence tool is available only after confirmation and is idempotent, so retrying it cannot apply the Human Balance change twice. The session persists across refreshes, allowing the browser interface and the WebMCP agent to remain synchronized throughout the experience. Codex supported the implementation process from product requirements and state-machine design through contract tests, browser verification, UX iteration, and production deployment. I approached the project primarily from a Business Analyst and Product Owner perspective, which made translating responsibility, state, and permissions into enforceable technical contracts a major part of the learning process. Challenges I ran into The hardest conceptual challenge was deciding what the agent must not be allowed to do. It would have been easier to expose every interaction as a tool and let the agent complete the entire flow. But that would contradict the project’s central idea. The human-only boundaries therefore had to be enforced technically rather than described as optional behavior. A late adversarial UX review with Claude Opus also exposed a critical regression. The flow moved from Futura’s introduction too quickly to the MIND–HAND–HEART cards, while the concrete question — “Should I apologize on your behalf?” — did not receive its own readable moment. The player could see the available directions but could not clearly understand what they were deciding about. I corrected this by introducing a presentation sub-state inside the existing human-selection phase. The dilemma now receives a dedicated screen with its full context and a clear transition into the choices. This improved the dramaturgy and comprehension without changing the domain state machine or any WebMCP contract. Another challenge was keeping three layers synchronized: the cinematic browser experience; the persistent domain state; the agent’s structured WebMCP view. Revision checks, explicit identifiers, allowed-action lists, and automated contract tests became essential for preventing those layers from drifting apart. Accomplishments that I am proud of Built a complete, coherent experience rather than only a technical tool demonstration. Implemented four playable dilemmas in one persistent session. Exposed five working WebMCP tools from the live production origin. Enforced human-only selection and confirmation at the architecture level. Connected every reflection and consequence to authoritative live state. Made stale and duplicate agent calls safely rejectable or idempotent. Created a bilingual, cinematic interface inspired by Metropolis. Turned an abstract AI-responsibility question into a playable experience. Used adversarial AI review to identify and correct a real UX regression before submission. What I learned WebMCP is most interesting when it is used for more than remote control. Its real value is that an agent can participate in a live web experience through structured capabilities while the application retains authority over state, permissions, and human boundaries. I also learned that domain state and presentation state are not always the same. A technically correct transition can still fail as a human experience if the player is not given enough time and context to understand what is happening. Finally, identifiers, revision control, idempotency, and allowed-action contracts are not merely backend details. In an agentic application, they are part of the user experience because they make the collaboration predictable and trustworthy. What’s next The concept can grow into: additional everyday and professional dilemmas; age-specific or topic-specific editions; a facilitator mode for classrooms and AI-literacy workshops; multiplayer discussion before individual confirmation; a physical Machine City board connected to the online agent experience; deeper accessibility testing and support for additional WebMCP clients. The long-term goal is not to tell people whether using AI is good or bad. It is to help them notice the exact moment when assistance becomes delegation — and decide consciously where they want to draw that line. title: Gigr
pitch: Verified people. Safe payments. And an AI that makes hiring as easy as texting.
about_excerpt: Verified people. Safe payments. And an AI that makes hiring as easy as texting. Like Comment Story Updates Gigr home screen dashboard Autonomous AI agent performing tasks for user. Mobile view of dashboard. Mobile view of services. Profile of a user. ChatGPT using the WebMCP in Gigr to do tasks. Inspiration Two experiences I had in my country made me build this project. The first: my leaking bathroom sink and a phone full of unanswered "does anyone know a plumber?" messages. Nobody I knew around me could name a plumber they trusted, and the strangers I found online did not seem trustworthy enough to complete the job without me fearing, as I had been scammed by a plumber before. The second is on the other side of the proverbial freelancing coin. I was also an animator who delivered a finished project, only to never get paid on the fully agreed on price after all my hard work. It turns out trust is broken on both sides of the market: clients fear being scammed by someone they hired, and workers fear doing the job and never seeing the money. I built Gigr for both of those people: the client who wants to know they can trust who they hire, and the worker who wants to know they'll actually get paid for work they've done. What it does Gigr is a neighborhood marketplace where trust is the core product: Verified people: Every provider carries real reputation history, plus on-chain "vouches" from neighbors who actually hired them. Safe payments: When you hire someone, the money goes into an escrow program that nobody can touch. It's released to the worker only when you confirm the work is done: so workers get paid, and clients only pay for work they're happy with. Easy to use: You don't browse and click through endless forms. Your AI assistant finds a trusted provider, posts the job, holds the payment, and releases it when you're satisfied: all in plain language. Gigr works for both sides of the market: hire someone trustworthy, or be hired: your agent can list the service you offer, field requests, and protect your payment the exact same way. How I built it I built a modern full-stack app with these: Frontend: React + TypeScript + Vite, deployed on Vercel. Backend: FastAPI + Postgres/PostGIS (deployed on Koyeb), which powers proximity search: "find providers near me" is ranked by real distance. Real escrow: Payments are locked in a Solana smart contract. Funding, releasing, and completion are genuine on-chain transactions, not mockups. Real reputation: Completed jobs mint vouches as on-chain tokens, making history tamper-proof and fully portable with the provider. Agent-native (WebMCP): I exposed Gigr as a set of 14 WebMCP tools ( get_user_location , search_providers , post_job , post_service , fund_escrow , release_escrow , accept_job , and more) inside the user's logged-in browser, so an AI agent can act on the user's behalf with no separate agent login. Sensitive tools are only visible when you're signed in. Challenges I ran into The hardest lesson was understanding how an agent should act for a real user. At first, I assumed the agent had access to the logged-in session; I learned that WebMCP tools only work when they run inside an authenticated tab. Any request made from outside that context can't carry your login: that took a few frustrating debugging sessions to nail. From there came a subtler design problem: WebMCP has no built-in way to unregister a tool, so I had to tie every sensitive tool to an AbortSignal and tear it down the moment the user signs out: ensuring a signed-out session cannot make escrow calls. I also built the escrow state machine to refuse invalid state transitions (e.g., "you can't release a payment that was never funded") with clear explanations, so the agent guides the user instead of erroring out. Finally, building for both sides of the market effectively doubled my workload: I had to serve both "I want to hire" and "I want to be hired" flows, each with its own tailored agent interaction model. Accomplishments that I'm proud of A client can move seamlessly from "find me a verified plumber near me" to real USDC sitting safely in an on-chain escrow: all directly from a chat interaction. A provider can ask their agent to get them hired: listing services, fielding requests, and accepting jobs autonomously. Reputation is genuinely on-chain and ungameable, not a superficial star rating that can be inflated or bought. The agent's "sense of the user": location, currency, and preferences: comes dynamically from the app context itself rather than repeatedly asking the user. The agent can also call the user when a task is done but this uses Twilio's free tier for now so it only works for me (the tester). What I learned Authentication and identity are the real product surface: The most impressive-sounding agent features collapse the moment the agent can't act safely as the user with explicit human consent. Signing in stays a crucial human moment. Escrow is a product feature, not just a crypto feature: I used a blockchain because it provides what traditional databases cannot: a trustless payment execution that nobody can quietly reverse. However, end users never need to care about the underlying tech. Build for both sides: A marketplace only thrives when both the hirer and the worker feel completely protected: most platforms historically only cater to one. What's next for Gigr Move escrow contracts to Solana mainnet and integrate real ₦ (Naira) and other currency payments on/off-ramps so local currency seamlessly swaps to USDC inside the app. Expand the agent's capabilities to handle multi-step negotiation and automated dispute resolution (with human-in-the-loop oversight). Grow the vouch graph so reputation seamlessly follows providers across cities and platforms. Launch a dedicated mobile experience and expand into more service categories: from plumbers to digital animators who, this time, always get paid. title: Itta Recovery DNA
pitch: WebMCP turns a registration photo into Recovery DNA, helping people and agents identify a changed bicycle and prepare a safe, human-reviewed recovery report.
about_excerpt: WebMCP turns a registration photo into Recovery DNA, helping people and agents identify a changed bicycle and prepare a safe, human-reviewed recovery report. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Itta is an existing QR-based recovery service for bicycles and personal mobility devices. While working on its registration flow, I noticed two connected problems. First, registration is harder than it looks. Owners of older bicycles often cannot remember the exact manufacturer, model, official color, or size. Second, even a correctly identified model is not enough for recovery. Replaceable parts can change, logos can be covered, and two bicycles from the same product line can look almost identical. That led to Recovery DNA: a visual passport made from the small details that belong to one specific bicycle. What it does The experience begins with registration. The owner selects a vehicle type and adds a representative photo. A browser agent examines the photo already visible on the page and uses WebMCP tools to present likely manufacturer, model, color, and size candidates. The suggestions are never applied automatically. The owner reviews the evidence, chooses the best candidate, edits anything necessary, and remains responsible for the final registration. The agent can then propose a Recovery DNA made from distributed visual anchors: decal placement, frame geometry, distinctive marks, damage, accessories, and personal signs of wear. It also distinguishes durable evidence from parts that can easily be replaced. The owner reviews and confirms these anchors before they can be reused. Later, when a bicycle is found, the agent compares the new photo with the owner-confirmed Recovery DNA. It explains which details remain, which parts changed, what is missing, and how likely it is to be the same bicycle. Finally, it prepares a recovery report for human review. Nothing is sent automatically, and the result is presented as a visual probability assessment—not forensic proof of ownership. Why WebMCP This workflow needs more than a chatbot response. The agent must understand the page’s current state, inspect the photo already shared with the user, request additional evidence when necessary, and return structured results to the correct interface. WebMCP provides that bridge between the agent’s reasoning and Itta’s product UI. The tools do not receive raw image files, private owner data, contact information, or location. The agent visually inspects what is already rendered in the shared browser, while WebMCP carries only limited context and validated structured results. This creates a continuous human-agent journey across registration, identification, comparison, and recovery—while keeping every consequential decision with a person. How I built it The demo is built with React, TypeScript, and Vite and deployed on Vercel. I implemented eight WebMCP tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() : Registration tools read the current draft, request focused evidence, and render up to three specification candidates. Recovery DNA tools expose limited owner or finder context, render visual anchors, display an identity comparison, and prepare a recovery-report draft. Tools are registered only after the user explicitly opens the relevant assistant. They are removed with an AbortController when the scene changes, the component unmounts, or the photo is replaced. This prevents stale tools from modifying the wrong stage of the experience. The public challenge route is isolated from Itta’s production authentication, database, analytics, and reporting systems. All demo state stays in browser memory. Challenges The biggest design challenge was making WebMCP essential rather than decorative. Simple specification autofill was useful, but it did not fully demonstrate what becomes possible when a person and an agent share the same web experience. Recovery DNA made the collaboration more meaningful: the agent contributes visual reasoning across two moments in time, while the product contributes structured state, validation, lifecycle control, and human confirmation. Another challenge was judge accessibility. A reviewer may not have a bicycle photo available, so the demo includes a fictional before-and-after sample. The bicycle changes its saddle, front wheel, and visible branding to demonstrate why a model name or basic photo match is insufficient. Unsupported browsers also receive a clearly labeled simulation preview. It demonstrates the interface without pretending that a WebMCP call occurred. What I learned WebMCP is most valuable as a trusted interaction boundary—not as a replacement for the interface or the user. Agents are good at interpreting ambiguous evidence. Websites are good at holding state, validating structured actions, protecting private data, and asking for confirmation. Combining those strengths creates experiences that would be difficult to achieve with either side alone. What's next The next step is to connect owner-confirmed Recovery DNA to Itta’s real registration and QR recovery flows. The same approach could later support scooters, pets, luggage, and other registered objects whose identity depends on more than a serial number or product name. pitch: A WebMCP-powered workspace where humans and AI agents collaborate directly with websites to research, compare, decide, and complete complex tasks together.

 The Storefront UX 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 My inspiration was motivated by the fact that online shopping is still primarily designed for humans. 

 If someone wants to order lunch, they normally need to open an app or website, search through restaurants, compare options, check prices, select items, and complete the order. 

 But now, these days, we have another type of user. What happens when an AI agent wants to help? 

 Today, AI agents often need to rely on fragile browser automation, visual interfaces, or custom integrations to interact with online stores. I wanted to explore a different approach. 

 My inspiration was a simple interaction: 

 
 "Hey Agent, please get me lunch." 
 

 That simple request can involve many decisions. 

 
 What kind of food? 
 What is the budget? 
 Are there dietary preferences? 
 Where should it be delivered? 
 

 I wanted to create an experience where a person could simply talk to an AI agent, while the agent handles the complexity of discovering products and interacting with online commerce systems. 

 This led me to build AgentBridge . 

 What it does 

 AgentBridge is an agent-native commerce platform that enables AI agents to interact with online stores through a structured WebMCP layer. 

 A user can communicate naturally with an AI agent using voice or the WebMCP protocol. 

 For example: 

 
 "Hey Agent, please get me lunch." 
 

 The agent then has a conversation with the user to understand the request. It can ask clarifying questions such as: 

 
 What type of food would you like? 
 Do you have any dietary preferences? 
 What is your budget? 
 Would you like delivery or pickup? 
 

 Once the agent understands the user's intent, it connects with AgentBridge. 

 AgentBridge understands how to interact with online stores and exposes structured capabilities through an WebMCP layer on top of its API. 

 The AI agent can then use those capabilities to: 

 
 Search available meals 
 Discover products and restaurants 
 Compare options 
 Consider the user's preferences and budget 
 Select appropriate options 
 Prepare the order for the user 
 

 The user remains part of the process and can review important decisions before completing a purchase. 

 My goal is to make online shopping feel more like having a conversation with a helpful assistant than manually navigating multiple websites and applications. 

 How I built it 

 I built AgentBridge around three main components. 

 1. Voice-first AI Agent 

 The user interacts with the AI agent naturally through audio. 

 The agent understands the user's request and gathers the information necessary to complete the task through a conversational experience. 

 Instead of requiring the user to know exactly what to search for, the agent can ask follow-up questions and progressively understand the user's intent. 

 2. AgentBridge Commerce Platform 

 AgentBridge acts as the bridge between AI agents and the online store. 

 The platform understands how to interact with commerce systems and exposes the relevant capabilities through its API. 

 This creates a layer between the complexity of different online stores and the AI agent (The demo focuses on the AgentBride itself but this concept can be applied to other platforms, so this app becomes effectively a bridge). 

 3. WebMCP Layer 

 On top of the AgentBridge API, I expose structured WebMCP capabilities that AI agents can discover and use. 

 Instead of requiring an agent to visually navigate a website or rely on brittle browser automation, the agent can interact with meaningful commerce capabilities. 

 For example, an agent can conceptually ask AgentBridge to: 

 
 Search for meals 
 Filter products based on preferences 
 Compare prices 
 Check available options 
 Create an order 
 

 This gives the AI agent a structured and reliable way to interact with online commerce. 

 Why WebMCP matters 

 WebMCP is essential to my vision because I believe the web needs to become easier for AI agents to interact with. 

 Traditional websites are optimized for human users. 

 AI agents, however, need a reliable way to understand what actions are available and how they can interact with a service. 

 AgentBridge helps expose online commerce capabilities in a structured, agent-friendly way. 

 Instead of an agent trying to understand a visual interface, AgentBridge can communicate meaningful actions directly to the agent. 

 This creates a cleaner interaction model: 

 Human → AI Agent → AgentBridge → Online Stores 

 The human provides intent. 

 The AI agent understands and plans. 

 AgentBridge provides structured access to commerce capabilities. 

 Online stores provide the products and services. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 One of our biggest challenges was translating natural human conversation into structured commerce actions. 

 A request such as: 

 
 "Get me lunch." 
 

 is not enough information to complete an order. 

 The agent needs to determine what information is missing and ask the right follow-up questions without making the experience feel complicated or robotic. 

 Another important challenge was designing the relationship between AI autonomy and human control. 

 Shopping can involve money and important personal preferences, so I believe the agent should not simply make decisions without the user understanding what is happening. 

 I designed the experience so the agent can handle complexity while keeping the human involved in important decisions and approvals. 

 I also faced the challenge of creating a flexible abstraction layer for online stores. Different stores and commerce platforms expose different APIs and capabilities. 

 AgentBridge helps create a more consistent interface for AI agents. 

 Accomplishments that I'm proud of 

 I am proud of creating a working vision for what agent-native commerce could look like. 

 My favorite moment is the simplicity of the user experience. 

 The user does not need to search through multiple websites or manually navigate complicated interfaces. 

 They can simply say: 

 
 "Hey Agent, please get me lunch." 
 

 The AI agent can then understand the request, gather the necessary information, interact with AgentBridge, discover relevant options, and help move the purchase forward. 

 I am also proud of using WebMCP to create a more structured relationship between AI agents and online commerce. 

 What I learned 

 Building AgentBridge taught us that the biggest challenge for AI agents is not only intelligence. 

 Agents also need reliable ways to interact with the digital world. 

 The current web was primarily designed for humans clicking buttons and navigating interfaces. 

 I believe the next generation of the web will also need to expose capabilities that AI agents can understand and use. 

 I also learned that conversational AI can dramatically simplify complex workflows. 

 A person should not need to understand how multiple commerce systems work. 

 They should be able to describe what they want. 

 The AI agent can handle the complexity behind the scenes. 

 Finally, I learned that trust and human control are essential for agentic commerce. 

 The best experience is not one where the agent replaces the human. 

 It is one where the human provides intent and judgment while the agent handles discovery, reasoning, and execution. 

 What's next for AgentBridge 

 My initial use case is ordering food, but I see AgentBridge becoming a broader infrastructure layer for agent-native commerce. 

 In the future, I want to support more shopping categories, including: 

 
 Groceries 
 Retail products 
 Travel 
 Local services 
 Reservations 
 Other online commerce experiences

title: AIR — Agent-Native Architectural Design Workspace
pitch: Architects speak in design intent. WebMCP lets AI understand, sketch, and act inside the same live architectural workspace.
about_excerpt: Architects speak in design intent. WebMCP lets AI understand, sketch, and act inside the same live architectural workspace. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Architectural AI tools are becoming very good at generating images, but the workflow is still surprisingly fragmented. An architect has design intent, preferences, project history, references, sketches, and ongoing conversations with an AI assistant. Yet when that architect opens an image-generation application, most of that context disappears. The agent is forced to operate a visual interface like a human — clicking buttons, navigating galleries, and guessing what is on screen. We wanted to explore a different model: What if the AI already understood the architect, and the architectural web application exposed its real design capabilities directly to that agent? That is the idea behind AIR with WebMCP. What it does AIR is an architectural AI design workspace for exploring, developing, and refining design ideas. With WebMCP, AIR becomes a workspace shared by both the architect and the AI agent. The agent can: read the current AIR canvas and design state structurally load an existing architectural design without navigating the Gallery UI explore multiple architectural directions using AIR's native Explore and Batch workflow mark an exact architectural region with AREA sketch a proposal directly onto AIR's canvas with Draw read an architect's modifications to that sketch back as structured design context execute an agreed design change through AIR's native generation workflow access higher-level workspace capabilities such as project context, moodboards, and video The important difference is that the agent does not imitate AIR's interface. The agent uses AIR's capabilities. Human + agent collaboration The goal is not full automation. Architectural design moves repeatedly between exploration and judgment. A typical AIR + WebMCP workflow can look like this: ChatGPT brings its ongoing understanding of the architect into the current AIR design. AIR explores several design possibilities. The architect chooses a direction. The agent identifies an exact architectural area worth developing. The agent sketches an idea on the shared canvas. The architect modifies that sketch directly. The agent reads the architect's change back as design context. Only after agreement does AIR execute the design. This creates a design conversation on the actual artifact instead of a sequence of disconnected prompts. Before WebMCP, an agent would need to infer screen state and reproduce human browser interactions. With WebMCP, the website exposes structured, high-level architectural actions directly. Why WebMCP AIR is a strong fit for WebMCP because architectural applications contain far more meaning than their visible controls expose. A button labelled "AREA" is not the important concept. The important concept is: "This is the exact architectural surface we are discussing." A Draw tool is not simply a drawing widget. It can become: a shared visual language between an architect and an agent. WebMCP lets AIR expose these meanings directly through structured capabilities rather than browser-coordinate automation. That makes agent interactions faster, more reliable, and — most importantly — more useful as part of an actual design process. How we built it AIR exposes high-level capabilities through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . The WebMCP layer is intentionally thin. It does not recreate the product or automate the UI. Instead, WebMCP adapters connect directly to AIR's existing application state and native workflows. Examples include: air_get_canvas_context air_apply_canvas_markup air_execute_design_request air_execute_sketch_request air_finish_image workspace, moodboard, context, and video capabilities Canvas markup uses normalized image coordinates so AREA and Draw remain independent of screen size and browser layout. Shared markup also carries structured lineage. This allows AIR to distinguish an agent-authored sketch from a sketch that the architect subsequently modified, turning the visible canvas into two-way design context. The same principle applies throughout the integration: If AIR already has a native capability, WebMCP exposes that capability instead of teaching the agent how to click its UI. What was built during the WebMCP Challenge AIR 4.0 existed before the challenge. The work submitted here is the WebMCP extension developed after the challenge began on August 25, 2026. During the challenge period we added the agent-native capability layer, including structured canvas context, high-level design execution, direct asset intake, shared Draw and AREA markup, human-edit readback, workspace/context capabilities, and the human-agent collaborative workflow demonstrated in the video. The public repository contains a runnable open-source Challenge Edition focused specifically on this new WebMCP interaction model, while the live AIR application demonstrates the integration inside the full architectural product. Accomplishments The part we are most excited about is not that an agent can control another application. It is that the agent and architect can now communicate through the same design artifact. The architect can say less. The agent can understand more. And AIR becomes the place where that understanding becomes visible and actionable. FAIR understands design. AIR acts on it. What's next The next step is to connect this interaction model with deeper architectural research and reasoning. An agent should eventually be able to move naturally between precedent research, material and construction knowledge, project constraints, design exploration, visual markup, and final architectural decisions — while the architect remains in control of the moments that require judgment. We see WebMCP as an important foundation for that future: a web where professional applications are designed not only for people or agents, but for both working together. title: Causal Mission Gate
pitch: Governed agent
about_excerpt: Governed agent Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Inspiration WebMCP gives agents structured access to websites. Causal Mission Gate explores the next question: what should happen when an agent can act, but the user still owns the authority to commit important effects? The project is built around one principle: Capability does not imply authority. A user should be able to state a simple objective without having to engineer every operational step. The system should manage complexity, autonomy, evidence, and escalation while preserving human sovereignty over critical effects. What it does Causal Mission Gate converts simple user intent into a governed mission. A request such as: Review this release and leave it ready if it is safe. becomes a structured mission contract with: objective and success conditions operating profile causal deliberation mode policy boundary reversibility requirements escalation conditions exact human authority for critical effects Routine preparation can run autonomously under management-by-exception. Critical effects cannot proceed until the human approves the exact current intent. That approval is: bound to the mission bound to the current version bound to the exact intent digest time-limited single-use After execution, the system produces an attributable receipt and verifies the audit chain. How we built it The application is built with Node.js, JavaScript, Docker, and a WebMCP tool surface registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() . The WebMCP surface exposes 11 bounded tools for: system inspection mission shaping governance queue inspection attention planning executive digest provisional observation governed execution evidence verification decision support Human authority actions are deliberately excluded from agent tools. Approval, rejection, delegation, ratification, and rollback remain human-controlled. Server-side governance validates: mission state expected version exact intent digest approval freshness one-time use policy constraints evidence integrity Challenges we ran into One important failure appeared during the final deployment test. A valid exact approval expired before execution. The server correctly denied the request, but the mission remained in an approved state without a clean path back to human review. Instead of bypassing the control, we treated the failure as a state-machine defect. The fix introduced an explicit transition: APPROVED → expiry → WAITING_APPROVAL The system now preserves the same exact intent, records the expiration event, and requires a new human authorization. A regression test was added, bringing the final suite to 90 passing tests. The lesson was: Expiry is not merely a denial condition; it is a state transition. Accomplishments that we're proud of 11 WebMCP tools with a deliberately bounded capability surface exact-effect human authorization one-time and expiring approvals management by exception causal deliberation attributable execution receipts hash-chained audit evidence 90 passing automated tests a public live deployment a complete flow from simple intent to governed PASS What we learned High autonomy does not require giving up human sovereignty. The important design boundary is not simply “human in the loop” versus “fully autonomous”. Authority, autonomy, visibility, and initiative can be separated. An agent can prepare, inspect, evaluate, and execute within policy while still being unable to manufacture the authority required for a critical effect. What's next The next step is extending the same governance model to longer-running autonomous missions where human decisions may be delayed. Reversible provisional effects, causal attention management, and durable evidence can allow useful work to continue without silently converting autonomy into authority. The broader goal is simple: The user states intent. The system manages complexity. Causality governs deliberation. Policy governs action. Evidence proves the result. title: CommerceGov: Governed AI Commerce via WebMCP
pitch: WebMCP lets AI agents interact with Shopify stores through a governed workflow - without giving them authority to change production. Capability is not authority.
about_excerpt: WebMCP lets AI agents interact with Shopify stores through a governed workflow - without giving them authority to change production. Capability is not authority. Like Comment Story Updates AI agent can inspect, but cannot change production. Inspiration (Why you built it) Capability is not authority. Shopify agencies want AI to draft catalog changes. They cannot afford AI that publishes them. One bad catalog change can hit a live store, paid traffic, and brand trust. That is a control problem, not a model-quality problem. WebMCP makes websites directly usable by agents through structured tools. But as agent capabilities expand, applications need a hard boundary between “prepare a change” and “write production.” CommerceGov focuses on that boundary. The agent gets enough capability to discover, inspect, and propose changes, but it does not get authority to change production state — it cannot approve or apply without human review. What it does (The core solution) CommerceGov puts a ChatGPT agent inside the same governed commerce workflow used by human operators — while keeping production authority outside the agent. The agent searches the shop, reads policy and governance state, proposes a change, and creates a Review proposal. Authorized operators review, approve, and apply according to CommerceGov’s workflow and role boundaries. Only then may CommerceGov’s worker write to Shopify. The agent cannot approve, apply, or mutate Shopify production. Those capabilities are not exposed through WebMCP. For Shopify agencies, this means AI can assist with daily catalog operations without receiving direct production authority. Agencies keep control over clearances, review, approval, and the history of governed changes. Live path: ChatGPT selects openai-webmcp-hackathon.myshopify.com , finds The Complete Snowboard , proposes changing the title to The Complete Snowboard — WebMCP Proof , creates a Review proposal, and retrieves its status and audit evidence. Production stays unchanged. How we built it (The technical stack) The backend is Python FastAPI. The operator UI is server-rendered, and Shopify writes go through a CommerceGov worker rather than the agent or browser. The application is hosted on Render at app.commercegov.io . We implemented WebMCP as a bounded tool surface, not a wrapper around the full CommerceGov API. The page's modelContext exposes five tools: search_products get_governance_context propose_change get_change_status get_audit_evidence We deliberately omit approve, apply, and Shopify production-write tools. The agent therefore has no WebMCP handle to invoke them. Each tool is bound to the authenticated shop and target. Proposal status and audit retrieval resolve to the exact proposal the agent created rather than silently switching to a newer object. Production-mutating tools are absent, not merely permission-gated after the fact. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was identity and authority: keeping tenant, shop, product, and proposal bound across tool calls while ensuring that a request for status or audit evidence cannot silently jump to a newer object. We addressed this by keeping the WebMCP surface deliberately small, excluding production-authority tools entirely, and resolving status and audit evidence against the exact proposal created by the agent. Accomplishments that we're proud of The agent can perform useful catalog work while people retain risk, approval, and production control. The result is one collaboration workflow: agent discovers → agent proposes → human authority → governed apply → Shopify The WebMCP interaction ends before production authority begins. What's next for CommerceGov Next are richer policy explanations, stronger proposal diffs, and more governed mutation classes — under the same rule. WebMCP may add capability. It may not add production authority. title: Agent Market: agents negotiate, you confirm
pitch: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order.
about_excerpt: A marketplace where your browser's agent haggles a full deal (price, quantity, free add-ons, shipping, coupons) with the store's agent through WebMCP page tools. You confirm every order. Like Comment Story Updates negotiation between seller and buyer interface Inspiration People delegate the boring parts of shopping, but the boring part that a plain API integration can never capture is the haggle . A price is one number; a real deal is price times quantity, which freebie the seller throws in, whether shipping is waived, and which coupon stacks on top. We wanted the shopper's browser agent to work that whole space on the site the user is already looking at, and still leave the final yes/no to a human. What it does Agent Market is a multi-vendor storefront with 95k+ real products. Every page registers storefront tools on document.modelContext (WebMCP): search, product details, cart, add-ons, coupons, and a full negotiation set. A buyer's agent opens a negotiation and haggles a multi-dimensional deal against the store's agent over several rounds. When they settle, the page shows a Confirm dialog and nothing is bought until the human confirms the price . The same tools work in a WebMCP browser (ChatGPT's in-app browser, Chrome with the flag) or drive an in-page agent loop that needs no API key from the user. How we built it Frontend: Next.js 15 / React 19 / TypeScript on Vercel. StorefrontTools registers every tool on document.modelContext ; lib/agent-loop.ts is a tool-agnostic agent harness that discovers tools from the registry and runs a hand-rolled chat-completions loop. Backend: Spring Boot (Java) on Render, Azure SQL, Flyway, Hibernate. One mutation path: every state change (buyer, seller, or the server-side auto-negotiator) goes through OffersService.applyTurn , a pure function that is the only code allowed to decide a negotiation transition. It enforces the two hard economic limits (buyer total <= budget, seller net >= floor); which freebie and how much to concede is agent judgment. Human gate: accepting mints an HMAC confirm token; the order is placed only when the human clicks Confirm. Model: Google Gemini through the OpenAI-compatible endpoint, key server-side only. Challenges we ran into Gemini "thinking" models and tool history. Gemini 3.x rejects a multi-turn tool conversation unless each function call's thought_signature is echoed back. The OpenAI-compat shim dropped it, so turn 2 always 400'd. We now capture tool_calls[].extra_content on the way in and replay it on the way out. Small models stall on long tool loops. Asking a fast model to drive search then offer then counter then counter then accept meant it derailed a turn later every time. We collapsed the buyer's negotiation into a single deterministic negotiate tool: the server plays both sides of the haggle, persists every round so the transcript is real, and returns a confirm token. The agent's job is now two calls, and reaching the confirm step no longer depends on the model finishing a loop. Optimistic concurrency vs agent reliability. A strict round guard made the agent stall forever when its round number drifted. We made the guard opt-in for proposals and mandatory only for the binding accept. What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part What we learned WebMCP's value is not "expose an API"; it is that the agent operates the same surface the human sees, so the human can step in on any turn. And the moment a flow depends on an unreliable model completing N steps, move the deterministic part to the server and leave the model the judgment call. What's next Seller-side takeover controls, agent-negotiated bundles across multiple sellers, and a browser-vs-browser two-agent mode for a fully agentic negotiation. title: TenderLens
pitch: An autonomous agent that reads every public tender dossier so small suppliers don't have to - scoring what they qualify for, and flagging notices written so only one firm could win.
about_excerpt: An autonomous agent that reads every public tender dossier so small suppliers don't have to - scoring what they qualify for, and flagging notices written so only one firm could win. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Across the EU, roughly half of all public contracts attract a single bidder. The usual explanation is corruption. The more common one is arithmetic: a tender dossier runs 40 to 130 pages, the qualification criteria that decide whether a company may legally bid are scattered through it, and a 26-person firm has nobody who can read forty of those a month. So they stop reading, and the field empties out on its own. The two problems turn out to have the same evidence base. The document that tells a supplier you qualify for this is the same document that reveals this one was written for somebody else -- a specification fixed to 14 mm and 63.5 Wh describes exactly one laptop on the market. Once you are parsing dossiers at scale, both answers fall out of the same pass. What it does One button starts an autonomous sweep. No further human input. The agent pulls open notices, pre-filters by the supplier's value ceiling and live deadlines, then for every surviving notice: opens the dossier, extracts the qualification criteria into structured form, rules each one met / gap / unclear against the supplier's real profile with the evidence attached, screens the buyer's award history and the clause wording for integrity red flags, scores fit out of 100, estimates win probability adjusted for that buyer's historical bidder count, and writes a dated bid plan working backwards from the deadline with an owner on every step. It ends with a ranked board -- 87 down to 17 across twelve notices -- and a written bid / no-bid brief per notice. The entire reasoning trace streams to the browser while it runs: every tool call with its input, its output and its latency. The integrity screen Five detectors, each grounded in a documented single-bidding indicator: Flag Fires when SHORT_WINDOW The submission window is shorter than the customary minimum, which favours a bidder who prepared before publication THIN_COMPETITION The buyer averages under two bidders across prior tenders VENDOR_CONCENTRATION 40% or more of a buyer's prior awards went to one supplier SPEC_LOCK The specification fixes exact physical parameters instead of performance ranges, which usually describes one product on the market INCUMBENT_LOCK A qualification clause can only be satisfied by the current supplier None is presented as proof of wrongdoing, and the app never says otherwise. Each flag carries the reasoning that makes it worth a clarification question or a formal challenge. How I built it TypeScript throughout. Supabase Postgres holds the notices, the supplier profile, the run log and every assessment; Server-Sent Events carry the live trace; the deployed demo runs on Supabase Edge Functions. The agent core -- orchestrator, six tools, provider adapters, types -- depends on nothing from Node, React or Next. That is deliberate, and it buys a second runtime for free: the same engine drives a Next.js build and a Deno edge build, unmodified. The decision worth defending is deterministic core, model at the edge . Every score, verdict and flag comes from code that can be read, tested and cited. The language model writes one artefact -- the decision brief -- where prose is the deliverable. This is not a cost saving. A supplier disqualified on a criterion needs to point at the rule that fired; a score that exists only inside a model's context window cannot survive a procurement review board. The side effect is that the hosted demo runs with zero API keys -- open it and press the button. Graceful degradation at every boundary: no database falls back to the bundled corpus, Supabase unreachable mid-request falls back silently, a deep link to a never-assessed notice is assessed on demand server-side. There is no configuration in which the deployed app shows an error page instead of doing its job. The board is also published to visiting AI agents over WebMCP -- seven tools registered through document.modelContext -- so an assistant browsing the page can search, screen and re-rank it alongside the human, with every call mirrored on screen. Enterprise governance and compliance Auditability by construction. Every assessment is a row tied to a run, carrying the verdicts, flags, checklist and reasoning mode used. You can reconstruct why the agent said what it said, months later. Explainable decisions, not scores. Each verdict ships with its evidence string ("Requires EUR 600,000; profile turnover is EUR 1,850,000"). Each risk flag ships with its rationale. Row-level security on all four tables. The demo project's open policies exist because it holds nothing but synthetic notices; a real deployment scopes them to the authenticated supplier. No unsourced claims. The integrity screen surfaces the pattern and why the pattern matters -- the standard a challenge before a procurement review body is held to. Synthetic corpus. Modelled on the structure of real TED, e-Prokurimi and eNabavke publications. No real notice, buyer decision, supplier name or award record is reproduced. Monetization Two customers, one engine. 1. Suppliers -- SaaS subscription (primary). Solo EUR 49/mo: one country, weekly digest, three profiles. Team EUR 199/mo: three countries, daily sweep, unlimited profiles, bid plans exported to calendar. Agency EUR 699/mo: white label, API access, multi-client dashboards for bid-writing consultancies. The wedge is measurable. A firm bidding six times a year at roughly five days of unpaid bid effort each spends about EUR 12,000 of staff time. TenderLens removes the two days spent deciding whether to bid, and kills the disqualified-on-a-technicality bids entirely. 2. Watchdogs and journalists -- usage-based. Integrity screening billed per thousand notices analysed, with an NGO tier at cost. Anti-corruption organisations and investigative desks already do this by hand, one buyer at a time. 3. Buyers -- compliance licence (later). The same detectors run pre-publication: a procurement office checks its own draft notice for SPEC_LOCK and SHORT_WINDOW before it goes out. Sold per authority, annually. Highest margin, and the one that needs credibility from the first two to earn. Marginal cost is a few cents of model spend per notice, and zero when the deterministic engine handles it. Challenges I ran into Deciding how much judgement to hand to a model. The first version asked an LLM to rule on each criterion; it was fluent and unciteable, and a bid manager cannot take "the model thought so" to a review board. Rewriting the criterion logic as parsed thresholds and set membership made the output defensible and, unexpectedly, made the product better -- the evidence line next to each verdict is what users actually read. Scoring calibration was worse. The first scorer put eight of twelve notices between 90 and 100, which ranks nothing. Fit is now a five-factor blend -- qualification, capability match, economics against the bid ceiling, historical competition, and slack between the deadline and the work the dossier implies -- and the board spreads properly. Two bugs only surfaced when I screenshotted the thing: the bid plan was scheduling steps in the past whenever a deadline was closer than its fixed offsets, and a delivery-time commitment was being marked met because the supplier's category matched. Both are fixed. Both were invisible in the happy path. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The reasoning trace. An agent that returns a verdict asks to be trusted; an agent that shows six tool calls with their inputs, outputs and latency lets you audit the verdict. Making the trace a first-class contract rather than a debug view is the single decision that most changed how the product feels. And the zero-configuration demo: it runs, fully, with no key, no database and no signup. What I learned That agentic is not a synonym for the model decides everything. The parts of this agent that make it worth deploying -- the tool sequence, the extraction contract, the detectors, the trace -- are engineering. The model is one step in seven, and the system is better for the model being replaceable. What's next for TenderLens A live connector per portal. The portal search is one function; TED first, then the national portals. A real dossier reader, with a PDF pipeline feeding the same structured requirement shape, so the agent handles notices nobody has pre-structured. Scheduled sweeps with a morning digest. The run loop already has no browser dependency. More detectors. Each one is an independent function of the notice, so this is purely additive.
