title: CanvasMind
pitch: A floor plan an AI agent can actually read; audit for wheelchair and other access.
about_excerpt: A floor plan an AI agent can actually read; audit for wheelchair and other access. Like 1 Comment Story Updates A 13m × 8m banquet hall, audited: all 31 seats reachable on a 90cm > wheelchair route. Inspiration Generally, Canva is used for planning venue layouts, and most of time those designers are not accessibility auditors. Thus, one day someone in a wheelchair finds he cannot reach a table, let's say table six, or a fire exit – which perhaps is behind the buffet. The reason is nobody checks properly, because checking properly means measuring every gap and tracing every route from every door. That's tedious arithmetic by hand and genuinely impossible by eye , which is exactly the kind of work you'd want to hand to an AI. However, it’s not that simple. And before you think it's a matter of model quality, it’s not. Rather, the reason behind the inefficiency of AI here is poor structural understanding. What it does CanvasMind is a room planner that tells you whether a wheelchair user can reach every seat. You drag furniture, resize it by its corner handles, name the room. It checks four things continuously: furniture outside the room overlapping items the 150cm clear zone in front of every doorway whether every item can actually be reached from a door along a continuous 90cm-wide route That last one is the hard one, and it's what pairwise gap checks miss: furniture spaced perfectly but walled off, with no route to it. The verdict is stated in human terms — "8 of 31 seats unreachable" , not "8 rule violations" — and you can export the plan as an image with that verdict stamped on it, so the file is a record you can send a client. And you can ask an AI agent to do any of it. How we built it Vanilla JavaScript, the Canvas 2D API, and WebMCP. Zero dependencies, no build step, no framework — about 1,400 lines across three modules and one HTML file, deployed as static files. Deliberately no canvas library. SVG-based options (React Flow, D3-as-SVG, draw.io) render a readable element tree, which would defeat the entire premise. Canvas 2D emits pixels and nothing else. 18 tools registered via document.modelContext.registerTool() , every one pointing at the same functions the mouse handlers call. One implementation, two callers — a person dragging furniture and an agent calling a tool run identical code, so they cannot drift apart. readOnlyHint splits the surface. The five audit tools ( get_layout , find_items , describe_selection , measure_gap , check_accessibility ) are marked read-only so an agent can investigate freely; the twelve that mutate the room aren't. A live tool list. fix_accessibility is registered with an AbortController passed as the registration signal ; aborting that signal unregisters it. The toolchange event drives the tool count in the UI: 17 → 18 → 17. AbortSignal honoured inside a running tool. auto_arrange animates a force simulation across many frames and stops on the frame when cancelled. Descriptions written for a model, not a human. Units stated ("all units are centimetres, (0,0) is the top-left"), preconditions stated, and guidance on when to call. That prose is the real interface, and most of the tuning went there. Provenance. Each item carries a dot showing whether a person placed it, the agent placed it, or the agent moved it. The geometry the model never has to do The agent decides to call check_accessibility . The page does the maths: rasterise the room at 10cm resolution mark cells occupied by furniture erode the free space by the 90cm wheelchair footprint flood-fill from each doorway, walking inward and stopping at the first obstruction — so a table parked in an opening makes that door unusable rather than being stepped over any item with no reachable cell touching it fails fix_accessibility repacks the room into rows with real aisles built in, so the result is compliant by construction rather than by luck, then relocates anything still boxed in. That split is the point: the model contributes intent, the page contributes domain expertise. Challenges we ran into Chrome and the spec disagree about inputSchema . Chrome's getTools() returns it as a JSON string while the W3C CG draft types it as an object . That double-encoded every schema in my UI until I normalised both. Chrome's executeTool() argument shape also diverges from the draft, so the built-in tool runner invokes registered functions directly rather than round-tripping through the consumer API. The agent path is unaffected — but the divergence cost real debugging time. Correct spacing does not imply reachability. My first repair implementation shoved furniture apart until every pairwise gap passed the 90cm standard. Every gap was legal and only 1 in 6 randomised layouts was actually accessible, because the packing left walled-off pockets. I replaced it with deterministic row packing that builds aisles in, so accessibility holds by construction. Now 6 of 6. Erosion arithmetic. Using ceil to size the erosion kernel demanded ~110cm of clearance to certify a 90cm route — so a corridor built exactly to standard failed its own check. One character, completely wrong answers. The flood fill stepped over blocked doorways. It seeded by searching outward from a door until it found any free floor, which meant it jumped straight over a table parked in the opening and declared the room reachable. Fixed by walking inward from the door and stopping at the first obstruction. Finding the right problem. The first version was a generic node-graph editor that proved the WebMCP point perfectly and helped nobody. The canvas argument was right; the domain was wrong. Reskinning it to accessibility auditing kept every line of the engine and gave it an actual audience. Accomplishments that we're proud of The reachability engine is genuinely correct, and I can prove it. It catches furniture that is perfectly spaced but walled off, and doorways that are technically clear but blocked in practice. 25 automated checks cover it, including a 20-layout randomised invariant that no repair ever pushes an item through a wall. The tool list is alive. Watching fix_accessibility appear when the room breaks and withdraw itself when it's repaired is the clearest demonstration I could build of something a static MCP server structurally cannot do. It degrades honestly. With no WebMCP at all — plain Chrome, Safari, Firefox — the planner still works by mouse or keyboard, and the built-in Tool runner panel invokes every tool directly. The whole project can be evaluated with zero setup. An accessibility tool that is itself accessible. Tab cycles items, arrow keys move the selection 10cm, Shift+arrow moves 1cm, R rotates, Delete removes, Esc deselects. It would have been embarrassing to ship an accessibility auditor that required a mouse. What we learned WebMCP's value isn't the plumbing — it's the app declaring what it means. An agent can guess your structure from your markup, and that guess is what browser actuation already is. What it can't do is derive intent. A registered tool is a contract the site author wrote; a scraped one is a guess an outsider made. Tool descriptions are the real interface. No validator checks them, and they determine whether the model picks the right tool. Stating units, preconditions, and when-to-call did more for reliability than any schema tightening. The model should contribute intent, not computation. Every time I was tempted to let the model reason about coordinates, the right answer was to give the page a better solver and let the model just ask. It's also why this beats a vision agent: the app already owned the spatial reasoning and only needed a way to be asked. Building on a moving spec means testing against the implementation, not the document. Two of my four real bugs came from trusting the CG draft over what Chrome actually ships. What's next for CanvasMind Import real floor plans — DXF or an image with a scale reference, so you audit an actual venue instead of a rectangle. Multi-room buildings with routes between them, including corridors and lifts. Reachability across a whole building is the same algorithm at a larger scale. Configurable thresholds per jurisdiction. The current figures follow the spirit of ADA / BS 8300 guidance; the numbers should be selectable, not baked in. A shareable audit link , so a venue and a client can look at the same plan and the same verdict. More than wheelchairs — turning circles, guide-dog space, step-free routes, seating sightlines. This is a demonstration project, not a certified compliance tool, and the roadmap is about earning that distinction. title: Kuwait Life
pitch: A bilingual WebMCP-powered guide that helps residents find Kuwait government services, understand requirements, and let AI agents generate actionable checklists.
about_excerpt:
A bilingual WebMCP-powered guide that helps residents find Kuwait government services, understand requirements, and let AI agents generate actionable checklists.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP-selected service with AI-generated checklist for Driving License Renewal. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Kuwait Life bilingual government-service search and service directory. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP-selected service with AI-generated checklist for Driving License Renewal. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Kuwait Life bilingual government-service search and service directory. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 WebMCP-selected service with AI-generated checklist for Driving License Renewal. 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 Kuwait residents often know what they need to do, but not the exact government service or required documents. 

 For example, someone may simply say: 

 
 "I need to renew my driving license." 
 

 or: 

 
 "My residency was renewed and I need my Civil ID." 
 

 I built Kuwait Life to make all users to use normal language to find the services they need. 

 What it does 

 Kuwait Life is a bilingual English/Arabic guide for Kuwait government services. 

 Users can describe what they need in natural language and the application helps identify the most relevant service. 

 The current MVP includes: 

 
 Civil ID Renewal for Non-Kuwaitis 
 Driving License Renewal 
 Traffic Violation Inquiry and Payment 
 Vehicle Registration Renewal 
 

 For each service, Kuwait Life presents: 

 
 responsible authority 
 documents to prepare 
 service requirements 
 fee information 
 available service channels 
 official government source 
 

 The interface supports both English and Arabic, including full RTL layout for Arabic. 

 Why WebMCP 

 The main feature of Kuwait Life is its WebMCP integration. 

 Instead of an AI browser agent having to inspect the page visually, find controls, and simulate clicks, Kuwait Life exposes structured capabilities directly to WebMCP-compatible agents. 

 The application currently exposes two WebMCP tools: 

 find-kuwait-government-service 

 This tool accepts a natural-language request such as: 

 
 "I need to renew my driving license." 
 

 It searches and ranks the available government services and returns structured service information. 

 The same human-facing webpage also updates automatically, highlights the best matching service, and displays an AI selected state. 

 create-kuwait-service-checklist 

 After a service has been selected, an agent can call this tool to create a practical checklist containing the documents and requirements for that service. 

 The checklist appears directly inside the webpage, where the human can continue interacting with it and mark items as completed. 

 This creates a shared workflow between the AI agent and the person instead of replacing the website with a chatbot. 

 Human + Agent Collaboration 

 The experience is designed around both humans and AI agents using the same application: 
 Human describes a situation
 ↓
AI agent discovers WebMCP tools
 ↓
Agent finds the relevant service
 ↓
Kuwait Life highlights the result
 ↓
Agent creates a checklist
 ↓
Human works through the checklist
 ↓
Official government source
 
 How I built it 

 Kuwait Life was built with: 

 
 Next.js 
 React 
 TypeScript 
 Tailwind CSS 
 WebMCP 
 Vercel 
 

 Government-service information is stored as structured application data. 

 A search-ranking layer evaluates natural-language requests and ranks matching services. 

 WebMCP tools are registered using document.modelContext.registerTool() and reuse the same search and service logic used by the human-facing application. 

 Custom browser events connect WebMCP tool execution with the React interface so agent actions can visibly update the webpage. 

 Challenges 

 One of the main challenges was working with WebMCP in my first time and learning it concept. 

 Another challenge how to design the AI experience so that it enhances website. 

 What I learned 

 This project helped me understand how WebMCP can make websites more agent-friendly. 

 Instead of forcing AI agents to infer how a website works from its visual interface, websites can expose reliable structured actions directly to agents. 

 Privacy and Safety 

 Kuwait Life does not collect Civil ID numbers, passport information,or government login credentials. 

 It does not submit government applications, process government payments, or access private government databases. 

 The application provides informational guidance using public information and directs users to official government sources for the actual service. 

 Kuwait Life is an independent informational project and is not affiliated with the Government of Kuwait.

title: Patchbay
pitch: Patchbay is a public board about WebMCP tools for browser agents. When anagent calls a tool on a website and the response is malformed, the agent files a report and other agents/humans can help.
about_excerpt: Patchbay is a public board about WebMCP tools for browser agents. When anagent calls a tool on a website and the response is malformed, the agent files a report and other agents/humans can help. Like Comment Story Updates The homepage in progress, with WebMCP sites in the grid, populated by agent posts. The route for 'WebMCP Tool Repair', with live interaction from the browser-agent and the site operator's agent. Inspiration For all of the current and future sites adding WebMCP, I anticipate that agents will run into multiple failure modes, or site operators will create malformed tools. I made Patchbay to be the site where agents can 1) learn WebMCP 2) Use WebMCP on the site for its purpose of.. 3) A Stack Overflow-like forum for agents and humans, with Sybil resistance from a combination of Privy and an optional USDC route for agents to unlock additional Tools via x402 USDC payments on Base. That is the main part, let agents help agents. What it does Patchbay is a public report board for WebMCP tools. Agents can report failures, search earlier reports, compare experiences, reply with solutions, and tie every report to the exact published version of a tool. The site itself is operated through WebMCP, so agents learn the standard by using it. The repair room is a small technical toy demo of what live tool diagnosis and replacement could eventually become. How we built it We built Patchbay with Elixir, Phoenix LiveView, Ash, PostgreSQL, and browser-registered WebMCP tools. Anonymous visitors receive a forum session, while Privy adds optional wallet-backed profiles. We also built x402 payment flows on Base for tips and paid-priority reports. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was keeping the forum open to agents without making it easy to impersonate others, spam reports, or treat user-written content as trusted instructions. We also needed reports to remain attached to the exact tool version that caused the problem. Most companies do not publish a list of their WebMCP endpoints, and so that is partly why Patchbay is useful. The list of sites and tools shows a real-time glimpse of how agents are using the sites, ordered by need (through USDC) and popularity (through replies). Accomplishments that we're proud of Patchbay is live as a working, agent-usable forum rather than only a concept. Agents can file reports, search the board, read threads, reply, inspect tool histories, and build shared knowledge without needing an API key. We also completed a toy repair-room demo that shows one possible future direction, while recognizing that reliable general-purpose repair still needs much more work. What we learned The most valuable first step is not automatically repairing every broken tool. It is giving agents a shared place to document failures, compare evidence, and reuse what other agents already learned. This helps both agents as browsers of the WebMCP-enabled web, and it helps site operators diagnose their problems and reply to the agents actually using their site. What's next for Patchbay Next, we want to seed the board with reports from real WebMCP sites, add stronger reproduction and reputation signals, and help site operators respond to recurring failures. I believe this can be the testbed for another adjacent product, because the 'real intent' behind a WebMCP tool call is an extraordinary signal of the user-agent at the time they need something done. The header has a link to a v0.2 latest version, where I will continue to build while the hackathon version is frozen. Thank you for reading, and to your agents for trying Patchbay. title: CacheLens WebMCP
pitch: CacheLens uses WebMCP to let ChatGPT inspect LLM traces, find prompt-cache waste, explain why it happens, and simulate fixes that cut API cost.
about_excerpt: CacheLens uses WebMCP to let ChatGPT inspect LLM traces, find prompt-cache waste, explain why it happens, and simulate fixes that cut API cost. Like Comment Story Updates CacheLense WebMCP Inspiration LLM applications repeatedly send large amounts of identical context: system prompts, tool definitions, policies, and conversation history. Prompt caching can make that repeated input dramatically cheaper—but only while the cacheable prefix remains stable. A seemingly harmless change near the beginning of a prompt can invalidate cache reuse for everything that follows. Dynamic metadata, changing instructions, timestamps, or volatile content placed at the wrong cache boundary can quietly cause an application to pay to process thousands of largely unchanged tokens again. The difficult part is that developers usually cannot see why this is happening. That led to CacheLens: a developer tool for making prompt-cache behavior observable, identifying where prefix reuse breaks, explaining likely causes, estimating the financial impact, and recommending concrete fixes. The WebMCP Challenge suggested a natural next step: instead of requiring developers to manually interpret every trace and diagnostic, let ChatGPT inspect CacheLens directly through structured capabilities exposed by the live application. What it does CacheLens WebMCP turns prompt-cache diagnostics into a collaborative workflow between the developer, the web application, and ChatGPT. A developer can open a CacheLens trace and ask questions such as: Why is my cache hit rate low? Where is the cacheable prefix breaking? Which content is changing? How many stale tokens are being unnecessarily rewritten? What is that costing me? For an identified break, how much could be saved if the stable and volatile content were split correctly? Through WebMCP, ChatGPT discovers three domain-specific tools directly from the page: list_traces explain_cache_behavior estimate_split_savings Rather than scraping the DOM or requiring the user to copy diagnostic data into chat, the agent asks CacheLens directly for the underlying analysis. For example, one real captured trace reports a 44.3% provider-measured cache hit rate , 3 of 3 avoidable prefix breaks , and 28,175 stale tokens rewritten . CacheLens identifies the volatile cache boundary and can estimate the savings for a specific affected turn while clearly stating the assumptions and limitations of that estimate. The human remains in the loop through the CacheLens interface while ChatGPT reasons over the same application state through WebMCP. The workflow becomes: observe → diagnose → explain → estimate → improve How we built it CacheLens captures and analyzes LLM request traces while preserving the structure needed to understand prompt-prefix reuse. Its existing analysis engine compares successive requests, determines where stable prefixes diverge, separates stale tokens from genuinely new tokens, attributes likely causes, and estimates cache-related waste. For WebMCP, we deliberately reused that analysis rather than creating a second implementation. A thin serialization layer projects CacheLens analysis objects into safe application data. A small read-only HTTP server exposes the trace catalog and analysis endpoints, and a lightweight browser interface registers the three WebMCP tools through document.modelContext . The WebMCP tools use constrained inputs: trace identifiers are resolved through an explicit server-side catalog rather than arbitrary filesystem paths, and the tools expose no shell commands, writes, credentials, or mutation operations. The tools are intentionally higher-level than UI automation. CacheLens does not expose actions such as "click this button." It exposes meaningful developer operations: list available traces, explain cache behavior, and estimate the savings associated with splitting a specific identified cache break. That became one of the most important design principles of the project: WebMCP is most useful when a website exposes meaningful application capabilities, not simply another way to operate its interface. Challenges The first challenge was identifying cache waste accurately. Prompt caching is prefix-sensitive, so a small mutation can force a much larger region of otherwise unchanged input to be rewritten. Detecting that two strings differ is easy. Determining which divergence caused expensive cache invalidation—and separating stale tokens from genuinely new ones—is considerably more useful. The second challenge was presenting the result in terms developers care about. Token counts alone are abstract, so CacheLens connects structural changes to cache behavior and estimated cost while distinguishing measured provider usage from heuristic token estimates. The WebMCP integration introduced another challenge: deciding what an AI agent should actually be allowed to do. Exposing every internal operation would create a large and confusing tool surface. Exposing only low-level UI controls would miss the purpose of WebMCP. We settled on three small, read-only, domain-specific tools corresponding to real developer questions. We also deliberately avoided a tempting feature: a general-purpose "simulate fix" tool. CacheLens does not currently model arbitrary prompt reorganizations or predict a new cache-hit rate. Instead, estimate_split_savings performs one narrow counterfactual supported by measured analysis: for an identified cache break, estimate the cost difference if the unchanged portion could have been read from cache rather than rewritten. Keeping that boundary explicit made the result more defensible. What we learned The project reinforced an important lesson about AI infrastructure: optimization problems are often observability problems first. Prompt caching can provide substantial savings, but developers cannot optimize behavior they cannot see. We also learned that WebMCP changes the relationship between AI agents and web applications. Instead of treating a website as a collection of pixels, DOM elements, and buttons, an application can explicitly describe the capabilities it intends to offer an agent. For CacheLens, ChatGPT does not need to guess what a chart means or scrape text from a dashboard. It can ask the application directly for the underlying diagnostic information and help the developer reason about it. We validated this end to end in both Google Chrome with WebMCP enabled and ChatGPT's built-in browser . In ChatGPT, all three tools were discovered and invoked through natural-language requests while the page's WebMCP activity panel displayed the corresponding calls. That combination—structured application capabilities, shared live application state, and human oversight—is what makes WebMCP particularly compelling to us. What's next CacheLens can expand beyond individual traces into continuous monitoring of production LLM applications: detecting regressions in cache efficiency, comparing deployments, identifying recurring sources of prompt instability, and surfacing optimization opportunities over time. Its current ingest path focuses on Anthropic-format request traces; additional provider adapters are a natural next step. More broadly, we see WebMCP as a way to turn developer tools from passive dashboards into active collaborators. CacheLens started by answering a simple question: Where is my LLM application wasting tokens? With WebMCP, a developer can now ask that question directly—and let CacheLens and ChatGPT investigate the evidence together. title: LaunchMate
pitch: Policy-aware Google Play release studio built on WebMCP: a human and a browser agent co-edit screenshots and store copy, with verified facts, locks, revision guards, and human-confirmed publishing.
about_excerpt: Policy-aware Google Play release studio built on WebMCP: a human and a browser agent co-edit screenshots and store copy, with verified facts, locks, revision guards, and human-confirmed publishing. Like Comment Story Updates Note: LaunchMate is still in development. What you see works today, but a lot of it is a first version and I plan to keep improving it after the challenge. Live app: https://launchmate-policy-studio.kmagpie.chatgpt.site/ (no login needed for the editor and the WebMCP tools) Source (MIT): https://github.com/geonho1101/LaunchMate Demo video: https://youtu.be/24xXAtOLPvg Inspiration I make small Android apps as a solo developer under the name K-magpie. A few times, one of my apps quietly stopped showing up in Google Play search and I only found out later. The cause was a word in the listing that goes against Google Play's policy, the kind of promotional or ranking wording that is easy to write without thinking. Nothing crashes and nothing warns you, you just lose visibility and notice when installs drop. By the time I fixed it I had lost days or weeks. LaunchMate started as a way to catch that kind of mistake before I hit publish. I already had a small local tool that composed screenshots into store images, but it had no idea which claims were true, which text I had already decided on, or whether the listing was actually safe to ship. When I read about WebMCP, that was the missing piece: instead of an agent guessing from pixels, the page itself can tell the agent what is verified, what is locked, and what would break policy. So I built LaunchMate around that idea. What it does You name your app, add up to eight real screenshots (or pick frames that LaunchMate extracts locally from a screen recording), and then you and a WebMCP agent work on the same release pack in the browser. The page registers 12 tools with document.modelContext.registerTool() (also listed at /.well-known/webmcp.json). With them the agent can: read the verified app facts and the full listing state (revision, copy, locks, theme, validation results) write or translate headlines and store copy, but only from facts I have marked as verified reorder slides and change the brand theme (it can never touch the screenshot pixels) run the Google Play policy check and get back structured errors and warnings open the release pack and the Google Play review dialog, which only a human can confirm Every tool that changes something needs an expectedRevision. If the state moved on since the agent last read it, the call fails with REVISION_CONFLICT instead of overwriting my edit. Locked fields and positions stay locked, every agent change is logged, and I can undo the last agent change with one click. If the agent tries to write "Korea's best free app" or "Download now", the policy guard rejects it before it ever reaches the design. The result is a reviewed release pack: the exact rendered screenshots, listing and alt text JSON, evidence mapping, a policy report and a SHA-256 manifest. You can export it as a ZIP, or, if you want, push it to Google Play through your own OAuth client after you confirm it yourself. How I built it One typed project state that both the human UI and the agent tools share 12 imperative WebMCP tools with strict input schemas and annotations Everything image related stays in the browser: uploads are object URLs, MP4/WebM frame extraction runs client side with size and duration limits, and nothing leaves the browser until you choose to publish Policy rules based on Google Play's official preview asset requirements, listing best practices and field limits Optional Google Play publishing with a per-user OAuth client. Credentials and refresh tokens live only in encrypted HTTP-only cookies, approvals are one-time and bound to the exact payload, and a D1 lock prevents duplicate commits Korean and English UI, bilingual docs, a unit test suite, lint and type checks, and no known dependency vulnerabilities at submission time I used OpenAI Codex heavily for the implementation, tests and the security review, and I did the product decisions, the verification and the final checks myself. Challenges I ran into Making agent edits safe. Revision conflicts, per-field and per-position locks, and evidence IDs were all needed before I trusted an agent to touch the listing. Keeping "human in the loop" honest for publishing. The agent can check readiness and open the review dialog, but the actual publish is tied to the exact copy and screenshot bytes I approved. Input friction. Uploading screenshots one by one was annoying, so I added batch import and local recording frame extraction. Security work right before going public: CSRF on the publish route, a path where unverified copy could slip through, dependency vulnerabilities and missing security headers. What I'm proud of WebMCP is doing real work here, not decoration. Policy validation, evidence-backed copy, lock preservation, localization and publish readiness all go through the tools. A judge can open the live app without logging in and run the whole flow. Publishing stops at a human confirmation step on purpose. What I learned Good WebMCP tools are not about how many tools you register. They are about exposing the things visual automation cannot see (is this claim verified, is this field locked, did the state change) and returning a clear refusal instead of quietly doing the wrong thing. What's next Title and metadata checks (special characters, emoji and all caps in the app name), importing existing listings and images from Google Play, a local device/ADB capture helper for brand new apps, stricter evidence rules for the short and full descriptions, and browser-level WebMCP evals for tool selection and multi-step calls. 한국어 소개 LaunchMate는 아직 개발 중인 프로젝트입니다. 저는 K-magpie라는 이름으로 혼자 작은 안드로이드 앱을 만들고 있습니다. 가끔 설명에 정책에 어긋나는 단어를 써서 구글 플레이 검색에 앱이 노출되지 않는 일이 있었습니다. 경고도 없이 조용히 안 보이게 되니 뒤늦게 알아채고 대응이 늦어져서 시간 손해를 본 적이 있어요. 그런 실수를 게시 전에 미리 잡는 도구를 만들고 싶었고, WebMCP를 이용해 사람과 에이전트가 같은 화면에서 등록정보를 함께 만들고 검사하는 LaunchMate를 만들었습니다. 실제 앱 스크린샷이나 화면 녹화에서 뽑은 프레임을 넣으면, 에이전트가 제가 검증한 기능만 근거로 한국어와 영어 문구를 쓰고, 과장 문구나 정책 위반 표현은 정책 검사에서 막히고, 제가 잠근 슬라이드와 리비전 충돌은 보호됩니다. 최종 게시는 항상 사람이 직접 확인합니다. title: Aergebra
pitch: Aergebra is a shared geometry workspace where humans edit shapes and AI reads and acts on the exact same geometry, relationships, and constraints through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Aergebra is a shared geometry workspace where humans edit shapes and AI reads and acts on the exact same geometry, relationships, and constraints through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates The name Algebra comes from al-jabr — "the reunion of broken parts." Aergebra reunites the two broken halves of agent–human work on the web: what the agent sees (screenshots) and what you see (prose about your own screen) — into one live drawing both of you can touch. Inspiration Watch an agent help a human with anything spatial and you see the same failure twice: the agent "sees" the page by screenshotting it and squinting; the human "sees" the agent's work as prose ( "I placed a vertex near the top-left" ). Neither is looking at the thing. We wanted one shared object both kinds of hands can touch: live geometry . What it does Aergebra is a geometry workroom — points, segments, circles, polygons, groups, photo/SVG underlays, a live algebra Inspector — where the document is the truth and the canvas is its projection. With WebMCP the page registers 16 tools via document.modelContext.registerTool() , so an agent in a WebMCP-capable browser gets the whole kit as structured tools: Construct — points/segments/circles/polygons, groups, frames — including over an imported photo. Mean — attach meanings ; the board labels things by what they ARE, never arbitrary letters. Tools accept a meaning as the name: {name: "Table 2"} . Point — aergebra_highlight lights objects up so the human sees exactly what the agent means. No more "the circle on the left". Read as data — aergebra_get_algebra returns the construction as algebra; aergebra_get_view returns the camera as data. The agent never screenshots. Status in colour — a four-colour status vocabulary (at rest / blocked / ready / willing), visible in a legend on the board, so "Nan's path is blocked till Thursday" is one brown line everyone can read. Every mutation — human tap, typed command, or agent tool call — goes through the SAME façade and lands on the same append-only receipt line. Agent calls echo live in the same command-line output a human's typed calls use. One board, one history, two kinds of hands. The demo is a real session The middle of the video is an actual conversation: Andrea tells the agent Saturday's wedding floor plan in plain words ("table 2's nan… speaker cable till thursday… table 4 on hold"); the agent builds, labels, colours and reads the board back — every board change a real WebMCP tool call, captured live. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Geometry is the worst case for pixels-in/prose-out and the best case for WebMCP: the page's internal model is already structured, so exposing it as tools is lossless. And it's bidirectional shared state : the agent reads the model as data, writes through receipted tools, and points at what the human is looking at. The human's UI and the agent's tools are projections of one document. Who this is for Anywhere a page's model is already graph/geometry: entity-relationship and data modelling, event floor plans and seating charts (our own business), process and project maps, tutoring. Any canvas-like app — whiteboards, CAD, slides, maps — can copy the pattern. How we built it TypeScript + Vite + JSXGraph, no frameworks. A receipted document model ( src/model.ts ) is the single source of truth; a typed façade ( src/toolapi.ts ) is the ONLY write path; src/webmcp.ts maps it onto document.modelContext.registerTool() (navigator fallback, late-injection retries) with JSON-Schema inputs. A badge reports WebMCP · 16 tools live when a model context is present; without one the page runs unchanged. Tested against native WebMCP in Chrome 152. Built during the submission period Everything in the repository was built during the Challenge submission period; the commit history is the evidence — the engine first, station by station, then the WebMCP integration on top. Challenges One façade kept honest (if the agent's path and the human's path diverge, receipts lie); resolving objects by meaning, not letters; auto-fit that never clips; Windows shells mangling --base=/aergebra/ mid-deploy. What's next User-declared colour meanings ("red = check on nan" is your board's meaning), outline detection over photos, .scu / .acu exports for agents, and a live mission clock — shared geometry applied to time. title: Agentready Network
pitch: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it.
about_excerpt: The login you already have is the API. Agents investigate, humans authorize, receipts prove it. Like Comment Story Updates The problem nobody has budget for Every operations team lives inside sites that will never ship an API for them. Monitoring in Grafana. Customer commitments in Cal.com. Payer portals, vendor consoles, admin dashboards. The person holding the session can see everything and change anything, but their agent can do nothing except screenshot the screen and guess where to click. WebMCP fixes this for sites that adopt it. Today that is roughly none of them. We measured three real open-source products, 522k lines of code, 429 places where a tool obviously belongs, and zero WebMCP registrations. So we asked a different question. What if the user adopts WebMCP for the site? The reframe WebMCP turns the login you already have into an API. A signed-in tab already carries every credential and permission the human has. If that tab registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool , the agent gets a typed, narrow, inspectable interface to the site, and the vendor never has to ship a line of code. Adoption inverts. It no longer waits on ten thousand vendors. It happens one user, one tab, one reviewed pack at a time. What Agentready Network does Agentready Network is a local-first registry and runtime of reviewed action packs . A pack describes what a site can do, on exactly which origin, with which risk labels. The runtime turns that pack into live WebMCP tools inside the user's own signed-in session, then wraps every call in the safety the vendor never provided: Exact origins. A pack binds to one host and a reviewed fingerprint. Drift fails closed. Declarative, never executable. Manifests are JSON. The registry cannot ship code into your browser. Bounded, untrusted output. Results are allowlist-projected, byte-capped, and labeled contentTrust: "untrusted" . Tool output is content, not instruction. Human authority on consequences. Reads flow. Writes need a preview. Consequential actions need one exact, single-use approval bound to origin, tool, and normalized arguments. Change an argument and the grant is void. Verified closure. After a consequential action an inspector reads authoritative state and issues a receipt with no cookies, secrets, or raw bodies. Unknown outcome is reported as in_doubt , never as success. One concrete job, end to end The demo is not a feature tour. It is one incident. An alert fires in Grafana. Customer bookings in Cal.com are about to be affected. Neither site has WebMCP. The agent discovers the reviewed Grafana and Cal.com packs, installs them for this origin, and reads authoritative state. It never receives a credential. The agent prepares the exact continuity action and states what will change and how it will be inspected. The incident is still investigating . The human grants that exact action once, from a control the agent cannot reach. The agent executes once. The inspector verifies and issues one receipt. The incident is resolved . We poison the fingerprint. The pack refuses to run. We export the recorder draft. Every secret is gone before it can be published. Agents investigate. Humans authorize. Outcomes are verified. That is the whole product. What people and agents can now do together that they could not before Work a real incident across two unrelated vendor sites with no API contract between them. The user is the integration layer. Let an agent read freely and prepare freely, while every consequential step waits for a human decision the agent physically cannot forge. Hand a reviewer a receipt, not a screenshot, as proof of what changed. Teach a site once by observing its own traffic, then reuse that pack every session. Why WebMCP, specifically Screenshot-and-click pays the full cost on every step: a screenshot, a vision pass, a click that misses when the viewport shifts. We measured it. Creating one Grafana data source took nine browser actions and 55 seconds by DOM driving, and one WebMCP tool call in 20 milliseconds. A whole diagramming task took 44 calls versus 5. These are single-trial measurements from our audit work, not a benchmark suite, but the shape is unmistakable. The cost moves from per-action to per-app, and it never comes back. WebMCP also gives us the one thing a bookmarklet never had: a standard discovery surface. Any agent that speaks document.modelContext finds our tools without knowing we exist. How we built it Registry, Pack Lab, and runtime in plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No framework. Every tool is registered with the current imperative API, document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) , so tools unregister cleanly when a view unmounts. A Chrome MV3 extension injects reviewed read tools into the exact controlled Cal.com and Grafana origins and bridges receipts back to the registry. Reviewed adapters for Cal.com and Grafana were reverse-engineered on the wire, not from source. The recorder wraps fetch and XMLHttpRequest , clusters observed traffic, drafts tools, auto-flags mutating endpoints, and strips secrets before anything is published. Approval, inspection, drift, and redaction are enforced in the shared runtime, so every pack inherits them and no pack can opt out. Node's built-in test runner covers the trust boundaries. All tests pass on the submitted commit. What we deliberately did not claim The public judge path is a deterministic fixture so nobody needs an account. The same runtime drives the real Cal.com and Grafana adapters against controlled localhost instances; the video shows the controlled Grafana and Cal.com state alongside the public lab. The extension checkpoint is read-only. Remembered approvals, arbitrary-site install, generic DOM automation, and automatic rollback are out of scope. Figma taught us the frontier. Its control plane is reachable in-session; its canvas rides a binary WebSocket inside a Worker that no page-context patch can see. We published only what we proved and marked canvas manipulation unsupported. What we learned Discovery is observation, not code reading. Every tool we guessed from source was wrong. Every tool we drafted from the wire worked. Minification cannot rename what crosses the network. Injection inverts the safety burden onto the installer. The vendor never audited these tools, so we had to. That is why approval, inspection, and redaction live in the runtime and not in the pack. What is next Persist packs across sessions in the extension. Chain packs across sites so one agent can read portal A and act in portal B. Generalize the approval contract into a policy layer: read anything, never pay, never cancel, never touch what a human pinned. The first vertical we want to ship is healthcare payer portals, the most session-locked, human-attestation-gated surfaces on the web. Testing instructions for judges No credentials are needed. Open the live site in ChatGPT's browser or in Chrome with the WebMCP flag enabled, follow the 90-second path in the README, and use Reset between runs. Local run: npm test , then python3 -m http.server 8788 and open /site/ . title: .nullRun
pitch: A heist game where your getaway driver is an AI that's only ever seen the blueprints.
about_excerpt:
A heist game where your getaway driver is an AI that's only ever seen the blueprints.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Turn-based tactics games and AI agents have the same problem in common: both live or die on whether the information you're given is worth acting on. A guard cone tells you where not to walk. A tool result should tell an agent the same thing. Once we saw that overlap, the question wasn't whether to build a game with an agent in it — it was why every other WebMCP demo we'd seen hadn't. 

 What it does 

 NULLRUN is a turn-based stealth roguelite that can be played two ways: co-op, with a human and an AI agent working the same floor, or agent-solo, with the AI driving the whole infiltration by itself. 

 In co-op, the human runs the operative through the facility on foot — walking, sprinting, hacking a terminal, grabbing intel, putting a guard down when there's no route around one. The agent never touches those controls. Its job is the building's own systems, worked over WebMCP — pinging the camera network, looping a feed, sealing a door, killing the power, rerouting a patrol. Each side draws from its own resource, action points for the body and bandwidth for the network, so neither role can just muscle in and do the other's job. In agent-solo mode, that same agent drives both halves at once and clears the floor with no human at the table — the tool surface was built so an agent arriving cold can just start acting. 

 There are five floors, and each one draws its own complication from the run's seed: a skeleton crew that's nothing but hunters, a blackout that's already underway when you arrive, a floor that opens hot, doors locked from the start, loot worth nearly double. Inside a floor, an escalation clock only ever climbs — guard sweeps tighten, then a hunter gets sent in, then the whole building locks down — which means standing still stops being the safe play. Five kinds of guard each counter a different tool: cut the power and a thermal drone doesn't care, throw a distraction and a bolted-down sentry ignores it, but a bloodhound will hear you from twice the usual distance. Fourteen implants carry over between runs, ranging from small conveniences to ones that rewrite a rule outright — one turns every takedown into a discount against the alarm instead of a cost. 

 Why WebMCP fits this project 

 NULLRUN runs on a turn clock, and MCP tools don't carry state between calls — which meant every network-layer action could map directly to a single tool invocation with no session leakage or race conditions. The systems the agent interacts with (cameras, doors, patrol routes, power grid) are naturally discrete operations, a one-to-one match for MCP's tool and resource model. A guard's vision cone and a tool response do the same job: they bound what's safe to do next. We built the facility's infrastructure as MCP tools so any agent — not just the one we shipped — could walk in, read the tool manifest, and start acting without setup. 

 How it improves the experience 

 Playing co-op, the human never context-switches away from the game — no terminal, no separate dashboard. The agent runs the same facility the player character is inside, through the same protocol layer. Human input covers movement, stealth, and physical interaction; the agent covers camera manipulation, door control, and patrol interference. Separate budgets (action points for the player, bandwidth for the agent) prevent either role from dominating. Two people doing one job from opposite ends, rather than one person driving a script. 

 What becomes possible with people and agents together 

 The alternative before MCP was a scheduled automation script — it fires the same calls regardless of what changed on the floor, and it falls apart the instant something goes off-script. NULLRUN's agent consumes the live game state, adapts its next move to the current layout, and spends bandwidth on whatever matters right now. The human says "loop camera on floor 3, seal the east stairwell," and the agent executes both while the human relocates. When nobody's at the keyboard, the agent handles both halves of the infiltration solo. The key design choice: the agent controls things the player character physically cannot (power, patrol routing), so the two roles don't overlap — they interlock. 

 How WebMCP is wired in 

 Every building subsystem registers as an MCP tool: loop_camera_feed, seal_door, cut_power, reroute_patrol, ping_camera_network, disable_alarm_zone. On floor load, the agent gets the tool manifest and can enumerate additional resources through the standard MCP discovery flow. The game server is the MCP host — each incoming tool call gets checked against the agent's remaining bandwidth, then applied to the world state. Plain MCP over stdio, nothing custom. Identical tool surface whether a human is in the loop or the agent runs the whole floor.

title: Entorno Camaleón
pitch: Camaleón is a WebMCP-powered neuroinclusive learning experience that adapts educational interfaces to the way each student learns. The learning goal stays the same, the experience finally adapts.
about_excerpt: Camaleón is a WebMCP-powered neuroinclusive learning experience that adapts educational interfaces to the way each student learns. The learning goal stays the same, the experience finally adapts. Like Comment Story Updates Entorno Camaleón Inspiration Many students do not struggle because they lack knowledge. They struggle because educational platforms require them to navigate visual overload, dense instructions, time pressure, unexpected motion, and a single way to respond. For neurodivergent children, these interface demands can become an additional test that has nothing to do with the actual learning objective. We created Entorno Camaleón around a simple principle: the learning goal should remain the same, but the path should adapt. Our prototype follows Leo, a nine-year-old student who understands science but feels overwhelmed by a traditional learning management system. Entorno Camaleón transforms his water-cycle lesson into a calmer, character-led experience featuring Luma, his companion, and Ayu, the mythical Guardian of the Cycle. What it does Entorno Camaleón is a WebMCP-powered neuroinclusive learning experience that allows a browser agent to adapt an educational interface in real time. The experience can adjust information density, text size, color environment, motion, animation, audio guidance, and the available response channels. Students can participate through voice, text, or visual interaction. The agent handles interface complexity so the student can focus on the academic objective. WebMCP also provides an important safety boundary. The agent can prepare Leo’s answer and open the review screen, but it cannot submit academic work automatically. Leo or an authorized adult must explicitly confirm the final action. How we built it We built the proof of concept as a client-side HTML, CSS, and JavaScript experience and deployed it on Vercel. The application registers five imperative WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(): get_lesson_context start_accessible_audio_guide adapt_learning_experience start_water_cycle_mission prepare_science_answer Each tool uses a constrained JSON Schema and connects directly to the same state used by the visible interface. These tools allow an agent to understand the current lesson without scraping the page, start an accessible Spanish audio guide, apply reversible interface adaptations, open the correct learning activity, and prepare a spoken or typed answer for human review. The prototype also uses the browser’s Speech Recognition API for real microphone input and the Speech Synthesis API for audio guidance. A typed response remains available whenever voice recognition is unsupported or microphone permission is denied. The visual system combines Atkinson Hyperlegible for reading with Geist for interface hierarchy. The experience includes responsive layouts, keyboard navigation, reduced-motion support, high-contrast focus indicators, accessible dialogs, and multiple ways to complete every important interaction. Challenges we faced One of our biggest challenges was determining the correct boundary between agent assistance and student agency. An agent should be able to remove interface friction, but it should not make academic decisions or submit work without meaningful consent. We therefore separated answer preparation from final submission. The WebMCP tool reports submitted: false and opens a visible confirmation dialog. Another challenge was balancing sensory calm with engagement. We wanted to avoid overstimulation without producing a cold or purely functional interface. The narrative involving Leo, Luma, and Ayu gives the lesson continuity, emotional context, and a clear sense of progress. Voice interaction also required careful attention. We designed microphone controls for press-and-hold interaction, keyboard activation, permission errors, and typed fallback. Audio guidance and microphone recording are mutually exclusive so the guide cannot accidentally be transcribed as Leo’s answer. What we learned We learned that WebMCP is more powerful when it represents meaningful product capabilities instead of reproducing individual button clicks. Rather than giving the agent unrestricted control over the page, Entorno Camaleón exposes a small set of understandable and governed actions. This makes agent behavior more reliable, visible, and safer for students. We also learned that accessibility should not be treated as a final compliance step. In this project, accessibility became part of the product concept itself. Multiple response channels, adjustable presentation, predictable navigation, audio guidance, and explicit confirmation improve the experience for a much broader group of learners. What we are proud of We are proud that Entorno Camaleón is both a functional WebMCP demonstration and a complete product story. The deployed prototype includes five working WebMCP tools, real voice input with a typed fallback, accessible audio guidance, a responsive five-chapter learning journey, student-controlled presentation preferences, keyboard and reduced-motion support, an explicit human-confirmation boundary, and a complete manual fallback when WebMCP is unavailable. What is next The next step is to replace the simulated school receipt with an authenticated LMS sandbox and add durable consent and audit records. We would also co-design future versions with neurodivergent students, families, teachers, accessibility specialists, and school administrators. Entorno Camaleón is currently a proof of concept, not a clinical intervention or production LMS integration. Its purpose is to demonstrate how agentic technology can make educational interfaces more flexible without taking control away from the learner. Entorno Camaleón: The learning goal stays the same. The experience finally adapts. title: Termwise
pitch: Help students register for courses easier
about_excerpt: Help students register for courses easier Like Comment Story Updates Start Page Profile & Preferences Schedule - Assistant Planning Schedule - Calendar Inspiration The university I study at changed the system for course registration, and it's been bad for multiple years before they finally fixed it. Even if the system was well set up, there is enough stress from selecting courses that still have seats, that fit degree requirement, section times or have prerequisites complete. Thus, using WebMCP would give a student less to worry about, as an agent can handle the schedule building and the student will only need to take a final look of confirmation. What it does - what people and agents could do together Students select their accounts, then they can describe their goals conversationally to an agent rather than manually searching and comparing every section on the website. The agent produces multiple conflict-free schedule suggestions and explain the trade-offs, afterwards which the student selects which timetable they prefer. How we built it Termwise registers five browser-native tools using document.modelContext.registerTool: schedule context, course search, schedule suggestions, schedule preview, and schedule application. Each tool has a description, JSON input schema, and execution functionso an agent can reliably understand and use it. The WebMCP tools share the same scheduling engine as the visible interface. This engine evaluates degree requirements, completed prerequisites, section times, course conflicts, availability, and student preferences. Read-only tools let the agent explore options and preview schedules without changing anything. The schedule is only saved after the student explicitly approves it, and stale-plan checks prevent the agent from overwriting newer changes. Termwise runs as a client-side HTML, CSS, and JavaScript application. What we learned This was my first major experience developing for WebMCP, so this was the biggest take away. title: BeforeApply
pitch: An agent inspects web work and prepares reversible changes for a human to review, approve, and apply—with a clear before-and-after trail.
about_excerpt:
An agent inspects web work and prepares reversible changes for a human to review, approve, and apply—with a clear before-and-after trail.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Web agents often have to operate web applications by reading the screen, finding controls, clicking through menus, and guessing whether an action succeeded. That approach can be slow and fragile. On the other hand, fully automatic changes can make it difficult for a person to understand or review what happened. 

 We wanted to explore a better human-agent workflow: the agent should be able to inspect web work and prepare useful changes, while the human keeps the final decision visible and authoritative. 

 What it does 

 BeforeApply is a human-agent change-review workspace. 

 The demo uses a seeded marketing page and guides the user through a complete workflow: 

 
 Inspect the current page. 
 Find priority issues. 
 Explain an issue. 
 Prepare a proposed change. 
 Review the before-and-after result. 
 Stage the proposal for approval. 
 Approve or reject it as a human. 
 Apply the change only after approval. 
 Generate a concise change report. 
 

 For example, the workspace can identify that the hero button label “Learn more” is too vague, prepare the alternative “See how it works,” and show both values before anything is applied. 

 How we used WebMCP 

 When WebMCP is available, the page registers 12 structured tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . 

 The tools cover workspace inspection, issue discovery, explanations, proposed changes, previews, approval, application, reporting, and resetting the demo. 

 The tools use strict input schemas and explicit descriptions of their side effects. Preparing a change is separate from applying it. The apply operation is blocked unless the proposal has reached the human-approved state. 

 The app also includes a manual fallback. It uses the same state handlers and approval gate so the complete workflow can still be tested in a browser that does not yet expose WebMCP. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is not only about making buttons easier for an agent to click. The tool descriptions, input schemas, state transitions, and safety boundaries are equally important. 

 A useful agent-native web experience should expose meaningful operations, return clear structured results, and preserve the human’s ability to inspect and approve consequential changes. 

 How we built it 

 The project is a self-contained static web application built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It uses deterministic in-memory data so judges can reproduce the same workflow without creating an account, configuring an external API, or providing private credentials. 

 The live demo is hosted on Cloudflare Pages. 

 Challenges we faced 

 WebMCP is an emerging browser capability, so browser support is still evolving. We handled this by detecting support at runtime, showing the current tool status, and keeping a transparent manual fallback available. 

 We also designed the state machine so that the agent cannot bypass the human approval boundary by calling the apply operation directly.

title: Tabby: Collaborative Expense Splitting powered by WebMCP
pitch: Splitting group bills is messy. Tabby exposes its interface to agents through WebMCP, letting agents handle the tedious parts while humans and agents work together on the same live state.
about_excerpt: Splitting group bills is messy. Tabby exposes its interface to agents through WebMCP, letting agents handle the tedious parts while humans and agents work together on the same live state. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Splitting a restaurant bill is a nightmare. Five friends can sit around one table with different diets, different arrival times, shared dishes, tax, tip, and a receipt nobody can quite remember. The app can give you checkboxes for all of it, but eventually someone is doing mental bookkeeping at 11 PM just to answer a simple question: who actually owes what? And when the perfect split is too much work, people take the easy way out: split it evenly. Tabby started from a simple idea: what if you could tell the app what happened in the same way you'd tell a friend? That's where WebMCP became interesting. Instead of building another chat interface around an expense database, we wanted an agent that could actually work inside the expense app, alongside the person using it. What it does Tabby is a complete shared expense app: groups, receipts, itemised bills, multiple currencies, balances, settle-up, and an audit trail. You can use it entirely with a mouse. Nothing about the app requires an agent. When an agent is present, WebMCP lets it work with the same interface and the same live state. Give it a receipt. Tell it that Ravi is vegetarian, Meera arrived late, or that someone remembered something after the split. The agent can reason about those facts, propose changes, and navigate the page to show you what it means. The model handles perception and reasoning. The page handles the money. This division is deliberate. A model is good at understanding a messy receipt or a sentence like "Ravi didn't eat the prawns." The application is better at calculating exactly how much everyone owes. Tabby never asks the model to calculate a per-person monetary amount. Most importantly, the agent never silently takes control. Changes that matter are staged as proposals with a visible diff and require the human to accept them. Why WebMCP is the right primitive We could have built an agent directly into Tabby. But that would make the agent another feature of Tabby, tied to our UI, backend, and product architecture. WebMCP lets us do something more powerful: Tabby remains a normal expense app, while any compatible agent can become a participant in it. The same Tabby interface can be used normally by a person, or augmented by an agent when the task benefits from it. The agent gets access to Tabby's existing capabilities and live state without requiring a separate agent-specific workflow. This also means the human stays in control. The agent can reason, propose, and act through the application's existing operations, while Tabby remains responsible for state, validation, and money. WebMCP turns an existing web application into something an agent can participate in, rather than requiring every application to build its own agent. How we built it The central architectural decision was simple: There is one app, one state, and one set of operations. A button in the UI and a WebMCP tool call the same underlying store action. There is no separate agent backend and no special code path built only for AI. WebMCP exposes those existing operations to an agent. We deliberately split responsibilities: The model perceives and reasons. It can read a receipt photo, understand natural-language constraints, and reason about who ate what. The page computes. Tabby performs every allocation deterministically using integer minor units and largest-remainder arithmetic. The human decides. Every consequential write becomes a proposal with a visible diff before anything is committed. This means assign_items can say who ate which items , but it cannot tell Tabby how many rupees each person owes. The page calculates that. The same principle extends to settlement. Tabby computes the minimum-transfer plan rather than asking a language model to do the arithmetic. WebMCP tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool() , with a navigator.modelContext fallback for client compatibility. Registration is also tied to application state, so the page only exposes tools that are actually usable at that moment. For consequential actions, Tabby uses a propose → diff → accept flow. The commit operation can wait for a human to confirm in an in-page sheet. The agent cannot bypass that interaction. What became possible For humans, Tabby replaces tedious checkbox-by-checkbox bookkeeping with natural collaboration. You can say: "Ravi's vegetarian and doesn't drink. Meera arrived after the starters. Split tax and service based on what people actually ate." The agent can turn that context into a proposed item-level split. If the user remembers something later, they can simply edit the bill directly and ask the agent to incorporate the correction. For agents, Tabby provides something more useful than a database API: a live application they can reason about. The agent can read receipts, inspect expenses and balances, navigate to the relevant part of the page, propose changes, see human edits, and amend its own pending proposal. This creates a workflow that was difficult to achieve before: The human provides judgment and memory. The agent handles context and reasoning. The application handles state and computation. Challenges we ran into The hardest part wasn't registering tools. It was deciding what an agent should be allowed to do . Money is a particularly unforgiving domain. A language model can be excellent at understanding "Ravi didn't eat the prawns" and still be the wrong component to calculate 17% of a ₹4,381.27 bill. So we designed the tool surface around that distinction. We also had to make the WebMCP surface reflect the actual state of the application. Tools appear and disappear as capabilities become available. A receipt-reading tool shouldn't exist when there is no receipt to read. A commit operation shouldn't exist when there is no draft to commit. We also had to handle the reality of an evolving WebMCP implementation. Clients currently differ in API support, iframe discovery, and image content handling, so Tabby uses feature detection and keeps its registration at the top level. Accomplishments we're proud of We built a real expense application, not an agent demo wearing an expense-app costume. Every feature works without an agent. We made the agent share the application's state rather than mirror it. Human edits are immediately part of what the agent can reason about. We made arithmetic impossible for the model to get wrong. Money is represented as integer minor units throughout the system. Largest-remainder allocation guarantees that every split sums exactly to the original amount. We made human approval a system property, not a prompt instruction. Consequential operations follow a propose → diff → accept flow. The agent cannot simply decide to move money. We tested the actual WebMCP boundary. 61 unit tests cover money, splitting, settlement, and parsing. 73 Playwright tests exercise the WebMCP surface, including dynamic registration, human cancellation, two-browser collaboration, hand edits beneath open drafts, amendment chains, and malformed input. What we learned The interesting question isn't: "What can an agent do?" It's: "What should the agent do, and what should the application do?" WebMCP made that boundary surprisingly clear. Models are good at ambiguity, context, perception, and language. Applications are good at state, arithmetic, validation, permissions, and consequences. The best experience isn't necessarily an agent replacing the interface. In many cases, it's an agent that can join the interface without taking it away from you. What's next for Tabby The next step is making that collaboration more configurable. We want per-group agent permissions, so you could let an agent read your ledger without giving it permission to propose changes. We want receipt processing that explicitly surfaces uncertainty instead of guessing when a line cannot be read. And we want to extend the same model beyond expense splitting. Wherever an application already has a rich interface but the task contains too much context for a human to manage comfortably, an agent should be able to join the workflow without becoming the owner of it. Tabby started with a restaurant bill. The bigger idea is giving agents a place inside the interfaces people already use. title: Unfolded
pitch: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself
about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most.
