title: Care Command Center + WebMCP
pitch: A doctor-led command center where agents prepare clinical review and staff tasks from simulated camera and mobile observations.
about_excerpt:
A doctor-led command center where agents prepare clinical review and staff tasks from simulated camera and mobile observations.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 A training drill changes local state without external staff messaging. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Care Command Center overview with source feeds and a clinician review queue. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Source filters help an agent narrow camera and mobile observations. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 An observation is prepared for human review; no automated clinical action occurs. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 A training drill changes local state without external staff messaging. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Care Command Center overview with source feeds and a clinician review queue. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Source filters help an agent narrow camera and mobile observations. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 An observation is prepared for human review; no automated clinical action occurs. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 A training drill changes local state without external staff messaging. 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 Doctors and hospital leaders move between camera views, mobile observations, staff calls, and task lists while trying to keep clinical judgment clear. An agent can help gather context and coordinate the right role, but it should not turn an uncertain image into an autonomous diagnosis or treatment order. Care Command Center explores that boundary with a public, simulated environment containing no patient imagery or live hospital connection. 

 What it does 

 Care Command Center presents simulated fixed-camera and mobile observations, a clinician review queue, staff availability, and an activity log. Its six WebMCP tools let an agent: 

 
 summarize the command center; 
 list observations by status, urgency, and source type; 
 prepare one observation for clinician review; 
 draft a task for a staff role; 
 read simulated role availability; and 
 run a coordination drill. 
 

 Preparing an observation highlights the matching card and returns a verification checklist. Drafting a task leaves it pending. A doctor or authorized operator must independently verify the situation and use the visible Approve & queue action. The staff acknowledgment shown in the demo is simulated. 

 Why WebMCP 

 Without WebMCP, an agent must infer meaning from a dense dashboard and simulate clicks. With WebMCP, the page exposes a small typed contract that maps directly to its state. The agent can reliably answer “What needs review?”, “Prepare this observation for me,” or “Draft a task for the duty nurse” while the doctor stays in the same interface. 

 This creates a practical human-agent boundary: the agent compresses navigation and coordination, while the clinician retains the consequential decision. 

 What judges should notice 

 
 WebMCP leverage: the agent invokes native typed tools backed by page state; it does not scrape labels or replay brittle clicks. 
 Execution: one continuous workflow goes from an urgent simulated observation to review preparation, a structured staff-task draft, doctor approval, simulated staff acceptance, and an audit entry. 
 Potential impact: hospital leaders can coordinate observations and staff from one interface without hiding uncertainty or transferring clinical authority to the agent. 
 Creativity and ambition: the prototype applies browser-native agent tools to camera, mobile, clinician, and staff coordination while defining a realistic boundary for safety-critical work. 
 

 How we built it 

 The app is a dependency-free static site built with accessible HTML, responsive CSS, and JavaScript modules. webmcp.mjs registers six imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(). Each tool has a JSON Schema, a precise description, and an explicit side-effect boundary. The summary, observation-list, and staff-directory tools declare readOnlyHint: true. 

 The WebMCP adapter calls the same state functions used by the visible interface, so agent and human actions cannot drift into separate behavior. Pure functions cover queue ordering and the draft -> approved -> queued -> accepted task transition. Tests verify both operational rules and the public tool contract. 

 Challenges 

 The hard design question was what an agent should do when a camera or mobile image could be clinically important. A direct diagnose_patient or change_device_setting tool would be unsafe and misleading. We instead created prepare_clinical_review: it highlights the observation, returns a checklist, and states clearly that no diagnosis, prescription, device change, or staff message occurred. 

 Staff coordination follows the same boundary. draft_staff_task creates a structured, pending task. The human must approve it before the simulated staff inbox accepts it. A real WhatsApp adapter is intentionally not connected. 

 Accomplishments 

 
 Six working WebMCP tools discovered and executed in a WebMCP-enabled browser. 
 A visible workflow from simulated camera/mobile observation to clinician review and staff-task approval. 
 Separate clinical and operational safety boundaries. 
 A reproducible public demo with no accounts, private data, or external systems. 
 Tests covering queue and approval behavior plus a public MIT-licensed repository. 
 

 What we learned 

 For agent-facing clinical workflows, descriptions and approval boundaries matter as much as schemas. The useful role for an agent is often to collect context, prepare work, and make uncertainty visible. The doctor remains accountable for the decision. 

 What's next 

 Future work could add institution-approved authentication, secure mobile capture, camera and device adapters, EHR links, staff-channel adapters, immutable audit storage, role-based policy, localization, and a formal clinical-safety evaluation. Any real deployment would require privacy and security review, named-user access, retention limits, validation, and independent clinical governance.

title: SafeGuard
pitch: Every signal a WebMCP page declares can lie. SafeGuard proves it, then fixes it with a Human Mandate.
about_excerpt: Every signal a WebMCP page declares can lie. SafeGuard proves it, then fixes it with a Human Mandate. Like Comment Story Updates SafeGuard Inspiration WebMCP gives a web page a new power: registering tools that an AI agent can invoke. The browser's consent dialog is built from strings the page authors — its name, its description, its readOnlyHint. So I asked a simple question: what happens when the page lies? Nothing in the current design stops it. SafeGuard makes that trust gap concrete, then closes it. What it does SafeGuard is a self-contained browser demo — a virtual café exposing six tools — that demonstrates four real attacks on WebMCP's consent surface: Label mismatch — the dialog says "Donate $1", but the tool changes the account email. Hidden instruction — a harmless coupon also silently upgrades the membership to a paid plan. Tool substitution — a rogue script re-registers the trusted donate tool with the same name and description, but swapped code. Read-only lie — a tool declares readOnlyHint: true , so the dialog promises "no changes", but it actually closes the account. Then it shows the fix: a Human Mandate — rules the human grants up-front — that intercepts every mutation and checks the runtime effect primitive ({ action: … }), never the tool's declared name, description, or read-only flag. A violating call is refused before any dialog can lie. It runs live: six real WebMCP tools registered through document.modelContext, discoverable by any agent in Chrome with WebMCP enabled. How we built it Plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript — no framework, no backend, no build step. State can only mutate through a single Effects.apply() gateway, and the Mandate intercepts every call through it. That capability boundary is why a hidden second effect, a swapped tool, or a read-only lie is caught exactly like a blatant one. The repo also ships THREAT-MODEL.md (a reusable trust-boundary checklist plus a concrete proposal for the WebMCP spec) and mandate.json (a machine-readable policy), because the mandate is data, not UI. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is brand new — gated behind an origin trial and a browser flag, with sparse docs and moving spec details (the entry point, registerTool's return type, and AbortSignal requirements all shifted across Chrome versions). Running the demo against the real document.modelContext — not a shim — meant getting an origin-trial token for the hosted domain and testing headlessly across Chrome 149–152, including a 151 regression where tool invocations failed closed without an AbortSignal. The bigger challenge was conceptual: proving the consent surface is the weak point, not just asserting it. Each of the four attacks had to corrupt a different WebMCP primitive, so the demo stays a precise spec argument rather than a toy. Accomplishments that we're proud of The demo runs against the real WebMCP API — six tools genuinely registered through document.modelContext on the live site, not a simulation. And the Human Mandate is a real capability boundary: every state mutation flows through one gateway that checks the runtime effect primitive, so all four attacks — including the ones that lie inside the consent dialog — are caught by the same rule engine. That is the "person and agent together" idea made concrete: the human grants bounded authority up-front, the agent acts inside it, and a standing check sits between them. What we learned The consent dialog is built from page-authored strings, so it is only as honest as the page. Any guardrail that reasons about a tool's name, description, or readOnlyHint can be defeated by a lying page; the only trustworthy thing is what the tool actually does at runtime. That is why the mandate checks effect primitives, and why the spec proposal pushes for structured, machine-readable effects in tool results, verified readOnlyHint, and registration identity. What's next for SafeGuard Three spec-shaped fixes follow directly from the four attacks: structured, machine-readable effects in tool results; verifying readOnlyHint against those effects instead of trusting it; and registration identity so a "trusted" name can't be silently rebound. I'd love to prototype the first of these against a real agent. title: Hyphened - A 3D Neural Motion Studio
pitch: An experimental 3D studio for browser-native neural motion. Autoregressive diffusion runs through WebGPU, while WebMCP lets AI use the same live production controls as people.
about_excerpt: An experimental 3D studio for browser-native neural motion. Autoregressive diffusion runs through WebGPU, while WebMCP lets AI use the same live production controls as people. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Hyphened came out of a much larger attempt to build a living open-world simulation. The path looked roughly like this: At first, I had a game concept and a lot of questions about simulated worlds. I wanted worlds with history, physical space, autonomous actors, and events that continue without the player watching. Then I spent a long time trying to define the simulation framework itself. I explored journals, world laws, causal graphs, actor perception, action possibilities, branching, replay, and ways for people or models to participate without directly changing world state. Some of this produced useful ideas. Some of it produced an absurd amount of prose. The crowd simulation became the first serious reality check. Large populations, navigation, changing regions, and long-running activity forced the framework ideas to deal with actual runtime problems. Core Time grew out of the time-related part of that work. It became responsible for logical clocks, playback, history, seeking, branching, and replay. This deserved its own framework because the same time problems existed outside open-world simulation. WebGPU Engine grew from a different set of pressures. The browser needed a real way to run persistent GPU systems. Physics, rendering, crowds, and machine learning all needed to share resources and execute in a known order. The physics work made those requirements much stricter. A large GPU simulation cannot depend on JavaScript rebuilding84 reby rebuilding its state every frame. That pushed the engine toward persistent GPU state, fixed capacities, runtime commands, and clearer ownership. Around the same period, I started experimenting with machine learning on the GPU. That included tensor execution, policy learning, and an AI4Anim motion-matching demo. A lot of that code later disappeared, but it proved that learned behavior could run inside the same engine as simulation and rendering. Then NVIDIA released ARDY. It was an autoregressive diffusion model for human motion, driven by language and spatial constraints. It happened to need almost every system I had already been building. ARDY gave the work a concrete body. Time became a motion timeline. GPU state became a moving character. Spatial constraints became waypoints. History became the previous motion needed to generate the next motion. Rendering and physics could finally operate on the same actor. Hyphened came from turning that technical work into something I could actually use. It is a focused motion-production environment inside the larger open-world effort. WebMCP changed the project again. An agent could finally enter the same scene I was watching, use its real authoring operations, inspect, I could inspect the timeline, change something, play the result, and look at what it made. That last step is probably the clearest expression of what I was reaching for in the early simulation documents. The original idea involved model-driven actors with bounded access to a living world. Hyphened makes a small but real version of that possible. What it does Hyphened is an experimental 3D neural motion studio that runs in the browser. It uses NVIDIA's ARDY model to generate human motion through autoregressive diffusion. I can arrange prompt-conditioned motion on a timeline, place waypoints, direct multiple actors, cut between cameras, add physical objects, play the scene, and capture the result. The model is about 380 MB. It downloads into the browser and runs locally through WebGPU. The GPU handles model execution, motion reconstruction, character skinning, physics, and rendering. Hyphened also exposes its authoring operations through WebMCP. An agent can inspect the current scene, read the timeline, add actors, change their motion, edit waypoints and cameras, control playback, and capture visual evidence. The person and the agent work on the same scene. That is the part I care about most. How I built it The first browser implementation focused on matching the released ARDY model. I worked through checkpoint loading, transformer execution, diffusion sampling, tokenizer decoding, motion reconstruction, skeleton transforms, and skinning. The early version loaded the real model before it could produce useful live motion. Click-to-move was the first meaningful interaction. A click on the floor became a root-position constraint at a future frame, and ARDY generated the movement needed to reach it. That exposed the hardest part of the model. ARDY generates motion in short windows. Each new window depends on previous motion, prompt conditioning, random state, spatial constraints, and coordinate recentering. The new result then has to join the existing motion at exactly the right frame. I rebuilt the runtime several times while trying to make that work continuously. One version used a large application scheduler. Another used workers and service layers. One used a state machine with more than a thousand lines of control logic. Later versions tried shared generation queues for multiple actors. Most of that machinery is gone. Each failed design exposed a real rule. Slow generation could not control playback speed. Each actor needed independent history. Generated motion needed to remain one continuous sequence. JavaScript could issue commands, but it could not remain the owner of the generated result. The current design gives Core Time responsibility for authored time, playback, seeking, and history. WebGPU Engine owns GPU execution, resources, physics, and rendering. The learned-motion code generates retained motion on the GPU. Hyphened composes the scene around those systems. I directed the project while several generations of Codex agents wrote most of the code. That allowed the project to move very quickly. It also meant that entire architectures could appear before anyone had properly reviewed them. Deleting bad machinery became as important as building new capabilities. Challenges I ran into Motion failures are extremely visible. A small error in history or timing can make an actor jump, freeze, drift, disappear, or twist into a broken pose. Performance has been difficult for the same reason. Model inference and rendering share one GPU. Earlier runtimes performed too much model work near the display loop, so a slow diffusion step could become a visible pause or frame jump. The browser adds more limits. The model takes time to download and load onto the GPU. WebGPU support still varies. The original ARDY text encoder is much larger than the motion model, so Hyphened currently relies on a library of prepared prompt embeddings and a separate encoder for new prompts. Agent authoring introduced another set of problems. A tool call can succeed while the visible result is wrong. The agent needs temporal readouts, useful errors, stable scene identity, and images that let it judge its own work. The project history is also messy. There are hundreds of ARDY-related commits, several large rewrites, and some changes made under severe time pressure. I am still reviewing and simplifying that work. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The real ARDY checkpoint runs in the browser through WebGPU. It does not depend on a hosted motion-generation API. The project grew from one actor performing one prepared prompt into a timeline-based environment with multiple actors, motion prompts, waypoints, cameras, physics, persistent scenes, and agent authoring. I am proud that Core Time, WebGPU Engine, physics, and learned motion now participate in one visible product. These systems came from different parts of the open-world project, and Hyphened gives them a practical reason to work together. I am also proud of the WebMCP loop. An agent can work with the actual scene, move through its timeline, make changes, and capture what happened. That was an idea in the earliest simulation-framework documents. It now exists in a form I can use. What I learned Architecture shows up on screen. Bad time ownership becomes a frame jump. Bad history ownership breaks a motion transition. Bad GPU ownership stalls the interface. Bad authoring boundaries let an agent report success while the scene is visibly wrong. I also learned that the browser can support a serious combination of machine learning, simulation, physics, and rendering. Coordinating them is much harder than getting each one to run alone. The early simulation work makes more sense to me now. An agent needs access to a world's real objects, time, available actions, and observations. Giving it a chat box outside the world does not create that relationship. What's next for Hyphened Hyphened still needs faster scene loading, a clearer workspace, better characters, more motion, and stronger visual review. The learned-motion code also needs to finish becoming a reusable

title: ELANE - Agent-Ready Fashion Shopping with WebMCP
pitch: ÉLANE lets shoppers and AI agents build an outfit from trusted product data, then create a personal concept preview without uploading the customer’s photo to the store.
about_excerpt: ÉLANE lets shoppers and AI agents build an outfit from trusted product data, then create a personal concept preview without uploading the customer’s photo to the store. Like Comment Story Updates What inspired me Online fashion shopping involves many small decisions. A customer may know the occasion, budget, size, colour, and style they want, yet still need to move between product pages, filters, the shopping bag, promotional details, and policy pages. An AI agent can help, but relying on screen navigation alone is not always reliable. The agent may have to infer product details, selected sizes, garment images, prices, and the current bag state from different parts of the interface. I wanted to create a shopping experience in which the customer and agent work with the same visible state. I was especially interested in personal outfit previews. This led to a simple idea: bring your own agent to preview your personal look . The customer can keep a full-body photo inside their own agent conversation. ÉLANE provides the agent with references to the exact garments staged on the website. A compatible image-generating agent can then create a personal outfit concept before the customer decides what to buy. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP ÉLANE uses WebMCP to give an agent structured access to the same catalog, Style Studio, shopping bag, promotions, and store policies that the customer can see. After an outfit is staged in the Style Studio, the agent can call the read-only read_look_render_kit tool. The tool returns one public garment image for every staged item, together with the selected size, garment layer, and a concise generation brief. The agent therefore does not need to guess which clothes are present by examining a screenshot. It receives structured references directly from the website and works with the same Style Studio state that is visible to the customer. The customer also does not need to upload their photo to ÉLANE. The photo stays inside the customer’s agent conversation and is never received or stored by the website. The generated image is presented as a visual concept, not as evidence of exact fit, sizing, material, proportions, texture, or drape. This demonstrates the value of WebMCP clearly: the website supplies trusted product information and controlled actions, the customer supplies their personal context, and the agent connects the two. How it creates a better user experience Instead of manually working through filters and comparing numerous products, the customer can describe the result they want in natural language. In the demo, the customer asks for a polished smart-casual outfit for OpenAI DevDay 2026 in San Francisco, with a budget of CAD 1,500. The agent searches the live catalog and stages a complete four-piece men’s outfit in size M. The selected look costs CAD 1,100 and appears in the visible Style Studio. At this stage, the shopping bag remains empty because staging an outfit is only a preview. The customer then attaches a clear full-body photo to the agent conversation and asks for a personal preview of the staged outfit. The agent calls read_look_render_kit , receives references to the four exact garments, and creates the concept inside the conversation. The customer’s photo is never sent to ÉLANE, and the shopping bag remains unchanged. After reviewing the concept, the customer makes a separate request to add the outfit to the shopping bag and apply an eligible promotional offer. The agent rechecks the staged look and current bag, adds the four items in size M, evaluates the promotion terms, and applies ATELIER15. The visible total changes from CAD 1,100 to CAD 935 after a CAD 165 discount. The demo stops before checkout. No payment is collected, and no order is placed. The agent can also read ÉLANE’s current shipping, return, refund, delivery, and promotional policies. This allows it to explain store terms accurately without leaving the shopping experience or changing the customer’s bag. What people and agents can do together The customer provides the personal part of the decision: the occasion, budget, style preference, photo, size, and final approval. ÉLANE provides structured catalog information, the current Style Studio state, exact garment references, controlled shopping actions, promotion rules, and policy information. The agent connects these two sides. It can understand the request, find compatible products, stage an outfit, create a personal concept using its own image capability, and perform only the shopping actions explicitly approved by the customer. The customer and agent share one visible working state. When the agent stages an outfit or updates the shopping bag, the customer can see the same result on the page. This workflow would be difficult to make dependable through screen navigation alone. An agent would otherwise need to infer product information, selected items, sizes, garment images, prices, and bag state from multiple parts of the interface. WebMCP provides structured results, allowing both the customer and agent to understand what was selected, what was visualized, what changed, and what still requires approval. How I built the project I built ÉLANE with React 19, TypeScript, Vinext, Vite, and Tailwind CSS, with Codex assisting throughout development, debugging, testing, and documentation. The website functions as a complete human-operated storefront in browsers without WebMCP. Compatible clients receive an additional native, page-scoped tool layer. ÉLANE registers 22 imperative WebMCP tools directly through document.modelContext.registerTool : eight read tools and fourteen write tools. These tools cover catalog discovery, natural-language search, Style Studio state, outfit staging and refinement, exact garment references, shopping-bag operations, promotions, and store policies. Each tool uses a closed input schema, side-effect annotations, runtime validation, and lifecycle cleanup. Tool handlers read or update the same React state used by the human interface, helping the agent’s response remain consistent with what the customer can see. Read operations and state-changing operations are deliberately separated. Catalog, bag, promotion, policy, and render-kit reads do not change the shopping experience. Staging an outfit changes the Style Studio but not the bag. Adding products or applying a promotion requires a separate, explicit customer request. The automated verification suite checks all 22 storefront registrations, the two policy-route registrations, 20 output-budget boundary fixtures, and one generated preview asset for every product in the 88-item catalog. It also runs TypeScript validation, linting, WebMCP contract checks, and a production build. Challenges I faced The first challenge was keeping the Style Studio and shopping bag separate. A visual preview should never quietly become a purchase action. I designed the flow so that staging and refining an outfit are safe and reversible, while bag and promotion changes require clear customer intent. The second major challenge was personal image generation. There are many possible garment combinations, but I did not want the website to collect customer photos. I addressed this by creating the read-only read_look_render_kit tool. It returns references to the exact staged garments, allowing the customer’s own compatible agent to use those references with a photo already present in the conversation. Another challenge was natural-language catalog search. Customers do not always use exact product names. I added ranked search, aliases, stop-word handling, optional collection and price filters, and deterministic pagination to make product discovery more reliable. I also had to keep tool results compact enough for dependable agent reasoning. The implementation uses bounded responses and output-budget checks while still providing enough information for the agent to verify that it has reached the end of a result set. What I learned I learned that WebMCP works best when it improves an existing website instead of replacing it. Customers should still be able to browse normally, while agents receive structured tools for the same visible experience. I also learned that tool boundaries are as important as tool capabilities. Reading information, creating a preview, changing the shopping bag, applying a promotion, and beginning checkout should not be combined into one operation. Customers need to understand what changed and what still requires their approval. Another important lesson concerned privacy. Personalisation does not always require sending private information to every website involved in a workflow. In ÉLANE, the customer’s photo can remain with their chosen agent while the boutique provides only the selected garment references. Finally, I learned that smaller and more specific tool outputs make agent behaviour more reliable. title: LuxeSalon & Spa — WebMCP Autonomous Storefront
pitch: LuxeSalon & Spa turns a normal booking site into one an AI agent can search treatments, check live stylist availability, and book an appointment.
about_excerpt:
LuxeSalon & Spa turns a normal booking site into one an AI agent can search treatments, check live stylist availability, and book an appointment.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 I'd already spent a few hackathons this year building agent-driven tools for local businesses — a WhatsApp front-desk agent for salons and clinics being one of them. The recurring problem was always the same: to let an agent act on a business's behalf, you had to build a whole separate backend integration for it, replicating auth and state that already existed in the web app. 

 WebMCP flips that. Instead of standing up a server-side API just so an agent can act, you expose the tools directly in the browser, in the same JavaScript that already runs your app. When the WebMCP Challenge came up, a salon booking flow felt like the perfect fit — it's a pattern (search → check availability → book) that's instantly understandable in a 90-second demo, and mirrors exactly the kind of local-business use case I'd been building toward already. 

 What it does 

 LuxeSalon & Spa is a booking storefront that an AI agent can operate directly, not just describe. It registers four tools on document.modelContext : 

 
 salon.search_services — find treatments by keyword, category, or budget 
 salon.get_available_slots — check live stylist openings for a service and date 
 salon.book_appointment — propose a reservation, gated behind a human confirmation step 
 salon.get_booking_status — look up an existing booking by reference or phone number 
 

 Every tool call reacts live in the UI — the catalog filters as the agent searches, the schedule panel highlights the chosen slot, the appointments drawer opens when a booking is checked. A built-in Agent Inspector panel also lets anyone watch tool calls happen in real time, without needing dev tools open. 

 How we built it 

 I forked the WebMCP pattern from vercel/shop 's reference PR (#498) into a fresh Next.js app, then built out the salon's own domain model — services, stylists, time slots, and bookings — backed by a React context. 

 Each tool's inputSchema was written as strict JSON Schema aimed at an LLM reader rather than a human one: field descriptions spell out exactly what format and values are expected, since that's what the agent actually reasons over when deciding how to call a tool. 

 The part I spent the most care on was book_appointment . Chrome's WebMCP security guidance is explicit that state-changing tools shouldn't commit silently, so instead of booking immediately, the tool suspends on a Promise and surfaces a confirmation modal — the appointment only becomes real once a human clicks "Approve & Confirm." Read-only tools are marked with readOnlyHint: true ; the booking tool isn't. 

 Testing went through three layers: a custom in-app inspector for quick iteration, Google's official Model Context Tool Inspector Chrome extension to verify the tools were actually reachable via the real browser API, and finally a Gemini-backed agent inside that extension calling the tools from plain-language prompts — not scripted JSON. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 WebMCP is Chrome-only right now. I do most of my daily browsing in Safari, so development and testing ended up split across two browsers — build and iterate anywhere, but every real verification had to happen in Chrome behind chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . 
 The flag needs a real relaunch, not just quitting the browser. I lost real time thinking my tool registration code was broken, when it was actually a stale flag state — document.modelContext simply wasn't injected yet. 
 Vercel's preview URLs are login-walled by default. Right before wrapping up, I nearly submitted a preview deployment link that silently sits behind Vercel's SSO protection — invisible to anyone without account access. Caught it just in time and switched to the public production alias. 
 Building a genuine human-in-the-loop pause , not a fake one — the booking tool's execute() had to actually suspend on a real Promise tied to a user click, so an agent calling it truly waits on a person, rather than the UI just cosmetically showing a modal after the fact. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 Verified spec compliance the hard way: not just "the code looks right," but confirmed via Google's own inspector extension and a live Gemini agent successfully discovering and calling the tools from natural language. 
 A confirmation flow that's a real safety mechanism, directly reflecting the WebMCP security guide's read-only-vs-action distinction, rather than a decorative modal. 
 Going from a forked reference PR to a fully deployed, agent-tested, submission-ready storefront solo, inside the hackathon window. 
 

 What we learned 

 
 WebMCP's actual value isn't just "another API" — it's giving an agent access to a page's real client-side state and logic, instead of screen-scraping a UI built for humans. 
 Tool descriptions are a UX surface too, just for a different reader. An agent decides whether and how to call your tool based entirely on how well you've described it. 
 Agentic tools need the same "don't trust the caller blindly" instincts as any other security-sensitive code — read-only actions can run freely, but anything that spends money or commits a resource needs a checkpoint a human controls. 
 

 What's next for LuxeSalon & Spa — WebMCP Autonomous Storefront 

 
 Extend from a single salon to a small directory of local Bengaluru businesses, closer to the original WhatsApp front-desk concept this grew out of. 
 Add cancel_appointment and reschedule_appointment tools, plus stylist-specific search. 
 Look into a WebMCP polyfill so agents in non-Chrome browsers can still discover and call the same tools. 
 Apply for the Chrome Origin Trial so the experience works for real users without requiring the testing flag.

title: Creative Community Orchestrator
pitch: From creative needs to the right plan, tools, and actions - powered by WebMCP
about_excerpt: From creative needs to the right plan, tools, and actions - powered by WebMCP Like Comment Story Updates Creative Community Orchestrator From the right plan to the right creative action — powered by WebMCP. Inspiration Adobe's community is full of creators asking practical questions: Which Creative Cloud plan is right for me? Will Premiere Pro run on my machine? Which app or feature should I use for this? How do I solve this creative problem? Creators often know what they want to accomplish , but not which plan, product, capability, or workflow will get them there. Creative software is particularly challenging for agents because the right answer often depends on structured context that is easy to miss when interpreting webpages: region, student eligibility, plan contents, product-specific system requirements, checkout destinations, and capabilities inside individual applications . An agent might return US pricing to a student in India, retrieve generic Creative Cloud requirements when asked about Premiere Pro, or suggest manual editing techniques without discovering that Photoshop has a specific capability — Harmonize — designed for the problem. The agent understands what the creator wants, but it cannot always reliably discover what the creative ecosystem can offer. That inspired Creative Community Orchestrator : use WebMCP to make the creative ecosystem structured and discoverable to agents, helping creators move from intent to the right action faster. What it does Creative Community Orchestrator connects a creator's intent and context to the right plan, product, capability, workflow, and action. A design student in India can ask: "I need Photoshop, Illustrator and occasional video editing. Which plan should I get?" The agent can use her needs, region, and eligibility to find a relevant plan and regional offer, check product-specific compatibility, and guide her to the appropriate checkout path. The same approach extends to creation: "Clean up these jewelry photos, give them a premium campaign look, and create an Instagram post and launch flyer." The agent can discover capabilities the creator may not know exist and connect them into a workflow: Firefly → Photoshop + Harmonize → Adobe Express The creator describes the outcome. The agent discovers the path. This reduces searching, conflicting information, and dead ends — creating a more direct path from intent → confidence → action . How we built it We built Creative Community Orchestrator as a human-browsable website for exploring creative goals, workflows, capabilities, products, and plans. Using WebMCP , we expose key capabilities as structured semantic tools for external agents, including: Plan recommendation and regional pricing Product-specific compatibility Checkout navigation Creative capability discovery Cross-product workflow composition The tools accept structured context such as region, eligibility, product needs, device context, and creative goals , and return structured results agents can use in subsequent steps. This lets an external agent move from: intent → tool discovery → verified information → capability discovery → workflow → action without relying on brittle DOM interpretation or requiring creators to understand the structure of the creative ecosystem. The website remains fully usable by people through its normal interface, while WebMCP gives agents a structured interface to the same ecosystem. Creators use the UI. Agents use WebMCP. Both access the same creative ecosystem. Challenges we ran into One of the biggest challenges was turning a fragmented creative journey into structured context an agent could reliably use . Plan recommendations depend on region, eligibility, required apps, pricing, and compatibility, while creative questions require mapping natural-language intent to the right capability. Capability discovery was especially interesting. Users rarely ask for features by name. Someone might say, "the lighting on this object doesn't match the scene," and the agent needs to connect that problem to Photoshop Harmonize . Another challenge was deciding what should become a WebMCP tool . Instead of exposing every button or UI interaction, we focused on meaningful creator intents: recommend a plan, check compatibility, discover a capability, find the correct purchase path, and compose a workflow. We also wanted the website to remain useful to humans while becoming understandable to agents , without turning the experience into another chatbot. Accomplishments that we're proud of We're proud that the project demonstrates WebMCP across a connected creator journey: Plan discovery → Regional pricing → Compatibility → Checkout → Capability discovery → Creative workflow The agent can move beyond recommending broad products and discover specific capabilities such as Harmonize based on the creator's actual problem. For a creative workflow, the collaboration can look like: Firefly → create the campaign treatment Photoshop + Harmonize → refine the composition and resolve the lighting mismatch Adobe Express → create the Instagram post and launch flyer Meera doesn't need to know beforehand which plan fits her needs, that Harmonize exists, which application contains it, or how multiple creative products can work together. At the same time, the experience remains fully human-browsable while exposing the same ecosystem to external agents. What we learned Our biggest learning was that the agentic web isn't only about helping agents perform actions — it's also about helping them discover what actions are possible . Creators think in outcomes: "Which plan fits me?" , "Will this run on my machine?" , "Make this composition look natural," or "Turn this into a campaign." They shouldn't need to know the exact plan, product, feature name, or navigation path first. Previously, creators had to translate their needs into the product ecosystem themselves: research plans → compare prices → check requirements → discover products → find features → assemble a workflow With WebMCP, that responsibility can be shared: Creators provide intent, context, and creative judgment. Agents discover, verify, recommend, and orchestrate. WebMCP becomes the bridge between creator intent and product capability . What's next for Creative Community Orchestrator Next, we want to expand Creative Community Orchestrator into an agent-accessible support layer across the creator journey . That includes troubleshooting : a creator could say, "My Premiere Pro export looks washed out," and the agent could discover relevant product-specific guidance instead of returning generic results. We also want to connect feature discovery directly to feature access . If the agent discovers that Harmonize is the right capability, it should take the creator to the exact feature, product experience, or relevant page where they can learn more or start using it. Our vision expands the journey to: Choose → Verify → Discover → Troubleshoot → Navigate → Create So creators can stay focused on what they want to accomplish , while agents reliably discover how the creative ecosystem can help them get there. People describe what they want to accomplish. Agents discover what's possible and help them act on it. From creative intent to creative action — with WebMCP. title: Your AI Can Now Choose Your Health Tests: medtests webmcp
pitch: Your AI can now discover the right health screening, ask the right questions, and guide you through it — using WebMCP.
about_excerpt:
Your AI can now discover the right health screening, ask the right questions, and guide you through it — using WebMCP.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI can already talk about your symptoms. But when it needs a structured screening tool, the experience breaks. 

 You leave the conversation, search for a test, complete it on another website, then bring the result back. 

 We wanted to remove that gap. 

 What if a health website wasn't just readable by an AI — but actually usable by it? 

 What it does 

 Medtests makes structured health screening tools available to AI agents through WebMCP. 

 An agent can discover available screenings, retrieve the questions, guide the user through them, score the answers, and return the structured result. 

 For example, instead of only answering: 

 "Could these symptoms be ADHD?" 

 an AI can use Medtests to start a relevant screening flow and guide the user through it. 

 The user doesn't have to figure out which page to open or copy information between an AI and a website. 

 How we built it 

 We turned Medtests from a traditional website into an agent-accessible website using WebMCP. 

 The browser exposes five tools: 

 
 list_screenings 
 get_screening 
 score_screening 
 get_crisis_resources 
 get_chat_analysis_protocol 
 

 The tools are registered through the browser's WebMCP interface using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . 

 The application is written in JavaScript and deployed on Cloudflare Workers with Wrangler, with deployment through GitHub. 

 The important architectural decision was simple: 

 Instead of building another chatbot, we made the website itself callable by AI agents. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Health screening is a good example of why agent interfaces need structure. 

 An agent shouldn't have to scrape a webpage and guess what a button, question, or score means. 

 We had to turn human-facing interactions into explicit tools with predictable inputs and outputs, while keeping the existing website useful for humans. 

 We also had to separate screening from diagnosis. Medtests provides structured screening tools and results — not medical diagnoses. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We built a working WebMCP layer on top of a real health website. 

 The same resource can now serve two users: 

 Humans can use the website. Agents can use the tools. 

 No separate AI product is required. 

 That is the part we're most excited about. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP changes what a website can be. 

 For the last 30 years, websites have primarily exposed interfaces for humans: pages, forms and buttons. 

 Agents need something different: capabilities with names, schemas and structured results. 

 Once those capabilities exist, the website stops being something an AI merely reads. 

 It becomes something the AI can use. 

 What's next 

 Medtests is the first use case. 

 The bigger idea is to make useful parts of the web agent-native — so an AI can move from explaining what someone could do to actually helping them do it. 

 The web was built for humans to click. WebMCP lets agents act.

Like 1 Comment Story Updates Ikuyo trip home Ikuyo trip timetable ChatGPT and Ikuyo Ikuyo task list Ikuyo expense list [Disclosure: the following is written with help AI correcting grammar and sentence structure; the idea and draft is originally human-written] Inspiration Travel planning is a living conversation of ideas, changes, and constraints. A useful itinerary must preserve all of that context. I want to empower people with agents, not replace them in the planning process. What it does Ikuyo is a collaborative itinerary workspace for travellers and their agents. Through WebMCP, agents can read a trip and create or update activities, accommodations, day plans, tasks, expenses, and comments. The result is not a one-off itinerary, but a shared plan that remains editable, visible, and understandable to the people travelling. The problem Planning a trip with an agent is a back-and-forth process of tuning and refining, not one-shot prompting. People need to feel in control of their plans while staying flexible when they change. Chat apps do not feel flexible enough, while spreadsheets are too rigid. What collaboration looks like The user asks the agent to draft a realistic travel plan around the fixed bookings, with a few itinerary suggestions. The agent creates it using Ikuyo's WebMCP tools. The user then studies and revises the plan, asking the agent for more suggestions. The agent sees the latest changes through WebMCP and uses them to give further suggestions. This goes back and forth until both parties are happy with the final itinerary. Why Ikuyo does not have an in-app agent In today's landscape, LLMs evolve very quickly, and everyone's preferred agent changes often. Committing to a specific agent provider requires significant ongoing maintenance for Ikuyo. It also conflicts with my goal of keeping users in control. Instead of providing an agent for users, I expect them to bring their own agent to help with travel planning. Why WebMCP is essential Because I expect users to bring their own agents, they would otherwise need to copy and paste information between Ikuyo and an agent's chat interface. This is inefficient. Another option is for the agent to control Ikuyo through browser automation. That is not ideal either: Ikuyo is built for people, so an agent must read and guess at HTML elements before performing actions. This makes each operation slow and unreliable. WebMCP solves this by exposing Ikuyo's product actions as tools with typed input and output schemas. The agent can discover the current trip, create and update itinerary objects, and read comments and costs from the live source of truth. Tool availability follows the user's role: viewers can read, editors can plan, and owners manage sharing. Destructive operations remain deliberate, human-confirmed UI actions. How we built it This project started in 2024, when I had the idea of making a Google Calendar-like web application for travel planning. The application uses React and Radix Themes for the frontend, MapTiler for maps, and PHP/Laravel/MySQL for the backend. It originally used InstantDB, but I migrated away from it in late August after its shutdown announcement. The calendar grid uses CSS Grid, and all frontend time and date calculations use Temporal. During this hackathon, I extended the application to support WebMCP, with the help of LLM agents (GPT-5.6). I imported Modern Web Guidance's WebMCP skill and used it while building. Afterward, I tested a range of prompts to fine-tune the tool descriptions so future agents can fill them in correctly. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was treating WebMCP as more than another function for calling backend APIs. I had to consider it from the user's point of view and align the UI capabilities with the WebMCP tools, so they could call the existing backend APIs more efficiently. I also adjusted some backend API fields to make them more intuitive for agents to use. The application initially focused on people, so I naturally built it around adding or editing one object at a time. However, when agents performed operations one by one, they were still slow to reach the desired outcome even when the plan was already synthesised in the context. I then added batch versions of the WebMCP tools so agents could create and edit itinerary activities more efficiently. Accomplishments that we're proud of I'm proud that this travel-planning application now integrates deeply with agentic capabilities. People can bring their preferred agents to interact with the site while remaining in control of their own travel plans. What we learned I learned that building for agents is different from building for people. People receive hints through the visual UI, while agents can access only the tool descriptions. I therefore need to fine-tune the capabilities so agents can operate correctly and efficiently. I also learned that agents work faster than people, so they need ways to batch-create and batch-edit activities. What's next for Ikuyo I have used Ikuyo to plan my own travels, and other people have shared that they completed trips using it. However, it still lacks some human-to-human collaboration capabilities, such as expense splitting and combining. It also needs better support for travel plans that span multiple regions and time zones. Those are the areas I plan to tackle next. A live dashboard where you and your agent can design and manage your restaurant

 Inspiration 

 After first learning about the WebMCP Challenge, I ran through a list of ideas I always wanted to try building: an outfit generator, a groceries tracker and recipe book, a sleep productivity app, and others, but none of these seemed to really fit the use case. Then, while sitting down at a restaurant with a few friends, a waiter accidentally brought us the wrong item. An honest mistake, something that I'm sure most people have experienced, and one of the difficulties that come with managing a restaurant. After coming home, and following a bit of research into restaurant software, I decided to build a live restaurant manager, where a manager can operate from a live view of their restaurant, aided by an agent to lessen the workload on the employees. That product is now Sous. 

 What it does 

 Sous is a live dashboard where you and your agent can design and manage your restaurant. 

 Starting with design mode , both a manager and an agent can rearrange and edit the floor layout to design or match their restaurant. Each table has its own controls, with the ability to change the size, number of seats, name, and waiter section. With WebMCP integration, the agent could simply be given a picture of the restaurant and call tools to match the in-app layout to the real thing. 

 Service mode is where you actually run the restaurant. Assigning tables, taking orders, delivering orders, and managing all the work in between happens here. Humans can perform all the functions, but the agent side is where it shines. By connecting the agent to a Yelp waitlist, a live feed, or other sources of information, it can automatically track and manage everything that is happening within the restaurant, with all the changes reflecting visually for the manager to see. WebMCP allows the agent to manage all the smaller functions, with only physical interactions left to employees, lessening the friction that comes with running the restaurant. 

 How we built it 

 As I am non-technical, this project was mostly built with the help of Claude. The app runs on React, Vite, and TypeScript, and all changes on it are saved locally to the user's browser without the need for logging in, so there is no backend or database. It runs similarly to the apps seen in OpenAI's WebMCP showcase. 

 WebMCP's whole author-facing surface is registerTool : a name the agent calls, a description it decides with, an inputSchema for the arguments, and an execute that runs. Sous makes that call once, over a table of 30 definitions, rather than writing thirty literal copies of it, so grep registerTool src/webmcp.ts finds the wiring, and src/tools.ts holds the tools themselves. 

 Challenges 

 Since this was my first time building an app, naturally it was filled with challenges, especially since I don't have a technical background. One of the biggest problems I came across was realizing midway that the app did not really match my vision. While AI has been a huge help in this challenge, I had essentially allowed it to build everything from scratch, without providing a list of exactly how I wanted the app to look and function. The main canvas in the middle took multiple iterations, including hours spent in Claude Design, before I arrived at something I believed fit the app. 

 Takeaways 

 As I mentioned above, I had multiple other app ideas before Sous, but I never got myself to actually build them out until now. The WebMCP Challenge finally pushed me to build my first app, and that experience is definitely my biggest takeaway from this challenge. Also, while I knew about APIs and MCPs before, this challenge introduced me to WebMCP, and seeing and building the possibilities myself makes me excited for the future of this technology. 

 What's next for Sous 

 Sous is an app I built on a whim with Claude Code, but it does help solve a problem that many restaurants face. Past this challenge, Sous could be integrated with existing POS systems in restaurants and other software like Yelp or Stripe, in order to help it move past simply being a dashboard and become an all-in-one app for restaurant management. Likely, this would include building out the backend, so that will be another learning opportunity for the future.

title: Vitals Incident Room
pitch: AI agents and engineers investigate, remediate, and verify production incidents together.
about_excerpt: AI agents and engineers investigate, remediate, and verify production incidents together. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Vitals Incident Room Dashboard Vitals Incident Room Agent Capabilities Vitals Incident Room Architecture Inspiration Vitals started with a simple frustration: when a production incident happens, engineers rarely investigate it in one place. They jump between dashboards, logs, traces, deployment history, alerts, and remediation tools, manually connecting the dots under pressure. While exploring WebMCP, I saw an opportunity to rethink that workflow. AI agents are increasingly capable of reasoning about complex engineering problems, but traditionally they have had to interact with web applications through the UI or through completely separate integrations. That creates a gap between what an agent can reason about and what it can actually do. So I asked: What if the observability application itself could expose its capabilities directly to an AI agent, while the engineer and agent remained in the same workspace? That became Vitals Incident Room , an experiment in what an agent-native incident-response workflow could look like. I wanted to go beyond "add a chatbot to a dashboard." The goal was to make the agent a genuine participant in the incident lifecycle while keeping the human in control of consequential decisions. What it does Vitals Incident Room is a WebMCP-powered incident-response workspace where engineers and AI agents investigate, remediate, and verify production incidents together. For demonstration, a checkout-api service experiences a severe latency and error-rate regression shortly after deployment v2.8.3 . The agent can discover and invoke structured WebMCP tools to: inspect service health, query metrics, compare deployments, inspect distributed traces, search operational logs, analyze the gathered evidence, prepare a remediation, apply an approved remediation, verify recovery. The investigation can look like: get_service_health ↓ query_metrics ↓ compare_deployments ↓ inspect_trace ↓ search_logs ↓ analyze_incident The agent correlates those signals and identifies the most likely cause: a database query regression introduced in v2.8.3 . It can then prepare a rollback to the last known-good version. However, the agent cannot authorize its own action. prepare_remediation ↓ HUMAN APPROVAL ↓ apply_remediation ↓ verify_recovery ↓ RESOLVED The remediation changes the application's simulated system state, and the final verification checks that both latency and error rate have actually returned to acceptable levels. The result is a shared workflow rather than a chatbot sitting beside an observability dashboard. How I built it Vitals Incident Room extends existing Vitals observability work with a focused browser-based Incident Room designed specifically around WebMCP. The application is built with TypeScript and React, with a deterministic simulated observability environment so the complete workflow can be reproduced without requiring real production credentials or infrastructure. The architecture separates the WebMCP layer from the application domain: Architecture Layer Component Responsibility Human Engineer Reviews evidence and authorizes consequential actions Web App Incident Room Presents shared incident state and workflow Agent Interface WebMCP Tool Surface Exposes structured capabilities to the AI agent Agent AI Agent Discovers tools, gathers evidence, analyzes the incident, and executes approved actions Observability Metrics · Logs · Traces · Deployments Provides the signals used for diagnosis Analysis Evidence Correlation Combines signals into a ranked root-cause hypothesis Remediation Prepare → Approve → Execute Proposes and safely applies the remediation Verification Recovery Checks Confirms latency and error-rate recovery before resolution Core flow: Engineer → Incident Room → WebMCP → AI Agent → Observability Data → Evidence Analysis → Remediation Proposal → Human Approval → Execution → Verification The WebMCP layer exposes nine focused tools with explicit schemas and annotations. Read-only investigation capabilities are separated from state-changing operations, and operational logs are explicitly treated as untrusted content. I also made the demo stateful. A rollback doesn't simply change a label from "failed" to "resolved"; it changes the simulated deployment, latency, error rate, and database-query performance. Verification then reads that new state. This gives us a deterministic cause-and-effect loop: v2.8.3 ↓ latency regression ↓ agent investigation ↓ rollback to v2.8.2 ↓ metrics recover ↓ incident resolved Most importantly, I designed the human approval boundary outside the WebMCP action surface. The agent can prepare a remediation, but only the engineer can authorize it. Challenges I ran into The biggest challenge was deciding how much of Vitals to expose. Vitals already covers a broad observability workflow, and my first instinct was to make everything agent-accessible. That quickly became the wrong direction. A large collection of loosely connected tools would demonstrate API coverage, but not why WebMCP fundamentally changes the product. I narrowed the project to one complete incident-response journey and treated everything else as secondary. Another challenge was making an agent-driven workflow believable without depending on real production infrastructure. I solved that with deterministic metrics, logs, traces, deployment history, and mutable runtime state. This lets us make the entire experience reproducible while preserving realistic relationships between the signals. I also had to think carefully about authority and safety. An agent that can investigate an incident and then immediately authorize its own rollback creates a dangerous feedback loop. I separated proposal, approval, execution, and verification so the human remains responsible for the consequential decision. Finally, WebMCP is an emerging browser capability, so I had to pay close attention to tool schemas, browser support, registration behavior, tool annotations, and the difference between a WebMCP-capable webpage and the agent consuming those tools. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I'm most proud that the project evolved beyond a conventional "AI + dashboard" demo. The agent can actually compose multiple capabilities exposed by the webpage: Health + Metrics + Deployment history + Traces + Logs ↓ Evidence-based diagnosis I'm also proud of the human-in-the-loop safety model. A consequential action cannot be executed until it has been explicitly authorized by the engineer, and recovery is not declared until the post-action state passes verification. Another accomplishment is that the demo is completely deterministic. I can reset the environment and reproduce the same incident, investigation, remediation, and recovery sequence without relying on external production systems. Incident Room also deliberately treat operational log data as untrusted content. That distinction matters in an agentic environment because data discovered by a tool should not automatically become an instruction to the agent. Most importantly, Vitals Incident Room gave us a concrete answer to a question the project started with: What does an observability application look like when an AI agent is a first-class participant rather than an add-on chatbot? What I learned My biggest lesson was that WebMCP is most interesting when it changes the workflow, not when it merely exposes functions. A collection of tools is easy to demonstrate. Designing a workflow in which an agent can discover, compose, and act on those tools while sharing state with a human is much more interesting. I also learned that tool design is effectively part of product design. Names, descriptions, schemas, output structures, side-effect annotations, and error behavior all influence how reliably an agent can use an application. Another important lesson was to separate: Evidence ↓ Analysis ↓ Authorization ↓ Action ↓ Verification That separation made the application easier to reason about and gave us a much clearer safety model. Finally, I learned that the best agent experiences are not necessarily fully autonomous. In many engineering workflows, the strongest design is agent speed + human judgment . What's next for Vitals Incident Room This challenge version is intentionally focused on one incident-response journey. The next step is to connect that workflow to real observability infrastructure. Future versions could support real Prometheus metrics, OpenTelemetry traces, production log providers, deployment systems, and runbooks while preserving the same WebMCP interaction model. I also want to explore richer agent collaboration, including: incident timelines that agents can continuously update, safer remediation strategies such as canary changes, richer evidence graphs and dependency analysis, post-incident report generation, agent permissions based on risk and environment, multiple engine

title: Fabric
pitch: Fabric turns your devices into one living runtime where AI agents build, run, and hot-swap WebMCP tools using available files, cameras, compute, and human input as capabilities change in real time.
about_excerpt: Fabric turns your devices into one living runtime where AI agents build, run, and hot-swap WebMCP tools using available files, cameras, compute, and human input as capabilities change in real time. Like Comment Story Updates Fabric lets an agent combine capabilities across desktop, laptop, and mobile to compile a new WebMCP photo-search tool during conversation. Fabric makes people part of the runtime by routing a camera request to user’s phone, continuing the cross-device workflow with their input. Fabric detects a disconnected device, replans the affected tool, and hot-registers version two under the same name and schema. Fabric: WebMCP Tools Across Your Devices Fabric connects your devices so agents can build, run, and hot-swap WebMCP tools from whatever files, cameras, compute, and people are available right now. Try Fabric Live · Explore the Source Code (MIT) · Watch the Demo Inspiration: One Fabric for People, Agents, and Devices AI agents are capable reasoners, but the moment they need to operate in the physical world, they run into a hard boundary: the tools and data they need are fragmented across multiple devices and humans. The draft contract PDF is saved on your laptop. A signed paper addendum is sitting physically on your desk. Your phone has the macro lens to photograph it clearly. A workstation desktop in the next room has an idle discrete GPU capable of lightning-fast inference. You are sitting in the middle of all of it, holding the judgment and authority needed to approve the final action. Today, bridging these disconnected islands turns you into a copy-paste courier. You email attachments to yourself, AirDrop photos between folders, upload private documents to remote cloud APIs, and manually synchronize three separate screens. The agent understands the high-level intent, yet it remains trapped inside a single browser tab. Fabric was built around a straightforward question: What if your devices did not need custom native agents or centralized cloud storage to collaborate? What if an agent could treat your entire personal device ecosystem, and the people in the room, as a single, ad-hoc capability fabric? Open a link on your laptop, point a phone or tablet at a QR code, and click a link on your desktop. In seconds, every screen negotiates an ad-hoc peer mesh. The agent inspects the room, sees what each device and human can do, compiles task-specific WebMCP tools on the fly, and gets straight to work. What It Does Fabric changes the agent experience from a passive chat interface into an active, multi-device team that dynamically organizes around whatever hardware is in the room. Dynamic Multi-Device Plug-and-Play You start a session on whatever device is in front of you. As other hardware enters the room, scanning a QR code or opening a URL seamlessly adds that device to the fabric without requiring software installations, browser extensions, or synchronized system accounts. Each device automatically contributes its natural strengths: Smartphones contribute high-resolution cameras, mobility, and personal photo libraries. Laptops offer local document stores, working directory access, and active workspace management. Desktops and Workstations volunteer hardware-accelerated compute, idle GPUs, and high-throughput batch processing. Tablets contribute stylus inputs, touch annotations, and review surfaces. Humans contribute real-world perception, contextual judgment, and explicit approval. Fluid, Local-First Execution Once devices join the fabric, the agent orchestrates tasks across them based on which node is best suited for each sub-task. For instance, when you ask the agent to search your personal photo library for a specific tax receipt, Fabric plans a distributed pipeline. Instead of uploading your camera roll to a server, the phone executes an on-device vision model locally in its browser engine. It generates vector embeddings right on the device, sends compact floating-point scores across an encrypted peer-to-peer channel, and transfers only the single matching image preview to your laptop display. Your personal media stays entirely private and local. First-Class Human Collaboration Rather than treating human interaction as an unhandled exception where the model halts, Fabric treats human judgment as an intrinsic stage of the tool pipeline. When generating a verified legal dossier, the agent can initiate a multi-device pipeline: It pulls the digital draft from your laptop filesystem. It pushes an interactive capture prompt directly to your phone screen, asking you to photograph the missing physical document. The moment you capture the image, your phone runs in-browser optical character recognition and pipes the extracted text back into the pipeline. Before any final document is stamped and exported, an interactive verification card pops up on your tablet or phone, displaying the extracted metadata with an approval toggle. You review the summary, tap Approve, and the agent completes the export. Human intent and physical actions blend directly into the execution graph alongside automated compute. Self-Healing Topology Because physical hardware is dynamic, devices frequently disconnect, sleep, or move out of Wi-Fi range. Fabric actively monitors node presence. If your desktop drops offline while performing vector calculations, Fabric immediately detects the missing node, re-routes the pending pipeline stages to run on your laptop processor, and hot-swaps the underlying tool implementation while keeping the exact same tool interface active. The agent continues the conversation uninterrupted. Why Fabric Is a Strong Fit for WebMCP Most WebMCP implementations register a static, pre-compiled set of tool definitions when the browser initializes. Fabric approaches WebMCP as a dynamic runtime compilation target : Just-In-Time Tool Synthesis: Instead of exposing fixed endpoints, the host inspects the live device mesh and synthesizes custom, validated execution graphs tailored to the user's specific prompt. The Web as a Strict Permission Sandbox: Fabric reaches local hardware, cameras, and filesystems exclusively through standard browser capabilities explicitly granted by the user. The agent gains powerful multi-device physical reach without obtaining unrestricted operating system access. Schema-Preserving Hot Swaps: When the physical topology changes, Fabric preserves the tool's external identifier and JSON Schema contract while hot-swapping the internal execution graph, avoiding model hallucinations caused by disappearing or mutating tool schemas. Cloudflare Architecture Fabric uses Cloudflare Workers and Durable Objects to provide an ultra-low-latency edge coordination layer for the peer mesh: Transactional Edge Coordination: A dedicated Cloudflare Durable Object manages each room, maintaining an authoritative, ordered log of peer presence, ICE candidate exchanges, and active capability leases. The Durable Object persists compiled tool graphs to transactional storage, allowing pipelines to recover seamlessly if the host browser reloads. Low-Cost Edge Parking via WebSocket Hibernation: Fabric leverages the Cloudflare WebSocket Hibernation API. When a room is idle, the Durable Object is evicted from active worker memory while maintaining open client WebSocket connections. The edge fabric remains parked and available indefinitely at virtually zero idle compute cost until an incoming frame wakes it up. Signaling and Data Transport Fallback: Browsers negotiate direct peer-to-peer WebRTC DataChannels using the Durable Object as an SDP signaling bus. SCTP-framed DataChannels deliver high-throughput binary tensor and image streams with zero server hops. If symmetric NATs or corporate enterprise firewalls prevent direct peer traversal, the Durable Object automatically falls back to an encrypted, zero-knowledge relay mode. How WebMCP Is Implemented The WebMCP integration layer lives in app/src/webmcp/ and connects ad-hoc peer networks directly into standard browser agent contexts: Dynamic Registration via registerTool : When a task is planned, Fabric compiles the pipeline into a validated Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) and registers it immediately using document.modelContext.registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) . Each registration is bound to a dedicated JavaScript AbortController . When topology updates occur, Fabric invokes abort() , cancels the pending runtime pipeline, and re-registers the updated DAG under the same name and input schema. Validated Execution Pipelines: Instead of generating unverified code strings, the planner outputs a structured pipeline blueprint. Fabric checks every step, data flow, and device lease before calling registerTool . Adaptive Client-Side Inference Engines: Workstations and Desktops: Utilizes Transformers.js running CLIP ViT-B/32 through WebGPU with fp16 half-precision GEMM kernels, delivering sub-50ms vector generation.
