 Inspiration 

 Applying for jobs can be exhausting. You can spend hours searching through listings, comparing requirements, figuring out where your skills fit, and writing a different cover letter for every application. 

 AI agents can make a lot of that process much faster. They can search, analyze job descriptions, identify skill gaps, and even write application drafts. But there is one part we didn't want an agent to handle on its own: actually submitting the application . 

 That led us to the idea behind EzApply . 

 We wanted to build something where the agent takes care of the repetitive work, while the candidate stays in control of the decisions that matter. When we came across WebMCP , it felt like a natural fit. Instead of an agent trying to scrape a page or interact with a UI blindly, WebMCP lets the website expose structured tools that an agent can use directly. 

 So we thought: what if applying for jobs felt less like filling out endless forms and more like having an AI co-pilot? 

 That's what EzApply is built around. 

 What it does 

 EzApply is a Job Application Command Center built with WebMCP. 

 The agent can take a job from discovery all the way to a ready-to-submit application, but the candidate always has the final say. 

 We currently expose six WebMCP tools: 

 
 search_jobs — Finds jobs based on keywords, salary requirements, and remote preferences. 
 score_job_fit — Compares the candidate's skills with a job's requirements and calculates a fit percentage. 
 identify_skill_gap — Shows which skills are missing and gives suggestions for improving the candidate's resume. 
 generate_application_draft — Creates a tailored cover letter and sends it to the Approval Queue. 
 save_to_drafts — Saves changes made by the candidate to an AI-generated application. 
 submit_application — Handles the final submission, but only after the candidate explicitly confirms it. 
 

 Human-in-the-Loop Approval 

 This is the part of EzApply we're most proud of. 

 AI can prepare an application, but it doesn't get to decide when it is submitted. 

 Every generated application goes into an Approval Queue . The candidate can read the cover letter, make changes directly, and then approve it. 

 The submit_application tool also checks for candidateConfirmation: true inside its execute() function. This means the safety check isn't only part of the interface. The tool itself refuses to submit an application without explicit confirmation. 

 We wanted this to be a real safety boundary rather than just a button that looks like one. 

 Agent Console 

 We also wanted users to understand what the agent was actually doing. 

 The Agent Console displays WebMCP tool calls as they happen, including timestamps and status information. This makes the agent's actions visible instead of turning the whole process into a black box. 

 The 1-Click Pipeline 

 EzApply also has a one-click workflow that demonstrates how the tools can work together: 

 Search → Score → Identify Skill Gaps → Generate Draft → Human Review 

 The agent handles the tedious parts in sequence, while the candidate takes over when a decision actually matters. 

 How we built it 

 One of our goals was to keep the project simple enough that the WebMCP integration remained the focus. 

 The entire application is contained in a single HTML file of roughly 70KB , with inline CSS and JavaScript and no production dependencies. 

 We register our tools through document.modelContext using WebMCP's registerTool() API and provide proper inputSchema definitions so an agent knows what each tool expects. 

 For example: 
 document . modelContext . registerTool ( { 
 name : "search_jobs" , 
 description : "Searches available tech jobs by keywords, salary, and remote status." , 
 inputSchema : { 
 type : "object" , 
 properties : { 
 query : { 
 type : "string" , 
 description : "Job title or skill keyword" 
 } , 
 minSalary : { 
 type : "number" 
 } , 
 remoteOnly : { 
 type : "boolean" 
 } 
 } , 
 required : [ "query" ] 
 } , 
 execute : async ( input ) = > { 
 const results = jobs . filter ( j = > matchesQuery ( j , input ) ) ; 

 return { 
 success : true , 
 count : results . length , 
 jobs : results
 } ; 
 } 
 } ) ; 
 
 We also added a small in-memory modelContext fallback. If WebMCP isn't available in the browser, the app can still be explored normally. When WebMCP is available, the same tools are exposed through the native protocol. 

 For the interface, we went with an aviation-inspired command-center theme. Job cards look like boarding passes, jobs have flight-style codes, and the overall interface is designed to feel like you're managing a journey from discovery to application. 

 The project is deployed on Vercel using Vite as a minimal static setup. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Getting the human approval step right 

 We didn't want the approval step to feel like unnecessary friction. At the same time, we didn't want to hide an important decision behind a single confirmation button. 

 We ended up using an inline-editable application draft so the candidate can make changes without leaving the workflow. The approval card is intentionally prominent, making it clear that this is the point where the human takes control. 

 Making WebMCP visible 

 One challenge with a protocol like WebMCP is that most of the interesting work happens behind the scenes. 

 A user doesn't necessarily know that an agent just called search_jobs or score_job_fit . 

 That's why we built the Agent Console. It turns those normally invisible interactions into something users can actually watch, which also helped us understand and debug the agent workflow while building the project. 

 Keeping everything in one file 

 We deliberately challenged ourselves to keep the application lightweight. 

 Instead of reaching for a framework, component library, or large collection of dependencies, we built the application with plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. 

 That made the project easier to deploy and kept the focus on what we were actually trying to demonstrate: WebMCP and human-agent collaboration. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 Six working WebMCP tools that can be used together as a complete workflow 
 A 1-click agent pipeline that demonstrates tool orchestration from job search to application draft 
 A genuine human approval boundary for the final submission step 
 The candidateConfirmation check is enforced inside the tool itself, not just in the UI 
 A complete application in roughly 70KB with zero production dependencies 
 A real-time Agent Console that makes agent activity transparent 
 A polished interface that makes an otherwise abstract WebMCP concept easy to understand 
 

 What we learned 

 Building EzApply changed how we think about agents on the web. 

 The biggest lesson was that agents don't always need to control the entire experience. In many cases, the better approach is to give the agent well-defined tools and let the human remain responsible for important decisions. 

 WebMCP made that model much easier to explore. Instead of relying on DOM scraping or trying to interpret screenshots, the website can expose structured tools with clear inputs and outputs. 

 We also learned that human-in-the-loop isn't necessarily a compromise . The approval step actually makes the experience feel safer because the user can see exactly what the AI produced before anything important happens. 

 And because the tools run directly in the browser, we were able to build and deploy the prototype without creating a separate backend just to demonstrate the agent interaction. 

 Most importantly, EzApply showed us a different way of thinking about the web: not just as pages that agents have to figure out, but as experiences that can actively provide agents with useful capabilities. 

 What's next for EzApply — WebMCP Job Command Center 

 EzApply is currently a prototype, but there are several directions we'd like to take it. 

 Real

title: ZipCheckup Agent
pitch: 88 million Americans are served by a water system with a violation on record. This page turns that record into six WebMCP tools an AI agent can call - and never returns a zero it doesn't have.
about_excerpt: 88 million Americans are served by a water system with a violation on record. This page turns that record into six WebMCP tools an AI agent can call - and never returns a zero it doesn't have. Like Comment Story Updates Six WebMCP tools over 42,679 US ZIP codes - real federal data, not sample data. ZIP 01004: one metric known out of fourteen. Every other field returns an explicit unknown with its reason - never a zero. Michigan, lead under 0.005 mg/L: 466 passed, 209 failed, 492 excluded because nobody measured them. Shared state: the agent and the person write to the same list. Rows show who added them. A letter to the water utility, built only from facts on the record. Ten asserted, three unknowns turned into questions instead of claims. Inspiration Ask any assistant whether the drinking water at an address is safe. You will get a confident paragraph. It will often be wrong, and nothing on the page could have stopped it. Eighty-eight million Americans are served by a water system with a health-based violation on record. That number is not a guess - it is 4,268 of the 10,517 public water systems in the dataset behind this project. The information is public. It is just buried in federal databases in formats no homebuyer will ever open, so people ask a model instead, and the model reads a table cell and cannot tell a measured zero from a blank nobody filled in. Most projects in this hackathon will make it faster for a model to read a page. This one changes what a model is allowed to say. What it does Six WebMCP tools over 42,679 US ZIP codes, 10,517 water systems, 282 million people . This is not sample data - it is ZipCheckup's production dataset, reviewed and accepted into the AWS Registry of Open Data, built from EPA SDWIS, published Consumer Confidence Reports and EPA radon zones. The agent can look up a ZIP, compare several, explain what a metric actually measures and against which legal threshold, search the whole country, write to a shortlist the person is watching, and draft a letter to the water utility. Two things make it different from a nicer API wrapper. First: a value cannot arrive naked. Lead comes back with the EPA action level of 0.015 mg/L and the citation 40 CFR Part 141 Subpart I in the same payload. The model cannot misquote a number it never read off a page, and cannot lose the threshold that gives the number meaning. Second: absence is never zero. When the public record holds no value, the tool returns an explicit unknown with the reason and a field stating what that absence does not prove. There is no code path in this project by which a missing measurement reaches an agent as 0 . Search a state for safe lead levels and you get three numbers, not one: measured and passing, measured and failing, and how many ZIPs nobody measured at all. For Michigan under 0.005 mg/L that is 466, 209, and 492 excluded for missing data - and the payload says, in words, that exclusion is a data gap and not a safety finding. That third number is the one every conventional site drops. It is also the one that decides whether a family trusts a house. What people and agents can do here that they could not before The shortlist is shared state, not a display. The agent's tool and the person's Add button call the same function in the same store. Rows carry who added them, flash when written, and can be deleted by the person. An activity log prints every call with its arguments and its known/unknown counts. So the person is not reading a report about what the model did. They are watching it work on the same object, and they can overrule it mid-flight. And the session ends with something they keep: a letter to the water system serving that address, composed only from facts whose status is known. An unknown value physically cannot reach the letter body, because the composer reads from nowhere else - everything unknown becomes a question to the utility instead of an accusation. When the dataset publishes no contact for that system, the tool returns resolution: "unresolved" and refuses to name a recipient rather than inventing a plausible one. An agent that will not name an address it cannot verify is a different kind of software than one that will. How I built it Six tools on document.modelContext.registerTool under one page-level AbortController . The badge in the header reads the registration back through getTools() , so it is evidence rather than a claim. "Revoke all" fires abort() and the count drops to zero live via toolchange - the correct demonstration of cancellation now that unregisterTool is gone from the spec. No framework, no bundler, no API key, no build step. Clone it and run npx serve web . Every compatibility decision was measured on Chrome 152, not read: navigator.modelContext is gone (the spec moved to document on 2026-04-23), getTools() is async and returns inputSchema as a string on Chrome 149-153, and title defaults to "" rather than undefined . Any one of those silently breaks a live demo. For browsers without native WebMCP, the page vendors the polyfill as a pinned 24 KB IIFE. For judges with no agent attached, an on-page console builds a form from each tool's own inputSchema . And scripts/mcp-bridge.mjs re-exposes whatever getTools() reports as a stdio MCP server, so agents outside a browser can drive it too - it hardcodes no tool names, so it tests the registration instead of reimplementing it. What I am proud of The honesty is enforced by code, not by discipline. One envelope module is the only exit from the data layer, so a missing value cannot become a zero anywhere downstream - not in a comparison, not in a ranking, not in a letter. 84 assertions run in real Chromium against the deployed URL , not localhost. They assert that no unknown is serialised as 0 , that an unmeasured ZIP is never ranked best or worst, that the word "unknown" cannot appear in a letter body, and that an agent's write renders a row the human can see, attributed to the agent. I pointed a real coding agent at the tools without telling it which to use. It found them from their descriptions, chained them, and carried the contract into its own prose unprompted: "These blanks do not mean zero, clean, compliant, or safe." That is the whole thesis working end to end, in a model I did not write. What I learned Registration takes an afternoon. Deciding what a tool is allowed to say takes the rest of the week - and that is the actual work of the agentic web. Once the page owns the shape of the answer instead of the model inferring it from markup, honesty stops being a prompt you hope holds and becomes a property you can enforce at the boundary. That generalises far past drinking water. What's next Every civic dataset in the country has this problem, and every one of them is about to be read by an agent instead of a person. Water is where I started because the stakes are legible - lead does not care whether the record was digitised. Next: the PFAS, flood, wildfire and air-quality layers already sitting in the same open dataset. The Chrome origin trial on the deployed domain, so any visitor on 149+ gets the native path with no flag. And then the ordinary web. Local service businesses answer the same three questions all day - do you serve my address, when are you free, what will it cost. Those are tools, not paragraphs. This project is the proof that an agent-callable page can be rigorous about what it does not know, which matters far more once the answer is about someone's home. title: TBR
pitch: TBR is a private reading list your AI can understand and manage, turning your reading history into smarter recommendations—without accounts, scraping, or guesswork.
about_excerpt: TBR is a private reading list your AI can understand and manage, turning your reading history into smarter recommendations—without accounts, scraping, or guesswork. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Like many readers, I kept adding books to my reading list faster than I could finish them. When it was time to choose my next book, the list itself wasn’t much help. That made me wonder: what if my reading list could understand my taste and explain it directly to an AI? What it does TBR helps me track books I want to read, have finished, or gave up on. I can search Open Library, rate books, import my Goodreads list, and explore patterns in my reading. I can also ask an AI agent to search and manage my shelves. It can learn which authors I love, what I tend to abandon, and what I’ve enjoyed recently before recommending my next book. How I built it I built TBR with Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS. It has no backend or login—my library stays privately in my browser, while book information comes from Open Library. I created seven WebMCP tools and connected them to the same store as the interface. When an agent adds or updates a book, I see the change immediately. Challenges I ran into The biggest challenge was WebMCP’s 1,500-character output limit. I couldn’t send an agent my entire reading history, so I designed TBR to turn it into a compact taste profile. I also worked around differences between WebMCP implementations, imperfect catalogue results, and the risks of public data. I also made sure destructive actions always require human approval, to prevent agent "fixes" doing more harm than good. Accomplishments that I’m proud of I’m proud that TBR feels like a real reading app rather than a technical demo. It works without AI, needs no account, and keeps me in control of my data. The taste profile is my favourite part. It can turn a large library into useful observations, such as identifying my favourite authors or noticing who I repeatedly abandon. What I learned I learned that building good agent tools involves much more than exposing a few functions. Tool names, descriptions, errors, safety labels, and response sizes all affect how reliably an agent behaves. I also learned that an agent doesn’t always need more data—it often needs better context. Letting my application summarize what it already understands produces better results with less noise. What’s next for TBR I’d like recommendations to consider more than ratings, including genre, reading pace, recent interests, and what I’m in the mood for. I also want to improve catalogue matching, add more ways to import and export my library, and expand compatibility as WebMCP develops. title: OpenPath Studio
pitch: People set the learning goal. Agents weave the open web into a transparent, editable path.
about_excerpt: People set the learning goal. Agents weave the open web into a transparent, editable path. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Project The problem The open web contains excellent learning resources, but turning them into a realistic learning path is fragmented work. A learner or teacher must search across sites, compare formats and levels, inspect reuse terms, calculate a time budget, choose an order, and keep the plan current. A conventional browser agent can click through that workflow, but it has to infer meaning from visual controls and repeatedly reconstruct the page's state. Why WebMCP is the right fit OpenPath Studio makes the website's learning-planning capabilities explicit. Its WebMCP tools let an agent read the current goal, search a structured catalog, compare resources using stable IDs, build a time-bounded draft, add or remove items, reorder the path, mark progress, and export the result. The agent operates on the same client-side state and interface the person sees, so it never bypasses the product experience. WebMCP is not an API wrapper added for the challenge. It is the interaction model that makes the collaboration reliable. Schemas remove ambiguity, tool outputs keep context compact, read-only annotations distinguish discovery from action, and the activity ledger makes every state change visible. A better human experience The person still leads. They define the topic, level, schedule, and preferences. The agent handles catalog search, comparison, sequencing, and repetitive edits. Every recommendation includes its source, provider, duration, level, format, URL, and license metadata. The draft remains fully editable with human controls, and it works without an agent as a progressive enhancement. Publishing demonstrates a deliberate trust boundary. The agent can activate and prepare an annotated HTML form, but the form does not use toolautosubmit . A person must visibly review the title and learner, then click Publish. No data leaves the browser in this prototype. What people and agents can now do together Before WebMCP, an agent had to scrape filters, guess at card actions, and infer an ordered plan from the DOM. OpenPath lets the human state a goal in natural language while the agent composes multiple reliable domain actions against live browser state. The result appears immediately in the same interface for inspection and correction. The human contributes judgment and consent; the agent contributes speed, consistency, and structured comparison. Example collaboration: “Build me a 5-day beginner path on web accessibility with 30 minutes per day.” The agent calls build_learning_path with explicit constraints. The person reviews the visible draft and asks for a practical checklist. The agent searches, adds the resource by stable ID, and moves it to position two. The person marks progress or changes the sequence manually. The agent prepares publication and waits for human confirmation. How WebMCP was implemented OpenPath registers 11 imperative tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() and exposes one declarative publish_learning_path form. The prepare_publish_review imperative tool provides a cross-client bridge that opens and optionally prefills the same visible checkpoint but can never submit it. JSON Schemas validate inputs. Read-only and untrusted-content annotations communicate tool safety. Tool output stays concise. An AbortController manages registration lifecycle, and the site sends origin-isolation and tools permission headers. Both agent and human actions reuse the same state layer and are recorded in a visible activity ledger. The app is built with Next.js and React, has no external runtime dependencies beyond the framework, needs no account or API key, and stores its workspace locally. It is responsive, keyboard accessible, reduced-motion aware, and fully functional in manual mode. title: CircuitForge
pitch: CircuitForge is a browser-based digital logic simulator where AI agents and humans build, test, and debug circuits together in real time using WebMCP.
about_excerpt: CircuitForge is a browser-based digital logic simulator where AI agents and humans build, test, and debug circuits together in real time using WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates 1 CircuitForge in action. Inspiration I built CircuitForge because I was struggling in my digital circuits class. Building combinational logic by hand or using clunky desktop simulators is frustrating, and one tiny wiring error can take hours to track down. I wanted to use modern AI to help design and debug my circuits, but standard AI assistants completely break when faced with visual canvas tools. They rely on screenshots and pixel coordinates, which fails miserably when pins are a few pixels wide and wires overlap. Instead of forcing AI to squint at a canvas and guess where to click, I wanted to give it direct, semantic access to the underlying mathematical graph of the circuit. What It Does CircuitForge is a browser-based digital logic studio where humans and AI agents collaborate on the exact same circuit in real time. For Humans: A clean visual canvas to place gates, route wires, and build computers from scratch. For AI Agents: A WebMCP control plane with 19 native tools to inspect, build, and verify circuits without ever "seeing" a single pixel. Key features include: Modular Synthesis: Agents can build subcircuits (like an OR gate made of NANDs), test them, and package them into reusable custom ICs. Automated Verification: Instead of guessing if an LED is on, agents run a full truth-table verification that systematically tests every input combination. Signal Tracing: Tools to trace signals upstream/downstream and find floating inputs. Shared Viewport: Agents can pan and zoom the camera so the human and AI are always looking at the same part of the board. How We Built It We built CircuitForge as a 4-tier web app bridging modern web standards with a compiled WebAssembly simulation engine: Simulation Core: A modernized, browser-safe version of Sebastian Lague's Digital Logic Sim, running in Unity WebGL/WASM. C# Semantic Bridge: A custom command dispatcher that executes typed graph mutations (adding gates, toggling pins) directly on the C# netlist. TypeScript WebMCP Host: A Vite frontend that registers our tools into the browser's document.modelContext with strict Zod schemas. Dual-Agent Support: Built-in browser WebMCP (for ChatGPT/Chrome) and a standalone WebSocket relay so external CLI agents (like Claude Code or Codex) can control the canvas too. Challenges We Ran Into The Opaque Canvas: WebGL renders straight to the GPU, so there are no DOM nodes for gates or wires. Automation tools just see a blank <canvas> . We solved this by serializing the internal C# graph into clean, typed JSON snapshots that the AI can read directly. Async JS vs. Single-Threaded WASM: JS is async, but Unity WebGL runs single-threaded. Blocking the main thread froze the browser. We built a custom async request map with UUIDs so JS could fire a tool call, yield to the event loop, and wait for C# to resolve the Promise via a .jslib extern. Timing and Physics Bugs: When agents packaged subcircuits, long chip names would clip through the pins. We had to write an auto-sizer algorithm. We also had to fix race conditions during truth-table verification by forcing the simulation to "settle" for a few physics cycles before reading the outputs. Accomplishments That We're Proud Of True Agentic Control: We built a system where AI can design complex logic purely through code and semantic tools, completely bypassing the hallucinations of computer vision and OCR. Autonomous Hierarchical Design: It was awesome to watch the AI take a prompt like "build a 3-input OR gate using only NANDs", wire it up, verify the truth table, package it as a custom chip, and then immediately use that new chip to build a majority function. Works Everywhere: Whether you're using an in-browser agent or an external CLI tool like Claude Code, it interacts with the live canvas seamlessly. What We Learned Canvas apps can be agent-native: You don't need to sacrifice rich WebGL graphics to support AI agents. You just need to expose the underlying data model via WebMCP. State tracking matters: Adding monotonic revision numbers to every tool call completely fixed race conditions between the human clicking and the AI placing components. Digital logic is perfect for AI: Because boolean logic has strict, unambiguous mathematical rules, it's an incredible benchmark for testing an AI's ability to reason and self-correct. What's Next for CircuitForge Full CPU Architectures: Moving beyond basic gates to build full 8-bit CPUs with registers, decoders, and RAM. Interactive Tutor Mode: An AI tutor that generates circuits with subtle bugs (like floating inputs or race hazards) and helps students debug them step-by-step. HDL Support: Adding tools to compile Verilog/VHDL directly into interactive CircuitForge schematics. title: Zingposts
pitch: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust.
about_excerpt: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browsing old cars, boats, campers, motorcycles, and machinery is fun. Managing the hunt is not. Good finds get lost across tabs, marketplace search misses obvious matches, alerts are rigid, research lives in scattered notes, and negotiations have no shared memory. A three-way trade is almost impossible to reason about cleanly. Zingposts starts from a different premise: the marketplace should be equally legible to people and their agents without embedding a model in the product. The site owns its native listings and structured deal workflow, while outside listings can be tracked as clearly labeled snapshots. What it does Zingposts is a complete peer-to-peer marketplace and durable workspace for interesting things. People can browse realistic native inventory, create and publish listings, upload photos, save finds, build boards, set alerts, keep research notebooks, message sellers, prepare offers, and create structured multi-party trade rooms. Outside finds can be tracked without confusing them with Zingposts-owned inventory. A connected outside agent receives a compact persistent core plus one focused pack drawn from 121 structured WebMCP tools. It can search with compound criteria, compare candidates, organize boards, tag and rank finds, record cited research and inspection risks, monitor price changes, draft communications and offers, calculate acquisition cost, propose trade scenarios, and coordinate the shared gallery, focus, or thumbnail canvas. The human uses the same structure through a canvas-first interface. Zingposts itself contains no LLM. The centerpiece is the shared canvas: an outside agent opens a durable session, places a shortlist, recommendation, or focused question beside the marketplace objects, and pauses only when human judgment matters. The person can inspect the exact listings and rationale, choose an option or add context, and return structured guidance. The agent reads that durable response on its next tool call and continues. This is turn-taking over shared marketplace objects, not a chatbot transcript. The loop now extends across visits. get_workspace_resume returns the last acknowledged checkpoint, everything that changed since, structured blockers, human responses, proposal status, and safe next actions. An agent can acknowledge the checkpoint only after processing it, so “come back later” is an explicit protocol rather than a hope that conversation context survived. For broad edits, the agent can prepare a sourced, versioned change set instead of making a trail of one-off mutations. Zingposts previews each proposed change in plain language, checks the expected object versions, and lets the person selectively accept only the changes they want. Agents cannot approve their own change sets. Completed deals can be recorded as private outcomes, and transparent aggregate patterns report counts, prices, and reasons without inventing a model-generated score. Either side can arrive first. A person can explore immediately in a prototype workspace, then replace a test email and verify the real address through Supabase only when work reaches the marketplace boundary. One Bring my agent click copies the canonical guide URL. Or an unauthenticated agent can inspect five setup-only tools and open a prototype handoff for the person. Once the person signs in, safe private tools appear automatically to an outside agent operating that browser document. Independent 12-hour revocable sessions remain available through one-use invites or codes for separate-browser or unattended work. The human remains in control. Publishing, enabling notifications, sending a message, submitting or responding to an offer, and inviting a trade participant stop at a visible confirmation gate. Every human and agent action is attributed, and reversible work can be undone. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer intent from buttons and screen position. That is brittle for a marketplace with dozens of interdependent objects: listings, boards, research, alerts, conversations, offers, people, assets, and constraints. WebMCP gives Zingposts a stable collaboration language. “Find pre-1980 boats under $15,000, put the best four on a board, record the title risks, and draft a message to the strongest seller” becomes a sequence of typed, attributable actions. The human can watch the same state change, refine it directly, and approve the parts that cross a consequential boundary. That makes the product meaningfully better with an agent—not merely automatable. How we built it Zingposts uses React 19 and Next.js on Netlify. Supabase Auth provides verified human sessions, Supabase Postgres holds marketplace, identity, agent-session, and workflow state, and Supabase Storage holds listing photos. Versioned SQL migrations keep direct browser access locked behind row-level security. The browser client exposes 121 declarative tools through the WebMCP modelContext surface, but only five setup tools while signed out. After the person signs in, AbortSignal-managed registration keeps a compact persistent core plus one replaceable focused capability pack, so navigation never accumulates an oversized registry or silently unlocks business actions. get_agent_bootstrap returns setup guidance while signed out, then canonical browser-delegated identity, workspace, attention, active collaboration, capability index, and guide version after sign-in. activate_capability switches the focused pack without moving the person; open_for_human_review is optional. The action layer derives canonical human and agent identity on the server, prevents duplicate profiles, enforces ownership and state-transition enums, creates reviewable drafts, writes attributed activity, stores inverse operations for undo, supports idempotency keys and optimistic versions, returns stable deep links and WebMCP-native structured errors, and converts consequential operations into pending confirmations. Isolated QA runs register only their own artifacts, provide an exact cleanup preview, and require human approval before deletion. The marketplace is seeded with original project-owned imagery and realistic records so the full human-agent workflow is understandable immediately. WebMCP registration is document-scoped, while Zingposts durably stores connection profiles, scopes, alerts, boards, research, drafts, versions, and audit history. The public /for-agents guide and /api/agent-guide contract show agents how to reconnect safely without storing an invite, code, or stale catalog. Challenges The main design challenge was not adding more agent power; it was deciding where that power should stop. We separated preparation from commitment. Research, organization, comparison, and drafting can proceed quickly. Communication, publication, notifications, invitations, and financial commitments pause for the human. We also designed external-listing tracking so provenance stays honest. Zingposts can organize an outside find, but it never claims that its cached price, availability, or seller statements are authoritative. Accomplishments A coherent marketplace, not a WebMCP proof of concept 121 tools spanning authentication, onboarding, resumable work sessions, versioned proposals, outcomes, canvas views, discovery, organization, negotiation, and multi-party trade Agent-first and person-first onboarding with a five-tool setup surface before human sign-in Durable agent-to-human-to-agent turn-taking with a unified attention queue Explicit resume checkpoints and structured blockers for work that continues across agent runs Sourced, versioned change sets with semantic previews and selective human acceptance Private outcome recording with transparent, non-AI aggregate patterns Live agent activity, exact-payload approval, idempotency, dry runs, structured errors, and stable deep links No built-in AI or model dependency Supabase human authentication plus opaque invite URLs, code fallback, and single-use, expiring, revocable agent sessions—without password or session sharing Persistent bootstrap plus navigation-independent focused capability activation Structured errors, strict workflow transitions, optimistic concurrency, and namespaced QA cleanup Durable attribution, confirmations, and undo Native seller photo upload and publishing workflow Clear separation between owned listings and outside tracked snapshots Production build, automated API smoke tests, desktop browser testing, and mobile verification What we learned Human-agent collaboration works best when both sides operate on the same durable objects. A board is better than a chat-only list. A research notebook is better than an ephemeral summary. A pending confirmation is better than asking the model to remember which action is sensitive. We also learned to separate document-scoped WebMCP

title: Wishlist Concierge
pitch: An agent + human co-curation layer for Sylius 2.0 wishlists
about_excerpt: An agent + human co-curation layer for Sylius 2.0 wishlists Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Planning a gift for someone means opening a dozen browser tabs, clicking filters that never quite match your intent, mentally adding up prices, then abandoning the cart when you realize the total blew past your budget. We asked ourselves: what if the storefront could understand "birthday for my nephew" and do the search, curation, and budget math for you while still giving you, the human, full control over what gets added to your cart? What it does Wishlist Concierge exposes 12 imperative WebMCP tools on a Sylius 2.0 storefront, covering the full gift-planning lifecycle: Find products by theme (tags); hard match on tags first, then soft match on product name, then fallback to all channel products Build & curate themed wishlists, add or swap products, reorganize at will Apply a budget constraint using a knapsack algorithm over quantity × ChannelPricing, with active catalog promotions discounts factored in; Return a human-readable explanation of what was chosen and why Move selected items into the Sylius cart and hand you the token to proceed How we built it The entire project is a Sylius 2.0 plugin with the Sylius Wishlist plugin providing the persistence layer. The key architectural choice was single-source-of-truth tool definition: Each tool is declared once via a #[ModelContextTool] attribute on its shop controller action with a name, description, input DTO class, path params, confirm/destructive hints, all in one place. A ModelContextToolCollector service introspects these attributes at compile time, resolves each tool's route via the Symfony router, and produces a JSON manifest. The frontend registry.js fetches that manifest and calls document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, {signal}) for each — so adding a tool means writing a controller method and a DTO, not touching JavaScript at all. Server-side, a ToolContractValidator kernel.request listener deserializes every incoming payload against the DTO's #[Assert] constraints and returns deterministic 422 envelopes on failure. As a bnous, the schema the agent sees is the schema the server enforces. The frontend uses two Stimulus controllers. A toolbox modal that dynamically renders a run form for every registered tool, and a toast controller for live feedback via webmcp:* custom events. Accomplishments that we're proud of The single-source-of-truth tool definition. A tool lives once as a #[ModelContextTool] attribute and that single declaration drives the manifest, the frontend registration, the server-side validation, and the toolbox UI. No duplicate schema, no drift, no manual sync. What we learned WebMCP changes the agent & web relationship. Instead of agents screen-scraping your UI, you hand them structured tools with typed schemas. That means better agents (clear contracts) and safer apps (no ambiguous click paths). Single source of truth is everything for developer experience. When a tool is defined in one place and everything else is derived, adding a new tool is a 5-minute task. Structured error shapes make agents better. Once the server returns {"error":"Validation failed", "message":"...", "violations":[{field,message}]}, the agent can reason about what went wrong and fix its next call - the feedback loop closes. What's next for Wishlist Concierge Real-world testing Extend the knapsack algorithm to consider stock levels and quantity discounts, not just unit price × quantity. title: Quorum
pitch: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged.
about_excerpt: Scheduling, negotiated by your agent — approved by you. Humans and AI agents vote, counter-propose, and converge on a meeting time together via WebMCP, with every agent action visibly logged. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Group scheduling is a negotiation over everyone's constraints - and it's still done by making humans click checkboxes in polls. When WebMCP launched, we realized the missing piece was never a smarter poll: it was letting each person's AI agent join the negotiation itself . Quorum is our answer: scheduling, negotiated by your agent - approved by you. What it does Quorum is a meeting scheduler where humans and agents are equal participants in the same live session. Humans get a normal UI: candidate times, yes/maybe/no voting, counter-proposals. Agents get seven WebMCP tools registered by the page itself - they can read the event state, join on their human's behalf, vote with reasons, counter-propose new times, and rank the slots. Every action lands in a shared negotiation log tagged HUMAN or AGENT , and only the human organizer can accept proposals or lock in the final time. Agent proposes; human approves. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Scheduling is a multi-step, stateful interaction - exactly where screen-scraping agents fail. With WebMCP, the page tells agents what's possible via typed, self-describing tools. In testing, an agent that had never seen the app correctly chained four tools on the first try (read state -> join -> vote with a conflict note -> report the winner) purely from the tool descriptions. What people and agents can do together that wasn't possible before A mixed negotiation - some parties human, some agents - on the same page, in real time, with full mutual visibility. Before WebMCP, agents couldn't reliably operate voting UIs built for humans, and sites had no way to declare what actions they support. Quorum shows the new shape of the open web: agents handle the tedium, the audit trail keeps trust, and humans keep the final word. How we built it Vanilla JS frontend + Express backend, live-synced over server-sent events. Every WebMCP tool executes the same functions the human UI uses , tagged via: "agent" - one code path, one audit trail: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "submit_availability", description: "Submit availability for candidate slots on behalf of your user…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { responses: { type: "array" } }, required: ["responses"] }, execute: async ({ responses }) => submitAvailability(responses, "agent"), }); Deployed on Vercel; Upstash Redis keeps event state consistent across serverless instances, with a per-stream Redis poll so every open tab stays live. The visual design was created in Claude Design and implemented as a hand-written design system. Challenges we ran into - Serverless broke our state. Events lived in memory; on Vercel, an SSE stream landed on a different instance and couldn't find the event. We added a storage layer (Upstash Redis in production, in-memory locally) and cross-instance live updates via polling. - The WebMCP API surface is still moving (document.modelContext vs the earlier navigator.modelContext), so we wrote a small adapter that registers against whichever exists. - Tool descriptions are prompts. Agents chained our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say when to call each tool and what to fetch first. Accomplishments that we're proud of - **A never-before-seen agent used our app correctly on the first try.** In our final test, a Gemini-backed agent autonomously chained four tools - read the event state, joined as a new participant, voted with a conflict note attached to the right slot, and reported the winning time - guided by nothing but our tool descriptions. That's the whole WebMCP promise, working. - **One code path for humans and agents.** Every WebMCP tool executes the exact same functions the human UI calls - so the audit log, validation, and permissions are identical no matter who acts. No parallel "agent API" to drift out of sync. - **Trust as a first-class feature.** The negotiation log tags every action HUMAN or AGENT in real time, organizer-only tools are genuinely scoped, and an agent can never finalize a meeting on its own. - **A one-click seeded demo event**, so any judge can see a mid-negotiation session - votes, an agent counter-proposal, a live log - in under ten seconds, then take over as the organizer. - **Shipping the full journey in days**: idea -> working local app -> designed UI -> deployed on Vercel with Redis-backed state that survives serverless cold starts. What we learned - **Tool descriptions are prompts.** Agents started chaining our tools correctly only after we rewrote descriptions to say *when* to call each tool and what to fetch first ("Call this first to understand the current state"). Designing for a model reader is a real skill, and WebMCP makes it part of frontend work. - **The trust problem matters more than the automation problem.** The feature people react to isn't that agents can vote — it's seeing exactly what an agent did on your behalf, and knowing the final decision always needs a human. - **Serverless changes your assumptions.** Our in-memory state worked perfectly until the first live SSE request landed on a different instance. Moving to Redis-backed storage with cross-instance live updates taught us to design for "any request, any instance" from the start. - **Build for a moving standard defensively.** WebMCP's surface has shifted between Chrome previews (`document.modelContext` vs `navigator.modelContext`), so a small adapter layer saved us from breaking on every browser update. What's next for Quorum - **Calendar integration**, so your agent votes from your real availability instead of being told your constraints. - **Agent-to-agent negotiation rounds** - agents exchange counter-proposals automatically until they converge on a shortlist, and humans only see the final choice to ratify. - **Invites addressed to agents**: send an event link straight to someone's assistant, which handles everything and pings its human only for approval. - **Richer constraints in tools** - recurring meetings, time-zone fairness scoring, and "must attend / optional" roles that agents can reason about.  Inspiration
Modern web apps crash on unexpected null checks or bad inputs, causing lost carts, churn, and 3 AM on-call alerts. We asked: Why do biological systems heal wounds in real time, while web apps shatter at the first error? With the new W3C WebMCP standard, we realized we could embed an AI immune system directly inside browser memory to detect, diagnose, and repair broken code instantly.
⚙️ What It Does
AutoFix.run is a self-healing frontend engine that fixes crashes in under 2 seconds with zero page reload:
WebMCP Flight Recorder: Buffers user clicks, DOM mutations, and component stacks.
Gemini Root-Cause Diagnosis: Dispatches crash dumps via WebMCP to synthesize surgical AST patches.
AST Safety Auditor: Blocks prototype pollution, arbitrary network calls, and unsafe evaluations before execution.
Zero-Downtime Hotpatching: Injects the verified fix straight into browser memory, preserving active user state and unfreezing the UI.
Git PR Automation: Generates clean Git diffs and ready-to-merge GitHub pull requests.
🧗 Challenges We Faced
Hotpatching Without State Loss: Swapping code in a running React bundle without refreshing the page or losing user inputs required careful in-memory prototype interception.
Preventing Hallucinations: Constraining Gemini via strict JSON schemas and AST invariant assertions so it only produces surgical, runnable code fixes.
High-Demand API Reliability: Built an adaptive circuit breaker that seamlessly cascades across Gemini flash models if an endpoint hits temporary 503 limits.
🏆 Accomplishments
Achieved sub-1.8s Mean Time to Repair (MTTR) from crash to live heal.
Demonstrated zero state loss across an authentic 2.7k★ React Calculator and an enterprise e-commerce checkout funnel.
Native browser-level WebMCP implementation (window.navigator.modelContext) instead of an external chat wrapper.
📚 What We Learned
WebMCP transforms the browser from a passive display into an active, intelligent host.
Neuro-symbolic design wins: Combining LLM reasoning with deterministic AST security checks is essential for running generated code safely in production.
Production web software no longer needs to be fragile—it can have its own immune system.

title: Symbiosis
pitch: Symbiosis is a shared control plane where AI agents and humans work together. Agents do the work while humans monitor, make judgments and approve key decisions - all in one visible workflow.
about_excerpt: Symbiosis is a shared control plane where AI agents and humans work together. Agents do the work while humans monitor, make judgments and approve key decisions - all in one visible workflow. Like Comment Story Updates Human direction, agent execution Inspiration AI agents are becoming dramatically more capable. At the same time, the services we use every day are becoming increasingly agent-friendly through technologies like MCP. That creates a new problem: as agents become capable of doing more work on our behalf, we need better ways to give them work, set priorities and boundaries, step in when human judgment is needed, and review what they have done. Chat is great for giving an agent one task. It is less suited to overseeing an ongoing workload. Then came WebMCP. WebMCP gives us the tooling we need to make this relationship work particularly well. What it does Symbiosis is built around the symbiotic relationship between a human and their AI agent companion. The human plans the work, prioritizes tasks, defines constraints, reviews results, and makes the decisions that require human judgment. The agent works through that queue autonomously using the tools and capabilities it already has. It reports progress, records results, and pauses for a decision when necessary before continuing. In short: The agent executes. The human oversees, prioritizes, and decides. Symbiosis makes that relationship visible in one shared workspace, with tasks moving between Backlog, Working, Needs Decision, and Done as the human and agent collaborate. How we built it Symbiosis itself was built collaboratively with AI, which felt particularly appropriate for the project. I used ChatGPT to explore and challenge the original product idea, gstack to turn that concept into a detailed product and engineering design, and Codex to help implement and test the application. A major design goal was keeping the architecture deliberately small. Symbiosis is the coordination layer - it does not try to duplicate the reasoning, web access, coding tools, email integrations, or other capabilities the agent already has. Challenges we ran into Our first iteration was built around a single workboard. It worked, but it quickly became clear that the model was too limited. Jobs could not be reused easily, workflows were difficult to compose, and the overall experience lacked the flexibility we wanted. Through further iteration, we developed a three-level system of flows → workboards → jobs. Flows orchestrate workboards, and workboards execute jobs. That hierarchy gave us a much more elegant and reusable way to model agent workflows. Instead of rebuilding a process from scratch every time, users can define small reusable jobs, group them into workboards, and then combine those workboards into larger flows. The challenge was finding a structure that stayed simple enough to understand while still being powerful enough to support loops, delays, schedules, human decision points, and more complex workflows. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are particularly proud of the flows → workboards → jobs system. Its reusability is one of the most powerful parts of Symbiosis. Jobs can be defined once and reused across different workboards, while workboards can become reusable building blocks inside larger flows. This turns agent interaction from a sequence of one-off prompts into something that can be structured, repeated, refined, and reused over time. We are also proud that WebMCP feels fundamental to the product rather than being added simply for the hackathon. Symbiosis relies on WebMCP as the coordination layer between the human-owned workflow and the user's existing AI agent. What we learned The biggest thing we learned was where WebMCP is genuinely useful. WebMCP works extremely well as a bridge between a conversational AI agent and a website. It allows the agent to understand structured application state, take actions, update progress, request decisions, and continue working while the human interacts naturally through chat. We also learned what it is less suited to. Trying to make the entire agent experience happen inside the webpage itself weakens one of WebMCP's biggest advantages: the agent already has its own context, identity, tools, and conversational interface. The strongest pattern we found was to let the website act as the structured control surface while allowing the agent to remain where it already lives. That separation became one of the core design principles behind Symbiosis. What's next for Coop Queue The immediate focus would be UI and UX refinement, clearer and richer tool outputs, and more advanced flow-control capabilities. One particularly exciting area is intelligent conditional loops, where a flow can evaluate the result of a completed job and decide what should happen next based on that data. We would also like to add better reporting, notifications, execution history, and visibility into long-running workflows. Beyond that, the most important next step is user testing. We want to see how people actually use persistent agent workflows in practice, where they want more control, and where they are comfortable giving their agents more autonomy. title: Semantic Loop DevOps Demonstrator
pitch: A shared schema-design workspace where people shape the model visually and WebMCP agents inspect, edit, seed, and export the same live project.
about_excerpt:
A shared schema-design workspace where people shape the model visually and WebMCP agents inspect, edit, seed, and export the same live project.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Database design often splits into two disconnected experiences. A person works visually in a browser while an AI assistant receives pasted fragments, guesses at current state, or drives the page through brittle clicks. That gap makes collaboration slow and risky: the person cannot easily review what the agent believes, and the agent cannot reliably act on the model the person is seeing. 

 Solution 

 Semantic Loop turns the browser page into a shared, structured workspace. The person can continue using the visual schema editor while an agent discovers purpose-built WebMCP tools on that same page. The agent can inspect the current project, create or revise a schema, add sample data, and export the project through typed operations. Every change flows through the application's real React state, so the interface immediately shows the result for human review. 

 This is stronger than generic browser automation: the agent works with domain concepts such as tables, columns, keys, sample data, and project exports instead of screen coordinates or incidental DOM text. 

 Why This Matters 

 The target users are developers, data architects, product teams, and technical operators who need to turn requirements into a reviewable data model. WebMCP gives them a collaboration loop that was previously awkward: 

 
 A person describes intent and watches the model evolve. 
 An agent reads the exact current project state. 
 The agent proposes or applies a structured change. 
 The person reviews the result in the visual interface and can edit it directly. 
 Either participant can continue from the same state and export a portable result. 
 

 That shortens the path from conversation to an auditable artifact while keeping the person in control of the visible source of truth. 

 How We Used AI 

 
 WebMCP-enabled agents operate the application through explicit, typed tools rather than DOM scraping. 
 A provider-neutral server-side gateway supports optional natural-language schema, data, visualization, and artifact generation using Gemini, OpenAI, or Anthropic when the operator configures credentials. 
 The core WebMCP demonstration is designed to remain usable without sharing any provider credential: judges can exercise the page-state tools and review their visible effects directly. 
 

 How We Used Codex 

 Codex helped inspect the existing codebase, separate pre-challenge product work from the new challenge contribution, design the WebMCP tool boundary around the application's existing state model, implement and test the adapter, harden the no-secret judge path, and prepare the Netlify and Devpost materials. Human review remained the decision point for project selection, rules acceptance, product positioning, and final submission. 

 Key Features 

 
 A visual React schema-design workflow that remains usable by a person. 
 Discoverable WebMCP tools with JSON schemas and focused descriptions. 
 A single shared project state for human UI actions and agent tool calls. 
 Structured read, create, update, sample-data, and export operations. 
 Visible feedback after agent mutations so the person can review the outcome. 
 A no-secret judge path for the core WebMCP flow, with multi-provider AI features as an optional enhancement. 
 Browser code never receives provider keys. Local development can load them using macOS Keychain, production reads protected Netlify secrets, and the gateway sends credentials only to the selected provider over HTTPS. 
 Portable project export for continuing the work outside the current browser session. 
 

 WebMCP Tools 

 The source registers these tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . 

 webmcp/tools.ts defines registerWebMcpTools ; webmcp/useWebMcpTools.ts mounts the document.modelContext.registerTool registration into React. export_project returns files: [{name, mediaType, content}] . 

 Architecture 

 The application is a Vite-built React 19 and TypeScript single-page app. React Context and a reducer hold the canonical project state. The WebMCP adapter registers browser-native tools, validates structured inputs, and dispatches through that existing state boundary. UI components subscribe to the same state and immediately render agent-initiated changes. Browser persistence keeps the working project local, and the export path produces a portable project representation. 

 Gemini, OpenAI, and Anthropic are optional service integrations behind one provider-neutral server-side boundary. They are not the state store and are not required for the basic WebMCP tool demonstration.

title: Zingposts
pitch: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust.
about_excerpt: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browsing old cars, boats, campers, motorcycles, and machinery is fun. Managing the hunt is not. Good finds get lost across tabs, marketplace search misses obvious matches, alerts are rigid, research lives in scattered notes, and negotiations have no shared memory. A three-way trade is almost impossible to reason about cleanly. Zingposts starts from a different premise: the marketplace should be equally legible to people and their agents without embedding a model in the product. The site owns its native listings and structured deal workflow, while outside listings can be tracked as clearly labeled snapshots. What it does Zingposts is a complete peer-to-peer marketplace and durable workspace for interesting things. People can browse realistic native inventory, create and publish listings, upload photos, save finds, build boards, set alerts, keep research notebooks, message sellers, prepare offers, and create structured multi-party trade rooms. Outside finds can be tracked without confusing them with Zingposts-owned inventory. A connected outside agent receives a compact persistent core plus one focused pack drawn from 121 structured WebMCP tools. It can search with compound criteria, compare candidates, organize boards, tag and rank finds, record cited research and inspection risks, monitor price changes, draft communications and offers, calculate acquisition cost, propose trade scenarios, and coordinate the shared gallery, focus, or thumbnail canvas. The human uses the same structure through a canvas-first interface. Zingposts itself contains no LLM. The centerpiece is the shared canvas: an outside agent opens a durable session, places a shortlist, recommendation, or focused question beside the marketplace objects, and pauses only when human judgment matters. The person can inspect the exact listings and rationale, choose an option or add context, and return structured guidance. The agent reads that durable response on its next tool call and continues. This is turn-taking over shared marketplace objects, not a chatbot transcript. The loop now extends across visits. get_workspace_resume returns the last acknowledged checkpoint, everything that changed since, structured blockers, human responses, proposal status, and safe next actions. An agent can acknowledge the checkpoint only after processing it, so “come back later” is an explicit protocol rather than a hope that conversation context survived. For broad edits, the agent can prepare a sourced, versioned change set instead of making a trail of one-off mutations. Zingposts previews each proposed change in plain language, checks the expected object versions, and lets the person selectively accept only the changes they want. Agents cannot approve their own change sets. Completed deals can be recorded as private outcomes, and transparent aggregate patterns report counts, prices, and reasons without inventing a model-generated score. Either side can arrive first. A person can explore immediately in a prototype workspace, then replace a test email and verify the real address through Supabase only when work reaches the marketplace boundary. One Bring my agent click copies the canonical guide URL. Or an unauthenticated agent can inspect five setup-only tools and open a prototype handoff for the person. Once the person signs in, safe private tools appear automatically to an outside agent operating that browser document. Independent 12-hour revocable sessions remain available through one-use invites or codes for separate-browser or unattended work. The human remains in control. Publishing, enabling notifications, sending a message, submitting or responding to an offer, and inviting a trade participant stop at a visible confirmation gate. Every human and agent action is attributed, and reversible work can be undone. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer intent from buttons and screen position. That is brittle for a marketplace with dozens of interdependent objects: listings, boards, research, alerts, conversations, offers, people, assets, and constraints. WebMCP gives Zingposts a stable collaboration language. “Find pre-1980 boats under $15,000, put the best four on a board, record the title risks, and draft a message to the strongest seller” becomes a sequence of typed, attributable actions. The human can watch the same state change, refine it directly, and approve the parts that cross a consequential boundary. That makes the product meaningfully better with an agent—not merely automatable. How we built it Zingposts uses React 19 and Next.js on Netlify. Supabase Auth provides verified human sessions, Supabase Postgres holds marketplace, identity, agent-session, and workflow state, and Supabase Storage holds listing photos. Versioned SQL migrations keep direct browser access locked behind row-level security. The browser client exposes 121 declarative tools through the WebMCP modelContext surface, but only five setup tools while signed out. After the person signs in, AbortSignal-managed registration keeps a compact persistent core plus one replaceable focused capability pack, so navigation never accumulates an oversized registry or silently unlocks business actions. get_agent_bootstrap returns setup guidance while signed out, then canonical browser-delegated identity, workspace, attention, active collaboration, capability index, and guide version after sign-in. activate_capability switches the focused pack without moving the person; open_for_human_review is optional. The action layer derives canonical human and agent identity on the server, prevents duplicate profiles, enforces ownership and state-transition enums, creates reviewable drafts, writes attributed activity, stores inverse operations for undo, supports idempotency keys and optimistic versions, returns stable deep links and WebMCP-native structured errors, and converts consequential operations into pending confirmations. Isolated QA runs register only their own artifacts, provide an exact cleanup preview, and require human approval before deletion. The marketplace is seeded with original project-owned imagery and realistic records so the full human-agent workflow is understandable immediately. WebMCP registration is document-scoped, while Zingposts durably stores connection profiles, scopes, alerts, boards, research, drafts, versions, and audit history. The public /for-agents guide and /api/agent-guide contract show agents how to reconnect safely without storing an invite, code, or stale catalog. Challenges The main design challenge was not adding more agent power; it was deciding where that power should stop. We separated preparation from commitment. Research, organization, comparison, and drafting can proceed quickly. Communication, publication, notifications, invitations, and financial commitments pause for the human. We also designed external-listing tracking so provenance stays honest. Zingposts can organize an outside find, but it never claims that its cached price, availability, or seller statements are authoritative. Accomplishments A coherent marketplace, not a WebMCP proof of concept 121 tools spanning authentication, onboarding, resumable work sessions, versioned proposals, outcomes, canvas views, discovery, organization, negotiation, and multi-party trade Agent-first and person-first onboarding with a five-tool setup surface before human sign-in Durable agent-to-human-to-agent turn-taking with a unified attention queue Explicit resume checkpoints and structured blockers for work that continues across agent runs Sourced, versioned change sets with semantic previews and selective human acceptance Private outcome recording with transparent, non-AI aggregate patterns Live agent activity, exact-payload approval, idempotency, dry runs, structured errors, and stable deep links No built-in AI or model dependency Supabase human authentication plus opaque invite URLs, code fallback, and single-use, expiring, revocable agent sessions—without password or session sharing Persistent bootstrap plus navigation-independent focused capability activation Structured errors, strict workflow transitions, optimistic concurrency, and namespaced QA cleanup Durable attribution, confirmations, and undo Native seller photo upload and publishing workflow Clear separation between owned listings and outside tracked snapshots Production build, automated API smoke tests, desktop browser testing, and mobile verification What we learned Human-agent collaboration works best when both sides operate on the same durable objects. A board is better than a chat-only list. A research notebook is better than an ephemeral summary. A pending confirmation is better than asking the model to remember which action is sensitive. We also learned to separate document-scoped WebMCP

title: jobContext: The Memory Layer for Your Career, Agent-Ready
pitch: Career searches scatter context across tabs, docs, and tools. With WebMCP, jobContext gives you and your agent one shared memory for every role and next move, directly in your signed-in browser.
about_excerpt: Career searches scatter context across tabs, docs, and tools. With WebMCP, jobContext gives you and your agent one shared memory for every role and next move, directly in your signed-in browser. Like 1 Comment Story Updates The memory layer for your career, with a live Claude MCP call composing a cover letter. Every new AI chat starts from zero. jobContext is the persistent memory. 12 domain tools, 104 actions, one capability layer across desktop, cloud, and mobile. Readiness-aware: Oura sleep, HRV, and recovery on the dashboard to time your outreach. The dashboard is itself an agent surface: every tool is registered in-page over WebMCP. Private by design: same origin only, tenant isolated, open schema, no lock-in. The signed-in cloud dashboard: priorities, pipeline health, and readiness at a glance. Pipeline with AI fitment scoring: a role weighed against the candidate’s real materials. A generated résumé, versioned and linked to its application, previewed in the app. ChatGPT discovers all 12 jobContext tools in-page through document.modelContext, with no connector or second login. Assessment detail: fitment 8/10 with strengths, risks, and evidence weighed against the saved résumé. Provenance gate: every claim traces to source context, with a verifiable pass or fail. Long generations run as async work items, then return with their trust report. A cross-site call to /mcp is answered 401 Unauthorized, so a hostile page cannot ride your session. Inspiration I built jobContext after getting laid off and finding that AI job-search help came with its own tax: every new conversation began cold. I was repeatedly re-explaining my resume, what I had shipped, which companies were already in my pipeline, people I had met, my STAR stories, and the way I write. The context existed, but it was scattered across documents, tabs, and past chats. Copying it into every fresh session was exhausting when I needed that energy for the search itself. I started by building a few small tools to stop re-explaining myself. They grew into jobContext. What I built jobContext is a living career workspace: applications, job search, materials, interviews, people, STAR stories, and the context behind them stay structured and persistent across sessions. It works as a desktop app, hosted dashboard, mobile companion, CLI, and MCP capability layer. It is not another chat that gives advice and forgets the work. The person owns the workspace and stays in the loop; an agent can help move real work forward inside it. For this challenge, I made the signed-in browser workspace agent-ready through WebMCP. A person and an in-browser agent can work from the same live pipeline: understand the search, find or assess a role, create materials, log the work, and leave the result where the person can inspect and use it. No new connector, separate OAuth flow, or blank-slate conversation is required. How I built it jobContext is built with Python, FastMCP, FastAPI, SQLite with a JSON audit trail, and a React dashboard. After authentication, the dashboard asks the live FastMCP server for its tool list and registers the returned names, descriptions, and input schemas directly with document.modelContext. When an in-browser agent invokes a tool, the bridge sends a same-origin JSON-RPC request to the same stateless /mcp endpoint used by other clients. The browser surface is not a second, hand-maintained API. It reflects the running MCP surface, so browser tools cannot quietly drift from the tools the app actually offers. The current surface has 12 consolidated tools and 104 actions behind them. Challenges I ran into More context is not better context. While improving document generation, I discovered that the system had accumulated more context about my writing style than about what I had actually done. That drove a retrieval-first redesign: token budgets, diagnostics, context ceilings, selective retrieval, and a clear separation between stored knowledge and prompt assembly. The lesson was simple: better context beats more context. “No setup” still has to be safe. I wanted the browser agent to work with the signed-in dashboard, not make someone configure yet another connector. But a session cookie is not permission to trust every browser request. The server accepts that session only for same-origin requests to /mcp; a cross-site browser request cannot use it, while deliberate bearer-auth MCP clients still work. A browser tool call is shorter than real document work. In-browser clients can time out before resume or cover-letter generation finishes. I added durable submit-and-poll generation so an agent can start work, return promptly, then retrieve the finished result instead of pretending a long-running job completed. A generated file is not a finished workflow. If a draft lands untracked, it creates another loose end. Generated materials now automatically create or update the relevant pipeline entry. A read-only Generation Trust Report lets the person inspect the claims checked, verdict, correction passes, and durable audit record. Trust has to be architectural. An interview question exposed a gap in my own system: I could observe non-deterministic AI output, but I could not yet prove that a generated claim was grounded. That became a deterministic provenance gate that checks factual claims against the source material on every generation and records the outcome. Prompt instructions alone were not enough. What I learned The useful unit of AI collaboration is not a prettier chat response. It is a shared, current workspace where the human can see what happened and decide what comes next. WebMCP matters because it lets a page describe its live capabilities at runtime. That is fundamentally better than making a person configure a second integration or maintain a browser-only copy of an API. Reducing friction can create more value than adding features. One of the most satisfying product moments was sharing a job from a phone and having the relevant workflow already waiting at the desk. Good agent systems need grounded context, clear permission boundaries, durable work, and inspectable results. Those are product requirements, not cleanup work after the demo. What changed during this challenge The original jobContext project predates this challenge. The WebMCP agent surface and its supporting hardening below were built during the submission period. The core bridge dynamically reflects the live FastMCP tool surface into document.modelContext and calls the signed-in, same-origin MCP endpoint. Agent-driven testing exposed and fixed workspace-aware assessment, validation, and interview-prep round-trip issues. I added provenance reporting, durable submit-and-poll generation for short browser timeouts, workflow instructions for in-browser agents, and automatic pipeline tracking for generated materials. WebMCP implementation synopsis The WebMCP work began by turning the existing hosted dashboard into an agent surface without creating a second browser-only tool API. The React app probes for document.modelContext, with the older navigator.modelContext alias retained as a compatibility fallback. After the user is authenticated, the bridge calls the live FastMCP server's tools/list endpoint, takes the returned tool names, descriptions, and input schemas, and registers those definitions with modelContext.registerTool(). When the browser agent invokes a registered tool, the bridge forwards the call as JSON-RPC over the same-origin, stateless /mcp endpoint already used by other MCP clients. That architecture means the WebMCP surface is generated from the server's real capability layer. There is no separately maintained list of browser tools to drift out of date. At submission time, the live surface exposes 12 consolidated domain tools with 104 actions. New server-side actions can appear in WebMCP automatically through tools/list rather than requiring a second implementation. The bridge also preserves the signed-in experience without turning the session cookie into ambient authority for arbitrary websites. Same-origin browser calls to /mcp may use the existing jobContext session. Cross-site requests are denied session-cookie authority using Sec-Fetch-Site, with Origin and Host checks as a fallback. Bearer-authenticated MCP clients and non-browser clients remain supported. This was built specifically so WebMCP could feel like part of the signed-in application while still enforcing an origin boundary around side-effecting tools. Browser agents also exposed operational gaps that were easy to miss in ordinary chat or direct MCP use. Long-running resume and cover-letter generation can outlive a browser tool-call window, so jobContext gained a durable submit-and-poll control plane. The agent can submit generation work, receive a work-item identifier promptly, and later poll for completion rather than holding the browser call open. Remote LLM clients were then given finite request timeouts and stale-run reporting so
