title: Understudy
pitch: Understudy uses WebMCP to turn one work sentence into a reviewed, executable playbook. Your agent asks for missing judgment, grows the process live, and routes evidence, recovery, and approval.
about_excerpt: Understudy uses WebMCP to turn one work sentence into a reviewed, executable playbook. Your agent asks for missing judgment, grows the process live, and routes evidence, recovery, and approval. Like Comment Story Updates The visitor’s agent loads the reviewed version, starts a run, and turns the graph’s rules into each owner’s task form. Recorded Pickup evidence cannot enter the Courier route. Understudy refuses the conflicting branch and preserves the submitted choice. Chat adds required weight, a delivery-method dropdown, owners, and Courier/Pickup conditions to the live process graph. A saved playbook keeps its fields, branches, approvals, versions, and run history ready for the next worker to reuse. The worker’s exact answer stays Draft evidence until one Save marks the reviewed playbook Human-confirmed. Lee reviews the customer-handoff evidence and approves it. The run preserves the values, actor, and human sign-off. After reload, a completed run can be reopened from history with its chosen route, evidence, actors, and event timeline intact. Start with one work sentence. Through WebMCP, the visitor’s agent asks focused questions while the process grows beside Inspiration Organizations already run on SOPs, ERP workflows, and explicitly programmed processes. Daily execution still depends on tacit judgment that rarely fits inside those systems: which weak signal means stop, which exception justifies a detour, how to recover, and when a handoff is actually safe. These gaps sit between formally defined steps. The operational record may say only "ran the schema migration on staging," while the experienced worker's judgment goes unrecorded. When that person is unavailable, the official process remains but part of its practical judgment layer disappears. We first tried the usual answer: put an LLM inside the app and ask it questions. WebMCP reverses that relationship: the page provides the tools, and the visitor brings a compatible agent. That made a different kind of collaboration possible — an agent apprenticed to the worker. It observes the work, asks for the judgment that is missing, and helps turn that knowledge into something the team can run. That is why it is called Understudy. What it does Understudy is a WebMCP layer that helps teams surface missing judgment through structured questions during real work, then encode the reviewed answers as a reusable process. It can start from an undocumented work event or an existing procedure, look for the gaps around the current task, and capture them as required evidence, decision criteria, recovery loops, ownership, and approval rules. One SDK script supplies observation, interviews, the process panel, and 21 WebMCP tools. Registered host actions add operation; the included process store and authenticated server guard add shared, governed execution. A visitor can begin in their compatible AI chat with one ordinary work sentence. Through WebMCP, the page presents the requested change as a human-readable “Use this as the starting point?” card. One confirmation saves the source record, opens Create process , and focuses the first question without asking the person to type the work again. The same flow is available from the page for people who prefer to start there. Capture. A person describes an ordinary work event in chat or on the page. Both entry points create the same reviewed source record. The visitor's agent reads the action journal, drafts the process around that event, and asks one focused question card at a time. For judgment-heavy steps the interview adapts from a concrete incident to observable cues, the tempting novice mistake, boundaries/exceptions, and failure/recovery. Questions, raw answers, authors, and timestamps stay attached to the relevant step as non-executable Draft evidence . Teach. The worker corrects the map directly — rename a step, adjust a branch, or explain a missing rule in chat. The agent reads those edits with get_map_edits , updates its next question, and leaves the revised map for human review. The existing Save as vN action confirms the whole map and its captured judgment together, changing Draft evidence to Human-confirmed ; there is no confirmation click after every answer. Saving a revision creates a new version with lineage. Older saved playbooks without elicitation metadata remain valid as previously reviewed versions. Operate. A saved playbook becomes assigned work. Contributor, Operations, and Reviewer roles receive their next task in order. Task cards render the playbook's typed data contract, including required numbers, booleans, acknowledgements, and dropdowns. Failure can route recovery work; reaching sign-off creates a review; the run survives reload. Enforce. The map is executable state, not a diagram. The page gives immediate guidance, while the server rechecks persisted transitions inside the storage transaction. It rejects work completed by the wrong role or out of order, branches that conflict with submitted evidence, forged approval completion, stale decisions after evidence changes, and edits to signed work. Reuse. When someone describes similar work later, Understudy explains which saved playbook matches and lets the person choose whether to start a new run. Execution evidence and new exceptions can inform a human-reviewed revision instead of silently changing the approved process. No site-owned LLM API key is required for these WebMCP interactions. The visitor's agent uses its own account, limits, and cost. How we built it Understudy SDK (TypeScript → bundled understudy.js ): an action journal, adaptive judgment-interview state machine, question and approval cards, a shadow-DOM process panel with a mini flowchart, and the WebMCP tool surface. Process engine: typed fields, role ownership, branch criteria, loop-backs that reopen the loop body, invalidation of superseded decisions, per-attempt audit events, review snapshots, and version lineage. Async human interaction: agent calls cannot wait indefinitely for a person. ask_user , run_action , and agent-requested deviations return a pending id; the agent polls for the real answer or approval outcome. Trust boundary: host and user text returned by read tools is labeled as untrusted data. Agent-requested host mutations have no force or global auto-approve path and wait for an on-page approval card. Normal accounts are bound to their authenticated session; only the disclosed judge account may switch among demo personas. Server guard (Express + Postgres on Railway): run updates are checked under the same lock used to persist them. The server derives actor and role from the session, recomputes order and branch evidence, owns approval completion, stamps attribution, and derives the run's active/completed status instead of trusting a browser claim. Two host apps: the React workspace demonstrates actions, persistence, role handoffs, and server enforcement. A deliberately plain, framework-free page demonstrates the one-script observation/tool tier. It does not pretend that one script can add an arbitrary application's database authorization. document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "resolve_decision", description: "Record a branch only when its saved criteria match evidence.", inputSchema: { /* stepId, branchTo, reason, measurements */ }, execute: async (input) => engine.resolveDecision(input), }) Challenges we ran into Human time is longer than tool-call time. Calls that waited for a person timed out, so we designed question and approval flows as pending-id + polling protocols. The agent's claim cannot be the record. An early agent could claim rowCountDelta: 0 after the assignee submitted 12 . Submitted task values are now authoritative; a conflicting branch is refused. The browser cannot be the security boundary. Earlier versions trusted browser-computed progress and persona strings too much. We moved actor, sequence, branch-evidence, approval, and completion checks into the server transaction and retain both the accountable persona and authenticating session. Retries expose stale state. Task and decision loop-backs must reopen the right work, clear current attribution, preserve historical attempts, cancel stale reviews, and invalidate superseded choices without erasing the audit trail. User text and instructions must stay separate. Work logs, labels, notes, and saved process content may contain instruction-like text. Read tools mark it as untrusted; authorization still comes from approval controls and server checks, never prompt wording. Automatable confirmation needs page UI. Native dialogs froze agent browsers, so destructive or state-changing confirmations became explicit page cards and two-step buttons. Business-language summaries are visible by default; raw action names and JSON remain available under Technical details. Testing required adversarial roles. We repeatedly attacked order, evidence, identity, retries, review delivery, concurrency, restoration, and malformed inputs. We d
video_title: Understudy WebMCP Chat Drives Graph 2m58 captioned
video_transcript_excerpt: Start in chat. Describe any recurring work, a database migration, quality check, incident response, or customer handoff through web MCP. Understudy turns the conversation into required fields, conditions, and branches. Here is one concrete example, a customer handoff. Understudy asks only what is needed to uncover the work before it, who owns each step, and which evidence controls the route. The page ships the tools. Each visitor brings their own agent. No site on Dell LM key is required. The conversation uncovers what comes next and who owns it. I answer on the page. Kim records the package. Park prepares the handoff. And Lee reviews the evidence. Now I teach the details, a required weight, and a delivery method drop down. Courier needs a tracking number. Pickup needs a collection code. I can correct the draft directly. The agent reads my edit and updates the actual process. A playbook is the team's saved version process. Starting a run turns the rules we just agreed on into each person's task form. Kim enters 12.5 kg and selects pickup. What if the agent tries courier anyway? The engine refuses. That contradicts the submitted choice. Following pickup activates Park's collection task. The drop down controls the route. A diagram can't refuse a bad past decision. This playbook just did. Park enters the collection code. The review appears automatically for Lee with the recorded evidence. Lee checks it and approves. The run records who did each step, what they submitted, and who signed off. A signed entry and review also work in a plain mobile browser, while desktop web MCP handles decision branches. After reload, the completed run remains in history and can be reopened with its evidence intact. In use a playbook, choose a saved process. The next person starts with the steps, inputs, branches, and approvals the team already taught. From one line of work to shared judgment to the team's next run, powered by web MCP. Through web MCP, the agent asks one expert question at a time. Answers stay draft evidence until the human states the playbook.

Formless - product that adapts to us, not the other way around. We're starting with healthcare, where that gap is most dangerous.

 Formless 

 Inspiration 

 
 "Empty your mind. Be formless, shapeless, like water. You put water into a cup; it becomes the cup. You put it into a teapot; it becomes the teapot." — Bruce Lee 
 

 For over 50 years, we've had to adapt to computers — learning their menus, their forms, their rigid abstractions. I wanted to flip that: software that 'takes the shape' of the person using it. 

 I started asking what a "formless" website or app would look like — one that, like water, takes on the most natural form for whoever and whatever it's serving. Healthcare felt like the sharpest place to test that idea given given my background, the increased need for accessibility and the fact that local models will soon allow us ot 

 Technology could help far more people understand their own health, but accessibility and fragmented data make it hard for most people to actually use AI to see where they stand in their health journey today. Formless is our glimpse of that future: a tool that takes many forms, helps people safely access their own data, and uses safe or local models to help them understand and make progress. 

 What it does 

 Formless is a tool for adaptive, "shapeless" software. We're starting with health as the first, most promising and hardest test case. 

 For health, Formless: 

 
 Make it possible for the app to change form while remaining functional and secure 
 Uses AI (local or otherwise privacy-safe models) to interpret that data 
 Shapes its output — explanations, visualizations, next steps — to the person's specific situation, rather than forcing everyone through the same fixed dashboard (not demonstrated in the demo) 
 

 How we built it 

 I wanted to build a real app that does something non-trivial, like pulling and visualizing real health data from EPIC. Security was top of mind so product for personal use only and no PHIs (sensitive health data) on any backend. The patient may decided to send data to be processed by an OpenAI model if they want.
Building blocks: Codex / Claude, WebContainer, NextJS, EPIC on FHIR, Vercel, WebMCP 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Getting real health data safely and legibly (formats, consent, access) without compromising privacy 
 Designing an interface that's genuinely adaptive rather than just a different fixed layout 
 Getting a local/safe model to explain health data accurately without overstepping into medical advice 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 A working end-to-end app built part time in a few days 
 Keeping the AI layer safe/local rather than routing sensitive health data through third parties 
 Proving the "formless" concept works on a real, high-stakes domain, not just a toy example 
 

 What's next for Formless 

 The real end goal splits reasoning from raw data access: a cloud "driving" model handles intent and orchestration, while a locally-trained model is the only component that ever touches raw patient data. 

 Please visit the README.md for more details. 

 Personal health apps won't replace clinics, but over time they can close the knowledge gap between visits — helping people understand and act on their own data without needing a costly, centralized system to interpret it for them.

FormPilot — Where AI agents and humans collaborate to conquer complex forms, with privacy you can trust.

 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 We've all been stuck on a confusing government form, googling what "Filing Status" means. We thought — what if AI could just sit next to you on the page and help? WebMCP finally makes that possible. 

 What it does 

 FormPilot lets an AI agent help you fill out complex forms (healthcare, loans, etc). You talk naturally — "My name is Alex, I live in Austin" — and the AI types it into the right boxes. It can explain confusing fields, catch errors, and prep the form for review. But it can never see your SSN or hit Submit without you. 

 How we built it 

 Vanilla JS, Vite, no backend. We registered 6 WebMCP tools using document.modelContext.registerTool() that let the AI read form state, explain fields, update values, and validate — all client-side. Forms are JSON-driven so adding new ones takes minutes. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Making sure the AI never sees raw sensitive data was tricky — we had to mask SSNs and income before returning them from the tool. Also, making the undo system feel instant when reverting agent changes took a lot of state management work. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 The AI genuinely can't submit without human approval. The privacy masking actually works. And we shipped two completely different forms (healthcare + business loan) with zero changes to the AI code — proving it's a universal platform. 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP is a game-changer. It turns websites from "things AI scrapes blindly" into "things AI cooperates with safely." Building the trust boundary between human and agent was the hardest and most rewarding part. 

 What's next for FormPilot 

 Adding more real-world forms (taxes, visas, DMV), multi-language support, and a form builder so anyone can make their own WebMCP-powered form without writing code.

title: Leaf
pitch: A design canvas your agent can use. Every layer is real HTML, and the editor registers itself as WebMCP site tools, so you and ChatGPT edit the same design at the same time.
about_excerpt: A design canvas your agent can use. Every layer is real HTML, and the editor registers itself as WebMCP site tools, so you and ChatGPT edit the same design at the same time. Like Comment Story Updates What it is Leaf is a visual design editor where every layer is a real HTML element with CSS styles. Open new.leafnode.app in ChatGPT's browser and the editor registers its own operations as WebMCP site tools. You and the agent then work on the same canvas. Why WebMCP fits Leaf Because every layer is DOM, the editor's operations were already structured and page-local: create an artboard, write HTML into it, read a swatch's fill, measure a text layer, pin a comment to a node. WebMCP lets the page hand those operations to whatever agent is in the browser, with no server, no extension, and no MCP client configuration. Leaf was an existing project I had been working on internally and the MCP server only worked with the local desktop app running. I'd considered creating a remote MCP server but it was a lot of work to get the interactions right, especially with screenshotting designs for agent feedback. WebMCP allowed me to quickly build a sort of remote MCP server that an agent can use without having the app running. How it makes the experience better The agent shows up on the canvas as a presence, its edits land in your undo history, and it reads the design as it is right now, including whatever you just changed by hand. In the demo I deleted the color directions I didn't want and left a comment on a swatch, "make this a bit warmer," the way I'd leave one for a teammate. The agent read the comment, warmed the swatch, updated its label, and carried that exact value into the guideline. Later it stopped and asked before pinning notes on the shared canvas. Code generators hand you a picture you can't touch; design tools have a canvas the agent can't see. Leaf is one canvas for both. What people and agents can do together Build a brand from foundations to applications in one sitting. The agent proposes a wordmark, two marks, three color directions, and a type pairing. You pick by hand. It assembles a one-page guideline from what survived, then builds a poster, an email header, and a landing page hero from that guideline on a new page, flagging its compromises as pinned comments you resolve. The canvas is the brief: nobody re-pastes brand rules into a prompt. I build landing page tooling for Shopify brands, and a new brand shipping a coherent page and email from one system, in about ten minutes of agent time, is the whole job. How WebMCP is implemented While a file is open, the app shell registers 27 tools with document.modelContext.registerTool : Reads: list_pages , get_basic_info , get_selection , get_tree_summary , get_node_info , get_node_styles , measure_text , find_nodes , get_canvas_layout , get_jsx , get_font_family_info Pages and camera: edit_pages , set_viewport Creation and mutation: create_artboard , write_html , update_styles , set_text_content , duplicate_nodes , delete_nodes , rename_nodes , move_nodes , set_node_visibility , rename_file Collaboration: list_comments , add_comment , resolve_comment_thread , finish_working_on_nodes Every tool dispatches through the same runtime the UI and Leaf's desktop MCP server use, so agent edits get the same validation, undo history, and persistence as a person's. Leaf existed before the challenge. The WebMCP integration and this local-only public build were done between August 26 and September 3, 2026; the repo's README has the timeline. Try it Open new.leafnode.app in ChatGPT's browser, or in Chrome with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing on. A first visit opens straight onto a canvas, and the Site tools indicator lists Leaf's tools. Then: "Build a 1440-wide landing page hero for a small-batch hot sauce brand: nav, eyebrow, headline, two buttons, fine print. Name every layer." Change the headline color by hand in the properties panel, then: "Match both buttons to the headline's new color." "Review the hero like a design lead. Measure the text, raise anything under 14px, and leave a comment pinned to any layer you changed." Built With node.js react typescript webmcp Try it out new.leafnode.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Aaron Escalona Like Share this project: Updates Aaron Escalona started this project — Sep 04, 2026 02:31 AM EDT
video_transcript_excerpt: Let's say we're starting a small batch hot sauce company called Midnight Chili Project. We want the brand foundations, so we give the agent a little guidance and tell it to use Leaf's web MCP tools and open it in the built-in browser. Leaf is a design tool where every layer is real HTML and it exposes its editor as a set of tools through web MCP. This is all a static site. There's no server, no traditional MCP server or built-in agent. We sped up the generation here to save some time. It gave us three color directions and two marks. I'll delete the ones I don't want directly on the canvas. And for the red, instead of picking a hex myself, I'll leave a comment on the swatch to make it a bit warmer. Now I asked for a one-page brand guideline from what's left. It reads the canvas as it is now, including my comment, warms up the red, and builds the brand guideline from the live values on the canvas. That's the whole system on one page. Then I ask it to use that guideline to build a poster, an email header, and a landing page hero. It creates a new page and builds all three from the guideline. Same palette, same type, same mark without me re-explaining any of it. Here it actually stops and asks before leaving comments on the canvas. I'll go ahead and say yes. It pins a couple of notes where it bent the system. I can read them and resolve them like I would with anyone else I'm working with. Under the hood, these tools run through the same editor run time as the UI. So, the agent's edits are validated and undoable just like mine. It's open source and you can try it now at new.leafnode.app.

title: InnerOS WebMCP Mission Control
pitch: A WebMCP coding control plane where a local AI proposes changes, InnerOS routes execution across real agent lanes, and every backend hop returns verifiable proof.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP coding control plane where a local AI proposes changes, InnerOS routes execution across real agent lanes, and every backend hop returns verifiable proof. Like Comment Story Updates Built for fastt operator workflows Trace every action from request to result Talk, coordinate, EXECUTE. Professional accesss for live presentations From prompt to physical action InnerOS WebMCP Mission Control Inspiration Most AI agents still interact with websites by looking at pixels, guessing what controls mean, and imitating human clicks. That is fragile for serious development, operations, and physical automation. We wanted a different model: the website itself should expose governed capabilities to the agent, while the human keeps a visible control room and every meaningful action remains verifiable. InnerOS already existed as our local-first multi-agent operating layer, coordinating local models, MCP/A2A agents, coding providers, infrastructure, evidence, and physical automation. For The WebMCP Challenge we built a WebMCP-native product layer that turns that infrastructure into one public, agent-operable development and operations cockpit. Live judge URL: https://webmcp.creatorcore.ai The core interaction rule Conversation is deliberation. Approval is the execution boundary. A user can talk to the local InnerOS Copilot for multiple turns, refine requirements, attach PDFs or source files, dictate a prompt by voice, change projects, and choose a different executor. None of that programs, registers, or physically executes anything. Only when the user is satisfied do they press Approve & Execute Plan . InnerOS then validates the selected project again and dispatches the latest refined plan through the selected lane. This gives Mission Control a clean universal workflow: Choose or create a project. Attach project context if useful. Converse with local Qwen and refine the plan. Choose AUTO / Local AMD / Codex / Cursor / AntiGravity. Press Approve & Execute Plan. Watch delivery, execution, verification, and evidence as different backend states. Delivery is not execution. Registration is not physical execution. A dispatch ID proves acceptance, not completion. A real browser development workspace The challenge build now goes beyond a one-shot demo console. Create Project Mission Control has an explicit Create Project action. Typing a new name into the Project field alone never creates anything. create_project_workspace creates a bounded local Git development workspace under the canonical InnerOS Projects root, initializes Git, and registers the project in Project Runtime. It deliberately does not create a GitHub or cloud repository behind the user's back. Before any coding dispatch, InnerOS verifies that the selected project exists and is a real Git workspace. PDF and source-code context Authenticated users can attach bounded PDFs and common source/text files. Attachments are stored privately per project and are passed to Qwen as read-only planning context . The Copilot now receives recent conversation history plus project-file context, so refinement is genuinely multi-turn rather than a chat UI that secretly sends only the latest message. Text PDFs are extracted locally; source/text files are decoded directly. If a PDF is image-only and no text can be extracted, the UI says so instead of pretending the model read it. A bounded portion of the same project context follows the execution brief after approval so the chosen executor can act on the relevant code/document information. Local voice dictation The voice button is local-first too. The browser records microphone audio using MediaRecorder, sends it to the authenticated WebMCP origin, and the server forwards it over loopback to our already-running local Whisper ASR service . The transcript comes back into the chat composer for review. Voice is dictation only. It never bypasses the approval gate. If local Whisper is unavailable, browser speech recognition is offered only as an explicit fallback rather than being mislabeled as local. Why WebMCP matters here WebMCP is not decorative in this project. It is the machine-facing interaction model. Instead of forcing an assistant to infer a human UI, the page publishes a compact set of semantic capabilities through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . The current public surface has 13 WebMCP tools : ask_inneros_copilot list_agents get_project_status create_project_workspace inspect_blockers dispatch_agent_action resolve_project_blocker get_execution_trace get_evidence dmx_create_scene dmx_status dmx_set_scene dmx_blackout The browser sees only those governed actions. InnerOS can coordinate a much larger private MCP/A2A fabric without exposing raw internal tools, private infrastructure, filesystem roots, model endpoints, or credentials. Local-first AI and execution lanes The primary Copilot is Qwen3-Coder 30B , served locally through vLLM on our AMD node. The live provider fabric exposes four coding lanes plus AUTO: AUTO — after approval, InnerOS chooses the cheapest capable local-first route; a bounded native capability may be used directly when appropriate. Local AMD / Qwen3-Coder — local vLLM + durable A2A/local execution, preferred under local-first policy. Codex — headless-capable when the live provider fabric proves CLI/auth/process readiness. Cursor — remote IDE/inbox when headless execution is not proven; delivery is not execution. AntiGravity — remote IDE/inbox unless a real runnable session is proven; completion requires returned evidence. Explicit lane selection remains explicit. If the user chooses Codex, Cursor, AntiGravity, or Local AMD, AUTO does not silently hijack that choice. Physical execution with AG-59 DMX The same control plane reaches the physical world through AG-59, the InnerOS DMX Stage Orchestrator . A judge can describe a lighting behavior that does not exist, refine it in conversation, approve it, and then watch the local AI create the new governed capability. After approval: Local Qwen designs one bounded declarative scene. Common aliases such as purple , blue , or disco ball are normalized into the canonical trusted vocabulary. AG-59 validates scene name, targets, colors, brightness, step duration, loops, and total duration. AG-59 atomically registers the scene in the live registry. Mission Control automatically discovers and selects the scene. The physical lights are still idle. The user separately presses Apply scene . Only then does dmx_set_scene drive the real fixtures. Raw DMX channels, fixture addresses, private topology, and rapid full-stage strobe are never accepted from public/model input. That separation is important: proposal != registration != physical execution . Proof, not theater Global Live Trace is designed around one question: how do I know this actually happened? Browser intent and backend confirmation are visibly separate: BROWSER events represent client-side intent and are not presented as backend proof. BACKEND · CONFIRMED events come from real server responses. Project creation is confirmed only after Project Runtime reports a real Git workspace. A provider receiving a task is not shown as running until process/session evidence exists. A DMX scene-registry change is confirmed only after AG-59 reports the new catalog. Voice is labeled Local Whisper only after the loopback ASR service returns a transcript. Every WebMCP request receives proof metadata including request ID, tool name, bridge identity, backend, timestamp, latency, whether execution is being claimed, and durable dispatch ID when applicable. Safety and trust boundaries The public browser never receives raw access to the private MCP runtime, local Qwen endpoint, local Whisper endpoint, physical DMX node, server paths, or credentials. Key rules: only allowlisted WebMCP operations are accepted; direct MCP access remains loopback-only; project names and local workspaces are bounded and verified; attachment size/type/context are bounded and project-scoped; private topology, paths, sessions, tokens, and credentials are sanitized; the Copilot cannot claim execution; conversation never executes; delivery is not treated as running; completion requires backend evidence; higher-impact host/cloud changes remain behind audited approval gates; DMX creation is declarative, bounded, revalidated, and separate from physical execution; local-first routing is visible instead of silently escalating to paid external compute. What is new for The WebMCP Challenge InnerOS and its underlying local multi-agent infrastructure existed before the challenge. The challenge-period work is the WebMCP-native product layer that makes it directly usable from an agent-capable website. Challenge-period work includes: WebMCP registration with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) ; the 13 public WebMCP contracts ; local Qwen3-Coder Copilot integration; real multi-turn conversation context; explicit approval-first execution semantics; local Git project creation from Missio

title: PantryOS
pitch: AI powered kitchen manager using WebMCP to recommend food to use, find recipes, track ingredients, and build smarter grocery lists.
about_excerpt: AI powered kitchen manager using WebMCP to recommend food to use, find recipes, track ingredients, and build smarter grocery lists. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Dashboard and AI activity Saved recipe Kitchen inventory Recipe matching Grocery planning Inspiration I do a ton of home cooking and managing the food in the fridge, can be a real hassle from what Ingredients I have to if they are expired or not. Inventory, recipes, and grocery lists usually live in separate places, leaving me having to compare dates, quantities, and missing ingredients manually. PantryOS explores a different model: Where I already implement AI for planning meals and recipes and managing leftover ingredients it instead homogenizes the information so an agent can access all of it at once. What it does PantryOS tracks ingredients across the fridge, freezer, and pantry, including quantities and expiry dates. It prioritizes food that should be used soon, finds suitable recipes, scales serving quantities, converts units, and can add missing ingredients to the grocery list. Instead of navigating several screens or finding recipes or copying information down and adding it to boxes of text manually the AI agent can automate this for you navigate fill out grab info from and expedite all this busy work so you can get back to your daily life. Here's an example of a use case Find a recipe for four people that uses the ingredients going bad, then add anything else I need to my shopping list. PantryOS turns that request into actual management actions keeping the interface and stored kitchen state up to date as you work or cook. Why WebMCP PantryOS is not a chatbot taped together alongside an application to manage your kitchen. Its features are exposed using structured WebMCP tools. The agent can inspect inventory, evaluate expiry dates, save and retrieve recipes, update quantities, and plan groceries without you having to feed it information about your kitchen and the recipes you have every time. What you end up with is a superior user experience, people can talk to agent in everyday language while PantryOS handles the multi-step coordination between inventory, recipes, serving sizes, and groceries. This also allows for further and more complex syncing of your information later on, the easy of use of the MCP allows for later hosted version of this demo to enable access by your AI agent wherever you are on the go. Human-agent collaboration The agent can prep and perform useful kitchen actions, but the person remains in control. Destructive actions like deleting recipes or throwing out food require confirmation to make sure the Agent doesn't run haywire and delete your grandmother long lost recipe. The activity panel records recent agent assistance, making it clear what is happening and what changed. How we built it PantryOS is a client-only React and TypeScript application deployed using Cloudflare Workers Static Assets. Zustand persists inventory, recipes, and groceries in browser localStorage . Its WebMCP tools register through document.modelContext . Every tool input is validated with Zod and described using a matching closed JSON Schema. Tool callbacks read current application state when they execute and call the same domain actions used by the interface. Automated tests cover tool contracts, persistence, malformed inputs, quantity conversion, grocery deduplication, cancellation, stale state, and confirmation races. What we learned The best agent tools don't feel like a background script or an entirely separate app. They work best when they can work with what you already have and you can see clearly their application. WebMCP made this feel like a more native interaction that just a automations or AI agent that is just added to a kitchen management app. Its quick simple to use and setup easy to for the AI to work with and access the correct information and allows me to use my already exiting workflow and models to do my tasks. What's next Future versions could add opt-in household collaboration and import integrations. I would like to have it persist across different browsers so you can access the info on the go. The submitted version intentionally remains local-first, client-only, and account-free so the WebMCP interaction is focused, private by default, and easy for judges to reproduce. But an increasing in scope and features is quite easy as there are tons of features I could have added that would be useful to me reminders, logs, side notes for recipes and so on that normal people use and interact with the kitchen everyday. title: ClawDeals
pitch: Your agent negotiates. You stay in control.
about_excerpt: Your agent negotiates. You stay in control. Like Comment Story Updates 1 Your agent negotiates. You stay in control. Every sensitive action leaves a policy decision, confirmation state and redacted receipt. The agent ranks synthetic e-bikes while showing why each candidate fits or violates the owner's policy. Your agent negotiates. You stay in control. Why ClawDeals? Think of your agent as a mechanical claw: reaching into the chaotic second-hand market to seize a great deal, while you keep a firm, unyielding grip on budgets, identity, and the final word. ClawDeals is the trust layer for agentic commerce. Buyer and seller agents can search, evaluate, and negotiate real-world deals, while humans retain explicit control over budgets, approvals, and contact details. The agent negotiates. It searches, ranks, questions sellers, and prepares offers through page-scoped WebMCP tools. The server enforces human limits. Budgets, owner approvals, reservations, and bilateral consent are re-checked server-side. A confirmation modal is never the security boundary. Every protected action stays verifiable. It produces a redacted receipt containing a request ID, an input hash, and the resulting policy verdict. Inspiration Current shopping agents excel at searching catalogs and adding items to carts. But peer-to-peer commerce is a different challenge: two independent people, asynchronous back-and-forth negotiation, strict budget caps, and personal contact info that shouldn't be leaked to an unknown bot. WebMCP gave us the missing in-browser contract: the agent receives structured, page-scoped tools, while the human keeps the final say on the exact same UI. Who this is for Peer-to-peer marketplaces (used bikes, electronics, furniture, housing) where negotiation is asynchronous, and an unconstrained agent could easily overspend or leak private identity. What it does A buyer delegates a Deal Mission: target price, hard budget, search radius, and item requirements. The agent executes WebMCP tools to search and evaluate listings against a structured policy_fit (which the human sees mirrored live as badges on the cards). The agent can open threads, ask technical questions (e.g. battery health), and stage offers. When an offer exceeds the mission budget, the platform halts the autonomous flow with APPROVAL_REQUIRED . The human owner reviews the action on /my/approvals/:id , can edit the counteroffer (e.g., adjust to €1,290), and approves it. Once accepted, the listing flips to RESERVED atomically. Contact details remain masked until both buyer and seller explicitly consent. How we built it Built on Next.js (Pages Router), TypeScript, React, PostgreSQL, and Supabase. WebMCP Integration : Tools register via document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) and listen to toolchange . We scope tools contextually: 5 public read-only tools on the main marketplace, expanding to 11 authenticated tools inside the judge sandbox. Security Boundary : Client confirmations are editable, but all policy rules (budgets, consent, reservations) are strictly re-checked server-side. Testing & Evals : Vitest covers tool schemas and redaction. Playwright runs deterministic synthetic sandbox journeys (Paris e-bike scenario). Adversarial tests verify prompt injection resistance, over-budget halts, and zero contact leakage. What we built during the challenge ClawDeals existed before August 25, 2026, making this an Existing project . Only the WebMCP capabilities built during the hackathon window are submitted for judging: Official imperative WebMCP runtime ( registerTool , AbortSignal lifecycle). Contextual dual-mode tool registry (5 public tools / 11 authenticated tools). Deal Mission engine and visual policy_fit card badges. Mission-bound negotiation ( start_thread , send_message , make_offer ). Server-enforced hard budget stops ( APPROVAL_REQUIRED ) and editable owner approvals. Atomic listing reservation ( RESERVED ) and bilateral contact reveal. Verifiable Agent Activity drawer and redacted receipts ( get_action_receipt ). Isolated judge hub with synthetic fixtures and one-click reset ( /webmcp-challenge ). Challenges we ran into Registering tools was straightforward; preserving a bulletproof trust boundary was the real challenge. When an agent can trigger payments or commitments, an in-browser confirmation dialog is insufficient. Sensitive write operations are idempotent and re-checked server-side, and contact details require two independent, server-recorded consents. We also kept our evaluation honest: a mocked modelContext in tests proves wiring, not real browser execution. We carefully separated local unit mocks, headless Playwright sandbox runs, and native browser verification. Accomplishments that we are proud of Real in-browser WebMCP tool execution without relying on generic DOM scrapers. 11 focused contextual tools instead of a single dangerous omnipotent function. Server-enforced budget protection that safely intercepts out-of-bounds agent counteroffers. Redacted audit receipts that let agents inspect past decisions without leaking secrets. Full end-to-end mission demonstration with synthetic Paris e-bike fixtures. What we learned Practical agentic commerce requires three distinct layers: An in-browser tool contract for the agent (WebMCP). A server-side policy contract for the platform (budget and identity gates). A consent contract for the human (approvals and bilateral reveal). What's next The isolated authenticated sandbox is live at https://sandbox.clawdeals.com/webmcp-challenge . Chrome 149+ (or Chrome 151 with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ) exposes the native runtime and our full 11-tool registry once the private judge key (provided in Devpost judge instructions) is entered. Public read tools remain testable without any key. title: Classmate
pitch: Paste a lecture. Video, captions, notes, and the board share one page. ChatGPT sits in the sidebar and writes on that desk — seek, highlight, draw — instead of narrating a screenshot.
about_excerpt: Paste a lecture. Video, captions, notes, and the board share one page. ChatGPT sits in the sidebar and writes on that desk — seek, highlight, draw — instead of narrating a screenshot. Like Comment Story Updates Thumbnail We can ask as many doubts as we want through out the lecture and get all of them answered by a single click in our agent with timestamps. Flashcards could be generated. We can even upload our own material and go through the lecture accoring to it. Classmate Paste a YouTube lecture. Video, captions, notes, and the board sit on one page. ChatGPT sits in the sidebar and actually uses that page — seek, highlight, draw — instead of talking about a screenshot. Live: https://classmate-steel.vercel.app/ How to try it This only works if ChatGPT has the page open in its own browser , not Chrome. Open ChatGPT desktop . Use Sol or Terra . Luna has WebMCP off, so skip it. Open ChatGPT’s built-in browser (the in-app one it uses to visit websites). Go to https://classmate-steel.vercel.app/ Paste a YouTube lecture on the page. In the sidebar chat (not the Ask box on the right), type: Study with me. If the header shows a tool count, you’re good. ChatGPT talks in the sidebar. Stuff happens on the page. Chrome still plays the video. Tools just won’t attach. Lost / Got it stay hidden. That’s normal. Ask on the page is not a chat. It pins a question at this timestamp. Talk to ChatGPT in the sidebar. Lost / Got it mark this moment — they only show up when tools are live. What it is ChatGPT is the conversation. The page is the desk. There’s one clock ( LectureEngine ). Video, transcript, slides, notes, and the board all follow playback.t . ChatGPT doesn’t watch the YouTube iframe. It reads what’s happening now , waits a bit, then writes on the desk so you can see it. You paste a lecture, say study with me, and it already knows what to do. The tools carry the instructions. You shouldn’t have to explain the site. Ask / Lost / Got it stay on the page. Next time ChatGPT reads classmate_get_now , the open questions are sitting there. It answers oldest first, next to the question — not only in the sidebar. How I built it Next.js, React, a single LectureEngine , WebMCP tools on the page, YouTube IFrame API, pdf.js, JSZip. Optional Speechmatics, AIMLAPI embeddings, Whisper, image gen. I started from the clock and worked out: Everything on screen comes from engine.now() . No second timeline. Then the tools. Reads tell the model what to do next. If something’s missing (captions, image gen, player), the tool says so instead of making it up. Then loading stuff: YouTube captions, PDF/PPTX, notes, VTT, a timing[] JSON file. Then matching speech to slides/notes — word overlap first, embeddings if you have a key, and anchors when someone pins a slide at a time. Then the desk UI: flip cards, quizzes, chalkboard, diagrams. Dark and quiet on purpose. It waits on video time , not wall-clock time. No screenshot of the iframe. Architecture ChatGPT talks. The page holds state. Tools are the bridge. Bit Where What it does Conversation ChatGPT sidebar (Sol / Terra) Talk. Not the canvas. Tools document.modelContext on the page ChatGPT calls these. Engine LectureEngine in the tab One clock: video, cues, slides, notes, board. Server Next.js routes Captions, metadata, STT token, embeddings, diagrams, Whisper. Flow is simple: ChatGPT calls a tool → execute() hits the engine → it gets JSON back ( now() / snapshot() ), not a picture of YouTube. The page hits /api/youtube/captions and friends when it needs to. What’s in the engine: Store What playback status, t , duration, rate cues[] captions slides[] deck notes[] from files, live, or the agent anchors[] “at this time, this slide” asks[] questions waiting for a reply, oldest first signals[] Lost / Got it board diagrams, cards, quizzes, margin notes That becomes now() , which both the UI and classmate_get_now use. Tools live on the top-level page , not in an iframe. Chrome-only = player, no hands. Fine. The YouTube player reports t and honors seek/play through a nonce so it doesn’t fight the engine. Data structures type Cue = { id, start, end, text } type Slide = { id, index, title, text, html?, imageUrl?, embedding? } type NoteBlock = { id, index, heading, text, t?, origin: "file" | "live" | "agent", embedding? } type Anchor = { id, t, slideId, noteIds?, label? } type DeskAsk = { id, at, text, reply: string | null } type StudentSignal = { id, kind: "confused" | "got_it" | "question" | "bookmark", at, text? } type NowSlice = { sessionId, playback, timecode, transcriptWindow, windowText, activeSlide, slideReason: "anchor" | "text-match" | "semantic" | "none", noteHits: { block, score }[], recentHighlights, recentSignals } If auto-match is messy, pin a slide. That anchor wins later: last t <= playback.t . Asks aren’t a second bot. unansweredAsks is everything still open. classmate_reply needs an askId (or a replies[] batch) so it can’t just answer the last one and ignore the rest. Notes remember where they came from. Change the video, live junk goes away. File notes and agent notes stay. Seek/play are one-shot requests with a nonce so YouTube doesn’t get stuck looping the same command. How the agent is supposed to work The how-to isn’t a paragraph you paste. It’s the description on classmate_get_session , and every read sends back howToStudy + next . Open the URL in ChatGPT’s browser. Tools register. Say Study with me . It calls classmate_get_session . You paste YouTube. Captions go into cues[] . Loop: observe_next (wait ~12s of the video , or Lost / Got it / Ask) then get_now . New idea, they’re lost, or they asked → highlight, pin, draw, cards, reply. On the page. Otherwise stay quiet. observe_next watches playback.t , not setTimeout(12000) . Pause the video, it stops waking. Seek isn’t “12 seconds passed.” Lost / Got it cut in immediately. Cite like [title, slide N, 4:12] . Don’t invent the rest of the lecture. Don’t screenshot YouTube. Captions ChatGPT can’t hear the video. If captions never hit the page, get_now is empty and it starts guessing. YouTube from a Vercel IP is annoying. The watch page lists caption tracks, then the actual fetch comes back blank. This is the fallback order: Step Try If nothing 1 Watch-page timedtext next 2 InnerTube Android player + json3 next 3 iOS / TV player next 4 get-youtube-transcript in the function (PoToken) next 5 empty cues “Listen with the microphone” Android is what usually works in production. The old local script that minted a PoToken in a child process doesn’t ship on Vercel, so the library runs in-process now. Mic is opt-in. You can’t captureStream a YouTube iframe, so we don’t grab the mic on every paste. Matching slides and notes now() just asks: given this second of the lecture, what’s relevant? Take playback.t . Grab cues from about 18s behind to 4s ahead. If there’s an anchor at or before now, that’s the slide. Else overlap the spoken window with slide text. Else embeddings, if you have a key. Same idea for notes: words, nearby timestamps, embeddings. Word overlap is the default so it doesn’t invent a heading like “JavaScript Loops” from a video that never said that. Auto-generated notes were doing that, so I killed them. Empty notes beat wrong notes. Calls I stuck with The page is the desk. If ChatGPT only talks, this is a YouTube tab with extra steps. Writes have to show up on screen. Tools explain the site. classmate_get_session is the playbook. You say one sentence. If we don’t have it, say so. No captions → listen. No image gen → chalkboard SVG. No WebMCP → hide Lost / Got it. Ask isn’t chat. A second box posting to an LLM would hide state. Questions live on the desk until they’re answered, oldest first. Wait on the video, not the clock. Paused shouldn’t keep pinging. A seek isn’t progress. Cards are cards. classmate_make_cards is a flip packet. Quiz is a separate packet. Don’t dump a wall of quiz text. You can export / load a timing[] JSON plus YouTube, mp4, PDF, PPTX, VTT, notes. The engine doesn’t care which door the data came in. What was annoying Captions on Vercel. Worked on my laptop, empty in production. InnerTube Android first, then in-process transcript, then mic. Wanting to screenshot YouTube. Can’t. Cross-origin. Put speech on the page instead. Tools not existing on first paint. We poll document.modelContext until they stick, then show the count. Only the last Ask got answered. First version used .at(-1) . Now it drains the queue. Fake notes. Distill hallucinated titles. Stopped that. YouTube setSize on the docked 16:9 player. Had to tell the adapter, not just CSS. What I learned A better prompt about a website isn’t the fix. The website has to be a tool. If the model’s clock is the chat turn, it’s always in the wrong chapter. If it’s playback.t , highlights start to mean something. If you asked on the page and the answer only exists in the sidebar, that’s two products. Putting replies next to the question is when this started feeling like a desk. S

title: Sân Chơi
pitch: AI-hosted Vietnamese folk playground: Ô ăn quan, Bầu cua, Múa rối nước, Gióng's Iron Garage & Rồng rắn lên mây — 5 games, 21 hang-proof WebMCP tools. sanchoi.app
about_excerpt: AI-hosted Vietnamese folk playground: Ô ăn quan, Bầu cua, Múa rối nước, Gióng's Iron Garage & Rồng rắn lên mây — 5 games, 21 hang-proof WebMCP tools. sanchoi.app Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration My 3-year-old nephew loves hearing Vietnamese folk tales and watching water puppet shows during Tết. But these centuries-old traditions — Ô ăn quan (Mancala), Múa rối nước (water puppet theatre), Rồng rắn lên mây (dragon snake chase), Bầu cua tôm cá (Lunar New Year dice), and the legend of Thánh Gióng riding an iron horse — are vanishing from children's daily lives. I wanted to build a digital "sân chơi" (playground) where an AI agent acts as the Game Master (Người Xướng Trò), hosting these folk games for kids, in Vietnamese, with full cultural authenticity. The OpenAI WebMCP Challenge was the perfect catalyst: what if the AI doesn't just talk about folk games, but actually runs them — managing game boards, rolling dice, directing puppet shows, chanting call-and-response, and feeding Gióng's iron horse? How I built it Tech stack: Vite + TypeScript, Three.js (3D water puppet stage), GSAP (animations), Web Audio API (synthesized Đàn Bầu, festive drums, gongs), zero backend — fully client-side with localStorage persistence. Architecture: Each game follows a strict split: rules.ts (pure deterministic game logic, no DOM) and scene.ts (Three.js/GSAP visuals). Agent tools live in tools.ts and call rules directly, returning JSON state instantly — animations fire as fire-and-forget side effects. The WebMCP integration registers 32 tools via document.modelContext.registerTool following the standard JSON Schema spec with inputSchema , annotations, and AbortController -based cleanup. A fallback mode exposes tools at window.__debugTools for DevTools testing outside ChatGPT. For audio, I synthesized traditional folk instrument sounds using the Web Audio API — no external audio files needed for the core experience, just procedural Đàn Bầu melodies and percussion. Challenges 1. The hang bug. The first version of Ô ăn quan awaited GSAP animations inside agent tool handlers. In headless/backgrounded browser contexts, requestAnimationFrame is throttled, so the agent hung forever waiting for an animation that never fires. The fix: agent-facing tools ( isAgent: true ) return game state immediately; animations run as void animate().catch(...) fire-and-forget promises. This pattern was then retrofitted to all 5 games. 2. Bầu cua's async dice. The dice-roll scene awaited animateDiceRoll before resolving bets. Same class of hang. Refactored to split roll logic from animation, applied the fire-and-forget pattern. 3. Zero-backend persistence. With no server, game state survives refreshes through localStorage — but only the last active game is saved. I built a save_progress tool and a "flustered game master" easter egg: if the agent does 5+ actions without saving, Chú Tễu pops up with "Người xướng trò bị rối!" (The Game Master is flustered!). 4. Cultural authenticity in code. Every game had to feel Vietnamese , not just reskinned Western games. Ô ăn quan uses relay-sowing rules unique to Vietnam (when your last seed lands in a small pit with >1 seed, you scoop and keep sowing). Water puppetry required understanding the 11th-century thủy đình stage and iconic tales like Cóc kiện trời (The Toad Sued Heaven). Gióng's Iron Garage is rooted in the legend of Thánh Gióng — a folk hero who grew instantly, rode an iron horse, and defeated invaders. What I learned Building agent-native web apps requires a fundamentally different mental model from human-facing UIs. The agent needs instant, structured feedback — it can't "see" animations. This means: Game logic must be pure and synchronous. The DOM is for humans; JSON is for agents. Tool descriptions must be precise enough for an LLM to understand the game's mechanics and cultural context without ever seeing the screen. Easter eggs and "funny hooks" keep the experience playful even when the agent is driving: zero-capture moves in Ô ăn quan make the pit shake indignantly, matching dice in Bầu cua trigger a "XỐC! BA CON!" celebration, and the water puppet applause meter rewards dramatic timing. The result is a new kind of interactive cultural preservation — not a video about Vietnamese folk games, but an AI that can host them.  Inspiration 

 We were inspired to build Thinking Map after seeing people struggle to communicate their ideas about what they wanted to build with CodeYam. CodeYam makes it easy to vibe code complex software applications but you still need to think deeply about what that software should do and how it should behave in various situations. Thinking Map helps with this but is not limited to software challenges. It is a general thinking tool. 

 What it does 

 Thinking Map is designed to help you think. Whether you want to plan a party, go on a trip, or build a software application, Thinking Map creates a robust user-experience for you and an AI agent to think about complex situations and challenges from multiple different perspectives while coming up with insights and devising experiments to move you forward. The visual experience and interactions complement the available agent chat, making the complexity of the project more understandable and easier to iterate on as you learn more and engage in experiments. 

 How we built it 

 Thinking Map was built using CodeYam to ensure a highly maintainable application. CodeYam let us vibe code it using both Codex and Claude Code. We were able to rapidly build and iterate on it over the course of just three days. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Our biggest challenge was creating a useful user-experience while sharing screen real estate with the agent in ChatGPT Desktop. We are still working to improve this. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We were able to build and iterate across a number of possible designs quickly over the course of just three days to create our submission. 

 What we learned 

 We were not aware of the WebMCP format but have been looking for a high quality way to supplement agent chat experiences with robust browser-based user experiences. We plan on leveraging WebMCP more going forward. 

 What's next for Thinking Map 

 We want to continue to improve the user-experience and the different ways Thinking Map can help you deconstruct your challenge and look at it from different perspectives. We also want to make it easier to engage in the experiments it suggests.

title: Every — real invoices from an AI browser, no sign-up
pitch: A marketing site that publishes 17 WebMCP tools, so an agent can make a real invoice for someone who has no account.
about_excerpt: A marketing site that publishes 17 WebMCP tools, so an agent can make a real invoice for someone who has no account. Like Comment Story Updates ChatGPT's built-in browser listing the 17 Site tools every.ai registers, beside the live generator page. Inspiration every.ai had two landing pages promising a free invoice generator and a free proposal generator to small service businesses. Neither had a generator behind it. We built one during the Challenge window, and made it agent-first from the first commit, because a generator is the one corner of a marketing site where "an agent fills in a form and gets a real result" is the whole product. Then we found the sharper reason to do it. Asked in plain language for "a free invoice tool I can use without making an account", ChatGPT recommended three competitors and then volunteered a correction about us: that Every requires a Google sign-up, so it does not qualify. It cited every.ai. Reading our marketing pages, that was a fair conclusion — the pages talk about trials and sign-in, because that is what the product needed before this week. That is the problem WebMCP actually solves. Search forms a view of what your site can do, and that view is stale the moment you ship. A page that publishes tools does not have to argue with the model. It just hands over the capability, and the agent updates. In our demo video you can watch that happen live : the agent tells the user Every needs an account, opens the page, and corrects itself on camera — "the earlier answer was indeed outdated: the page explicitly says no account is needed" — and then makes the invoice. What it does every.ai is a static Astro marketing site. It also registers 17 tools on document.modelContext , so an agentic browser can act for a visitor who has never signed up. They cover the whole arc of a visit. Decide. about_every and check_fit answer what Every is, what it costs from live pricing data, and whether it suits the business the visitor describes — including saying plainly when it does not. search_help answers from a build-time index of the site's own content and admits when it has no answer instead of guessing. Do. create_invoice , update_invoice , create_proposal , update_proposal , convert_estimate_to_invoice , get_document , list_my_documents and get_pdf create and revise real invoices, estimates and proposals. Not previews. Each one is created immediately, gets a public link, and is kept for 30 days. No account at any point. Leave. request_signup_link returns a single link that opens an Every account already holding everything the agent just made. open_app points existing customers at the right page. request_demo reaches sales. calculate_stack_cost and score_warm_lead expose the site's own calculators. get_more_tools records what an agent wanted and could not find, which becomes our roadmap signal. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP, and what is newly possible A free tool that only a human can operate sits and waits for a human. The visitor has to find the page, understand the form, and fill it in. WebMCP moves the tool to where the person already is — mid-sentence, in the conversation where they said "I need to invoice this client." Three things became possible that were not before: A stranger can transact with us. Not a demo account, not a sandbox: a real document at a real URL that they can send to their client, with no sign-up, created by their agent on their behalf. The page can correct the model. Our video is the proof. Static marketing copy loses that argument; a tool surface wins it, because the tool is the ground truth. We can hear demand. get_more_tools means an agent that wants something we do not offer tells us so, in the moment, in its own words. How we built it WebMcpTools.tsx is a headless React island mounted once on the site. It feature-detects document.modelContext (falling back to the deprecated navigator.modelContext ) and, on a browser without WebMCP, registers nothing and renders nothing. Each tool is registered with registerTool : a JSON Schema inputSchema , annotations ( readOnlyHint , and untrustedContentHint on anything relaying text a third party wrote), and an execute that calls the same typed API client the site's human-facing forms use — so a document created by an agent and one created by a person land in the same session and the same list. Two design rules shaped everything. Results are written to be read aloud. The agent, not our UI, is doing the talking, so every result is a short self-contained string that ends in a usable next step, and a test asserts each one fits the budget. Guest documents mirror the product. They live in a completely separate database whose every user-settable column matches the product table it will one day become, so claiming a document into a real account is an insert of the same columns — lossless, not a re-entry. Because no engineer has a WebMCP-native browser in CI, we wrote a small in-page polyfill that installs document.modelContext only when a page opts in with ?webmcp=polyfill and no real implementation exists. The same registration and execute() path then runs in ordinary headless Chromium, which gave us a node --test suite and a Python harness that hands the tools to a live Claude model and runs a real agentic loop against the page. Challenges we ran into Keeping the guest schema identical to the product's so that claiming is lossless rather than a reconstruction. Designing get_pdf to be genuinely useful while still capturing a lead. Writing results an agent can relay verbatim without a model misreading a phrase as a system error. The hardest one was restraint. Our first version of the sign-up tool emailed the link. An adversarial review called it what it was: an unauthenticated endpoint that sends mail from our domain to any address a caller names — roughly 1,200 sends an hour from one machine. We cut the send entirely. The agent already has the link in the conversation the person is reading, so delivery added nothing and risked our sending reputation. The tool returns the link and nothing else. Accomplishments we're proud of It runs on the real production data path, not a demo backend. Every document a tool creates is real and has a real claim path into the product. And the surface is honest under pressure: check_fit tells people when Every is not for them, and search_help says when it does not know. What we learned Designing for an agent is not designing an API. It is closer to writing for a colleague who will repeat what you said to a customer, word for word, without checking. That changes every string. What's next The Chrome origin trial, so Chrome and Gemini users can see the tools at all. Then WebMCP inside the signed-in product, so a customer's agent can operate their actual workspace in the same tab. New work vs prior work every.ai existed before the Challenge, and this submission is evaluated only on what was added during the Submission Period. All of it was built on 2026-09-02 and 2026-09-03 , inside the window, with dated commit history in the public repository: the tool layer, the polyfill, the test suite, the agent-simulation harness, the guest document store and its API, the generator pages, /for-agents , and llms-full.txt . Before this window, the two generator URLs were six-line landing stubs with nothing behind them and the site registered no tools at all. title: DungeonQ
pitch: Enter the unknown. Exit with proof.
about_excerpt: Enter the unknown. Exit with proof. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Completed synthetic proof queue with deterministic evidence and retained compensation history. DungeonQ landing page: a WebMCP-native synthetic security proving ground. Mobile view of the governed human-agent workflow. Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for DungeonQ Inspiration Adaptive cyber defense often jumps from detection straight to action. That is exactly where agent autonomy becomes dangerous: an agent that proposes a high-impact change should not be able to approve the same change. We built DungeonQ to make that boundary interactive, testable, and observable in judge-authored synthetic environments. What it does DungeonQ is a WebMCP-native synthetic security proving ground. A judge can provide a bounded Scenario Pack containing synthetic assets, signals, trust classes, policy thresholds, injected control failures, a requested effect, and expected invariants. A WebMCP agent admits the pack through a strict validator, runs a deterministic decision engine, explains the route and capability envelope, and requests human review. The tool surface then contracts: the agent never receives an approval tool. Only after a person approves the exact proposal digest and revision in the visible UI can the agent apply the browser-local synthetic effect, verify its receipt, compensate it, and return a replayable evidence digest. Three fixed-seed scenarios cover a controlled honey-credential replay, compound edge/evidence failure, and fresh-context false-positive recovery. Judges can also author their own packs and replay them through the browser or CLI. How we used WebMCP DungeonQ exposes state-shaped tools through document.modelContext: dungeonq_scenario_admit dungeonq_status dungeonq_simulate dungeonq_approval_request dungeonq_effect_apply dungeonq_receipt_verify dungeonq_effect_rollback dungeonq_evidence_export This is not a static wrapper around buttons. WebMCP makes the application meaningfully better because an agent can carry a complete new environment into the page, traverse a governed multi-step workflow, and lose capabilities as state changes. Human approval remains an intentionally missing capability. How we built it The dependency-free security core uses browser-safe JavaScript modules shared by Web UI, CLI, tests, and WebMCP. Admission enforces a 128 KiB document bound, closed fields, synthetic namespaces, content safety, cross-field references, budgets, scopes, and bounded arrays. The pure engine produces a canonical SHA-256 input digest, weighted risk score, route safety overlay, failure-composed capability set, exact proposal digest, and invariant results. A governed in-memory state machine binds approval, proposal digest, revision, expected prior state, and idempotency claim. Apply and compensation append protected receipts; Evidence Bundles cover the command transcript and hash-chained audit events. Vinext and the official Sites Vite plugin create the public ChatGPT Sites artifact without changing the core decision path. Challenges we ran into The hard part was not adding more agent power. It was designing a useful WebMCP experience where capability absence is part of the product: scenario replacement disappears after simulation, approval never exists as an agent tool, stale digests fail closed, compound failures can only remove capabilities, and recovery preserves prior evidence. Accomplishments that we're proud of A judge can bring a new synthetic environment through WebMCP, UI, or CLI. The same fixed-seed input produces the same engine result across adapters. The agent cannot approve its own proposal. All 127 non-empty combinations of seven injected failures are tested for monotonic capability reduction. Receipt and Evidence Bundle tampering are detected. Compensation is idempotent and preserves the original evidence chain. The live app contains no third-party browser asset, analytics, remote script, real credential, or production connector. What we learned The strongest human-agent experiences are not necessarily the ones with the most tools. A state-shaped capability surface can make authority, uncertainty, and recovery legible to both the agent and the person supervising it. What's next for DungeonQ DungeonQ deliberately stops at synthetic validation. A production path would require independently attested signals, durable state and claims, external evidence checkpoints, verified human identity, real policy distribution, isolated effect infrastructure, clock trust, and field acceptance. Those are future gates, not claims hidden behind a polished demo. title: Tengu and Boykot web mcp the art of interact with agents
pitch: A real Santiago restaurant and a real art-supply store expose menu, catalog, live stock and forms as WebMCP tools. The agent does the tedious part and stops: you send, you pay.
about_excerpt: A real Santiago restaurant and a real art-supply store expose menu, catalog, live stock and forms as WebMCP tools. The agent does the tedious part and stops: you send, you pay. Like Comment Story Updates Tengu Swag Boykot Flow Restaurants and small shops are the most-attempted and worst-served agent task on the web. Every assistant can find a restaurant. Almost none can do anything with one. The menu lives in a PDF or a photo, the prices are stale, and the booking widget is a third-party iframe an agent cannot reason about. So the agent guesses — and it guesses wrong about the one thing the diner is paying for. We run two real businesses in Santiago, Chile, and we felt this from the other side. Agents were already describing our menu and our catalog to people, from blog posts written years ago. We had no way to be the author of what agents said about us. But the thing that actually kept us from opening the door was not the reading. It was the booking. Nobody wants an agent that reserves a table, or buys $80,000 CLP of paint, on their behalf while they are looking away. So we built for the opposite: the agent does the tedious part and stops. What it does Two businesses that have nothing in common expose the same pattern. Tengu — a kappo omakase restaurant, average table $300–400k CLP. Five tools on the page: get_carta (the live menu with real prices, by section), buscar_plato (search dishes, cocktails, wines and sake), get_guia (long-form guides the restaurant wrote about bluefin, sake and kappo cooking), get_info, and the one that matters — preparar_reserva. Boykot — an art and graffiti supply store, about 3.000 SKUs. Thirteen tools: catalog search, product detail, brand list, quotes, stock subscriptions, promotions, project planning, colour cards — plus agregar_al_carro, ver_mi_carro and guardar_en_lista. preparar_reserva fills the reservation form on the page with the party size, date, time and name the agent gathered in conversation — and then stops. It does not submit. The form is left visible, filled, scrolled into view, with the fields the agent touched marked, and a notice above it that says so and offers to discard. The human checks it and sends it. agregar_al_carro does the same on the store side. The cart gets built. Nobody pays. That is the division of labour we wanted. The agent parses "a table for four next Friday, somewhere quiet, my wife doesn't eat raw fish". The human keeps the part that costs money and social capital. The restaurant's host still sees a normal booking arrive. The read tools matter for a subtler reason: grounding. An agent asked "what's the sake situation at Tengu" now answers from the restaurant's own words and tonight's actual list, instead of from a 2023 blog post. For the first time, the business is the author of what agents say about it. How we built it Eighteen tools across the two sites — five on Tengu, thirteen on Boykot — registered on document.modelContext (with navigator.modelContext as the deprecated alias), feature-detected so each page degrades to an ordinary website when the API is absent: var mc = document.modelContext || navigator.modelContext; if (!mc || typeof mc.registerTool !== 'function') return; Both sites carry origin trial tokens, so the API is native — no ?webmcp flag, no polyfill, nothing for the judge to enable. Open the URL and the tools are there. The in-page tools are deliberately thin: they proxy to the same /api/mcp JSON-RPC server each business already runs for out-of-page agents. A browser agent and a server-side agent get the same answers from the same source. One truth, two transports. The exception is the write-side tools — preparar_reserva and agregar_al_carro only exist in the page, because their whole job is to touch the DOM in front of a human and leave it there. Tengu is static HTML and vanilla JS on Vercel with zero npm dependencies on the page — the smallest attack surface we could manage for something that hands tools to an autonomous caller. Reservations persist to Postgres through SECURITY DEFINER functions behind row-level security that denies all direct access; the page never holds a database credential. Boykot is Next.js, backed by the store's live inventory. Deliberately not exposed: anything that spends money or commits the business. No payment, no confirmation, no cancellation, no order modification. The reservation engine has its own caps underneath — 8 tables per slot, rate limit per name and phone — and the agent surface sits strictly inside them. A tool we don't register is a tool that can't be jailbroken.
