title: RightsOps — Rights-aware Campaign Operations
pitch: WebMCP authority that disappears when the evidence behind human approval becomes stale.
about_excerpt: WebMCP authority that disappears when the evidence behind human approval becomes stale. Like Comment Story Updates Short description RightsOps is a WebMCP-enabled creative-operations workspace for preparing a three-asset social campaign against structured usage-authorization metadata. An agent can inspect evidence and prepare an exact manifest, but only a human can approve it. Approval causes the page to expose one parameterless WebMCP publish tool bound to that manifest. If a selected asset's evidence changes, the manifest becomes stale and the capability disappears. The agent must repair the campaign and regain exact human approval before it can perform a one-shot simulated publication. Inspiration Creative operations teams coordinate asset selection, territory, channels, commercial-use constraints, approvals, and publication across interfaces that were designed only for people. Giving an agent generic UI control makes the task faster, but it does not make delegated authority specific, current, or visible. RightsOps explores a stronger model: the website itself tells the agent which structured actions are valid now, and can withdraw a consequential action when its evidence is no longer current. What it does The seeded demo asks for three commercial assets for Japan across Instagram and TikTok for six months. The agent uses WebMCP reads to inspect eight candidate assets and prepares an exact manifest with versioned rights proofs. The human reviews and approves that manifest in the UI. Only then does an exact publish_approved_campaign_manifest-<id> capability appear. A deterministic external rights update increments one selected asset's evidence from v1 to v2. The interface visibly changes from 3/3 current to 2/3 current , marks the proof stale, and removes publish authority. The agent diagnoses the stale proof, finds a replacement, and prepares a new manifest. After human re-approval, a new one-shot publish capability appears. Executing it creates a server-generated append-only demo receipt and audit trail, then consumes the capability. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP WebMCP is not a convenience wrapper in RightsOps; its changing tool surface is the agent-facing expression of current application authority. Structured tools let the agent inspect campaign and rights data without scraping the visual UI. Dynamic registration lets the site expose publication only after a human has approved one exact manifest, remove it when evidence becomes stale, and expose a new manifest-bound operation only after repair and re-approval. This would be difficult to express safely through ordinary browser actuation. A click-capable agent can see a button, but the page cannot give it the same explicit, typed contract that an operation is read-only, decision-free, manifest-specific, and temporary. How it creates a better user experience The human stays focused on the consequential judgment: reviewing and approving the exact campaign. The agent handles structured investigation, candidate selection, manifest preparation, stale diagnosis, repair, and execution. The Capability Surface makes that delegation legible without developer tools by showing the server state, authorization count, observed WebMCP tools, and the causal reason publish authority appeared or disappeared. The site remains fully usable when WebMCP is unavailable, with a clear compatibility notice. WebMCP is a progressive enhancement that improves agent accuracy and collaboration without becoming the only way to operate the demo. What humans and agents can do together now Before this pattern, a human either performed the entire multi-step workflow or gave an automation broad access and manually checked whether its assumptions were still valid. In RightsOps, the agent can do the investigative and mechanical work while the human grants narrow authority for one reviewed artifact. The website automatically withdraws that authority if the supporting evidence changes, and the agent can repair the plan instead of acting on stale approval. How WebMCP was implemented The client feature-detects document.modelContext and registers imperative tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Read tools carry readOnlyHint: true . Every registration is scoped to an AbortController ; the state coordinator unregisters tools whose operations are no longer valid and then reconciles the judge-visible list through document.modelContext.getTools() . Server workflow state is the source of truth. toolchange events are retained only as telemetry. Draft and Stale expose manifest preparation; Review Ready deliberately exposes no approval tool; Approved exposes exactly one parameterless publish tool containing the approved manifest ID in its name; Published exposes receipt and audit reads. The publish callback awaits the server result before state synchronization removes the consumed registration. The server independently verifies that the exact manifest was approved, every rights-proof version is current, the manifest hash is unchanged, and the approval has not already been consumed. This preserves fail-closed behavior even if a client has not refreshed its visible tools yet. How we built it Next.js 16 and React 19 for the application and route handlers TypeScript and Zod for contracts and validation direct WebMCP Imperative API for browser tool registration Drizzle ORM and managed Postgres for server-authoritative workflow state Vitest for domain, server, UI, and WebMCP tests Vercel for the public deployment Codex for implementation, test iteration and verification. Challenges The hardest boundary was ensuring that dynamic client capabilities never became the security authority. Tool removal improves what an agent can discover and call, but server freshness and replay checks must independently reject stale or consumed operations. A second subtlety was avoiding cancellation of an in-flight publish call: the tool stays registered until execution completes, then Published-state synchronization withdraws it. Accomplishments A native WebMCP target-client run discovered and invoked every tool contract. The same session proved exact authority appearance, stale withdrawal, repaired re-approval, one-shot consumption, and refresh reconstruction. The human workflow remains complete when WebMCP is unavailable. Automated coverage proves stale-server rejection, replay rejection, reset from partial state, network diagnostics, and Approved/Stale/Published reloads. Judges can see the causal capability story directly in the product and in paused evidence frames. What we learned Dynamic tools are most valuable when their presence carries product meaning, not merely when they duplicate buttons. WebMCP gives a site a structured way to represent temporary delegation, but robust systems still need server-owned truth, exact binding, freshness checks, and replay protection. Observability also matters: a capability lifecycle is far easier to trust when the user can see why authority changed. What's next This hackathon build intentionally stays within a synthetic, deterministic scenario. A production version would require authenticated organizations, verified rights-data integrations, policy and legal review, durable audit retention, and authorized publishing-platform integrations. Those are not implemented or claimed here. Simulation and legal scope Rights metadata is deterministic structured demo input, not legal analysis or advice. The rights update and social publication are simulated. The WebMCP tool lifecycle, exact human approval, state transitions, database checks, stale/replay rejection, receipt generation, and one-shot consumption shown in the demo are implemented behavior. title: Vouchsafe
pitch: Three agencies hold one household's record and may not pool it. Vouchsafe screens that household for six benefit programs anyway by putting yes-or-no questions to four origins and receiving no records
about_excerpt: Three agencies hold one household's record and may not pool it. Vouchsafe screens that household for six benefit programs anyway by putting yes-or-no questions to four origins and receiving no records Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration To find out whether a household qualifies for heating assistance, food assistance, or a childcare subsidy, a caseworker needs facts held by three separate agencies, and those agencies are forbidden to share them. The restriction is legal rather than technical, which is why the usual answer (put it all in one database) is not available. So the household becomes the courier: a portal and a login for every agency, documents printed and re-keyed into six forms that all ask the same questions. Benefits go unclaimed because the process is exhausting instead of people not being able to qualify. WebMCP is the first thing that fits the actual shape of that problem. It lets a site offer a capability without handing over the data behind it, and it expresses consent as something the browser already understands: an origin. A server-side MCP integration cannot do this, because the agencies would have to trust a central integrator with the records themselves, which is the exact thing the law forbids. What it does Vouchsafe is a benefits screening workbench for a caseworker. They ask one question in plain language, and six programs are determined across three agencies in seconds, with the reasoning shown requirement by requirement. Each agency keeps its record at its own origin and answers only predicates. attest_income_below(threshold, tax_year) returns {attested: true}, never 34200. The release of information a client signs is expressed as exposedTo: [' https://vouchsafe-app.vercel.app']: this site may ask, and no other site may. The office ends up safer than before, not merely faster. A disclosure ledger shows every question that crossed an origin boundary, which field stayed at the agency, and what came back. After a full screening, it reads eleven questions asked, zero record fields disclosed. A caseworker who never had the income figure cannot leak it. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before An assistant can compose a decision across mutually distrustful origins that will not share data, and none of them has to trust the assistant, the broker, or each other with a record. Three things follow: Determination without disclosure. Utility Arrears Relief comes back eligible having asked nobody anything, because it is categorically eligible via heating assistance. The determination is derived entirely from another determination. Consent that is revocable mid-session, from the UI. Withdraw a release at the agency and its AbortController fires, toolchange reaches the broker, and the tool stops existing. The assistant does not refuse the question; there is nothing left to call. An honest third answer. Programs that needed the departed agency turn indeterminate, never ineligible. Absence of proof is not proof of ineligibility, which matters when the output is somebody's benefits. How we built it Four separate origins. Plain ES modules, no build step, zero npm dependencies. The three agencies register attestation tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { exposedTo: [' https://vouchsafe-app.vercel.app' ], signal }), each returning a minimal-disclosure envelope of {attested, predicate, agency, ref, ts} and nothing else. Revenue also registers get_income_record without exposedTo, as a control case: the broker cannot see it, and a "Probe the boundary" button demonstrates that live. The broker is a composer, not a forwarder. It discovers agency tools with getTools({fromOrigins}), calls them with executeTool(), and re-syncs on toolchange. It then registers six tools of its own for the assistant, so the agent sees one coherent surface rather than a pile of forwarded predicates, and never sees an agency tool at all. Challenges we ran into WebMCP is young, and most of the real work was discovering how it actually behaves rather than how we assumed it would. Six findings are documented in smoke/RESULTS.md. The three that shaped the architecture: getTools({fromOrigins}) is additive, not exclusive. It returns the caller's own tools alongside those of the requested origins. Before we caught it, the broker's own facades landed in every agency's bucket, so agencies read as online while their tools were missing. The broker now partitions results by tool.origin. executeTool() takes a JSON string and returns a JSON string, not objects, so arguments and results both need serialising and the response needs parsing twice. Registering a tool that already exists throws InvalidStateError: Duplicate tool name. Our toolchange handler was not awaiting its own callback, so two refreshes could overlap and the second collided with the first. Verification was its own problem: WebMCP does not exist in headless Chrome, so a normal headless test captures an empty, broken page. Every check drives a real headful Chrome over the DevTools Protocol instead, and cross-origin iframes are out-of-process, which needs Target.setAutoAttach with flatten: true to reach them at all. Accomplishments that we are proud of The central claim is measured rather than asserted. tools/verify-agent.js walks the entire agent path and scans every byte the assistant can see for the record values: leakedSecrets: [] across 9,940 bytes. tools/verify-revocation.js proves the revocation path against production, not a mock. ?selftest=1 runs seven assertions inside the live page, so a judge can check the claims without reading any code. Thirty-six unit tests cover the program graph and the envelope. The control case is the part we would point at first. A tool registered without exposedTo is not merely undocumented or unlisted; the broker genuinely cannot reach it, and the page lets you try. What we learned The important design decision was making the broker compose rather than forward. Proxying twelve agency predicates straight to the assistant would have been less code and a worse product: the agent would carry the burden of knowing which agency holds what, and every question would cross the boundary individually. Six facades that each consult several origins gave a better agent experience and a smaller disclosure surface at the same time. The second lesson was that a privacy claim is worth only as much as its instrumentation. "No records are disclosed" is easy to write and easy to break by accident, so the ledger counts real crossings and the verifier greps the agent's own view for the secret values. What is next for Vouchsafe The predicates here are hand-written per agency. The natural next step is a declarative attestation schema, so an agency can publish which predicates it answers without writing a tool by hand, and a signed attestation reference, so a determination can be re-verified later by a third party from the ref alone. Beyond benefits, the same shape fits anywhere a decision needs facts that are legally forbidden to pool: clinical eligibility, immigration casework, school enrolment, tenancy checks. The interesting property is not that the data stays put. It is that the consent to ask is a browser primitive an ordinary person can withdraw. A conventional interrogation answers by handing back the record. Income, filing status, etc. Vouchsafe asks a yes or no question instead. The black block is where the value would be. It never leaves the agency it's holding. Four separate origins, not one page with three panels. They exchange tools through Web MCP, a proposed browser API that lets a site offer tools directly to an assistant. This is the Department of Revenue. The broker cannot see that one and that's the control case. Six tools face assistant, and each one may consult three separate origins. Six programs, three agencies, one question at a time. The system says it cannot know, which is the honest answer. Four origins, six programs, and zero records. Thank you.

title: IntentLock
pitch: Your agent can act. You set the boundaries.
about_excerpt: Your agent can act. You set the boundaries. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI agents can perform real actions on websites, but malicious webpage content may try to change what the human requested. IntentLock explores how websites can give agents freedom while keeping humans in control. What it does A human sets purchasing rules such as: Maximum total: $100 Quantity: 1 Delivery: Office A Vendors: Approved only The agent may choose a suitable product. If webpage content tells it to order five items or change the address, IntentLock returns BLOCK with the exact reasons. Valid actions follow: Agent proposes → Website verifies → Human confirms → Execute once If the agent needs more authority, it must request permission from the human. How we built it IntentLock registers five WebMCP tools: get_mission search_products prepare_checkout request_authorization_change commit_checkout The application uses React, TypeScript, ChatGPT Sites, Cloudflare D1, and WebMCP. The optional GPT-4o mini feature explains product choices but cannot approve, block, or execute actions. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was showing that IntentLock is not simply a product filter. The agent proposes a real action, the website checks it against saved human rules, and execution requires confirmation. We also implemented mission versions, trusted catalog values, expiring tokens, and execute-once protection. Accomplishments that we're proud of Five working WebMCP tools ALLOW , BLOCK , and UNDETERMINED results Clear explanations for blocked actions Human-controlled permission changes Prepare, confirm, and commit workflow Replay and stale-action protection Public deployment and automated tests What we learned WebMCP tools are more than a better way for agents to navigate websites. Their structured handlers can become enforcement points. We also learned that LLMs are useful for explanations, while important authorization decisions should remain deterministic. What's next for IntentLock Next, IntentLock could become a reusable WebMCP security library supporting authenticated users, signed delegation rules, real commerce integrations, cross-site provenance, organizational budgets, and domains such as email, travel, finance, and cloud operations. title: Esbiko WebMCP Science Lab
pitch: Esbiko turns interactive science simulations into shared workspaces where people and AI agents configure, run, inspect, and compare real experiments through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Esbiko turns interactive science simulations into shared workspaces where people and AI agents configure, run, inspect, and compare real experiments through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Interactive science simulations are designed for people: learners move sliders, press buttons, watch animations, listen to sounds, and interpret measurements. For an AI agent, however, the same interface is ambiguous. It has to locate controls visually, infer their scientific meaning, approximate numerical values, determine whether an experiment actually ran, and scrape the result back from the page. I asked a different question: What if a human and an AI agent could operate the same scientific experiment together? Esbiko is an existing open-source science and mathematics learning platform with browser-based 2D and 3D simulations, classroom workflows, scientific visualisations, and media tools. For the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge, I extended Esbiko with a semantic agent-facing layer that makes its Doppler Effect laboratory directly understandable and controllable through WebMCP. The goal is not to replace the learner or hide the experiment behind a chatbot. The human should still see, hear, inspect, and modify the experiment. WebMCP gives the agent a precise way to act on that same scientific environment. The result is a shared scientific workspace where human intent, agent actions, visible simulation state, physics calculations, audio, and recorded output all remain connected. What it does Esbiko WebMCP Science Lab turns a live Doppler Effect simulation into an agent-operable scientific instrument. The current implementation exposes 11 semantic WebMCP tools . Two site-level tools allow an agent to discover and open WebMCP-enabled science simulations: list_science_simulations open_science_simulation Nine Doppler tools allow the agent to read and control the experiment: get_doppler_state configure_doppler configure_doppler_scene set_doppler_playback reset_doppler create_doppler_video get_doppler_video_status stop_doppler_video download_doppler_video An agent can configure source motion, source speed, emitted frequency, observer state, direction, sound type, and multi-source scenes. It can also direct a complete scientific video. The final production demonstration creates a 30-second, 9:16 two-vehicle Doppler experiment at an emitted frequency of 440 Hz and a source speed of 60 m/s . A Real Car Engine travels from left to right. It approaches the stationary observer, passes at 7.5 seconds, and then recedes. An Ambulance Siren then approaches from the opposite direction, passes the observer at 22.5 seconds, and continues away. For a speed of sound of 343 m/s, Esbiko calculates approximately: 533.29 Hz while approaching and 374.49 Hz while receding. The pitch difference is clearly audible in the generated video. While the agent is recording, the user can also watch the same directed motion happening in the live browser. After recording, the agent can inspect structured recording status, confirm that real audio was captured, wait until the file is ready, and download the final WebM. How I built it Esbiko uses the WebMCP Imperative API through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . The implementation is a progressive enhancement over the existing React application. Browsers without WebMCP continue to use Esbiko normally. Two persistent site-level tools provide discovery and navigation. Nine Doppler-specific tools are registered while the Doppler laboratory is active. A validated JSON-safe adapter connects WebMCP inputs to Esbiko's existing React state and scientific code. Semantic instructions such as approaching , receding , and explicit source directions are converted into validated physical parameters instead of arbitrary DOM interactions. Scientific results are never generated by an LLM. Esbiko's application code deterministically calculates values such as: Observed frequency Frequency ratio Percentage frequency shift Relative amplitude Sound level Motion classification The AI video workflow required an additional Doppler Director . The director creates an exact timeline from physical parameters using: distance = speed × time For the final 30-second story, each phase lasts 7.5 seconds and each vehicle travels 450 metres during each phase. The observer remains fixed at 500 metres. The recorder creates a deterministic 1080×1920 WebM and combines the rendered simulation with a real Web Audio track. Selected sound samples are preloaded before recording. Esbiko routes the Web Audio mix through an analyser and a MediaStreamDestination . Before accepting a recording, Esbiko checks that a measurable audio signal actually reaches the recording bus. A silent track is not treated as success. Most importantly, during AI-directed recording, the live browser motion, recorded motion, and Doppler audio are driven from the same deterministic director timeline . This keeps the audible pitch transition synchronized with the exact visual moment when each vehicle passes the observer. Challenges I ran into One of the hardest problems was not implementing the Doppler equation itself. It was keeping several real-time systems synchronized. Initially, the recorded video used a deterministic director clock while the sound was still driven by the ordinary browser simulation loop. Under the additional workload of rendering a 1080×1920 canvas and encoding WebM, browser frame timing could slow down. The vehicle in the video would reach the observer at the correct time, but the audio simulation could lag behind it. The Doppler shift was scientifically correct, but the audible pitch change did not always line up clearly with the visual crossing. I eventually removed that split-clock architecture. During AI recording, the audio source state is now derived directly from the same deterministic director timeline used by the live browser preview and recorded video. That made the higher-to-lower pitch transition clearly audible at the intended pass moments. Browser audio policy was another challenge. Modern browsers may prevent an AudioContext from starting without a human gesture. Esbiko preserves that browser security model and returns an explicit AUDIO_ACTIVATION_REQUIRED error when necessary. I also had to solve silent recording failures. Having an audio track attached to MediaRecorder does not guarantee that meaningful sound exists in it, so Esbiko performs a real analyser-based signal test before starting the recording. Finally, because Esbiko is an existing Progressive Web App, browser caching and Service Worker state had to be considered during production verification to ensure I was testing the current deployed revision. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I built an end-to-end WebMCP workflow inside a real existing educational application rather than creating an isolated WebMCP technical demo. The production system now demonstrates semantic discovery, navigation, scientific configuration, scene control, playback, physics-derived measurements, AI-directed recording, real audio verification, recording status, and downloadable scientific media. The final production test successfully demonstrated a 30-second two-vehicle scenario with a Real Car Engine and Ambulance Siren moving in opposite directions at 60 m/s. Both vehicles visibly move in the live browser while the recording is being created. The Real Car Engine passes the observer at approximately 7.5 seconds and the Ambulance passes from the opposite direction at approximately 22.5 seconds. In both cases, the transition from higher approaching pitch to lower receding pitch is clearly audible and synchronized with the visual observer crossing. Esbiko also supports a simpler 10-second single_pass mode where one continuous siren approaches for five seconds and recedes for five seconds, providing an especially clear A/B Doppler comparison. The implementation includes structured validation, bounded scientific inputs, explicit browser-audio errors, audio-signal verification, deterministic recording, shared human/agent state, and automated WebMCP contract and physics tests. The complete implementation, architecture, testing documentation, challenge evidence, deployment history, and MIT-licensed source code are public. What I learned I learned that the most useful WebMCP tools represent human intent , rather than mechanically exposing every UI control. A scientific user does not really want to say: "Move slider number three to pixel position 240." They want to say: "Show me a 440 Hz source approaching an observer at 60 metres per second." WebMCP provides a much better boundary for expressing that intent. I also learned that adding agent control makes the visible human interface more important, not less. The strongest workflow is not one where the AI operates invisibly in the background. It is one where the agent performs precise and repeatable operations while the learner can simultaneously see, hear, inspect, question,

 Inspiration 

 We wanted to explore how AI Agent can do more than just give instructions it can interact with a real web application and complete a task . 

 We chose a maze because it provides a simple and visual way to demonstrate this idea. By combining WebMCP with Amazon Bedrock , the AI Agent can understand the maze, find a valid path, make the moves, and verify that the player has reached the exit. 

 Our goal was to turn a simple maze game into an AI-interactive web application . 

 What It Does 

 Maze Escape is a browser-based maze game that can be played manually by a user or automatically by an AI Agent . 

 The AI Agent can interact with the live game using WebMCP tools . It can: 

 
 View the current maze and game state 
 Check the player's position 
 Check available moves 
 Find the shortest valid path using BFS 
 Execute the solution through the game 
 Verify whether the maze has been successfully completed 
 

 The project uses Amazon Bedrock for AI reasoning and WebMCP for interaction with the game. 

 In simple terms: 

 
 * You can play the maze yourself or ask the AI Agent to find the shortest path and actually solve it. * 
 

 How we built it 

 We built Maze Escape as a browser-based game using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript , with a Node.js backend and Netlify Functions for the AI integration. 

 1. Maze Game 

 The frontend manages the maze, player movement, timer, move counter, and game status. Users can navigate the maze manually using the available controls. 

 2. WebMCP Integration 

 We exposed the game's important functions as WebMCP tools , allowing a compatible AI Agent to interact directly with the running game. 

 The main tools include: 

 
 get_maze_state 
 get_player_state 
 get_available_moves 
 move_player 
 restart_game 
 get_game_status 
 find_solution 
 execute_solution 
 

 3. Maze Solving 

 We implemented Breadth-First Search (BFS) to find a shortest valid path from the player's current position to the exit. 

 This keeps pathfinding deterministic and reliable instead of asking the AI Agent to calculate every movement itself. 

 4. AI Agent 

 We integrated Amazon Bedrock using the Converse API. The AI Agent receives the user's request and can decide which WebMCP tools to use to inspect, solve, and verify the game. 

 5. Backend and Security 

 The Bedrock integration runs through a Netlify Serverless Function . AWS credentials are stored as environment variables and are never placed in the browser or frontend code. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Building Maze Escape involved solving a few important technical challenges: 

 
 * Connecting AI Agents with the live game: * We needed the AI Agent to access the actual maze state and perform actions, so we exposed the game's functionality through WebMCP tools. 
 Reliable maze solving: ** Instead of relying on the AI Agent to calculate every move, we implemented **BFS to consistently find a shortest valid path. 
 * Efficient tool execution: * Calling move_player for every step could require many tool calls. We added execute_solution to execute the complete path more efficiently. 
 * Amazon Bedrock integration: * Connecting the AI Agent to Bedrock required a server-side integration through a Netlify Function while keeping AWS credentials secure. 
 * Deployment and configuration: * We had to correctly configure Netlify environment variables, the Bedrock model identifier, and the serverless API so the AI Agent worked in the deployed application. 
 

 These challenges helped us build a more reliable connection between AI reasoning, WebMCP tools, and real-time web application actions . 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud of turning a simple maze game into a working AI-interactive web application . 

 Our key accomplishments are: 

 
 🤖 Built an AI Agents that can understand and interact with the live maze . 
 🌐 Integrated WebMCP tools for structured interaction with the game. 
 🧠 Implemented BFS to reliably find a shortest valid path. 
 ⚡ Added execute_solution to complete the maze efficiently with fewer tool calls. 
 ☁️ Integrated Amazon Bedrock for AI reasoning. 
 🔐 Kept AWS credentials securely on the server-side using Netlify Functions . 
 🚀 Successfully deployed the application as a live web app. 
 

 Most importantly, the AI Agent does not just explain how to solve the maze it can actually perform the actions and verify that the maze has been completed . 

 What we learned 

 Building Maze Escape helped us understand how AI Agents can interact with real web applications instead of only generating text. 

 We learned how to: 

 
 🌐 Use WebMCP to expose website functionality as structured tools for AI Agents. 
 🤖 Build an AI workflow where the Agents can understand, act, and verify . 
 🧠 Use BFS to find a reliable shortest path through a maze. 
 🔗 Combine AI reasoning with deterministic algorithms for better reliability. 
 ☁️ Integrate Amazon Bedrock using the Converse API. 
 ⚡ Use Netlify Functions to connect the web application with cloud AI services. 
 🔐 Keep AWS credentials secure by keeping them on the server side. 
 🛠️ Design tools that are simple and clear enough for an AI Agents to use effectively. 
 🚀 Deploy and configure an AI-powered web application for real-world use. 
 

 The biggest lesson we learned is that AI becomes more useful when it can interact with applications through well-defined tools and take real actions , rather than only explaining what should be done. 

 What's next for Maze Escape Game 

 We plan to extend Maze Escape from a single maze experience into a more capable AI-interactive application. 

 Our future plans include: 

 
 🧩 More maze levels and difficulty modes with larger and more complex mazes. 
 🎲 Procedurally generated mazes for a new challenge every time. 
 🤖 Smarter AI interactions with more WebMCP tools and improved agent workflows. 
 📊 AI performance tracking to compare solving time, moves, and efficiency. 
 👤 AI vs. Human mode to compare how quickly the AI Agent and players can solve the same maze. 
 🎨 Better visualizations showing how the AI Agent finds and follows a path. 
 🔌 Multiple AI model support so different models can be tested with the same WebMCP tools. 
 🌐 More real-world AI tasks beyond maze solving, using the same idea of giving AI Agents structured access to web applications. 
 

 Our long-term goal is to explore how WebMCP can make web applications more useful and interactive for AI Agents , allowing them to understand a task, use application tools, take actions, and verify the result.

title: a11y-mcp
pitch: Speak Thai, fill any English web form by voice. a11y-mcp reads forms aloud, fills them from your speech, and self-corrects — powered by WebMCP.
about_excerpt: Speak Thai, fill any English web form by voice. a11y-mcp reads forms aloud, fills them from your speech, and self-corrects — powered by WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Two failures, stacked. First, AI agents "use" the web by guessing which pixel is a button — and guess wrong. Second, accessibility tooling is built for English. Our lead user is a Thai person in front of an English-only visa, university, or airline form: it's well-marked-up and completely unusable if you don't read English, and nobody translates it. Screen readers mangle code-switched Thai. The same tool helps blind, low-vision, motor-impaired, and elderly users — so we built it as a capability, not a special-needs product. What it does a11y-mcp turns any semantically sound web form into typed tools an AI agent can call (via WebMCP / document.modelContext), then lets a Thai speaker read, fill, correct, and submit that form entirely by voice. You press a microphone, speak Thai, and GPT-4o-mini calls the page's tools while the page answers with structured, typed feedback instead of a red border. It reads the form aloud in Thai, fills each field from your speech (keeping names in Latin script, translating free text to English, matching dropdown options), self-corrects from typed validation errors, asks you in Thai when it isn't sure, and never submits without an explicit confirmation. How we built it TypeScript + Vite + @crxjs/vite-plugin, with Zod defining the tool boundary once for both JSON Schema and runtime validation. It's an MV3 extension with two content scripts bridged over postMessage: a MAIN-world script that reaches document.modelContext, registers the four tools (describe_form, read_form, fill_form, submit_form), and runs the GPT brain; and an ISOLATED-world script that owns the microphone and calls Paxa. GPT-4o-mini function-calling turns Thai speech into tool calls; Paxa Labs handles Thai text-to-speech (voice "yoyo") and translation; the Web Speech API handles voice input. Both APIs allow direct browser calls, so there's no proxy in the demo path. Challenges we ran into The WebMCP spec is unstable. The API had movedext to document.modelContext (deprecated in Chrome 150), so nothing worked at first. We instrumented the live Chrome 152 surface and dct: registerTool is async, there is no unregisterTool, duplicate tool names throw, getTools() returns inputSchema as a JSON strinarguments as a JSON string — none of which the docs said. We rebuilt against that. We also had to get the failed-vs-needs_human distinction righit, and work around audio autoplay needing a user gesture. Accomplishments that we're proud of The failed vs needs_human split: "failed" is reactive (the page rejected a value, so the agent retries), while "needs_human" is prensure, so nothing is filled and the agent must ask). A confidently-wrong value on a visa form is the failure mode that actually hurts peoplet. Error speech comes from stable Thai templates keyed by an enum — never model prose. And the read-back: a blind Thai user can finally percejust fill it. We verified the whole loop live in Chrome — one Thai sentence filled eight fields, translated the free text, matched a dropdown, rrected a bad ID number, and correctly left an unlabeled field empty. What we learned Don't trust the docs for an unstable API — instrument the runtime; it's the only truth. WebMCP's real value is constraint feedbnt can act on, versus a red border a human has to interpret. And accessibility and agent-usability turn out to be the same problem — a well-markeh. The Thai angle isn't a bolt-on; it's exactly the audience Western accessibility tooling has never served. What's next for a11y-mcp It works on sites with reasonable semantics, aells the truth when a site's markup is bad rather than filling wrong values silently. Next: move the API keys server-side and ship it publicly oncehind the Chrome flag. Deliberately out of scope for now — cross-page memory (a privacy design problem) and custom non- widgets.  Threadwise 

 Threadwise helps online shoppers find the right apparel size when every brand uses a different size chart. 

 The Problem 

 A shopper may wear a medium in one brand and a large in another. 

 Traditional size labels are too generic, and product pages often make it difficult to compare chest, waist, shoulder, and sleeve measurements. 

 This leads to uncertainty, poor fit, and unnecessary returns. 

 Our Solution 

 Threadwise lets shoppers enter their measurements and preferred fit, then compares them against each garment’s own size chart. 

 It returns: 

 
 A recommended size 
 A confidence score 
 Area-by-area fit details 
 Possible warnings 
 An alternative size 
 

 Threadwise also supports real product links. 

 A shopper can paste a product URL and the size-chart rows from that page, then receive a real-time recommendation without requiring marketplace scraping or retailer credentials. 

 Why WebMCP? 

 WebMCP allows Threadwise to expose structured tools that AI agents can discover and use. 

 The available tools include: 
 list_garments
get_size_chart
recommend_garment_size
compare_product_fits
analyze_product_link
 
 Instead of guessing from labels such as “medium” or “large,” an agent can call the appropriate tool, provide structured measurements, and receive an explainable result. 

 The shopper remains in control of their measurements and decisions. 

 Privacy First 

 Measurements stay in the browser by default. 

 Threadwise does not require an account and does not send body measurements to retailers. 

 The app does not use body photographs, infer sensitive personal attributes, or claim guaranteed fit. 

 Recommendations are presented as transparent estimates, not certainty. 

 Built For 

 Threadwise is designed for online apparel shoppers who want more confidence before ordering. 

 The same approach can later help independent apparel stores reduce size-related returns and improve product size charts. 

 What We Built 

 The prototype includes: 

 
 A responsive apparel catalog 
 Store-specific body and garment size charts 
 Unit conversion between centimeters and inches 
 Slim, regular, and relaxed fit preferences 
 Explainable scoring and confidence levels 
 Real product-link analysis using user-supplied chart data 
 WebMCP tool registration 
 Browser-only measurement handling 
 Accessible and responsive UI 
 

 Future Improvements 

 Future versions could support authorized merchant feeds, official retailer APIs, better garment-category models, and feedback loops based on anonymized fit outcomes. 

 Threadwise’s goal is simple: make apparel sizing feel less like guessing and more like an informed decision.

title: Replan - Agentic Travel Recovery
pitch: A flight-cancellation site where ChatGPT's own browser discovers and calls 12 WebMCP tools - rebook, hold a room, arrange transport - no custom agent built.
about_excerpt: A flight-cancellation site where ChatGPT's own browser discovers and calls 12 WebMCP tools - rebook, hold a room, arrange transport - no custom agent built. Like Comment Story Updates Natural-language travel constraints drive flight recovery through WebMCP. ChatGPT discovers and calls Replan's 12 WebMCP tools directly. The agent coordinates recovery while the human confirms consequential actions. A multi-step recovery coordinated across flights, hotel, ground transport, notifications, and budget. Inspiration Travel recovery is a good stress test for WebMCP because it is multi-step, stateful, and involves consequential actions. The scenario behind Replan is simple: imagine a nonstop flight to Miami being canceled the day before a cruise departure from PortMiami. The traveler needs to recover quickly while balancing constraints such as timing, hotel availability, ground transportation, and budget. I wanted to explore what happens when the website exposes its capabilities directly to an AI agent instead of requiring a custom conversational layer inside the application. What it does Replan is an agentic travel recovery app where a traveler sets goals and constraints in natural language while an AI agent discovers and operates the site's capabilities directly. The traveler can ask the agent to search for replacement flights, update constraints, hold a reservation, confirm a booking, rebook a hotel, arrange ground transportation, notify a contact, track the running trip cost, and generate an itinerary summary. The app exposes 12 WebMCP tools: ping search_flights search_flights_semantic update_constraints hold_reservation confirm_booking search_hotels update_hotel_reservation book_ground_transport notify_contact calculate_total_cost generate_itinerary_summary The human remains in control of consequential actions through explicit confirmation gates, while the agent handles the multi-step coordination. How we built it Replan is built with React, Vite, and TypeScript, deployed on Vercel. Convex powers the one live backend piece—the semantic-search vector index, reached from the browser tool through an HTTP endpoint, so no Convex client code ships in the runtime bundle. The key integration is WebMCP. The page registers its capabilities through the WebMCP API using document.modelContext.registerTool() . ChatGPT, in its in-app browser, discovers those tools and calls them from natural-language requests. There is no custom LLM, NLU, voice layer, or custom agent in the Replan codebase. The application exposes structured capabilities and lets the agent decide how to compose them. The 12 tools are registered statically at page load. Each tool validates its inputs and returns structured JSON, including structured errors that allow the agent to understand failed operations and recover. One of the tools, search_flights_semantic , uses natural-language semantic ranking backed by a live vector index with embeddings rather than simple keyword matching. I verified the complete interaction flow manually: 12/12 tools registered, 36/36 demo turns passed, 0 failures . Challenges we ran into One of the main challenges was designing tool validation and error responses so that an AI agent could recover from invalid or conflicting requests. Structured errors turned out to be especially important because the agent needs actionable information rather than only human-readable error messages. Another challenge was designing confirmation boundaries. Search and other reversible operations can be performed speculatively, but consequential actions such as confirming a booking need an explicit human confirmation step. The final challenge was compressing a 36-turn recovery workflow into a clear demonstration under three minutes without losing the important WebMCP interactions. Accomplishments that we're proud of I successfully exposed the complete travel recovery workflow through WebMCP without building a custom agent or natural-language processing layer. The final implementation has 12 WebMCP tools , and the complete human verification covered 36/36 turns with 0 failures . Most importantly, the entire recovery chain can be driven from natural language: the agent discovers the capabilities exposed by the webpage, composes multiple tools, handles state and constraints, and stops for human confirmation when an action becomes consequential. What we learned WebMCP changes the design boundary between a website and an AI agent. The website does not need to understand how the agent reasons. It needs to expose clear, reliable capabilities that an agent can discover and compose. I also learned that confirmation gates are not just a UI concern. They shape the tool design itself by separating safe, reversible operations from consequential actions. Finally, structured JSON responses and meaningful errors are critical when tools are being operated by an agent. They provide the information needed for the agent to adapt instead of simply failing. What's next for Replan - Agentic Travel Recovery The next step is to make the recovery workflow more realistic and flexible. Potential extensions include partial availability, multi-leg itineraries, more complex constraint conflicts, and broader use of live vector search across additional travel capabilities. The goal is to continue exploring how far a website can go when it exposes reliable, composable capabilities directly to an AI agent through WebMCP. pitch: Perso-xxl is a web extension that allows you to personalize your experience of the web like never before using AI tools. UX/UI are optimized for the average people, You are not average ! Let fix it !
about_excerpt: Perso-xxl is a web extension that allows you to personalize your experience of the web like never before using AI tools. UX/UI are optimized for the average people, You are not average ! Let fix it ! Like Comment Story Updates After, analytics tools added by the agent. Before Inspiration Websites are built for the average user, but everyone has different preferences, accessibility needs, and workflows. We wanted users to ask their existing AI agent to adapt any webpage for them, even when they do not own the website. What it does Perso-XXL is a browser extension that lets AI agents safely personalize webpages. Agents can change styles, hide or move elements, add safe interface components, create shortcuts, and remember the user's preferences. Changes are local, reversible, and saved for future visits. With WebMCP, capable agents use Perso-XXL directly. OpenRouter is only a fallback for users without a compatible agent. How we built it Perso-XXL exposes WebMCP tools such as inspect_page and apply_page_plan . The agent first receives short-lived, opaque target IDs. It then submits a structured modification plan. Perso-XXL validates the plan, checks that targets are still fresh, and applies it atomically. The extension uses a secure bridge between the page and extension environments. It also supports confirmation, cancellation, rollback, persistent modifications, and dynamically registered shortcuts. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was giving agents useful control without allowing arbitrary JavaScript, HTML, CSS, or selectors. Modern pages also change constantly, so inspected elements can quickly become stale. We addressed this with one-use snapshots, fingerprints, navigation checks, and target revalidation. We also had to support both normal Chrome extensions and built-in agent browsers, which expose WebMCP differently. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that Perso-XXL: Works on websites the user does not own. Lets existing agents personalize pages without another AI call. Rejects unsafe and stale modifications. Supports reversible and persistent changes. Turns saved workflows into callable WebMCP tools. Gives agents access to the user's style preferences. Includes automated browser, security, rollback, and adversarial tests. What we learned WebMCP is most useful when tools expose meaningful capabilities instead of raw DOM access. We also learned that data and presentation should be separate. A website can securely provide information, while the user and agent decide how to display it. Finally, reversibility is essential. Agents are more useful when users can safely experiment, inspect the result, and undo it. What's next for Perso-XXL Next, we want to: Move the OpenRouter fallback to a secure backend. Add encrypted preference synchronization. Improve accessibility-focused personalization. Expand the safe modification capabilities. Improve previews and explanations before applying changes. Support more browsers as WebMCP becomes widely available. Our long-term goal is to make web personalization belong to the user. title: Modelo
pitch: A notebook where the calculations and the narrative live in one place. Collaborate with your agent on building deterministic and interactive models.
about_excerpt: A notebook where the calculations and the narrative live in one place. Collaborate with your agent on building deterministic and interactive models. Like Comment Story Updates Notebook Page Homepage Inspiration Modelo is directly inspired by Decipad, a product I worked on in the past. At the time, LLMs were far less advanced, and few products had useful AI features. The project did not work out, but I always believed it was a great idea that needed agentic collaboration to feel complete. For this challenge, I rebuilt a minimal version of it. What it does Modelo is a local-first notebook. You can write prose with headings, paragraphs, and lists, as in any other rich-text editor. Between paragraphs, you can add model blocks: a number, slider, select, toggle, or formula. Each block declares a named variable. Typing @ in a paragraph inserts the value as an inline chip that reacts to model changes. This lets you build deterministic, interactive models and add a narrative around them. You can also create and save scenarios with predefined values to compare different outcomes. Everything you can do manually is also available through WebMCP tools. An agent can list notebooks, open them, read a model, set an input by name, or rename a variable and update every formula that uses it. Each writing tool reports what changed, what remains broken, and how well the page reads. How we built it Modelo uses React 19 and Vite, with no backend. BlockNote provides the editor and acts as the only source of truth. The document you see is the same document that the tools edit. MathJS evaluates the formula graph based on its dependencies, while Zod validates every argument at the boundary. WebMCP registration uses Chrome’s use-webmcp-tool hook. A single table in src/webmcp/tools.ts defines all 23 tools: their names, scopes, Zod schemas, descriptions, and run functions. The React layer loops through the table and registers each tool with document.modelContext.registerTool . The interface buttons call the same runTool function that the agent uses. Challenges we ran into Currency algebra was difficult. Registering each currency as a separate MathJS unit makes mixed-currency formulas return an error. In the future, we would like to add FX rates to support currency conversion. More generally, units require careful handling and many design decisions. Agent-written prose was another challenge. By default, agents focus on building the model rather than creating a clear and visually appealing narrative. I added sections to the tool calls to improve this. A section is more than a set of blocks: its paragraphs can mention variables that do not exist yet. The section tool resolves @names against variables declared in the same call, so a sentence can reference a formula that appears later. Accomplishments that we’re proud of I created one portable format for seeds, storage, exports, and agent payloads. The application is highly testable. Most importantly, a person and an agent can edit the same paragraph without either needing to know who made the previous change. What we learned A tool should always report what it changed. Without this feedback, agents make more mistakes than they should. The mutation report became the most useful information an agent receives. I also learned that tool descriptions are prompts. Two sentences explaining when to use write_section instead of insert_blocks changed agent behavior more than any schema did. What’s next for Modelo Next, I want to support sharing notebooks by link, which will require a small backend. I also want to add charts as a block type, so users can see scenario comparisons as well as read them. Other ideas include importing spreadsheet ranges as inputs and building a richer unit system that can convert values instead of only formatting them. title: Mend: Safe, verified website repairs with WebMCP
pitch: Mend helps you find website problems, review safe AI fixes, and verify the results, while WebMCP and security safeguards keep your source code and workflow under your control.
about_excerpt: Mend helps you find website problems, review safe AI fixes, and verify the results, while WebMCP and security safeguards keep your source code and workflow under your control. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Scan: find the issues that matter most Mend landing page: safe, verified website repairs Read-only source viewer mapped to the issue Understand: trace audit evidence to the source Proposed diff waiting for human approval Performance finding: hero image is larger than rendered Audit dashboard with performance, accessibility, SEO, and link scores Accessibility finding: email field without an associated label Connected repository with WebMCP tools ready Verify: compare results and prove the fix worked Inspiration Website audits tell you what is wrong, while coding agents can edit source code. The difficult part is the handoff between those systems. Mend turns that gap into one human and agent workflow. What it does Mend scans a website for accessibility, performance, SEO, and broken-link issues. It keeps evidence tied to pages and selectors, maps findings to authorized source hints, proposes a bounded patch, shows an exact diff, waits for explicit approval, records a branch-first change, and verifies the before-and-after result. Why WebMCP This is a structured sequence of actions, not a chatbot guessing which pixels to click. Mend registers 13 compact tools through document.modelContext: scan, summarize, list and inspect issues, inspect source, propose a fix, review the diff, request approval, apply the approved fix, verify, and compare audits. The agent and human see the same state, and the tools work in WebMCP runtimes that omit optional execution context. How we built it The app is Next.js and TypeScript with server-side bounded HTML checks, normalized audit models, a controlled demo repository, and deterministic fix and diff generation. WebMCP is feature-detected so the manual UX works in browsers without it. Human approval and applied state are bound to signed HTTP-only receipts, the browser workspace recovers after reload, and verification reruns checks against the actual patched source snapshot. The approval guard rejects unapproved changes and the checked-in main fixture remains untouched. What we learned The hard part was making the workflow trustworthy and legible. We kept evidence, confidence, diffs, approval status, and verification together, and added SSRF protections, timeouts, size bounds, safe path validation, reload recovery, and regression checks. Try it The deterministic demo repairs missing hero-image alternative text: Accessibility moves from 74 to 89, one issue resolves, and zero regressions are reported. The production workflow was verified end to end from scan through source-backed comparison.  Inspiration 

 I built Funk Trainer because learning funk rhythm has always been difficult for me. I wanted one place where I could see where chords land in the beat, hear the groove, find useful funk chords, and practice against drums instead of jumping between different tools. 

 What it does 

 Funk Trainer is a visual sequencer for practicing funk guitar. You can place chords on rhythmic subdivisions, change keys, explore funk chord voicings, generate grooves, and play along with drums.
The goal is to make where you play as clear as what you play. 

 How we built it 

 is an interactive web-based sequencer that keeps the visual grid, guitar, and drums synchronized. 

 also added WebMCP, exposing the trainer's controls as tools that an AI agent can use. An agent can change the key, generate a groove, select chords, and place beats in the sequencer. 

 This means you can ask something like "Show me a groove using the chords from Superstition" and let the agent translate its musical knowledge into the UI. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The main challenge was timing: keeping the sequencer, drums, guitar, and visual feedback synchronized while keeping the interface simple enough for practice. 

 Another challenge was designing useful WebMCP tools that let an agent control the application without needing to understand its internal implementation. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Turning something I personally struggle with into a tool I can actually practice with. 

 I am also excited about making the application agent-controllable through WebMCP. Instead of AI only explaining a rhythm, it can actually build that rhythm inside the trainer. 

 What we learned 

 Building the trainer reinforced that funk isn't just about which chords you play. The placement, subdivisions, silence, and relationship with the drums are what create the groove. 

 I also learned that WebMCP creates an interesting bridge between an AI's musical knowledge and an interactive application. 

 What's next for funk-trainer 

 The next step is connecting the agent to real song data. 

 For example, the agent could retrieve the chords and structure of a song from a platform such as Ultimate Guitar and then automatically plot those chords and their timing into Funk Trainer. this would speed up the process as Codex does not have to look on the internet but already has a reliable source. 

 From there, Funk Trainer could become a way to go from "I want to learn this song" to an interactive, playable rhythm exercise generated directly from the song. 

 The immediate change will be to add a an acoustic sound instead of a machine like one.

title: EpochX
pitch: Train an online classifier with your browser agent while humans control labels and model changes through WebMCP
about_excerpt: Train an online classifier with your browser agent while humans control labels and model changes through WebMCP Like 1 Comment Story Updates Label Loop Why we built it Software can rank uncertain samples, update a classifier, and calculate metrics. A person still needs to decide what an ambiguous example means. Most labeling interfaces expose this process as buttons and tables, leaving a browser agent to infer which actions are safe. We wanted the page to publish those operations directly while keeping label decisions under human control. Support-ticket routing gave us a small task with visible results. Label Loop classifies tickets as billing , bug , or access . What it does Label Loop runs an online multinomial Naive Bayes classifier in the browser. The session begins with nine seed examples, twelve unlabeled review candidates, and a fixed nine-item holdout set. The agent ranks unlabeled tickets by predictive entropy and can place up to three in the review queue. A person assigns each label through the page. The agent then trains a batch and evaluates the updated model. The interface shows probabilities, per-class F1, token weights, a confusion matrix, calibration, and log loss. A ledger records label provenance, while a separate trace records WebMCP calls. Model-setting proposals stay pending until a person accepts or rejects them. How we built it The project is a static Vite application with no backend or external model API. The classifier and session state run in page memory, so reloading creates a fresh deterministic session. For a document $d$ and class $c$, the model calculates: $$ P(c \mid d) \propto P(c)\prod_{w \in d}P(w \mid c) $$ Token likelihoods use Laplace smoothing: $$ P(w \mid c)=\frac{N_{w,c}+\alpha}{N_c+\alpha |V|} $$ $N_{w,c}$ is the count of token $w$ in class $c$, $N_c$ is the class token total, and $|V|$ is the vocabulary size. Each confirmed example increments these counts. Review candidates are sorted using normalized predictive entropy: $$ H(p)=\frac{-\sum_{c=1}^{K}p_c\log p_c}{\log K} $$ A value near one means the probabilities are close, so that ticket moves toward the front of the review queue. One-vs-rest log-likelihood differences show which tokens push the model toward each class. Holdout evaluation returns aggregate metrics without returning individual rows. How WebMCP is used The page registers nine tools with document.modelContext.registerTool : Tool Access Job get_training_state Read Model, queue, configuration, and metrics inspect_uncertain_samples Read Entropy-ranked unlabeled tickets inspect_model_diagnostics Read Features, confusion counts, calibration, and loss predict_ticket Read Probabilities, entropy, and route-or-review decision evaluate_model Read Aggregate holdout metrics inspect_training_history Read Checkpoints and label provenance queue_label_review Write A bounded request for human labels train_confirmed_batch Write Incremental training on confirmed examples propose_model_config Write A pending configuration proposal Each definition has JSON Schema and runtime validation. queue_label_review has no label input. Samples move through unlabeled , awaiting-human , confirmed , and trained states, and training accepts only confirmed examples. Configuration changes require a separate human action. Challenges WebMCP browser support was the first practical problem. We verified all nine tools in Chrome 152 and built a deterministic replay for ordinary browsers. Replay events are labeled local replay so they cannot be confused with external calls. The second problem was label provenance. Hiding a control in the interface would not prevent an agent tool from sending the same data. We removed labels from the review-request schema and made the training operation check sample state at runtime. Evaluation tools return aggregate metrics, feature weights, and confusion counts while omitting individual holdout examples and answers. We also corrected a misleading setting whose original name implied automatic training. It is now a review threshold. Predictions below it go to a person, and training remains limited to confirmed examples. What we learned Useful WebMCP tools matched domain operations instead of interface controls. queue_label_review gives the agent a clear capability and limit; a tool such as click_review_button would preserve the ambiguity of the page. Human approval also needs a technical boundary. Label Loop keeps label assignment out of the agent tool set and checks provenance again when training starts. Since the model runs locally, every displayed probability, token weight, and metric can be reproduced without an account or API key. title: InsurAsync
pitch: Insurance claims shouldn't need everyone on the same call at the same time to move forward.
about_excerpt: Insurance claims shouldn't need everyone on the same call at the same time to move forward. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration So, this whole idea popped into my head because of something that happened to a buddy of mine. His younger brother accidentally bumped his car into a university bus. It wasn't a huge crash or anything, but the car needed fixing, and it took ages, like weeks, for the insurance stuff to finally get sorted out. Now, this brother relied on that car to get to university every single day. For those weeks he couldn't drive, someone else had to give him a ride instead. And this happened every day, for a situation that honestly felt like it should have been wrapped up in a few days, not weeks. When I saw the WebMCP challenge, that whole experience just flashed back to me. The real bottleneck wasn't the accident itself, but the fact that everyone involved was stuck passing information back and forth manually. The insurance company needed paperwork from the car owner, and the repair shop needed approval from the insurance company. Nobody had a quick, direct way to just communicate with each other. That's when I realized this is precisely the sort of issue WebMCP is designed to tackle: instead of a person acting as the manual link between three different systems, let each party have actual tools that an agent can directly access. That's how InsurAsync was born. What it does InsurAsync is a demo insurance claim platform with three separate parties — a policyholder , an insurer , and a repair shop each with their own page and their own WebMCP tools: The policyholder's agent can file a structured incident report and upload documents. The insurer's agent checks real coverage terms, requests exactly the documents needed, and validates repair estimates against real policy limits. The repair shop's agent proposes and revises estimates based on real parts and labor pricing. A shared live log shows every step as it happens, so you can watch the whole negotiation unfold in real time. And importantly, the very last step, actually confirming the settlement, is something only a human can do. The agents can negotiate everything up to that point, but they can never be the ones to finalize it. How we built it I built InsurAsync with Next.js, using WebMCP's document.modelContext.registerTool() on each of the three party pages to expose real, callable tools. Every tool is backed by an actual API route with real validation logic, real coverage limits, real document requirements, real repair pricing, so an agent calling these tools gets back genuine data, not guesses. For persistence, I initially tried a simple file-based store, but once I deployed to Vercel I learned that serverless functions don't reliably share a filesystem between requests. I ended up switching to a real Redis database (hosted on Vercel) so claim data actually survives across requests and cold starts, something I tested thoroughly before trusting it for the live demo. To actually prove the WebMCP integration worked, I tested it with a real agent using ChatGPT's in-app browser, prompting it to file a claim, check coverage, upload documents, propose an estimate, and validate it all through the real tools, live, on the deployed site. Challenges we ran into Getting real persistence working. My first attempts (in-memory storage, then file-based storage) worked locally but silently failed once deployed, because serverless environments don't behave like a normal always-on server. Moving to Redis fixed this properly. Finding the right way to test WebMCP tools with a real agent. Chrome's WebMCP testing flag turned out to be inconsistent in exposing document.modelContext reliably in my setup, and regular ChatGPT browsing only reads page text, it doesn't call in-page tools. ChatGPT's dedicated in-app browser was the one that actually worked, and once I found it, the whole negotiation flow worked end to end on the first real try. A very small but very stubborn bug : I once had the code from my "revise estimate" tool accidentally pasted into my "propose estimate" file, which silently broke the flow with a confusing error message until I traced it back to a simple copy-paste mix-up. Accomplishments that we're proud of Getting the full three-party negotiation to actually work end-to-end, live, with a real agent not just simulated with manual API calls is the accomplishment I'm most proud of. Watching ChatGPT file a claim, get asked for documents, upload them, get a repair estimate priced and validated against real policy limits, all without me typing anything into a form, was the moment the idea stopped being a concept and became a real working thing. I'm also proud of getting the human-in-the-loop boundary right: the agents can do all the negotiating, but only a real person can click Confirm Settlement. That felt like an important line to draw, not just a technical detail. What we learned The biggest thing I learned is that WebMCP tools are only as trustworthy as the real logic behind them. It would have been easy to build tools that just returned made-up numbers, but the moment I wired every tool to real stored data actual coverage limits, actual document requirements, actual repair pricing, the whole demo became something I could actually trust watching an agent operate. That distinction, between an agent guessing and an agent calling a tool with real validation behind it, is the whole point of WebMCP, and building this made that click for me in a way just reading about it hadn't. What's next for InsurAsync Real authentication, so each policyholder, insurer, and repair shop sees only their own claims instead of the most recent one Real document uploads instead of file-reference placeholders Support for more incident types and more nuanced coverage rules A dispute/counter-offer flow, so an insurer and repair shop can go back and forth on an estimate more than once before it's approved Exploring what this pattern looks like for other multi-party processes with the same "everyone relays information by hand" problem — warranty claims, permit approvals, or multi-vendor project sign-offs Built With css javascript nextjs node.js react redis vercel webmcp Try it out insurasync.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Ismail Ajingi A final year computer science student at King Mongkut's University of technology Thonburi, KMUTT , Bangkok, Thailand Like Share this project: Updates Ismail Ajingi started this project — Sep 02, 2026 03:09 PM EDT

title: CaseFile
pitch: A murder. Five suspects. An AI detective at your side. Casefile is a game that uses WebMCP to let AI investigate, uncover clues, and build theories while you make the final deduction.
about_excerpt: A murder. Five suspects. An AI detective at your side. Casefile is a game that uses WebMCP to let AI investigate, uncover clues, and build theories while you make the final deduction. Like Comment Story Updates LandignPage Cases Investigation A murder mystery is supposed to make you think. But when you put an AI agent into the game, there is an obvious problem: what stops the AI from simply reading the entire case and telling you who the killer is? That question inspired Casefile . Casefile is an AI-native detective game built around the idea that an AI agent should be a co-investigator, not an answer machine . The player investigates a murder case while an AI agent investigates alongside them through WebMCP. Instead of giving the agent access to the entire game state, Casefile exposes structured investigation tools such as searching locations, discovering evidence, inspecting clues, interviewing suspects, and reconstructing timelines. The agent can perform real investigative actions and help the player connect information, but hidden evidence and the solution remain inaccessible until the investigation legitimately uncovers them. The human still has to make the final deduction. Why WebMCP? Traditional web agents have to interact with websites by interpreting the interface and figuring out what actions are available. WebMCP changes that by allowing a website to expose its capabilities as structured tools. That makes a detective game particularly interesting. Instead of asking an AI to click around Casefile and guess what buttons mean, Casefile gives the agent an actual investigative toolkit. The agent can reason about the case while using tools specifically designed for investigation. This creates a different interaction loop: Human observes → AI investigates → AI finds connections → Human evaluates the theory → Human makes the accusation. The goal was not to make the AI smarter than the player. The goal was to make the player better at investigating with the AI . How We Built It Casefile is a web application with multiple independent investigations. Each case has its own suspects, locations, evidence, timeline, deductions, and solution. WebMCP tools are registered directly by the application and operate against the currently selected case. The investigation state determines what information is available to both the human and the agent. Some of the core tools include: get_case_state — retrieve the player's current investigation state search_evidence — discover available evidence inspect_evidence — investigate discovered clues search_locations — investigate locations get_suspects — view known suspects interview_suspect — conduct interrogations build_timeline — reconstruct events submit_accusation — make the final accusation A major part of the implementation was ensuring that the agent cannot simply request the answer key . Hidden case data and solution logic are kept server-side, while WebMCP only exposes information that the investigator has legitimately unlocked. We also built the cases around deductions rather than simply collecting clues. Evidence can be incomplete, ambiguous, or misleading, meaning that finding a clue is not necessarily the same as understanding it. What We Learned The biggest lesson was that building an agent-native application is not just about adding an AI interface to an existing website. You have to rethink what information the agent is allowed to know and what actions the agent is allowed to perform . During development, we discovered that exposing too much case data—even indirectly—could completely undermine the game. We therefore treated the WebMCP tools as part of the game's rules, not just as an API. We also learned that good agent experiences require clear tool boundaries. Each tool needs to expose enough information for the agent to reason effectively without accidentally exposing information that should remain part of the mystery. Challenges The hardest challenge was balancing AI capability with human agency . If the agent knows too little, it becomes useless. If it knows too much, the game becomes a simple question-and-answer session. We also had to solve state isolation between multiple cases, prevent agents from bypassing evidence discovery, prevent premature accusations from revealing the solution, and ensure that sensitive case information was not shipped to the browser where it could be reconstructed. Testing the application with an actual WebMCP agent became an important part of development. Rather than only testing whether the UI worked for a human, we had to ask: "What happens if an agent tries to break the investigation?" That led us to build security and regression tests around evidence access, case isolation, premature accusations, timeline reconstruction, and client-side solution exposure. What Casefile Represents Casefile is our exploration of a simple idea: The future of AI applications may not be about AI doing everything for us. Sometimes the better experience is an AI that can act, investigate, and reason alongside us—while leaving the important decisions in our hands. With WebMCP, Casefile turns that idea into a game.
